en: we / our — and "my" for shared things

말 + 하다. Polite: 말해요.
Polite: 알아요 — also the everyday "got it / I see."
Polite: 몰라요 (mollayo) — a 르-irregular like 배불러요. Its own word, not 안 알다.

Polite: 친절해요.

The all-purpose formal apology — also "excuse me" when squeezing past someone.

커피 한 잔, 물 두 잔.
맥주 두 병. Also the standalone word for "bottle."

Same word family as 'typhoon' — both from Chinese 台風.
70% of Korea. Fall 산 + 단풍 is a national pilgrimage.
바다에 가요 covers 'go to the beach' — no separate word needed yet.
벚 (cherry) + 꽃 (M7's flower). Two weeks of national festival every spring.
The red-gold autumn leaves — and the maple they come from.
여름 휴가 — the sacred summer week.
학 (study) released — 방학. Work takes 휴가, school takes 방학.
여행을 가다 — go on a trip. Module 23 makes a whole journey of it.
스키를 타다 — ride skis, like every vehicle since M6.
눈 (snow) + 사람 (M1's person). You've been able to decode this since Module 1 — now it's official.
Konglish, clipped from 'air conditioner.' Summer's most beloved appliance.
바람이 불어요. Also blowing out candles, playing wind instruments.
비가 그쳤어요 — the rain stopped. Weather stops itself; no one stops it.
더워요 — ㅂ-irregular, and this module makes the whole family official.
추워요. Weather is 덥다/춥다; things (coffee, hands) use different words — later.
흐려요 — regular, mercifully.
맑아요 (말가요 by liaison). The batchim ㄺ reads ㄱ alone: 맑다 = 막따.
습해요. The 장마 special.
건조해요. Korean winters are famously 건조하다 — hence the humidifiers.
아주 더워요 — very hot. The neutral 'very.'
Officially 'excessively,' colloquially just 'so': 너무 좋아요 — I love it.
진짜요? — really?! Conversational gold. Its formal twin is 정말.
정말 감사합니다 — thank you so much. 진짜's slightly dressier sibling.
얼마나 더워요? — how hot is it? 얼마 (M9) grown an -나 and asking about degree.
The intercity kind; the KTX is Korea's bullet 기차.
비행 (flight) + 기 (machine). 비행기를 타다 — like every vehicle.
The IOU from Module 6's 역 note, paid. 버스 정류장 in full.
기차표, 비행기표 — glue the vehicle on the front.
Physical roads and figurative ways alike — 길을 몰라요 works for both.
역 근처에 있어요 — it's near the station. A position noun in spirit, joins the M6 family.
기사 + 님 — how you address any taxi or bus driver. The gap deck explains the title system.
자리 있어요? — is this seat taken? (lit. does a spot exist?)
Subway meetups live and die by 출구 numbers: 삼 번 출구.
출구's mirror — 입 (enter) vs 출 (exit).
Sino numbers + 번: 삼 번 출구 (exit 3), 몇 번 버스? (which bus?). Also counts times — 한 번 (once, native).
서울역 — pronounced 서울력, a sound-interlude special (ㄴ-insertion).
Second city, first beaches. 서울에서 부산까지 — the classic KTX bracket.
쭉 가세요 — go straight. Also 'continuously' — 쭉 living somewhere.
Where the 파란불 (blue light = green light) from the gap deck lives.
버스 요금, 택시 요금 — what the 카드 taps away.
교통카드 — the tap-everywhere transit card (T-money) — is 교통 + M9's 카드.
막 (last) + 차 (M3's tea… no — the CAR sense!). The night's deadline; the gap deck explains its social physics.
The generic 'place': 좋은 곳 (a good place — parseable after M24). Not 곧 (soon, M10) — batchim differs.
The 지하 in 지하철 — now you own both halves. 지하 일 층 = B1.
갈아 (switch) + 타다 (M6's ride). 갈아타세요 — the transfer announcement you'll actually hear.
길을 건너요 — cross the street. Polite: 건너요.
은행을 지나요 — pass the bank. Also time passing: 시간이 지나요.
세워 주세요 — please pull over. The taxi phrase, powered by M9's do-for-me machine.
버스를 놓쳤어요 — the universal excuse. Polite: 놓쳐요.
길이 막혀요 — traffic is bad (lit. the road is blocked). The gap deck has the metaphor.
얼마나 걸려요? — how long does it take? 삼십 분 걸려요. Time gets 'caught' on the journey.
주차해요. 주차장 — parking lot (장 = place, as in 정류장).
조심하세요! — careful! What everyone says when you leave in bad weather.
빨라요 — 르-irregular, joining 몰라요/배불러요. The 빨리 in 빨리빨리 is its adverb.
느려요 — mercifully regular.
편해요. 편의점 (M6) is literally the 편-store — convenience made retail.
위험해요! Also on every warning sign: 위험.
빠르다's adverb — and doubled, it's the national tempo from the gap deck: 빨리빨리.
Konglish, from 'apartment.' Most of urban Korea lives in one — whole skylines of numbered towers.
거 (dwell) + 실 (room). The same 실 hides in 화장실 — and in 침실, two words down.
A rare final ㅋ. Alone it sounds like 부억; add 에서 and the ㅋ wakes up — 부엌에서 (bueokeseo). The sound interlude, live.
침 (sleep — the one in 침대) + 실 (room). The bed's room, literally.
The shoes-off zone every Korean home has. Guests stop here until waved in — and the street stays here too (see 온돌 in the gap deck).
Konglish 'veranda' — the glassed-in strip where the laundry dries and the plants live.
The surface you sit on — and in Korea, often sleep on. The gap deck's 온돌 explains why it's the warmest seat in the house.
Konglish, five syllables, and a typing-drill boss fight.
A counter, like M5's set — with Sino numbers: 일 층, 이 층. 몇 층이에요? works in every elevator in the country.
Konglish. The ㅍ is doing the 'f' work — Korean has no f, so ㅍ covers the shift.
냉 (cold) + 장 (storage) + 고 (warehouse): a cold-storage-warehouse. Korean names appliances by job description.
세탁 (laundry) + 기 (machine) — the same 기 as 비행기, the flying machine.
열다 (open — below) + 쇠 (metal): 'open-metal.' The word is a tiny job description.
Korea sorts it strictly — food waste (음식물) gets its own bin, its own bag, and its own smell politics.
Thick enough to sleep under ON the floor — the 온돌 lifestyle's essential kit (gap deck).
Watch the vowels: ㅔ then ㅐ — the merged-sound pair, both ways, in one word.
옷 (clothes — official in the clothes module) + 장 (storage — the one in 냉장고). A clothes-warehouse.
One word for fire and the lights. 불을 켜요 — turn it on. And M7's 파란불? That was this 불 all along.
Moving boxes, travel bags, anything hauled. 이삿짐 — moving-day 짐.
Lights, TV, 에어컨 — 켜다 flips anything on. Its opposite is two letters and one irregular: 끄다.
ㅡ-drop family (아프다, 바쁘다, 슬프다…): 끄 + 어요 → 꺼요. Two letters, full irregular pedigree.
문을 열어요. Its noun child is up in the vocab: 열쇠, the open-metal.
A law-abiding ㄷ — 닫아요, unlike 듣다/걷다. Not every ㄷ misbehaves.
이사 is the move itself. Point the destination with M6's (으)로: 새 집으로 이사해요.
정리 = order, arrangement. Desks, closets, photos, your life — all 정리-able.
쓰레기를 버리다 — the natural pair.
Doors, phones, sentences, habits — 고치다 repairs them all.
ㄼ batchim reads ㄹ before a consonant — 널따 — but both letters wake with a vowel: 넓어요 (neolbeoyo). The sound interlude's rule, running live.
Regular ㅂ, like 입다 — 좁아요, no ㅂ→우 magic. The irregular family doesn't take everyone.
ㄺ batchim like M11's 맑다: 박따 alone, 밝아요 (balgayo) once a vowel follows.
ㅂ-irregular: 어두워요. Joins the 덥다/춥다/맵다 family.
ㅂ-irregular: 더러워요. The anti-깨끗하다.
ㅂ-irregular: 시끄러워요. Shouted alone — 시끄러워! — it means 'keep it down!'
조용히 하세요 — the librarian's setting. A 하다-adjective, so no irregular surprises.
Clips onto the front of a noun, no glue needed: 새 집, 새 침대, 새 핸드폰. It never stands alone — always the 새 something.
이웃사촌 — 'neighbor-cousins': the saying that a close neighbor beats a distant relative.
After a plain noun (수업 전에) or a verb wearing -기 (자기 전에). 전 = the time before.
After a plain noun (수업 후에) or a verb stamped past with -(으)ㄴ (먹은 후에). 후 = the time after.
몸이 안 좋아요 — 'my body isn't good' — is how Korean says 'I'm unwell' without naming anything.
M11's snow, same syllable — the homograph finally lands its second job. 눈이 와요, snow comes; 눈이 아파요, your eye hurts. Context referees.
코가 막혀요 — a blocked nose runs on M12's 막히다, the traffic-jam verb. Sinus congestion is nasal traffic.
입이 무거워요 — a 'heavy mouth' keeps secrets. The gap deck has more body-idioms like it.
One word for both — 목이 아파요 covers sore throats and stiff necks; context decides which hurts.
Sounds exactly like Sino 팔 (eight, M2). You have two arms, not eight — 팔이 두 개.
Also 'bridge' — a river's legs. Two homographs in one module; the 눈 problem is everywhere.
손 (hand) has 손가락, finger; 발 has 발가락 — 'foot-fingers.' Korean names toes with perfect logic.
Final ㅍ — 무릅 alone, but 무릎이 (mureupi) wakes it with a vowel. 부엌's rule, new letter.
The part that hurts from desks and floors alike. 허리가 아파요 — half of Korea, daily.
코 + 피: nose-blood. In K-dramas, studying too hard always ends in 코피. One vowel from 커피 (coffee) — order carefully.
눈 + 물: eye-water. The body compounds itself from parts you own.
감기에 걸리다 — you get 'caught' by a cold. M12's 걸리다 moonlighting; the same verb hangs, catches, and takes time.
M5's ten, M13's 열다/열쇠 — and now body heat. 열이 있어요, there's a fever. The 열 syllable works three jobs.
기침을 해요 — coughing is something you 'do' in Korean.
병 (illness) + 원 (house) = 병원 — M6's hospital, finally decomposed. M5's bottle-counter 병 is a homograph; get well before you count bottles.
건강에 좋아요 — 'good for the health' — is printed on half the food packaging in Korea.
Konglish. 스트레스를 받다 — you 'receive' stress (M9's 받다, promoted to psychology); 풀다 unties it.
Konglish. Standard kit in 미세먼지 season (M11's fifth season) and cold season alike.
The thing every Korean kid fears at the 병원. 주사를 맞다 — you 'receive' a shot, verb arriving in a later module.
간호 (nursing) + the job-사 from 요리사 and 의사. M4's build-a-job machine still runs.
담배를 피우다 — see the verb below for the smoke-as-bloom poetry.
The ㅡ-drop family's patriarch finally enrolls: 아프 + 아요 → 아파요. You've been saying its shape since M3's 배고파요.

A NEW irregular family — ㅅ vanishes before vowels: 나 + 아요 → 나아요. Rare and mostly used to wish people well: 빨리 나으세요. Sounds identical to M7's 낮다 (low) — this module's homograph festival extends to sound-twins.
For the moment of injury — 다쳤어요, I got hurt. 아프다 is for the hurting after.
ㅂ-irregular: 누워요. The doctor's 여기에 누우세요 — lie down here — runs on it.
M12's 세우다 (stop the taxi) was this verb's causative cousin — 'make it stand.'
Literally 'to make bloom' — 꽃이 피다, flowers bloom. Korean gave smoking its grimmest poetry.
걱정 alone is the noun. 걱정하지 마세요 — the sentence this module exists for.
The toast, the birthday wish, the grandmother's sign-off: 건강하세요.
Darker on paper than in speech — casual Korean 'dies' of hunger, heat, and homework hourly. The gap deck explains 죽겠어요.
목 (throat) + 마르다 (dries): thirst is a drying throat. 르-family conjugation: 목말라요.
힘이 없어요 — no energy: the universal symptom. 힘내세요! — the universal encouragement.
푹 쉬세요, 푹 자요 — the adverb of proper rest. Doctors prescribe it verbatim.
아직 아파요 — still sick. With a negative it reads 'not yet': 아직 안 먹었어요.
초등 (beginning-level) + 학교. The ladder starts here: 초등 → 중 → 고등 → 대.
중 = middle — the same 중 as 중국 (the 'middle country,' China).
고등 = high-level. Shortened to 고등학생's 고교 in headlines — Korean compresses what it says often.
대 (big) + 학교: the big school. Casually just 대학.
대학 + 학생, overlapped into one word. Korean loves a shared syllable.
학 + 년 (year) — spelled 학년, said 항년: the sound interlude's nasalization rule, live. 몇 학년이에요?
학 (study) + 원 (the institute-원 of 병원). The second school day: most Korean kids go after regular school — math 학원, English 학원, piano 학원, taekwondo 학원.
M5's half, second job: your homeroom. 3학년 2반 — grade 3, class 2 — is how Korean schools address a kid.
교 (teach) + 실 (room) — the room-실 family from 화장실/침실/거실 goes to school.
The teach-과목-book. 교과서 같다 — 'like a textbook' — describes suspiciously perfect people.
공 (blank) + 책 (book): a blank-book. M1's 책 finally builds a compound.
연 (lead) + 필 (writing tool). 연필로 쓰세요 — M6's (으)로 marking the tool.
Konglish at its most efficient — one syllable, borrowed whole.
지우다 (to erase) + -개, the tool-maker suffix — M13's 베개 (lean-tool pillow) has a classmate. An eraser is an 'erase-tool.'
칠 (paint) + 판 (board) — a painted board.
교수 + the respect-님 of 선생님/기사님. Address professors with it always — M12's title system applies double on campus.
수 (number) + 학 (study-of). The -학 suffix names every field — watch for it.
Not M6's train-역 — a homograph syllable in the wild. Korea's 역사 runs five thousand years and one alphabet promulgation you've already read about.
그리다's noun — a drawing is 'a drawn.' The pair below.
외 (outside) + 국 (country) + 어 (language — the 어 of 한국어/영어/단어). You are, at this very moment, doing 외국어 공부.
점 (points) + 수 (number). 백 점 — a hundred points — is perfection; M9's 백 moonlights in report cards.
The noun inside M10's 대답하다. 정답 — the correct answer — is the quiz-show word.
처음 배워요 — learning for the first time. Also inside the formal first-meeting greeting 처음 뵙겠습니다.
처음's opposite number. 마지막 수업, 마지막 문제 — and M12's 막차 carries the same 막.
배우다's other half. 선생님이 가르쳐요, 학생이 배워요 — the classroom in two verbs.
단어를 외워요 — this app's entire business model in one verb.
Ask + see: 보다 rides along to soften it — 'ask and see.' Not M1's 물 — the 물 here is from 묻다, to inquire.
틀렸어요 — wrong answer. This app has been telling you this word's meaning every time you miss a quiz question.
맞아요! — you've heard it as 'that's right!' since forever. Also the receiving end of M14's 주사를 맞다.
Sounds exactly like 있다 (to exist) — 잊지 마세요 vs 있지요. Spelling tells them apart; context does the rest.
그림을 그려요 — draw a drawing. Korean happily pairs a verb with its own noun.
졸업 = graduation. February in Korea: graduation season, flowers everywhere. Said 조러파다 — ㅎ merges per the sound interlude.
Knock-knock — 똑똑 — is also the sound of knocking. A smart kid and a knocked door share an onomatopoeia.
The highest Korean compliment a grandmother can pay.
부지런하다's shadow. 르-family: 게을러요 — lazy even in conjugation, dropping letters.
힘 (M14's energy) + 들다 (costs): something that takes your strength. 힘들어요 — the honest answer to how studying is going.
사무 (office work) + 실 — the room-실 family (교실, 침실, 거실…) clocks in.
M10's 회의 + 실. By now you can name any room in the building.
무슨 직업이에요? — M10's 무슨 asking the small-talk classic.
직 (duty) + 원 (member — the one in 회사원). Also who you call over in any shop: 직원.
Konglish. 우리 팀 — M4's warm 우리 extends to the office.
The title ladder in one office: 사장님 above, 부장님 mid-floor — always with 님, never a bare name. M12's title system pays rent here.
기 (record) + 자 (person). The 기 of 일기 (diary) and, yes, 기차 tickets — busy syllable.
The job-사 family grows: 요리사, 간호사, 변호사. Hear -사 at a job's end and you can guess the shape.
Received with two hands, read carefully, placed on the table — never pocketed unread. The card IS the person; treat it accordingly.
Konglish. 메일 alone also works — Korean rarely means postal mail by it.
월 (month — the one starting 월요일) + 급 (pay): month-pay. 월급날 — payday — is a small national holiday.
출 (out — the one in 출구 and 출발) + 장. Going out on duty.
회 (gather — 회사/회의's 회) + 식 (eat — 식당's 식): the after-hours team dinner that is officially optional and practically not. Round two is 노래방.
평 (ordinary) + 일 (day): M2's 주말 finally gets its opposite.
이번 주, 이번 달, 이번 회의 — 'this current one.' M12's 번 (number/turn) behind it: this-turn.
The native month — 이번 달, 다음 달 — and also the moon in the sky. One 달 orbits, the other invoices.
M6 gave you here/there/over-there for PLACES — 이거/그거/저거 is the same trio for THINGS. 이거 주세요 has been waiting since M9.
그 = near the listener, like 거기. 그거 뭐예요? — what's that you've got?
저 = far from both, like 저기. Point across the room: 저거.
The enrolled-going verb: 회사에 다녀요, 학교에 다녀요, 학원에 다녀요. 가다 is one trip; 다니다 is a routine with your name on it.
출 (out) + 근 (duty): heading out to duty. Said 출그나다? No — 출근해요, straightforward.
퇴 (retreat) + 근 (duty): the day's sweetest verb. 퇴근했어요? doubles as evening small talk.
야 (night) + 근 (duty). The 근-family tells the whole workday: 출근, 퇴근, and when things go wrong, 야근.
Email, packages, texts, people to the airport — and time: 주말 잘 보내세요, 'send your weekend well.'
부탁 is the favor itself. 부탁해요 — please do this for me; 잘 부탁드립니다 — the formal 'I'm in your hands' that opens every working relationship in Korea.
M8's 끝나다 is 'it ends'; 끝내다 is 'I end it.' One vowel of agency: 일이 끝났어요 vs 일을 끝냈어요.
돈을 벌다 — the reason for all the 근-verbs above.
People, restaurants, yourself: 제 소개를 하겠습니다 opens a thousand first meetings. 소개해 주세요 — set me up (also, famously, with dates).
복사기 — the copy machine — adds M15's tool logic to the 기 of 세탁기.
M8's 늦다 is late in general; 지각 is the official offense, recorded and frowned upon. 지각하지 마세요.
M15's 틀리다 is wrong answers; 실수 is wrong actions. 실수했어요 — own it, then move on.
발표 = the presentation. Feared equally in 교실 and 회의실.
일을 그만뒀어요 — I quit my job. 그만! alone means 'stop it!' — parents' favorite syllables.
중요한 것? Coming in M17. For now: 회의가 중요해요.
Korean needs backwards: 돈이 필요해요 — 'money is needed (to me).' The wanter takes a back seat, 있어요-style.
취미가 뭐예요? — the universal small-talk opener, right after job and age.
축 (kick) + 구 (ball). The -구 family names every ball game — watch it repeat below.
야 (field) + 구 (ball) — NOT the night-야 of 야근. Same syllable, different ancestor; the homograph radar stays on.
농 (basket) + 구. The -구 family complete: 축구, 야구, 농구.
Konglish. Racket sports take 치다 — hit-play — like the piano.
수 (water — the 수 in 수요일's water-day!) + 영 (swim). M10's 수영하다 was this noun wearing 하다.
등 (climb) + M11's 산: mountain-climbing — the national pastime of everyone's parents. Full gear mandatory, summit optional.
M7's 노래 + M8's 방: the song-room. 회식 round two, friendship's pressure test, and the gap deck's -방 economy flagship.
춤을 추다 — dance a dance, the way you draw a drawing (그림을 그리다). Korean likes its verbs to bring their own nouns.
사진을 찍다 — photos are 'stamped,' not taken. 사진 찍어 주세요 gets you a stranger's best effort anywhere in Korea.
축구 경기, 야구 경기. Also the province around Seoul, 경기도 — homograph, different hanja, same spelling.
손흥민 선수 — the title follows the name like 님 does. Also slang for anyone suspiciously good at anything.
Not 공원's 공, not 공책's 공 — this one bounces. Third job for the syllable; the count is now routine for you.
피아노를 치다 — struck, not played. Same verb as tennis; Korean files keys and rackets together.
Konglish — and a perfect homograph of Sino 기타, 'et cetera.' On forms, 기타 means 'other'; in bands, it means six strings.
독 (read) + 서 (book — 교과서's 서). What 책 읽는 것 becomes on a résumé.
Korea's comics — ancestor of the webtoon, the format Korea exported to the world's phones.
Konglish, but meaning K-drama specifically. Source of the 코피 nosebleed lore and half the world's Korean learners.
That ㄲ batchim collapses to ㄱ — 낙씨-ish. Also internet slang for clickbait: getting 낚시'd is getting hooked.
The strike-play verb: 피아노를 치다, 기타를 치다, 테니스를 치다. If it's hit or plucked, it's 치다.
Only ever with its own noun: 춤을 추다. A verb with one loyal partner.
Photos, stamps, dots, votes — 찍다 is the precise-press verb. 사진을 찍어요.
우리 팀이 이겼어요! — the sentence this verb lives for.
Also what the sun does at dusk — 해가 지다. Losing and sunsets share a verb; make of that what you will.
What 화이팅 is for. Korean cheering culture is choreographed, drummed, and completely sincere.
달리기 — running, the noun — is the -기 you know from 자기 전에 and 배우기, promoted to a hobby's name.
NOT M11's mountain-산 — a stroll, not a summit. 공원에서 산책해요.
M11's 여행 wearing 하다 — the pattern 수영/수영하다 taught you, running in reverse.
ㅡ-drop: 모아요. Stamps, figures, photocards, money — the collector's verb.
주말을 즐기세요 — enjoy your weekend. The hobby module's mission statement.
M10's 잘 fused into a verb: 노래를 잘해요. You've deflected with 잘 못 해요 since the gap deck — here's the machinery.
잘하다's shadow: 요리를 못해요. Said 모타다 — the ㅎ-merge from the sound interlude.
유명한 것들 await M17's own glue. For now: 이 선수가 유명해요.
Possessed, 있다-style: 인기가 많아요 — 'has much popularity' — is how Korean says something's a hit.
The 매-family: M5's 매일 (every day), 매주, 매달, 매년. One prefix, the whole calendar.
M7's 많다 as an adverb — and long overdue. 많이 먹어요! — eat a lot! — is Korean hospitality's core command. Said 마니; the ㅎ vanishes per the interlude.
Always with a negative: 별로 안 좋아해요 — don't really like it. The politest possible shrug. Alone — 별로예요 — it's a review score.
M4's 저 + possessive 의, squeezed into one syllable: 제 취미, 제 친구. The humble 'my' that matches 저.
The thing-word — casually 거, which you've already met inside 이거/그거/저거 (이 것 → 이거). With -는 in front, it turns whole verbs into things: 먹는 것, eating.
Korean chopsticks are METAL — flat steel, heavier than wood, a national skill-check. The 가락 means a slender stick; 손가락 (fingers) are hand-sticks.
Korea keeps the spoon at the table for rice and soup — scooping rice with chopsticks marks you a beginner. Note the ㄷ batchim where 젓가락 has ㅅ; both say t.
숟가락 + 젓가락, first syllables fused. Restaurants keep the 수저 in a table-side drawer — check under the table before asking.
Also the counter for servings: 밥 한 그릇 — one bowl of rice. Don't lift it while eating — Korean bowls stay on the table, unlike in Japan.
Konglish 'cup', one syllable. M5's 잔 counts the drinks; 컵 is the object itself.
Thicker and saltier than 국, served bubbling in stone or steel: 김치찌개, 된장찌개. One pot, table-center, everyone's 숟가락 — that's the culture.
The fermented backbone of Korean cooking. The 장 (paste/sauce) family: 된장, 고추장, 간장 — storage-장's delicious homograph.
고추 (chili) + 장 (paste) — the red engine of 떡볶이 and 비빔밥. Now a global pantry word in its own spelling.
Steamed, fried, or floating in 국 (만둣국). Cousin to jiaozi and gyoza — the dumpling diaspora runs through every border.
국수를 먹다 also means 'to attend a wedding' — noodle soup was the traditional wedding meal. 언제 국수 먹여 줄 거예요? = when are you getting married?
Chewy rice cakes for every occasion — moving day (M13's 이사 comes with 떡 for the 이웃), birthdays, exams (sticky 떡 helps you 'stick' to the pass list).
떡 + 볶이 (stir-fried — the verb 볶다 below): street-food royalty, gochujang-red, sold from every orange tent (포장마차).
삼 (three — M2's Sino!) + 겹 (layer) + 살 (flesh): three-layer meat. Grilled at your own table, wrapped in lettuce, the social meal.
돼지 (pig) + M3's 고기: pig-meat. Korean names meats by animal + 고기 — no separate 'pork/beef' words needed.
소 (cow) + 고기. The pattern from 돼지고기, and yes — 닭고기 (chicken-meat) exists too, when 치킨 isn't fried.
Not M16's gather-회 — this one is sliced and dipped in 고추장-vinegar. Coastal Korea's pride; 회 먹으러 갈까요? is a serious invitation.

The 김 in M3's 김밥 — seaweed-rice, finally decomposed. NOT the 김 in 김치 (that's from 침채, pickled greens, worn down by centuries). Also Korea's most common surname; a 김 씨 eating 김 wrapped 김밥 is unremarkable.
야 (field — the SAME field-야 as 야구) + 채 (greens). Field-greens; the homograph radar logs another repeat customer.
예약 = reservation. M5's 약속 promises a person; 예약 promises a table, a ticket, a haircut.
추천해 주세요 — recommend for me, please: the four syllables that unlock any menu you can't read.
Korea's delivery culture is world-final tier: anywhere, anything, absurdly fast. 배달 시키다 — with M3's 시키다 — is the operative phrase. Not M3's boat/stomach 배… or is it? (It isn't. Radar stays on.)
음 (drink — 음식's first half) + 료 + 수 (water — 수영's 수). The menu category above the food.
Konglish. Korean meals traditionally end with fruit or 식혜, but the 카페 conquered dessert — hence the meal-then-coffee two-stop ritual.
맛 (taste) + 집 (house): a taste-house — the place worth the pilgrimage and the line. Every neighborhood argues about its 맛집 list; that's half the fun.
The noun hiding inside 맛있다 (taste-exists) and 맛없다 since Module 1 — extracted at last. 무슨 맛이에요? — what flavor is it?
ㅂ-irregular: 싱거워요. The polite complaint; also said of people who joke weakly — a bland person, seasoning-wise.
ㅂ-irregular: 뜨거워요. M11's 덥다 is hot weather; 뜨겁다 is the hot bowl. English merges them; Korean won't.
ㅂ-irregular: 차가워요. 춥다 is cold weather; 차갑다 is the iced drink — and, metaphorically, a cold person.
ㅂ-irregular VERB: 구워요. 삼겹살을 구워요 — at your own table, tongs in hand; whoever grills, everyone eats.
The 볶 in 떡볶이 and 볶음밥 (fried rice). Menu-reading superpower: spot 볶, expect a hot pan.
라면을 끓여요 — the national midnight verb. 물이 끓어요 (it boils) vs 물을 끓여요 (you boil it) — the 끝나다/끝내다 agency split again.
The 비빔 in 비빔밥 — mixed rice. Mix it ALL, properly, before eating; a politely unmixed 비빔밥 is a small tragedy.
Drinking without 안주 is considered borderline reckless — the word makes eating-while-drinking a named institution. 치킨 is 맥주's official 안주 (M3's 치맥).
Literally 'dry the glass.' Juniors clink lower and turn slightly away to drink — M4's politeness system operating at the table.
한 (Korea) + 식 (food — 식당's 식). The set: 한식, 중식 (Chinese), 일식 (Japanese), 양식 (Western). Four cuisines, one suffix.
외 (outside — 외국어's 외) + 식 (food): outside-eating. 오늘은 외식해요! — the happiest household announcement.
된장찌개's soft white heart. 순두부찌개 — silken-tofu stew — is its bubbling starring role.
반말-only. Korean mostly AVOIDS 'you' — names and titles do the work — but between real friends, 너 is finally safe.
나 + 의 squeezed, exactly as 제 came from 저. The humble/casual pairs line up: 저/제 for politeness, 나/내 with friends.
Spelled 네, but here's the problem: it sounds exactly like 내 (my) AND like 네 (yes). Real speech dodges the pileup by saying 니 — 니 생일, your birthday. Written 네, spoken 니.
M5's 반 (half) + M4's 말 (speech): half-speech — the register with the endings snapped off. This module's entire subject, named.
Respect-speech — everything you've learned through Module 18. 반말's counterpart; knowing WHICH to use is the real fluency.
이다's opposite number — 아니에요 politely, 아니야 casually. You've said 아니에요 since M4; here's the dictionary form underneath.
별 (special) + 명 (name). Korean friendships mint nicknames aggressively; answering to yours is a membership card.
최 (most) + 고 (high): the highest. 최고야! with a thumbs-up is complete communication.
성격이 좋아요 — good personality — is the classic friend-recommendation. What 눈치 measures, 성격 is.
농담이야! — just kidding! The escape hatch after every risky sentence.
거짓 (false) + 말 (speech): false-speech. 거짓말! alone means 'no way!' — disbelief, not accusation. Usually.
비밀이야 — it's a secret — reliably guarantees the whole group knows by Friday.
Konglish. The ㅍ handles the f again, like 소파.
Konglish. Korean birthdays add 미역국 — seaweed soup — because your mother ate it after bearing you. Cake for the party, soup for the meaning.
오랜만이야! / 오랜만이에요! — long time no see, in both registers. M10's 오래 grew a suffix and became a greeting.
우 (friend) + 정 — THE 정, the bond the gap deck tries to translate. Friendship is literally 'friend-jeong.'
Where English splits heart and mind, Korean has one 마음. 마음에 들어요 — 'it enters my 마음' — is how things get liked.
무슨 소리야? — 'what sound is that?' — really means 'what are you talking about?' Nonsense is just noise.
M14's 목 (throat) + 소리 (sound): throat-sound. The compound machine never rests.
Not memory-the-faculty — memory-the-treasure. Photos, trips, songs: 추억 is what 사진 찍는 것 is actually for.
동갑이에요? — same age? — is the doorway to 반말. The gap deck explains why age-matching matters this much here.
Kids play, adults hang out — 놀다 covers both without embarrassment. 놀자! is the friendship imperative.
Also 'to make friends with' — context and eyebrows distinguish. 사귀자 is a confession; deploy carefully.
Couples 헤어지다, but so do friends at the bus stop — parting is parting; only context makes it sad.
싸웠어? — did you two fight? — the question that follows every suspicious silence.
화 (anger) + 나다 (comes out): anger emerges, weather-style — like 비가 와요, feelings arrive on their own. 화났어? — you mad?
M7's 웃다 (laugh) with a causative kick: MAKES laugh. 웃겨! — hilarious! Also, dryly: 웃기지 마 — don't make me laugh.
생일 축하해! Said 추카 — the ㅎ-merge the sound interlude promised would arrive with this exact word.
파티에 초대했어요. Being invited to a Korean home is rarer than it sounds — most socializing happens out; a home invite is a big deal.
연락해! — text me! The parting word of every good hangout. 연락이 없어요 — radio silence — is how worry starts.
The 친 of 친구. 친해요? — are you two close? — maps the social graph one edge at a time.
Call a name, call a taxi, sing a song — 노래를 부르다. 르-family: 불러요. 배불러요 was this conjugation shape all along.
인사 = the greeting itself, bow included. 인사해 — say hi — is how Korean kids are introduced to everyone, forever.
M15's 잊다 finally gets its opposite. 기억해? — remember? — the word 추억 lives on.
나를 믿어 — trust me. A regular ㄷ, unlike 듣다 — believing is easier than listening, conjugation-wise.
Konglish. 데이트하다 — the verb form comes free, 하다-style.
Konglish — and a lifestyle: 커플티 (matching shirts), 커플룩, couple rings. Korean coupledom is proudly uniformed.
Konglish. 솔로예요 — I'm single — said with pride, resignation, or strategy depending on the party.
M8's 전화하다 was this noun wearing 하다. 전화번호 — phone number — self-assembles two entries down.
Literally 'characters' — a text is just letters sent. 문자 보내 / 문자했어요 both work.
Konglish. Korea's is famously the world's fastest; complain accordingly.
와이파이 있어요? — free in nearly every Korean café; asking is routine, not rude.
One syllable of Konglish. Older speakers say 어플 (from 'application') — both survive.
배터리가 없어요 — the modern emergency. Not M3's 배, not M18's 배달's 배 — the radar logs another.
화 (picture) + 면 (surface): picture-surface. The thing you're reading this on.
M12's 번 grown up: 전화번호, 방 번호, waiting-line 번호표. Numbers that LABEL, not count.
영상을 봐요 — what half of all screen time is. 영화 is the theatrical big sibling.
Konglish compression: SELf + CAmera → 셀카. Korea coined it before 'selfie' reached English dictionaries.
Konglish 'notebook' — meaning the computer, always. The paper kind is M15's 공책.
M15's 답 (answer) + 장 (letter): an answer-letter. 답장해! — text back! The gap deck's 읽씹 is what happens instead.
통화 중이에요 — on the line. 영상통화 — video call — assembles from parts you now own.
영상 + 통화, exactly as advertised. Grandparents' favorite feature, worldwide.
M19's 비밀 (secret) + 번호 (number): a secret-number. The compound machine at its most literal — and the café wi-fi's second question.
The generic term; 문자 is specifically SMS-style texts. In practice, everything is 카톡 anyway (gap deck).
The formal word; M6's 핸드폰 remains the everyday one. Both Konglish, both everywhere.
댓 (responding) + 글 (writing). 악플 — malicious comments — is its dark twin; Korean internet culture takes both seriously.
In Korea this means the big character stickers — a paid economy of bears and rabbits doing feelings for you.
Konglish. Set five, trust none.
진동으로 하세요 — put it on vibrate: the cinema's opening announcement.
Not headline news — personal news: 소식 있어요? Any word from them? 소식이 없어요 is how distance is measured.
무 (without) + 료 (fee/material — genuinely the same 료 as in 음료수). Fee-less. Opposite: 유료, with-fee.
Phone-only — never in person. From 여기 보세요 (look here), worn smooth by a century of calls.
Also tops up transit cards (M12's 교통카드를 충전해요) — one verb refills both phones and fares.
르-family: 눌러요. Buttons, links, elevator floors, and the 좋아요 below.
검색해 보세요 — try searching it. What 모르다 leads to now.
Literally 'to raise' — you LIFT content onto the internet. 사진을 올렸어요.
M15's 지우개 was this verb + the tool suffix all along. Files, texts, chalkboards, regrettable posts — one verb erases all.
저장 = storage — the 장 of 냉장고, refrigerating your data. 번호를 저장했어요 — saved your number.
잃다 (lose) + M13's 버리다 (throw away) as an oops-completely auxiliary: lost-and-gone. 잊어버리다 does the same for memories — M15's 잊다, intensified.
전화를 끊다 — end the call (politely: after the elder hangs up first). Also quits things: 담배를 끊었어요 — M14's cigarettes, cut.
문자를 확인해요 — check your texts. The verb of the modern reflex; 확인 alone stamps documents and dialog boxes.
전화를 걸다 — you HANG a call, the same verb as hanging a picture. M12's 걸리다 (be caught/take time) is its passive cousin — the family reunion.
Korea says SNS — es-en-es — where English says social media. Konglish that recycled an acronym English itself abandoned.
M1's verb form, frozen into a noun: 좋아요를 눌러 주세요 — press the like. Grammar becoming furniture; the internet does this to every language.
청 (blue) + 바지: blue-pants. The 청 is the deep blue of 청바지 and celadon pottery both.
Also the bottom half of a 한복 — the word predates the miniskirt by centuries.
Konglish, casually just 티 — as in M16's 커플티.
Konglish. What M11's 겨울 demands and every drama's autumn scene is styled around.
Konglish 'one-piece' — a dress is one piece of clothing. Logic English forgot to apply.
잠 (sleep — 자다's noun) + 옷: sleep-clothes. The outfit 집에 오면 갈아입어요.
교 (school) + 복 (clothing): the -복 suffix dresses whole categories. Korean middle and high schoolers wear one; the drama industry never recovered.
M17's 수영 + 복: swim-clothes. The -복 family assembles itself.
한 (Korea — 한식's 한) + 복: Korea-clothes. Worn now for holidays, weddings, and palace photo days — rent one near 경복궁 and admission is free.
M8's 운동 + 화 (shoe): exercise-shoes. The -화 suffix walks: 운동화, 등산화 (hiking boots — M17's 등산).
The office-and-occasions shoes; 운동화's formal rival. The 출근 uniform, ankle-down.
Mandatory visibility: shoes come off at every 현관 (M13), so Korean sock game is played in public.
안경을 쓰다 OR 끼다 — head-things and fitted things share custody. The wear-verb table in Part 3 sorts it out.
M14's 목 (neck) + M20's 걸다 (hang) + 이: a neck-hanger. Two modules old and one module new, snapped together.
귀 + 걸다 + 이: ear-hangers. Same machine as 목걸이 — once you see the pattern, jewelry names itself.
커플 반지 — matching rings at 100 days — is standard relationship infrastructure (M19's 커플 culture, jewelry division).
지갑을 잃어버렸어요 — the classic emergency, M20's verb ready to report it.
장갑을 끼다 — gloves are fitted things, so they take 끼다. The taxonomy holds.
M14's 목 again — the neck stays busy: 목걸이 hangs on it, 목도리 wraps it, 목소리 comes out of it.
Where the 지갑 lives. 주머니가 가벼워요 — a light pocket — is a poetic way to be broke.
M7 taught the colors as [hue]+색; 색깔 is the word for color itself. 무슨 색깔이에요? — what color?
유행이에요 — it's in style. Korean trends move at 빨리빨리 speed; last season is archaeology.
Konglish. 제 스타일이에요 — it's my style — works for clothes, food, and, notably, people.
The formal twin of M9's 값-flavored asking. 가격이 어때요? — how's the price?
Konglish. An accessory, so it takes 하다 — 넥타이를 해요 — and quietly rules M16's 출근 dress code.
Shoes and socks only — 신발을 신다, its own noun built in. Korean assigns wear-verbs by body zone; the table in this module's Part 3 is the map.
Rings, gloves, glasses — anything that grips: 반지를 끼다, 장갑을 끼다. The snug-fit verb.
One removal verb undoes all the wearing verbs — democratic. 신발을 벗으세요: the 현관's standing order.
갈아 (switch) + 입다 — the same 갈아 as M12's 갈아타다, transferring between outfits instead of trains.
잘 어울려요! — it suits you! Also for couples and food pairings: things that harmonize 어울리다.
Peels apples, trims hair, and — at markets — cuts prices: 좀 깎아 주세요. Works at 시장 stalls; department stores will only smile.
멋 (style/flair) + 있다: style-exists — the 있다-factory's fashion branch. 멋있어요! works on outfits, people, and buildings.
어려 보여요 — you look young — lands as a top-tier compliment in age-aware Korea (M19's gap deck explains the stakes).
ㅂ-irregular: 가벼워요. Jackets, bags, footsteps, and — per M19 — thin-eared people who believe everything.
ㅂ-irregular: 무거워요. 가볍다's counterweight — and M19's heavy mouth (입이 무겁다) keeps secrets with it.
Half of South Korea lives in one metro area — 도시 is where the 아파트 towers and the 지하철 map both live.
Where 할머니 lives, the air is 좋다, and every K-drama hero eventually returns to heal.
The walkable world: your 편의점, your 맛집, your 세탁소. 우리 동네 — M4's warm 우리 applies automatically.
Rivers get 다리 — and M14 warned you: a bridge is a river's legs.
한 (the Korea-한 of 한식/한복) + 강: Seoul's river and its living room — see the gap deck for the 치킨-and-picnic civilization on its banks.
Where the real 맛집s hide. Korean urban charm is measured in 골목s per block.
M19's 놀다 + 이 + 터 (site): a playing-place. Every 아파트 complex has one at its center.
Also means glue — the school kind. M15's pencil case and the lawn share a syllable; the radar shrugs and logs it.
Korea has over three thousand. The famous one is next in the checklist.
The honeymoon-and-holiday island: volcanic, tangerine-scented, with its own dialect Seoulites can't follow. The -도 suffix marks islands and provinces both.
The 수 is water again — 수영's and 음료수's 수, pooled.
One dense syllable with a rare ㅍ batchim — 숲에 (supe) wakes it, per the interlude.
Also a baby's first birthday — the 돌잔치. Stones and first birthdays share a syllable; only one gets a party.
M13's 새 (new) has a flying homograph. 새 새 — a new bird — is legal Korean and a tiny poem.
The 별 in M19's 별명 (special-name) and M17's 별로 — the sky's version is the original. City skies ration them; 시골 skies pay out.
공기가 좋아요/나빠요 — checked daily like weather, because M11's 미세먼지 made air quality a conversation topic.
경치가 좋아요 — the view is good: the sentence every 등산 summit and café window exists to earn.
동 (moving) + 물 (thing): a moving-thing. 동물원 — the animal-house — is the zoo; the 원 you know from 병원 and 학원.
Technically puppy, practically every dog — Korean pet-speak upgrades all dogs to puppies forever. Also a term of endearment for children.
The sound interlude promised this word — go-yang-i, the batchim ㅇ that never slides. Street cats are 길고양이: M12's road + cat.
물 (water) + 고기 (meat): water-meat — Korean names the animal by its destiny. On the plate it's 생선; swimming, it's already dinner-in-waiting.
비가 그친 후에 — after the rain quits (M11's 그치다) — this is what the sky apologizes with.
세상에서 제일 — 'the most in the world' — is the superlative's favorite stage. 세상에! alone gasps 'oh my goodness!'
벌레가 있어요! — the apartment emergency. Also a suffix for obsessives: 공부벌레, a study-bug, is M15's hardest worker.
The school-trip picnic of every Korean childhood — 김밥 mandatory, mothers up at dawn rolling it.
야 (night — 야근's 야, not 야구's field) + 경 (scenery — 경치's 경). Seoul's 야경 from a mountain fortress is the tourism board's entire argument.
Smaller and older than a 동네 — the word carries stone walls and persimmon trees in it.
Water, forests, night, and thoughts — 깊다 measures them all. 밤이 깊었어요: the night has deepened.
ㅂ-irregular: 아름다워요. M1's 예쁘다 is pretty; 아름답다 is beautiful — scenery, music, and moments earn the bigger word.
Streets, subways, and feelings — one word for overcrowded and overcomplicated. 머리가 복잡해요: my head is complicated (= too much going on).
Looking as leisure: 시장 구경, 꽃 구경 (gap deck). 구경만 할게요 — just browsing — is shop-Korean survival kit.
르-family: 올라요. Mountains, stairs, and prices — all things that 오르다. M17's 등산 is this verb's noun habitat.
꽃이 피어요 — M14's 피우다 (make bloom → smoke) was this verb's causative all along. The 벚꽃 forecast tracks it nationally, to the day.
제 (order) + 일 (one — M2's Sino!): literally 'number one.' Park it before any adjective: 제일 맛있어요, 제일 좋아요.
A PARTICLE spelled exactly like the busiest verb in the course — 보다's fifth job, and this one isn't even a verb. B보다 A가 더 커요: A is bigger than B. The syllable has now fully unionized.
여 (travel — 여행's 여) + 권 (document — M5's book-counter 권, promoted to paperwork). The one thing 잊으면 안 돼요.
Konglish. Not the card — the stamp. Korea waives it for most tourists; the word matters going the other way.
관 (view) + 광 (light): viewing-the-sights. The whole industry in two syllables — and the base for the next two words.
관광 + 객 (guest — 손님's formal cousin). Tourists are guests of the view.
관광 + 지 (place). Where the 관광객 and their cameras concentrate.
외 (outside) + 국 (country) — M15's 외국어 minus its language. 외국에 가 봤어요? — been abroad?
외국 + 인 (person). What immigration forms — and curious grandmothers — will call you. Wear it lightly.
기념 (commemoration) + 품 (goods — M21's 명품's 품). Memory-goods: the 추억, purchasable.
The native word — 우리나라, 'our country,' is how Koreans say Korea (M4's 우리 at national scale). Sino 국 does the compounds; 나라 stands alone.
Konglish. Budget alternatives with their own flavor: 모텔, 게스트하우스, and the 찜질방 floor (M17's gap deck) for the brave.
박물 (broad things) + 관 (hall). The -관 suffix builds public buildings: 박물관, 미술관, 영화관.
미술 (fine art — where M15's 그림 hangs when it grows up) + 관. The -관 family's second member.
Seoul keeps five. 경복궁 — the grandest — waives admission if you arrive in M21's 한복: the rental shops next door are no coincidence.
M11's 바다 + 가 (edge): the sea's edge. 해수욕장 is the official swimming beach; 바닷가 is anywhere the land runs out.
온 (warm — 온돌's 온!) + 천 (spring). The floor-heating syllable, applied to bathing.
안내 (guidance) + 소 (place). The 관광 안내소 marks itself with an ⓘ and speaks English; this module aims to make that optional.
The direction-maker: 이쪽 (this way), 저쪽 (that way) — and M6's 왼쪽/오른쪽 were 쪽-compounds all along. 어느 쪽이에요? — which way?
M12's 건너다 (cross) + 편 (side): the crossed-to side. 길 건너편에 있어요 — it's across the street.
똑바로 가세요 — go straight. Also 'properly': 똑바로 하세요 is what teachers say when it isn't.
사 (four — M2's Sino) + 거리 (streets): a four-streets. A 삼거리 has three; Korean names junctions by counting.
Four syllables of pure Sino bureaucracy meaning 'crossing-walk-way.' M12's 신호등 stands guard over it.
The 판 of M15's 칠판 — a board again, now advertising. Korean streets stack 간판 five stories high; reading them is free vocabulary practice.
일정이 어떻게 돼요? — what's the schedule? Works for trips and Tuesdays alike.
유 (having) + 료 (fee) — M20's 무료 finally meets its twin. Check which one the 안내소 says before queueing.
M22's 세상 is the lived-in world; 세계 is the atlas one — 세계 여행 (world travel), 세계 지도 (world map). Feelings take 세상; geography takes 세계.
자유 여행 — independent travel, no flag-following. The next word is its opposite number.
단체 여행 — the guided tour: matching hats, a raised flag, military scheduling. 단체 사진 — the group photo — nobody escapes.
광 (wide) + 장 (place — 주차장's 장). 광화문 광장 is where Seoul gathers to celebrate and to protest, sometimes the same week.
수원 화성 — the fortress wall you can walk at sunset. Also the 성 in 성격 (M19) and family names; the radar logs a triple.
여행을 떠나요 — you 'leave on' a trip. More romantic than M8's 출발하다, which is for buses; 떠나다 is for chapters.
돌아 (turning) + 오다: come back around. Every trip's final verb.
돌아오다's mirror — back TOWARD somewhere else. 집에 돌아가요, said from the trip; 집에 돌아와요, said from home. M6's 오다/가다 geometry, still governing.
환 (exchange) + 전 (money): swap-money-do. Airport rates are famously the worst; the 명동 booths famously better.
The verb hiding inside M1's 잘 지냈어요? all along — 'have you been passing time well?' Twenty-two modules later, the machinery surfaces.
호텔에서 묵다 — overnighting, specifically. 지내다 spends time; 묵다 spends nights.
벌써 도착했어요? — here already? M14's 아직 (not yet) finally gets its opposite. Time flies; 벌써 is how Korean gasps about it.
거의 다 왔어요 — almost there: the sentence every backseat wants and every driver stretches.
A thought-view. 의견이 있어요? — any opinions? — opens the discussion; 좋은 의견이에요 approves one. Both run on this module's machinery.
이유가 뭐예요? — what's the reason? The polite way to ask M10's 왜 after the fact. The answer, half the time: 그냥.
The noun is a fact; topic-marked — 사실은… — it shifts into confession gear: 'actually…'. Korean signals truth-telling before telling it.
Konglish — M8's 신문 on a screen. 뉴스에서 봤어요 (saw it on the news) is how 소문 gets promoted to fact.
Things-heard: the 문 of M8's 신문 (new-hearings), minus the fact-checking. 소문 들었어요? — did you hear? — travels faster than 뉴스.
The noun inside M10's 이야기하다, standing alone at last: a story, a talk, a topic. 옛날이야기 — an old-days story — is Korean for fairy tale. Shortens to 얘기 in speech.
대 (facing) + 화 (speech — 전화's 화): face-to-face speech, the thing M20's phones keep interrupting. 대화가 필요해요 — we need to talk — four syllables of dread.
Measured on the 있다-chassis: 관심이 있어요/없어요. 관심 없어요 ends conversations; 관심 있어요 starts them.
진 (true — 진짜's 진) + 심 (heart): true-heart. 진심이에요? — do you mean it? 진심으로 — from the heart.
오 (wrong) + 해 (untangle — M10's 이해's 해): understanding, done wrong. 오해하지 마세요 — don't get me wrong — the sentence that always arrives one sentence too late.
반 (flip — not M19's half-반) + 대 (facing — 대화's 대): flipped-facing. 반대예요 — I'm against it. Also plain geometry: 반대쪽, the opposite side, with M23's 쪽.
옛 (old) + 날 (day), said 옌날 — the interlude's nasal slide, live. 옛날 옛날에 — 'long, long ago' — is how every 옛날이야기 opens.
The person 존댓말 (M19) was invented for. 어른이 되면 — when you become one — the 반말 rules stop being simple.
어떻다 wearing this module's badge: what-KIND-of. 어떤 사람이에요? — what are they like? — the question behind every friend-recommendation (성격이 좋아요, M19).
이렇다 + -ㄴ: 이런 날 — a day like this. Alone — 이런! — it's a wince: oh no.
그렇다 + -ㄴ — and M7's 그런데 was 그런 + 데 all along: 'that kind of situation, and…'. 그런 사람 아니에요 — I'm not that kind of person.
The trio completes M6/M16's geometry: this-kind, that-kind, THAT-kind. Alone — 저런! — it's the national sympathy noise: oh dear.

en: to be the same / be like
notes: 같아요 — it's the same; 교과서 같아요 (M15) — like a textbook. And the course's oldest adverb decoded: M9's 같이 (together) is 같다's adverb — doing it 'the same.'
똑 (exactly — 똑바로's 똑, M23, and the knock of M15's 똑똑하다) + 같다. 똑같아요! — identical! What twins and copied homework are.
달라요 — 르-family, the 몰라요/빨라요/불러요 shape. Badge form 다른 also means OTHER: 다른 사람 — someone else. Different and other share a word; Korean shrugs.
비슷해요 — the diplomatic middle between 같아요 and 달라요. 비슷한 것 — something similar — is what the shop offers when they don't have it.
The question adjective: 어때요? — how is it? 어땠어요? — how was it? (The ㅎ vanishes and the vowels fuse.) Its children run this course: M10's 어떻게 is its adverb, 어떤 its badge form.
궁금해요 — I wonder. 궁금한 것이 있어요 — I have a question — is what 관심 sounds like when it's polite.
착해요. M4's 친절하다 is kind BEHAVIOR; 착하다 is kind NATURE. 착한 사람 — a good soul. The compliment for kids and dogs alike.
이상해요 — that's weird. 이상한 소문 — a strange rumor. The mildest alarm Korean has; often said mid-smile.
특별해요. 특별한 날 — a special day; M25 is a whole module of them. Restaurant menus charge extra for this adjective.
무서워요 — ㅂ-family; badge form 무서운, like 매운. Scary AND scared: Korean lets context pick fear's direction. 무서운 이야기 — what 옛날이야기 turns into after dark.
대단해요! — impressive! The all-purpose wow: for marathons, for 매운 것 survivors, for anyone who finished Band 1.
부러워요! — I'm jealous! — said freely and warmly; in Korean, envy is a compliment. ㅂ-family, of course: 부러운.
젊어요 — said 절머요, the ㄻ batchim handing its ㅁ across (sound interlude, live exhibit). 젊은 사람 — a young adult. For kids it's M21's 어리다: 어린이 — young-one — is the official word for child.
솔직히 말하면 — honestly speaking — the opinion-starter that promises 진심 is coming. 솔직한 대답 — an honest answer — is what 글쎄요 postpones.
설명해 주세요 — please explain — M9's do-for-me machine pointed at confusion. What turns 오해 back into 이해.
The answer to 왜? that ends the conversation: 그냥 — just because. The gap deck's oldest resident finally joins the checklist. Also a softener: 그냥 물어봤어요 — just asking.
아마 비가 올 거예요 — it'll probably rain. Rides M8's guessing future; certainty is not the Korean way.
물론이에요! — of course! Agreement at full volume; 물론 alone works too. Literally 'no need to discuss.'
The question-softener: 혹시 알아요? — do you happen to know? Opens every polite ambush: 혹시… 시간 있어요? Also 'just in case': 혹시 몰라서 — because you never know.
서로 달라요 — different from each other; 서로 도와요 — help each other. The mutuality word: what M4's 우리 does internally.
The opinion airbag — deployed between question and answer to soften whatever's coming. 글쎄요… commits you to nothing. Drop the 요 among friends; M19 rules apply.
Sino numbers in front: 이천이십육 년. M11's native 해 does the poetry (새해); 년 does the paperwork.
The months are just Sino numbers + 월: 일월, 이월… 십이월 — nothing to memorize. Two got sanded smooth: June is 유월 (not 육월), October is 시월 (not 십월).
The third 일 on your radar: one (M2), work (일하다), and now DAY — 구 일, the 9th. M2's 내일 was 'the coming day' all along; a number in front means a date.
M11's native 날, grown official. 날짜가 어떻게 돼요? — what's the date? — is what you ask before booking 기차표.
달 (M16's month-moon) + 력 (record): the month-book on the wall. Korean ones print 설날 and 추석 in red — the days everything closes.
M5's 몇 + 일, fused and softened: 오늘 며칠이에요? — what's the date today? Spelled 며칠, never 몇일 — a spelling rule even natives wobble on.
The year that just left, said 장년 — the nasal slide again. 작년 겨울 — last winter.
올 + M11's 해 — the year we're standing in; no Sino version needed. 올해도… — 'this year too…' — the opening sigh of every resolution.
내 (coming — 내일's 내!) + 년: the coming year. Tomorrow and next year share a prefix; Korean optimism is decodable.
The when-noun. Bare after events: 추석 때, 시험 때. With the third badge for verbs: 어릴 때 — when I was little. (M1's 시간 is duration; 때 is the moment.)
그 + 때. 그때 봐요! — see you then! Also the storyteller's pivot: 그때… — and THAT's when everything changed.
M12's 지나다 wearing M24's past badge + M8's 주: the passed-week. 지난달, 지난번 — the prefix works the whole calendar. The badge builds words now, not just phrases.
The umbrella over 설날 and 추석 — the days half the country drives to visit the other half. 명절 연휴 is when the whole nation shares the same road at the same time.
Korea's biggest 명절, said 설랄: new clothes, deep bows to elders (세배 — rewarded in cash, 세뱃돈), and 떡국 for breakfast. Buses book out a month ahead.
M18's 떡 + M18's 국, self-assembled. Eaten on 설날 morning; finishing a bowl officially makes you one year older. Some children request seconds.
The autumn 명절 — thanks for the harvest, food for the ancestors, 송편 for everyone. Fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, so the 달 is always full.
The 추석 떡: pine-steamed, sesame- or honey-filled, folded into a half-moon. Family legend says shape a pretty 송편, get a pretty child. Grandmothers judge.
연 (linked) + 휴 (rest — 휴가's 휴, M11): rest-days holding hands. 삼일 연휴 — a three-day weekend — is what the whole country scans the 달력 for.
Konglish, five syllables of it. In Korea it's a COUPLE holiday — closer to Valentine's than to family dinner; M19's 솔로 famously suffer.
기념 (commemoration — M23's 기념품's first half) + 일 (this module's day): a marked day. Young couples run monthly ones — the 백일-counting culture of the gap deck.
결혼 + 식 (ceremony — the suffix behind 졸업식 graduations and 입학식 school entrances). Korean wedding-hall ceremonies run famously efficient; the buffet is where the reunion happens.
The native party. 돌잔치 — M22's 돌 note pays off: the first-birthday feast. 잔치국수 — feast noodles — because long noodles mean long life.
M13's 새 + M11's 해, exactly as 해's note promised. 새해 복 많이 받으세요 — the formula the whole country exchanges at midnight.
축 (celebrate — 축하하다's 축, M19) + 제: universities throw them in May, regions all year — mud, cherry blossoms, fireworks. The 불꽃축제 fills M22's 한강 every autumn.
Smaller than M4's 아이. Star of the 백일 and 돌잔치 in the gap deck — Korean babies headline two parties before they can walk.
M19's 커플, upgraded by paperwork. 부부 싸움 — a married quarrel — has its own proverb: 칼로 물 베기, 'cutting water with a knife.' No lasting damage.
몇 년에 태어났어요? — what year were you born? Age-aware Korea (M4's gap deck) asks early. Everyone's first verb, grammatically always in the past.
결혼했어요? is small talk, not a proposal — family curiosity, asked warmly. The noun 결혼 stands alone; add -식 for the ceremony, 신혼 for what follows.
가족이 모여요 — the family gathers: the whole point of a 명절. 모임 — a meetup — is this verb turned noun.
미 (not-yet) + 래 (come — 내일's coming-내 in another coat): the not-yet-come. What M8's 꿈 and 계획 are made of.
인 (person — 외국인's 인, M23) + 생 (life — 생일's 생): one person's run through time. Modern slang stacks it on anything peak: 인생 사진 — the best photo you've ever taken.
M6's 앞 + M6's (으)로: toward-the-front — in TIME. The future is ahead, and M24's 옛날 is behind; Korean walks facing forward.
미역 (seaweed) + M18's 국. New mothers eat it to recover; everyone eats it on their birthday in tribute to mom. NEVER before an exam — the gap deck explains the slip.
Received, not had: 복 많이 받으세요 — get lots of luck. Korean fortune is a delivery, and at New Year the whole country wishes you a big shipment.
초를 불어요 — blow out the candles, with M11's 불다. On the radar: 초 is also 'second' (the clock's tick) and the start-syllable of 초등학교 (M15). This one melts.
The alphabet from this course's first reading gets a national holiday — Sejong's 1446 promulgation, celebrated with a day off. Said 한글랄; the only holiday honoring a writing system you now read.
어버이 — the old word covering both 어머니 and 아버지 (M4) — plus 날. Carnations pinned to parents' chests, phone calls home. Not a day off; the affection is mandatory anyway.
신 (new — 신문's new-신) + 혼 (marriage — 결혼's 혼) + M11's 여행: new-marriage-travel, self-assembled. M22's 제주도 built an industry on it.
한국 문화 — what this module (and half your curiosity) is about. The 문 here is writing, not M6's door — the radar's last homograph lesson.
전통 음식, 전통 놀이, 전통 시장 — the adjective slot Korea fills most proudly. What 명절 exist to hand down.
조선 시대 — the Joseon era — is where half the dramas live. 요즘 시대에 — 'in this day and age' — is how elders open sentences about phones.
Five hundred years (1392–1910), one dynasty — the palaces, the 한복, and 한글 itself all date from it. When a drama says 조선, expect topknots.
여왕 — queen; 왕자 — prince. Also modern slang's favorite prefix: 왕만두 are king-sized dumplings. Royalty inflates portions.
세종 + 대 (great — 대학교's big-대) + 왕: the king from this course's first reading. His statue watches 광화문 광장; his alphabet carries your every sentence.
태극 (the red-blue yin-yang) + 기 (flag). The four black trigrams mean sky, earth, water, fire — a cosmology on a flagpole, waved hardest during World Cup season.

무궁 (never-ending) + 화 (flower): the national flower that blooms, falls, and blooms again all summer — the persistence was the point. Also the name of the slower, cheaper train (M23's KTX's humble cousin).
The alphabet itself, finally a checklist word — 26 modules after you learned to read it and one module after its holiday (한글날, M25). 한 (great/Korea) + 글 (writing).
태 (stomp) + 권 (fist) + 도 (way): the way of foot and fist. Korea's Olympic export — more practitioners abroad than at home, counted in the tens of millions.
한 (Korea) + 류 (flow), said 할류: the wave that carried 드라마, 케이팝, and probably you to this app. Coined abroad, embraced at home.
Konglish returning home: the K is for Korea. Idol lyrics mix 반말, 존댓말, and English mid-line — listening practice with choreography.
The folk song every Korean knows and no one can quite translate — 아리랑 itself means… nobody agrees. Hundreds of regional versions; one shared ache. UNESCO-listed.
예의가 없어요 — no manners — is a serious verdict here. Two-handed giving, the bow, elders eat first: 예의 is the operating system 존댓말 (M19) runs on.
One syllable, two solemn things: the floor-deep bow (세배 at 설날 is one) and the Buddhist temple in the mountains. The radar's parting gift — context bows to context.

The great November production run: families gather, hundreds of cabbages surrender, and a winter's worth of 김치 goes into the 냉장고 (or its dedicated sibling, the 김치냉장고). UNESCO-listed as heritage — the gathering, not the recipe.

The gap deck's famous untranslatable (M19), now officially on your checklist: the affection that accumulates between people who share time. 정이 많아요 — has lots of jeong — is among the warmest things said about a person.
첫 (first — 처음's prefix form) + M14's 눈-snow. Couples promise to meet when it falls; the forecast becomes romance news. 첫사랑 — first love — uses the same 첫, and the dramas use both.
지금 is now-this-second; 이제 is now-as-opposed-to-before — a hinge between chapters. 이제 할 수 있어요: I couldn't, and now I can. This module's word for a reason.
요즘 어떻게 지내요? — how are you these days? — the small-talk opener built from M23's 지내다. Long overdue; consider it the course's own 요즘.
The book (now app) this whole course secretly is — 단어 by 단어. Not M13's 전 or M23's warm spring: the radar files another 전.
The formal parent of the -어 family: 한국어, 영어, 외국어 — all children of 언어. What you've been building for twenty-six modules.
발음이 좋네요! — the compliment that follows 잘하시네요. Every rom in this app encodes it; the sound interlude was its training manual.
한국어 실력 — your Korean level, measured in what you can DO, not what you've memorized. 실력이 좋아요 is earned, not given.
What every 카페 review measures first: 분위기가 좋아요 — good vibe. People have it too; 분위기 있는 사람 is someone with presence.
The grandest of Seoul's five 궁 (M23) — the one whose note promised free admission in a rented 한복. 경복 means 'shining fortune'; the 복 is M25's luck-복.
Cloudy, gently fizzy, farmer-born. National law of pairing: rain outside demands 막걸리 and 파전 (green-onion pancake) — the sound of rain and frying oil are said to rhyme.
올해 목표 — this year's goal — written every January (M25's 올해도 sigh included). Yours said 'learn Korean'; look where that went.
자신 있어요! — I've got this — confidence measured on the 있다-chassis like everything else Korean values. Twenty-six modules is how it's earned.
M19's 놀다 turned noun: 놀이터 — playground; 윷놀이 — the 설날 board game of thrown sticks; 전통 놀이 — the whole folk-game shelf.
Traditions, promises, secrets, goals: 약속을 지켜요 — keep your word. What this module's nouns ask of the next generation.
깜짝 놀랐어요! — startled! (깜짝 is the jump itself.) The inner state whose outer voice is -네요 — this module's grammar and this verb are a matched set.
세상이 변해요 — the world changes; 마음이 변했어요 — feelings changed (the drama accusation). What 전통 resists and 시대 insists on.
노력하면 돼요 — just keep at it (M23's machine, pointed at yourself). The verb 화이팅 (M15's gap deck) exists to cheer for.
The 존 of 존댓말 (M19): respect-speech's own verb. 세종대왕을 존경해요 — a sentence most of the country would co-sign.
신기해요! — the traveler's word for good-strange: heated floors, self-opening doors, side dishes that refill. Pairs with -네요 like it was born for it: 신기하네요!
다양한 문화, 다양한 음식 — the badge form does brochures and truth alike. 다 (many) + 양 (kinds): many-kinded.
ㅂ-family to the last: 자랑스러워요 — I'm proud. Of 한글, of the 태극기 at a stadium — and, permitted just this once without the modesty deflection: of finishing Ring 1.
미 (beautiful — chosen for the sound of 'America') + 국 (country, M23's 외국's 국). The flattery is accidental; the 국 is systematic.
일 (sun — the radar's FOURTH 일: one, work, day, sun) + 본 (origin): sun-origin, where the day starts seen from the continent. 일본어 — Japanese — by the -어 machine.
중 (middle — 중학교's 중, M15) + 국: the Middle Country. Not phonetics — a worldview, two thousand years old. 중국어 by the -어 machine.
영 + 국, from 'England' — and the -어 machine's famous exception: 영어 is England's language, so 미국 speaks 영국's word.
From 'Deutschland' via hanja, said 도길 — the liaison carrying the ㄱ across (sound interlude). 독일어, 독일 사람, 독일 빵 — every machine applies.
Phonetic loan — the ㅍ handling the F, as always. 프랑스어를 배우는 것보다 한국어가 쉬워요, some say. 빵 — bread — actually arrived through Portuguese and Japanese, not French, despite the vibes.
Phonetic loan. 러시아어. On a world map in a Korean classroom, the biggest thing on it — 정말 크네요.
Phonetic loan. A top destination for 어학연수 (language study abroad) and working holidays — many Koreans' first 외국.
호 + 주 (continent) — the hanja shorthand for Australia. The other working-holiday giant; opposite seasons, so 호주 크리스마스 is a beach day.
동 (east) + M23's 쪽. The 동 of 동대문 (the East Gate) — old Seoul reads itself once you own the compass. The sun rises over the 동해.
서 + 쪽. Also the 서 of 서울? No — that one's native; the radar warns against over-decoding. Sunsets and the 서해 live this way.
남 + 쪽 — the 남 of 남대문 (Great South Gate) and 남학생. Warm winds, 부산, and 제주도 are all 남쪽에.
북 + 쪽. Colder weather comes from here, and the peninsula's other half is politely called 북한 — north-Korea, by this compass.
고향이 어디예요? — the warm follow-up once your country is known. Where 명절 traffic jams point (M25), and what 아리랑 aches about (M26).
남 (male) + 편 (side — 건너편's 편, M23): the male side of a 부부 (M25). Somehow twenty-six modules of family vocabulary arrived before the spouses did.
Your own wife. Someone ELSE's wife gets the honorific 부인 — the M4 noun-upgrade pattern (나이/연세, 집/댁), still sorting the world.
The honorific wife: 사장님 부인 — the boss's wife. Never your own (that's 아내 — humility rules, M4). Also a polite address for married women of a certain era.
Technically an uncle-by-marriage; practically every man over forty — the taxi 기사님's off-duty name. The gap deck explains the fictive-kinship system before you misfire it.
The casual clip of 아주머니 — the restaurant-running, line-cutting, umbrella-armed backbone of the nation. Address one as 이모 (M18) in a restaurant and eat better.
주 (master) + 인 (person — 외국인's 인): the shop's 주인, the dog's 주인. 주인아저씨/주인아줌마 — the owner, street-titled — runs every 가게 you've shopped at since M1.
교 (teach — 교실/교과서's 교, M15) + 수. Address as 교수님, always — the 님-ladder (M16) has no day off on campus.
The person M14's 병원 exists for. The -자 is a person-suffix (기자, 학자 — reporter, scholar); 환자 is the suffering-person.
군 (army) + 인 (person). Nearly every Korean man serves ~18 months — 군대 (the army) is where friendships pause, dramas set flashbacks, and 눈치 gets professionally trained.
여러 (several) + 분 (M5's counter wearing its honorific person-hat): 'honored severals.' How teachers, MCs, and flight attendants open every sentence aimed at a room.
M4's 말, honorific edition — the noun-upgrade pattern's flagship. 말씀하세요 — please speak. Humble twist: it also lowers YOUR words to an elder (말씀 드릴게요 — Ring 2 machinery, previewed).
M1's 집, upgraded for elders: 댁이 어디세요? — where do you live, honored one? The noun-honorific shelf now holds 나이/연세, 말/말씀, 집/댁 — and M25's 생일/생신.
교 (teaching) + 회 (gathering — 회사/회의's 회, M16). Korea's skylines glow with red crosses at night; about a third of the country attends one.
극 (drama) + 장 (place — 주차장/광장's 장). The older, broader word; 영화관 (M23's -관 family) is specifically the movies.
서 (writing) + 점 (shop). Where 책 (M1), 사전 (M26), and this course's imaginary paper edition live. The big ones double as Seoul's favorite meeting spots.
우체 (mail) + 국 (office — a THIRD 국 for the radar: country 미국, soup 떡국, office 우체국). Where 편지 and 소포 begin their journeys.
대사 (ambassador) + M23's -관 (public building). The place your 여권 (M23) hopes you never urgently need.
Where 유학 (study abroad) usually starts — shared rooms, curfews, and the fastest Korean immersion money can't buy. M15's school world gains a bedroom.
The raw street inside M23's 사거리 (four-streets), extracted. 길 (M12) is the way you take; 거리 is the street scene — 먹자거리, the let's-eat street, is the best compound in urban planning.
장 (place) + 소 (place — 안내소's 소): place-place, the formal one. 곳 (M12) is anywhere; 장소 is a venue with a purpose — 약속 장소, the meeting spot.
키가 커요/작아요 — height IS big or small; Korean has no 'tall.' The gap deck files the pattern next to 인기가 많아요 — measure by possession, as always.
편지를 쓰다/받다 — written with M10's 쓰다, received with M9's 받다, sent 한테 someone with this module's glue. Handwritten ones still rule Korean romance.

한 (China's Han dynasty — NOT Korea's 한국-한; the radar's subtlest catch) + 자 (character). The roots behind every compound this course decodes; 한글 replaced them for writing, but they still power the vocabulary.
M4's 우리-warmth at national scale: Koreans say OUR country, rarely 한국, when speaking Korean to Koreans. One word, written solid — the possessive pronoun fused into the map.
무슨 (M10) asks what KIND; 어느 asks WHICH ONE: 어느 나라, 어느 쪽 (M23's note, finally legal). Point at a set, pick a member.
만나서 반갑습니다 — glad from meeting you — the introduction formula. ㅂ-family: 반가워요, casually 반가워! The joy specific to seeing a person.
People take 한테 where places take 에: 친구한테 줬어요. The everyday spoken form; 에게 in writing. FROM a person is 한테서.
한테's formal twin — letters, lyrics, and books use 에게; conversation uses 한테. Same job, different register: the M19 lesson, applied to particles.
The honorific upgrade of 한테/에게: 부모님께, 선생님께, 사장님께. Travels with -(으)시- and 드리다 (M4/M9) — the politeness machinery moves as a set.
Korean plurals are optional — 들 appears mostly on people (사람들, 친구들) when the many-ness matters. Never where a number already counts: 세 명, not 세 명들.
들어 (entering) + 가다: enter, moving AWAY from the speaker. 방에 들어가요. The compound machine's flagship.
들어 + 오다: enter, coming TOWARD me. 들어오세요! — come in! — said while holding the door. The 가다/오다 compass decides, always from where YOU stand.
나 (emerge — M8's 나가다's 나) + 오다. Buildings, ovens, and search results all 나와요. 영화가 나왔어요 — the movie is out.
올라 (rising) + 가다. 산에 올라가요 — M11's mountains, M22's 오르다 in its everyday compound suit. Prices 올라가요 too, relentlessly.
내려 (descending — M6's 내리다, the get-off verb) + 가다. 고향에 내려가요 — Koreans go DOWN to their hometowns from Seoul, whatever the compass says.
내려 + 오다 — down toward me. 산에서 내려왔어요 — back from the summit, where M22's 경치 was.
걸어 (M6's 걷다, ㄷ flipped) + 가다: go on foot. 집까지 걸어가요 — the how folded into the going.
걷다 + 오다: arrive on foot. 학교까지 걸어왔어요? — you WALKED here? The compound answers how and which-way at once.
The errand verb: a round trip in one word. 시장에 다녀왔어요 — been to the market. The gap deck holds its famous formula: 학교 다녀오겠습니다.
가져 (가지다 — to have, this module's grip-verb) + 오다: have-and-come. 우산을 가져오세요 — bring an umbrella. Its mirror 가져가다 takes things away.
A many-jobs verb: lift and carry (가방을 들어요), money is spent (돈이 들어요), sleep is entered (잠이 들어요). The 들 inside 들어가다 — entering was its first job all along. ㄹ-drop: 듭니다.
The put-it-out verb: 돈을 내요 (pay), 숙제를 내요 (hand in), 화를 내요 (put out anger — the active cousin of M19's 화나다). 시간을 내다 — MAKE time.
To have, actively — 있다 states existence; 가지다 grips it. Spoken Korean squeezes it to 갖다: 갖고 있어요, I've got it. The 가져 of 가져오다.
Hands, fish, taxis, and opportunities: 손을 잡다, 택시를 잡다, 기회를 잡다. What the 돌잡이 baby (M25's gap deck) does to its future — the grab was this verb.
가방에 책을 넣어요. Sugar into coffee, coins into machines, 넣다 feeds them all. The gap deck's 눈에 넣어도 안 아프다 puts a grandchild in an eye, approvingly.
넣다's open-air twin: 책상 위에 놓으세요 — set it on the desk. Also release: M4's 말 놓으세요 was this verb, putting formality DOWN. Says 노타 — the ㅎ merge, live.
M9's 사다 finally meets its counterpart — 사고팔다, buy-and-sell, is commerce in one breath. ㄹ-family: 팝니다 on every shop sign (아이스크림 팝니다).
아기를 안아요 — holding M25's baby. Sounds like 앉다 (sit, M9) — 안자요/안아요 keep them apart in speech, context does the rest. The radar logs a sound-twin.
The raw verb inside M15's 물어보다 — 묻다 + 보다, ask-and-see. ㄷ-irregular like 듣다: 물어요. (A homograph 묻다 buries things — context, as ever, decides.)
The raw loss inside M20's 잃어버리다 — which was 잃다 + 버리다, lost-and-thrown-away, the compound machine dramatizing. 길을 잃다 — lose the way (M23's cheerful emergency).
Run AND jump — Korean bundles the burst of motion. 뛰지 마세요! — no running — on every pool deck. 달리다 is the sports-track runner; 뛰다 is everyday hustle.
What M22's 새 does, and M12's 비행기 (飛行 — flying-going) does professionally. ㄹ-family: 새가 날아요. M21's 옷이 날개다 gave you the wings; here's their verb.
Things sprout: 문제가 생겼어요 (a problem arose), 시간이 생겼어요 (time opened up), 여자친구가 생겼어요 (a girlfriend HAPPENED). Also looks: 잘생기다 — well-arisen — is handsome.
The raw verb inside M9's 도와주다 — ㅂ-family with a twist (돕다 → 도와요, the footnote M11's table promised). 서로 도와요 — help each other; M24's 서로 finds its verb.
The eruption verb hiding everywhere: 화가 나다 (M19), 기억나다 (M19), 소리가 나다, 땀이 나다. Feelings and happenings COME OUT in Korean; 나다 is the door they use.
M6's 안 is inside-the-boundary; 속 is inside-the-substance: 가방 속, 물속, 마음속 — where M19's 마음 keeps its secrets. 속이 안 좋아요 — my stomach (my insides) is off.
M6's 아래 is below; 밑 is right underneath, touching: 책상 밑에 — under the desk (where dropped pens go). The position-noun shelf gains its basement.
The middle of anything: 방 가운데에 (mid-room), 둘 가운데 (between the two). M6's position nouns finally get their center — and photos get their 가운데 자리, the spot everyone wants.
The noun inside M8's 끝나다/M16's 끝내다, extracted at last. 끝까지 — to the very end; 끝! — done! The double-consonant ㄲ start and ㅌ batchim make it a pronunciation exhibit all by itself.
M1's 자다, nouned: 잠을 자다 — sleep a sleep (Korean doubles up happily). 잠이 오다 — sleep COMES, like weather; 잠이 들다 — you fall IN. The gap deck files the insomniac's sentence.
The day's missing timeslot: 아침 → 점심 → 낮 → 저녁 → 밤, complete at last. 낮잠 — a daytime-sleep — is the compound for nap, and the argument for one.
Duration's word: 방학 동안 (during vacation), 세 시간 동안 (for three hours), 그동안 (all this while — the catch-up greeting's engine). Time gets a container.
M8's 손 (hand) + 가락 (strand): hand-strands. 발가락 — toes — are foot-strands; the body keeps self-assembling. What 잡다 grips with.
The plot-twist adverb: 갑자기 비가 왔어요. Dramas run on it; so does M11's weather. Often paired with 왜 갑자기? — why, out of nowhere?
Immediacy in space and time: 바로 옆에 (right next to), 바로 지금 (right now), 바로 그거예요! — that's EXACTLY it. M23's 똑바로 was 똑 + this.
계속 비가 와요 — it keeps raining. 계속하세요 — carry on. The adverb of not-stopping, which is also how Korean study works.
M5's 한 + M12's 번, fused: one-time — and softened into an invitation: 한번 해 보세요, give it a try (M16's try-machine's favorite passenger). 언제 한번 만나요 — let's meet sometime.
The raw moment inside M9's counter phrase 잠깐만요 (just-a-moment-please). 잠깐 들어오세요 — come in for a minute. Its formal twin 잠시 staffs announcements.

en: to be that way / be so
notes: The connective factory's engine. 그래요 — I see / that's right; 그래요? — really?; 그랬어요? — did it? ㅎ-family like 어떻다 (M24). Its children fill this module.
The WRITTEN but — books, news, exams. Say it aloud and you sound like an editorial; speech uses 그런데/하지만 (M7). Your first citizen of the written register (appendix S2's territory).
그렇다 + M20's -(으)면: if-that's-so. The full suit of 그럼; opens solutions: 그러면 내일 갈까요? — then shall we go tomorrow?
그러면, clipped by the 준말 machine. Doubles as a warm 'of course!': 그럼요! And closes conversations: 그럼, 내일 봐요. The most social two syllables in the language.
그렇다 + M10's -(으)니까: because-it's-so. Also the 'that's what I'm saying!' of agreement — 그러니까요! — the chorus of every gossip session.
그렇다 + M7's -지만: that's-so-but. Sits between casual 그런데 and written 그러나 on the register ladder — the connectives got the M19 treatment all along.
'If you ask why—': M10's 왜 + 하면. Opens the answer and usually lands on -기 때문이에요. English says because mid-sentence; Korean announces it first.
[noun] 때문에 — because of it: 눈 때문에, 너 때문에 (credit or blame; tone decides). The formal -기 때문이에요 answers 왜냐하면 — recognize now, produce in Ring 2.
The bare pointer inside 이거/이런/이쪽, finally naked: 이 책, 이 사람. The radar's FIFTH 이 — subject particle, two, tooth, and now this. Context has been sorting them for you all course.
그 사람 — that person; and Korean's closest thing to THE: 그 영화 — the movie we both mean. Rank 9 in the entire language; twenty-nine modules was long enough to wait.
The far pointer: 저 건물 — that building yonder. Yes, it looks exactly like 저 (I-polite, M1) — 저는 저 사람을 알아요 is legal and Koreans don't blink. Sentence position referees.
모든 사람 — everyone; 모든 것 — everything. Frozen in badge form (M24's -ㄴ, fossilized). Its adverb sibling 모두 counts the same crowd from outside the noun.
여러 나라 — various countries; 여러 가지 — several kinds. The 여러 of M27's 여러분, demoted back to civilian duty.
The any-pointer: with negatives it empties rooms (아무도 없어요 — nobody), with 나 it opens them (아무 때나 — whenever). The indefinite system's front door.
M24's 다르다 in badge form, so common it fossilized into its own word: 다른 사람 — someone else; 다른 거 있어요? — got anything else? The shop-counter essential.
그거's formal suit — writing and careful speech keep the 것 whole (M16 taught you the clip). 그것보다 — more importantly… — pivots whole conversations.
여기's written twin: signs, brochures, and announcements say 이곳 (이 + M12's 곳). 이곳에서 수영하지 마세요 — the pool sign, now fully parseable.
M22's 제일 in its written suit — 가장 큰 나라, 가장 좋아하는 노래. Speech says 제일; print says 가장; both crown the same winner.
The textbook's very — where speech says 아주/너무 (M11), writing says 매우. Your degree ladder now has dress shoes.
모두 왔어요 — everyone came; 모두 얼마예요? — how much all together? 모든 modifies the noun; 모두 stands alone and counts the crowd.
M9's 같이 in its ceremony suit — wedding invitations, anthems, and slogans say 함께. 같이 gets the coffee; 함께 gets the vows.
또 만나요! — see you again! — and the exasperated 또?! (AGAIN?!). M10's 다시 is redo-again; 또 is once-more-again. Small word, daily workout.
The promise-hardener: 꼭 오세요 — you MUST come; 꼭 연락할게요 — I'll definitely call. Softness with steel inside; Korean invitations run on it.
M10's 언제 + 나: whenever-you-look. M8's 항상 states a fact; 언제나 makes it warm — 언제나 환영해요, always welcome.
Two jobs: the warm truly (날씨가 참 좋네요) and the oh-right! of sudden remembering (참! 숙제 있었지). The grandmother's degree word and everyone's memory alarm.
M28's 잠깐 in uniform: 잠시만 기다려 주세요 — the announcement, the hold music, the elevator. Same moment, starched collar.
The hurry-warmly adverb hiding in M9's 어서 오세요 — 'come QUICKLY' softened into 'welcome.' 어서 먹어 — go on, eat — is grandmother for I love you.
뭐's full suit (M10 taught the clip first — the course's one deliberate backwards 준말). Writing and formal speech keep it whole: 이것은 무엇입니까?
The realization noise: 아, 알겠어요 — ah, got it. 아! before a sentence buys the brain half a second; Koreans deploy it constantly, and now so do you.
그렇다 in M19's 반말: 그래! — okay!; 그래? — really?; 그래 그래 — yes yes, I'm listening. The polite version is this module's 그래요.
아니요's 반말 clip — but its second job is bigger: sentence-initial 아니 means 'hold on, WHAT—': 아니, 왜 벌써 가요? Disbelief's favorite opener.
The national exhalation: pain (아이고 허리야), sympathy (아이고, 어떡해), exhaustion (sitting down after fifty), delight (아이고 예뻐라). Standing up, sitting down, and everything between. See the gap deck.
좋다's opposite, twenty-nine modules late — proof the course preferred 안 좋아요 (softer, more common) all along. ㅡ-drop family: 나빠요. 나쁜 사람, 나쁜 꿈, 나쁜 날씨.
M17's 즐기다 (enjoy), adjectived — ㅂ-family: 즐거워요. 즐거운 여행 되세요! — have a pleasant trip! — the send-off on every platform.
걱정하지 마세요 — don't worry — possibly the kindest -지 마세요 (M14). 걱정돼요 — I'm worried; 걱정이 많아요 — the 있다-chassis measures anxiety too.
생 (life — 생일/인생's 생) + 활 (activity): life as it's actually lived. 한국 생활이 어때요? — how's life in Korea? — the question every 외국인 (M23) fields.
그 + M11's 날, fused solid: the day we both mean. 그날 밤 — that night — is how every Korean story turns its most important corner.
그 + M28's 동안: the span since we last met. 그동안 잘 지냈어요? — the catch-up greeting M1's 잘 지냈어요 grows into once there's a gap worth naming.
The tens continue past M5's 스물: 서른 살 — thirty years old, the age every K-drama treats as a deadline. Ages native, money Sino — the split holds.
마흔 살. Confucius called forty 불혹 — the age of no doubts; Korean forty-somethings quote it wryly while doubting plenty.
쉰 살 — and the aigo-when-sitting age (M29's gap deck). One syllable; the ages get shorter as they get bigger.
예순 살 — the year before 환갑, the sixty-first-birthday feast that once earned its own 잔치 (M25). Modern medicine demoted the party; the word survives.
일흔 살. Not M2's Sino 일 — native through and through; the radar stays sharp to the end.
여든 살 — grandmother territory, where 아이고 예뻐라 (M29) gets said about YOU for visiting.
아흔 살. Beyond it, 백 살 borrows M9's Sino hundred — the native system retires at ninety-nine, like most of its speakers don't.
M26's 첫 (first-) + -째: first-in-order — and the firstborn child: 첫째는 딸이에요. Birth order is a lifelong job title in Korean families.
M5's 둘 + -째. 둘째 딸, 둘째 문제 — second in any lineup. The pattern continues: 넷째, 다섯째, as far as families and lists go.
M5's 셋 + -째. 첫째, 둘째, 셋째 — how Korean numbers its arguments, its children, and its New Year resolutions.
Rides like a counter, Sino numbers in front: 백 미터 — 100m. 센티미터 for the small stuff — 키 (M27) gets measured in it: 백칠십 센티미터.
Sino numbers in front: 이십 퍼센트 — 20%, the discount that starts wallets. Native alternative: 프로 (from Dutch 'procent') — older shopkeepers say 이십 프로.
What M23's 환전하다 converts 원 into. 십 달러 — ten dollars, Sino like all money. Not M16's 달 (month-moon) — the radar files the near-miss.
M5's 개 + M25's 월: month-units. Sino + 개월 = native + 달: 삼 개월 = 세 달, both three months. The hybrid-clock rule (M5), running one more system.
Paper, photos, tickets, blankets: 종이 한 장, 사진 두 장, 표 세 장. NOT the place-장 of 주차장 or the paste-장 of 된장 — the radar's busiest syllable gains a fourth job.
The kitchen's missing tool — 칼국수 is knife-noodles (hand-cut). 부부 싸움은 칼로 물 베기 (M25's proverb) finally shows its blade. 칼퇴 — knife-sharp on-time leaving — is office slang worth knowing.
식 (eat — 식당/식사's 식) + 탁 (table): the eating-table, where M18's 그릇 stays put and homework happens anyway. 책상 studies, 식탁 feeds.
The bathroom shelf begins. Korean gyms and 찜질방 fold them into 양머리 — sheep-head hats — a national craft skill acquired in childhood.
Native word, no decode needed — a rarity by Module 30. 비누로 손을 씻으세요 — wash with soap; M13's 씻다 gets its tool.
치 (tooth — the Sino twin of M8's 이) + M10's 약 (medicine): tooth-medicine. The compound machine does dental care.
치 + 솔 (brush), with the ㅅ glue the spacing interlude flagged (바닷가's trick). 칫솔이랑 치약 — the travel kit, in this module's own particle.
휴 (discard) + 지 (paper). Housewarming gift #1 in Korea (M13's 집들이): may your troubles unroll as easily. 휴지통 — the wastebasket it ends up in.
수 (water) + 박 (gourd): the water-gourd, summer's fruit-king — sold whole, halved at home, eaten by the family around one 식탁. 수박 화채 is the punch-bowl upgrade.
Winter fruit in Korea — greenhouse season peaks in January, and 딸기 뷔페 (strawberry buffets) sell out hotels. Not related to 딸 (daughter, M4); the radar checks anyway.
포도 한 송이 — one bunch. 청포도 the green kind, 포도주 the drink it becomes (주 = alcohol, 소주's 주 — the compound machine pours).
Konglish; the native citrus is 귤 — Jeju's tiny mandarin, winter's national snack. 오렌지주스 — the breakfast loanword double-header.
Said 닥 — the ㄺ batchim keeping only ㄱ (sound interlude, final exhibit). The animal behind M3's 치킨: 닭고기 is the meat, 닭갈비 the dish, 닭살 the goosebumps (gap deck).
The animal inside M18's 돼지고기, finally on the hoof. Dreaming of one (돼지꿈) means money's coming — buy a lottery ticket, tradition insists.
Ribs, grilled tableside: 소갈비, 돼지갈비, 닭갈비 — this module's animals, deliciously sorted. 갈비찜 for holidays (M25's 명절 tables groan under it).
냉 (cold — 냉장고's 냉, M13) + 면 (noodles — 라면's 면): cold-noodles, summer's answer. 물냉면 swims, 비빔냉면 gets M18's 비비다 treatment. Scissors arrive; say yes.
What 어린이날 (M25) distributes and dentists forgive. 사탕발림 — candy-coating — is flattery; Korean noticed the connection early.
Konglish. Valentine's in Korea runs backwards: women give 초콜릿 on Feb 14; men answer with candy on White Day, March 14. 솔로 (M19) observe Black Day in April, eating 자장면.
Konglish, five syllables. Also a scheduling word: a 샌드위치 데이 is the workday squeezed between two holidays — the 연휴 (M25) everyone petitions to bridge.
Konglish. 햄버거랑 콜라 주세요 — the counter script, in this module's own particle. Korean chains stack 불고기 patties; the machine adapts everything.
Konglish — the ㅍ handles the p-f border zone as usual. Korean pizza believes in corn, sweet potato, and 불고기; Italy has filed complaints.
Konglish. Its partner 사이다 is NOT cider — see the gap deck for the false friend and the slang it spawned. 치킨엔 콜라, the pairing law says.
M7's color set had a hole — the most Korean color of all: the 한복 of old was undyed 흰색, earning Koreans the name 백의민족, the white-clad people. 하얀색 is its softer twin.
The physical chest — and where feelings physically land: 가슴이 아파요 hurts sadder than M14's 아프다 usually does. M19's 마음 is the mind-heart; 가슴 is where it beats.
하나만 — just one; 너만 — only you. REPLACES 을/를 and 이/가 like M2's 도: 커피만 마셔요. Not M9's 만 (10,000) — the radar's final homograph filing.
딸기랑 포도 — strawberries and grapes, casually. M2's 하고's friendly twin; M19's register rules apply to particles too.
빵이랑 우유 — batchim words take 이랑, the 은/는 convention one more time. Friends and texts live here; formal writing switches suits.
딸기와 포도 — the written and. Books, news, invitations; 함께 (M29) is its favorite companion: 가족과 함께.
빵과 우유 — batchim takes 과, vowel takes 와 (backwards from your instinct; everyone's, at first). The and-with trio is complete: 하고 neutral, (이)랑 casual, 와/과 formal.
