The laughter consonant — ㅋ is the k of 크크. Intensity scales with count: ㅋ (dry), ㅋㅋ (amused), ㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋ (genuinely lost it). A single ㅋ can read as cold; calibrate.
ㅋㅋ's softer sibling — the h of 하하. Gentler, warmer, safer with people you 존댓말. Bosses get ㅎㅎ; friends get ㅋㅋ.
응 (casual yes) stripped to its consonant, twice. Pure 반말 — send ㅇㅇ to an elder and Reading 4's pressure rule becomes a workplace incident. The polite reply is still 네.
감사 clipped to two consonants — M1's 감사합니다 at maximum compression. Friends only; the full bow survives everywhere else.
Two vowels drawn as streaming tears — typography as emotion. ㅜㅜ cries a little less; ㅠㅠㅠㅠ floods. The rare slang readable with zero explanation.
One syllable of pure disbelief — good news, bad news, price tags. Often typed 헐… with the trailing dots doing the emotional labor. M29's 아이고 for the young.
짱이야! — the best! Prefixes too: 얼짱 (best face), 몸짱 (best body). A '90s survivor that refuses to age out — M19's 최고 with its tie loosened.
Standard Korean uses 완전히 (completely, adverb); slang drops the 히 and welds 완전 onto anything: 완전 맛있어, 완전 꿀잼. The degree ladder's off-the-books rung.
꿀 (honey — M3's shelf) + 잼 (재미, shrunk): honey-fun. The compound machine and the 준말 machine, in series. 꿀 alone prefixes anything good: 꿀팁, 꿀맛.
English 'no' through the adapter + shrunk 재미: no-fun. 꿀잼's evil twin; a review score in two syllables. 이 영화 완전 노잼이야 — condemned.
아이스 아메리카노, first-syllabled: the national beverage in two vowels. Hot is 따아 (따뜻한 아메리카노); the year-round iced loyalists are 얼죽아 — see the gap deck. Safe to say at ANY counter.
최 (most — 최고's 최, M19) + 애 (love): most-loved. Your favorite member, character, menu item. Fandom Korean's load-bearing word; 차애 is the runner-up.
Japanese 오타쿠 → 오덕후 → 덕후: a loanword localized twice. The activity is 덕질 (fanning-about), and 입덕 is the moment you fall in — an entire verb family grew from two syllables.
English 'insider' through the adapter, shrunk: the person at every 모임 (M25's 모이다). Konglish + 준말 in series — Reading 5 then Reading 4, the standard slang assembly line.
'Outsider,' same assembly line — 인싸's opposite, worn mostly with pride: 저는 아싸예요 means my weekend plans are excellent and private. 혼밥 (M18's gap deck) is aspirational here.
멘탈 (mental, adapted) + 붕괴 (collapse), both clipped: system failure of the self. 멘붕 왔어 — it ARRIVED, like M28's weather-states. A decade old and still fully alive.
심장 (heart — M24 진심's 심) + 쿵 (thud, onomatopoeia): the chest sound of sudden attraction. 심쿵했어! — my heart THUDDED. What 첫눈 (M26) and dramas are engineered to cause.
불 (fire) + 금요일 (M5's day-set): Friday, on fire. 불금인데 집에 있어? — it's BURNING FRIDAY and you're home? (Yes — 아싸 pride.) The work-week's finish line, named.
갑자기 (M28) 분위기 (M26) 싸해진다 — 'suddenly the vibe goes cold' — first-syllabled into one noun. The silence after a joke lands wrong; the word for it arrives even faster.
'Case by case' through the adapter, then first-syllabled: the universal it-depends. 사바사 (사람 by 사람) is its person-to-person spinoff — the template breeds.
Work-life-balance, adapted and first-syllabled. What M16's 야근 destroys and every job posting promises. 워라밸이 좋아요 — the modern 회사 compliment that matters most.
갓 (god, adapted) + 생 (life — 인생's 생, M26): the disciplined, 미라클모닝, gym-before-work life. 갓생 살자! — the New Year's resolution, slangified. 갓- prefixes anything superb.
진짜 (M11) compressed and tensed: 찐 맛집 — a GENUINELY good restaurant; 찐이야 — it's the real deal. The tensing itself carries the emphasis — sound symbolism doing grammar's job.
밀다 (push) + 당기다 (pull), first-syllabled: the strategic hot-and-cold of early romance. What 썸 (M19's gap deck) runs on. 밀당하지 마 — stop playing games — ends it.
The elder who lectures uninvited, opens with 나 때는 (back in MY day — punned as '라떼는'). Serious enough to appear in HR training; funny enough to tease your dad with. Use with 눈치 (M16).
갑 (the stronger contract party — gap deck explains the 갑/을 system) + -질 (the doing-of, derogatory): pulling rank, made famous by airline-nut incidents. Slang serious enough for newspaper headlines.
소소하지만 확실한 행복, first-syllabled: the good coffee, the clean bed, the 아아 at 3pm. Borrowed from a Murakami essay, naturalized completely — the anti-갓생, and its roommate.
The written 하고: 커피 및 차. Forms, menus, regulations — reading only. Say it aloud and the room checks whether you're reading a contract.
전화 또는 문자 — choose one, in print. M29's 또 (again/also) + 는: the or-word of forms and instructions. Its literary twin 혹은 haunts older books.
The restater: [complicated thing]. 즉, [simple thing]. Textbooks and news lean on it; teachers say it aloud as a verbal colon — the one written connective that escapes into speech.
The 그렇다 machine's most formal child (M29's family, in a judge's robe) — proofs, editorials, sermons. Speech uses 그래서/그러니까; print concludes with 그러므로.
The list-closer: 사과, 포도, 딸기 등. Doubled — 등등 — it trails off aloud. On every receipt, syllabus, and ingredients label; also 'back' (등이 아파요) — the radar files a homograph.
The forbidding suffix-noun: 주차 금지 (no parking), 사진 촬영 금지 (no photos), 출입 금지 (keep out). [Anything] + 금지 = don't. The sign vocabulary's sternest word.
One notch below 금지: 머리 조심? No — that's 조심; 주의 is the printed form: 미끄럼 주의 (slippery), 개 조심/맹견 주의 (beware of dog). Yellow signs speak it fluently.
사용 중 (in use — the bathroom door's word), 사용 금지 (do not use), 사용법 (instructions). The verb is 사용하다 — 쓰다 (M10) in a lab coat.
비상 (emergency) + 구 (opening — 입구/출구's 구, M12): the green running man above every theater door. The one sign word worth knowing before you need it.
고장 났어요 — it broke (breakdowns ERUPT, with M28's 나다); the taped-up sign reads 고장. What vending machines announce and elevators threaten.
영업 중 — open; 영업 종료 — closed for the day; 24시간 영업 — the 편의점 promise. The shutter vocabulary of every shop street.
공사 중 — under construction: the sign, the detour, the 6 a.m. drilling. Korea rebuilds constantly; this word narrates it.
중국's middle-中, hung after any noun: 영업 중, 공사 중, 통화 중, 회의 중. The busy-sign machine — see the gap deck for the full system. Also plain 'among': 이 중에서 — among these.
The verb on half of Korea's doors (미시오 — its 하오체 costume) and the 밀 of S1's 밀당. ㄹ-family: 밀어요. Pushing paperwork too: 미루다 is its procrastinating cousin.
The other half of the doors (당기시오), the 당 of 밀당, and appetite's verb: 입맛이 당기다 — a craving PULLS. Every door you've hesitated at, resolved.

대 (great — 대학교's 대) + 한 (韓, THE 한 of 한국) + 민 (people) + 국 (country): the Great Nation of the Han People. Passports, ballots, and stadium chants (대~한민국!) say this; everyday speech says 한국. New root 민 (people) — file it, every citizenry word to come uses it.

북 (M27's compass north) + 한. Only the South says this — the North calls itself 조선 (M26's dynasty word, still on duty up there) and calls the South 남조선. One peninsula, and each half names the other after its own map.

首都 head-city: where a country keeps its head. 서울 is the 수도 — and was under Joseon too, back when its name was 한양. Homograph alert: 수도 is also the water supply (수돗물 = tap water); context sorts the head from the plumbing.

통 (統 unite — NOT 교통's pass-through 통 (通, M12): two Sino 통s, same sound, different hanja) + 일 (one — M2's Sino 일): united-into-one. The 일 homograph party (one, work, day, 일본's sun) seats its most solemn member. 통일하다 to unify — the peninsula's pending verb since 1953.

경 (京 capital) + 기 (畿 royal domain) + 도 (道 province): the-province-around-the-capital — and it is exactly that, wrapped around 서울 on all sides. That capital-경 hides in 도쿄's hanja name 동경 and 베이징's 북경 too — see the world shelf.
Province names are two-city welds: 강릉 + 원주 = 강원. The mountainous east coast — ski country, summer beaches, and the 2018 Winter Olympics (평창). The 도 suffix stamps every province on the map.
충주 + 청주 = 충청, the weld again. The country's calm middle — 대전 anchors it, and its dialect is famously the slowest in Korea. Today it splits with compass syllables you own: 충청남도 / 충청북도.

전주 + 나주 = 전라 — with a spelling catch: 나주's 나 is written 라 mid-word (Sino words dodge word-initial ㄹ; tucked inside, the 라 surfaces). Said 절라도 (ㄴ+ㄹ→ㄹㄹ, the sound reading's rule). The southwest: Korea's rice bowl and its proudest kitchen — 전주 비빔밥 is the reference dish.

경주 + 상주 = 경상. The southeast — 부산, 대구, 울산 all live here, and its blunt, musical dialect stars in every gangster movie. Radar: this 경 is 경주's 慶 (celebration), NOT 경기도's 京 (capital). Two provinces, two different 경s.

인 (仁 benevolence) + 천 (川 stream): kind-stream. Korea's front door — 인천국제공항 (M12's 공항 wearing this module's 국제) is where you'll land. Sound-twin: 온천's 천 (M23) is a different hanja (泉, spring) — one syllable, two waters.

대 (big) + 구 (邱 hill). The inland giant of the southeast, and the hottest city in the country every summer — Koreans call it 대프리카 (대구 + 아프리카, from this module's world shelf). Apples and textiles built it; the heat named it.

대 (big) + 전 (田 field): big-field. The crossroads — KTX lines split here (M23's gap item passes through daily), and the national research labs cluster here. The 성심당 bread pilgrimage is optional but traditional.

광 (光 light) + 주 (州 town): light-town. 전라도's capital, which makes it — by that province's reputation — the best table in the country. The -주 is old Chinese 州 (administrative town), stamped on 경주, 전주, 충주, 상주… every weld-donor city wears it.

울 (蔚 lush) + 산 — yes, M11's mountain, sitting inside a city name. The industrial powerhouse: Hyundai's shipyards and car plants, the biggest paychecks in the country, and the container ships to show for it.

경 (慶 celebration) + 주 (州 town) — the city that lent its first syllable to 경상도. Silla's capital for nearly a thousand years; now 'the museum without walls' — burial mounds downtown, temples in the hills, every school trip's destination. Where Korea goes to look at its oldest self.

남 (compass south, M27) + 산 (M11): South Mountain — you could have decoded this one alone. Seoul's green center, N Tower on top, love-locks on the railing; the skyline photo you've seen IS this hill. Most Korean towns keep a 남산 of their own — south of the old center, every time.

종 (鐘 bell) + 로 (路 road): Bell Road — named for 보신각, the pavilion bell rung 33 times every New Year's Eve. Spelled 종로, said 종노 (ㄹ after ㅇ nasalizes — a street sign doing phonics). That -로 stamps street names nationwide: 세종대로, 강남대로…

동 (compass east) + 대 (big) + 문 (M6's door/gate): Great East Gate — one of the walled city's gates, decoded entirely from parts you own. 남대문 is the same machine pointing south (M27 promised this one). Both now mean their markets: 동대문시장 for fashion at 3 a.m., 남대문시장 for everything else.

덕 (德 virtue) + 수 (壽 longevity) + 궁 (palace — 경복궁's 궁, M26): Palace of Virtuous Longevity, across from 시청. Its stone-wall walk 돌담길 is Seoul's most famous stroll — and superstition says couples who take it break up (the divorce court used to sit at the end).

시 (市 city) + 청 (廳 government hall). The 시 radar grows: city 市, o'clock 시 (M5), 시험's 試 — one syllable, three jobs. Seoul's 시청 fronts the plaza (M23's 광장) and names the subway stop everything transfers through. Bonus homograph: 시청 (視聽) is also TV-watching — 시청자 = viewers.

제주도's (M22) volcano and South Korea's roof — 1,947 m, visible from every corner of the island. The 한 is 漢: 한강's and 한자's 한, NOT 한국's 韓 (M27's subtlest radar catch, still paying out). On top: the crater lake 백록담, white-deer pond.

설 (雪 snow — the 설 in 설탕, 'snow sugar', M3) + 악 (嶽 craggy peak) + 산: Snow-Peak Mountain, 강원도's granite crown. Fall starts here — the news tracks its 단풍 line (M11) down the country like a weather front.

백 (白 white) + 두 (頭 head) + 산: White-Head Mountain — the peninsula's highest (2,744 m), astride the 북한–China border, crater lake 천지 (heaven pond) on top. Radar: this 백 is white, NOT M9's hundred (百). The anthem's first line starts here — 동해 물과 백두산이… — so every Korean sings this mountain.

국 (country) + 가 (家 house — 가족's 가, M4): the country-as-household. The formal register of M23's 나라 — anthems, constitutions, and news anchors say 국가; everyone else says 나라. This module is one long 국-family reunion: 한국, 미국, 외국, 국내, 전국, 국제…

지 (地 earth/land — the 지 grounding 지도 'land-picture' and 지하철 'land-below-iron', both M12) + 역 (域 domain): any bounded patch of map. With this module's 마다 it becomes the thesis: 지역마다 — every region its own everything.

방 (方 direction) + 향 (向 facing). Radar: this 방 is NOT M8's room (房) — same syllable, different hanja, and the difference between asking for a direction and asking for a bedroom. M27's compass words are all 방향s; 어느 방향이에요? aims them.

位置 place-put: where a thing sits. Sound-twin of M6's 위 (above) — that one is native, this one Sino. The map-app word: 현재 위치 (current location) is the blue dot you'll follow through every 지역 in this module.

주 (周 around) + 변 (邊 edge): the ring around something. M6's 근처 is the place near YOU; 주변 is what surrounds a point — and it works on people: 주변 사람들 = the people around you. Radar: this 주 is neither week (M2) nor the city-stamp 州. The 주 pileup is real; hanja sorts it.

부 (附 attached) + 근 (近 near): the attached-nearby. 근처's formal cousin — news reports say 역 부근 where you'd say 역 근처. Radar: that 近 is NOT M16's work-근 (勤 of 출근/퇴근/야근) — two 근 families, one clocking in, one standing nearby.

국 + 내 (內 inside): inside-the-country. Spelled 국내, said 궁내 (ㄱ before ㄴ nasalizes — the sound reading, still lawyering). Radar: this 내 is inside 內, not 내일/내년's coming-내 (來, M25). 국내선 = domestic flights; its opposite is the next entry.

해 (海 sea) + 외 (outside — 외국's 외, M23): beyond-the-sea. Not a metaphor here: with the land border sealed, leaving South Korea means crossing water — every trip out IS overseas. 해외여행 is the compound on every travel-agency poster.

전 (全 all) + 국: all-country. Your third 전: 전화's electric-전 (電), 전에's before-전 (前), now all-전 — which is also 전주's 전, the 'complete' city. 전국 노래자랑, the nationwide song contest, has run on Sunday TV since 1980 — this word in its natural habitat.
국 + 제 (際 between): between-countries. Glued onto airports (인천국제공항), phone calls, and film festivals (부산국제영화제). Where 해외 is where you go, 국제 is what happens between the going.

동 (compass east) + 양 (洋 ocean): the east-ocean world. How Korean says 'Eastern' — 동양 철학 (Eastern philosophy), 동양화 (ink painting). Pairs with the next entry: M27's compass syllables doing civilizational work.

서 (compass west) + 양 (洋 ocean): the west-ocean world — Europe and the Americas as one cultural bloc. 서양 음식 (Western food), 서양 사람 (a Westerner). The ocean in both words is the one you cross to get there.

Through the adaptation machine untouched — Asia has no F, V, or TH to repair (the Konglish reading's easiest customer). The continent Korea anchors the east of; news and sports run on it: 아시안 게임, 아시아 최초 (first in Asia).
Europe through the converter: 유럽 — the P lands as a ㅂ batchim, no cushion needed. The graduation-trip cliché (유럽 여행) and the backpacker's default — now sayable with this module's 해외.

The converter earning its keep: Africa's F becomes ㅍ with an 으-cushion — a-peu-ri-ka, four syllables where English packs three. The F-rule from 커피 and 프랑스, applied to a continent — and the back half of 대구's summer nickname, 대프리카.

뉴 + 욕, two syllables. 미국's (M27) biggest city — not its capital, a distinction Korean quiz shows adore. Radar for fun: 욕 alone is the word for a swear word (욕하다 = to curse). New Yorkers would probably approve.

일본's (M27) capital. Its hanja name reads in Korean as 동경 — east-capital, with 경기도's capital-경 — and older Koreans still say it that way. The news switched to sound-borrowing decades ago: 도쿄, as Japan says it. One city, two Korean names, one 경.

중국's (M27) capital. Same double life as 도쿄: the hanja reading 북경 (north-capital — your compass 북 + that capital-경 again) versus the sound-borrowed 베이징. 북경 오리 (Peking duck) kept the old name; the nightly news took the new one.

프랑스's (M27) capital, silent S dropped at customs: 파리. Homograph classic: 파리 is also the housefly — so 파리에 파리가 있어요 (there's a fly in Paris) is the sentence no Korean textbook can resist. Neither could we.
영국's (M27) capital: 런던, no repairs needed at the border. Completes the five capital–country pairs on this shelf: 도쿄–일본, 베이징–중국, 파리–프랑스, 런던–영국… and 뉴욕–미국, the trick pair (see two entries up).

Stick it straight onto a noun: 날마다 (every day — M5's 매일, where 매 is the Sino 'every' and 마다 the native one), 주말마다, 지역마다. It swallows 이/가 and 을/를 whole, like 도 and 만. Also distributes: 사람마다 달라요 — different from person to person.

社會 gather-meet: society. Flip the syllables and you get 회사 (M4's company) — 會社, the SAME two hanja reversed. Society is the gathering; a company is a gathering incorporated. The 회 is 회의's (M10) meeting-회. One flip, three words decoded.

經濟 manage-and-aid: the economy. Yes, another 경 for the pile (경기도 京, 경주 慶, 경치 景 — all sorted in M31) — the syllable is crowded, the hanja never collide. 경제 뉴스 is half of every broadcast; the other half is two entries down.

政治 govern-manage: politics. Radar: this 정 (政) is NOT M19's 정 (情, affection) — government and warmth share a syllable, which Koreans find funnier every election. 정치인 = politician (M31's person-인 doing suffix work).

政府 govern-office: the government, the actor in half the headlines. Same govern-정 as 정치, plus 부 (府, office). Technically the module's only grade-C word — the 2003 list underrated it; the nightly news never has.

大統領 big-unify-command: the president — etymologically the great unifier-commander. The 통 is 統, the unite-통 of 통일 (M31). Said 대통녕 (ㄹ after ㅇ nasalizes — 종로's rule, one module later). Address one as 대통령님; the news drops the -님.

國民 country-people: the citizenry. M31's 국-family meets 대한민국's 민 (people) — the first compound you could have coined yourself. Said 궁민 (ㄱ before ㅁ nasalizes). As a prefix it nationalizes affection — see the gap deck's 국민 여동생.
敎育 teach-raise: education. Radar: this 교 (敎, teach) is 교회's and 교수's 교 (M27) — NOT 학교's (校, the school building). The national obsession M15 toured (학원, 수능) finally gets its abstract noun.

放送 release-send: broadcasting — flinging words into the air. A THIRD 방 (M8's room 房, M31's direction 方, now release 放); the radar barely blinks anymore. 방송국 = a broadcaster — and that 국 is 局 (bureau), not country: 결국's 국, further down this list.
廣告 wide-tell: advertising — telling everyone at once. Radar: this 광 is 廣 (wide), NOT 광주's 光 (light, M31). What you sit through before the video, and what 스킵 buttons were invented for.

Program through the converter: P→ㅍ and the ㅡ-cushion twice — 프로그램, five syllables where English packs two. TV 프로그램, computer 프로그램, both imports. Koreans clip it too (준말 law): a TV show is often just 프로.

人間 person-between: a human being. The 간 is 시간's (M1) — 間, between. To be human is to exist between others; the hanja is doing philosophy. This person-인 (人) also fronts 인기 (M17, people-energy = popularity) — but NOT 인천 (仁 benevolence, M31).

女性 woman-nature: the formal register of M4's 여자. Forms, news, and signage say 여성; conversation says 여자 — the register ladder M4 built for family words turns out to grade nouns in general. 여성복 = womenswear (M21's -복, still stamping).
男性 man-nature: 여성's pair. The 남 radar files a third card: man 男 (남자), south 南 (남쪽, 남산), and now the formal register splits them cleanly. 남성복 is one aisle over from 여성복.
民族 people-tribe: 대한민국's 민 + 가족's 족 (M4) — a people is the family scaled all the way up, says the hanja. 한민족 = the Korean people; on this peninsula the word carries real weight.

自己 self: oneself. Quoting's little helper — 자기가 맞다고 해요 (insists HE's right, M15's 맞다). And the K-drama staple: couples call each other 자기(야) — literally 'self, dear' — which is either romantic or grammatically alarming, your call.

當身 that-body: 'you' — handle with care. In songs, ads, and books it's the warm universal you; between spouses it's 'dear'; said to a stranger's face it means the fight has started. Rule: read it often, sing it freely, say it never — M4's name+씨 system exists so you don't have to.
戰爭 war. The 전 pileup seats a fourth: electric 電 (전화), before 前 (전에), all 全 (전국, M31), now war 戰. Korea names its war by start date — 6·25 전쟁, June 25th — the way M25 taught you dates work here.

平和 flat-harmony: peace — everything level, nothing burning. Which completes the 화 triple: speech 話 (전화), fire 火 (화나다's anger, M19 — also 화요일's Mars-day), harmony 和. Fire and harmony share a syllable; the radar's tidiest irony.

境遇 boundary-meeting: a case. News-speak's favorite if: 비가 올 경우 (should it rain — M25's -(으)ㄹ badge doing hypotheticals). Where English says 'in that case', Korean says 그런 경우에는 — M24's 그런, reporting for duty.

程度 measure-degree: the abouter. 한 시간 정도 = about an hour; 이 정도 = this much; 어느 정도 = to what extent (M27's 어느). And the 도-collection hits three in two modules: province 道, island 島 (both M31), degree 度.
方法 direction-law: a method is a direction with rules. The 방 is M31's 방향's (方). 다른 방법이 없어요 = there's no other way; 좋은 방법이에요 = now you're talking. Attach it to anything you're learning: 공부 방법, 요리 방법.
結果 tie-fruit: a result is the fruit your efforts tied off. 결혼's knot-결 (M25 — 結, literally tying) + 과일's fruit-과 (M30 — 果). 시험 결과 = exam results, the country's least favorite harvest.
內容 inside-contain: what's in it. M31's 국내-내 (內, inside), back on duty already. 책 내용 = what the book says; 무슨 내용이에요? = what's it about? — the question that unlocks every drama recommendation.
意味 intent-flavor: meaning — the formal register of M10's 뜻. 무슨 의미예요? and 무슨 뜻이에요? both work; one wears a tie. 의미가 있어요 = it means something (the 있다-factory, still hiring).
關係 connect-tie: a relationship. The 관 is 관심's (M24 — 關, the connecting gate): 관심 points AT something, 관계 ties you TO it. 관계가 없어요 doubles as 'unrelated' and 'none of my business' — tone decides.

變化 change-becoming: M26's 변하다 grown into a noun by -화 (化, becoming) — the same -화 hiding inside 문화 (M26: culture, the becoming-of-writing). The suffix industrializes: 세계화 globalization, 노령화 aging. 변화가 필요해요 = change is needed.

環境 ring-boundary: the environment — the ring around you, M31's 주변 with a degree. 환경 문제 (M7's 문제) is the news phrase; 환경을 지켜요 recycles M26's protect-verb. And yes, 境 is one more 경 — the pile grows, the hanja never blur.

硏究 grind-investigate: research — what 교수님 (M27) does between lectures. 연구실 is the lab/office every Korean grad student calls home. 연구 결과에 따르면… = according to research findings — this module's news frame, self-assembling.
部分 section-portion: a part. 이 부분 = this part — of the song, the movie, the problem (노래방 usage guaranteed, M17). One entry down: its big brother.
대 (big) + 부분 (part) = the big part: most. 사람들 대부분 = most people; 대부분 맞아요 = mostly right. Korean built 'most' out of two parts you own — arithmetic, not vocabulary.

點 dot: a point — 좋은 점/나쁜 점 (M24's badge) = strengths and weaknesses; 이 점 = this point, says every presenter. Radar: NOT 서점's 점 (店, shop — M27). Same dot scores your tests (점수) and reads your fortune (점을 보다) — one busy little dot.

Native, and hiding in plain sight since Reading 1: 한글's 글 — writing itself. 글을 쓰다 = to write (a post, an essay); 글자 = a written character. 한글 = the Korean 글 (M26). Twenty-plus modules to notice the second syllable — homograph-radar humility.

A counter for varieties, riding M5's native numbers: 한 가지, 두 가지, and M29's 여러 가지 (several kinds — you've been one syllable from this word since then). Homograph: 가지 is also the eggplant, so 여러 가지 가지 요리 = many kinds of eggplant dishes — a sentence Korean children find funnier than it is.

以上 from-here-up: 스무 살 이상 = twenty and up (M5's ages at the door of every bar); 세 시간 이상 = three-plus hours. Radar: NOT the 이상 in M24's 이상하다 (異常, abnormal) — 'twenty and up' and 'weird' spell identically and never meet.

最近 most-near: the news register of M26's 요즘. The 최 is 최애's most-최 (S1); the 근 is 부근's near-근 (M31) — most-near-in-time. When the anchor says it, it's 최근; when your friend says it, it's 요즘. Same ladder, one rung up.
結局 tied-situation: how it all wraps up. 결혼/결과's knot-결 + a NEW 국 — 局 (situation/bureau), not country 國. It's 방송국's 국 too. 결국 늦었어요 = late anyway, in the end — the word every drama recap leans on.

對하다 to-face. You'll almost never conjugate it raw — it lives in the frame [noun]에 대해서 (about) and [noun]에 대한 + noun (M24's badge, about-flavored): 한국 문화에 대해서 이야기해요. News Korean cannot function without this machine; now neither can you.

en: to be for; ~을 위해서 = for the sake of
notes: 爲하다 for-the-sake-of. Frame: [noun]을/를 위해서 — 가족을 위해서 일해요 (M16's verb, M4's family, one national work ethic). Monuments and anthems run on it: 나라를 위해서. Where 주세요 asks FOR things, 위해서 dedicates TO them.

通하다 pass-through: 교통's through-통 (通), finally conjugating. 말이 통해요 = our words get through — we CLICK (the best compliment your Korean can earn). [noun]을 통해서 = via: 인터넷을 통해서 (M20). Radar: this 通 is NOT 통일's unite-統 — two Sino 통s, same sound, different jobs.

One verb, two jobs: 저를 따라오세요 (follow me — M28's 오다 welded on) and 물을 따라 주세요 (pour — M9's machine). ㅡ-drop family (M7's table): 따라요. And the news frame: [source]에 따르면 = according to — 뉴스에 따르면, 연구에 따르면. Follow the source, pour the facts.

M28's 나다 eruption family, dramatic branch: 갑자기 나타났어요 (appeared out of nowhere — every drama's episode-one move). Results do it too: 결과가 나타나요 = the results show. What erupts (나다) eventually shows up (나타나다).

To feel: 분위기를 느껴 보세요 (M26's vibe through M16's try-machine). Its noun is 느낌 — the feeling, the vibe — made with the -ㅁ that also built 잠 from 자다 (M28) and 꿈 from 꾸다 (M8). Ring 2 will formalize that little machine; you've owned its products for months.
特히: M24's 특별하다's special-특 + the adverb-히 of 천천히/열심히 (M10) — special-ly, literally. Said 트키 (ㄱ+ㅎ merge — 축하's rule from M25). When a sentence needs a spotlight: 특히 이 부분 (especially this part).

The cool-headed already. M23's 벌써 gasps (already?!); 이미 shrugs (already, as established). News and essays run on 이미; your surprise still runs on 벌써. 이미 늦었어요 = it's already too late — 결국's favorite conclusion.

亦是 also-indeed: as expected. Standalone, it's the national applause word — 역시! (that's SO you / never doubted you). In sentences: 역시 어렵네요 (M26's -네요 noticing what you suspected all along). Learn it to praise friends; hear it whenever you do anything well.

없다 + -이: without. The adverb-factory -이 (많이's, M17) applied to absence: 문제 없이 (without a hitch), 돈 없이 (broke but traveling). 너 없이 살 수 없어 — every ballad's chorus, now fully parseable (M19 반말, M10 can-machine, this word).

이렇다 (M29's machine) + -게, the adverb-maker that was hiding inside 어떻게 all along (M24 decoded it; here's the factory). The demo word: 이렇게 하세요 = do it like this. Said 이러케 — the ㅎ+ㄱ merge from the sound reading.

그렇다 + -게: like that / so. Two jobs: manner (그렇게 하세요 — do it that way) and degree (그렇게 어려워요? — it's THAT hard?). The -게 machine works on any adjective: 크게 (loudly), 맛있게 드세요 (eat deliciously — what servers wish you).

저렇다 + -게: like THAT one, the far demonstrative doing manner work. 저렇게 살고 싶어요 = I want to live like that — said while pointing at someone else's life. M29's 이/그/저 geometry, now complete at adverb altitude.

네's formal twin — interchangeable, with 예 leaning stiffer (phone operators, the military). 반말 drops it to 어 or 응 (M19's rules). And a second job: 예 = example — 예를 들면 (for EXAMPLE — literally 'lifting an example', M28's 들다) opens every explanation. Plus 예의's courtesy-예 (M26) makes three.

姓銜 surname-title: the honorific of 이름 (M1). The noun-upgrade ladder from M4's gap item (나이→연세) climbs to names: 성함이 어떻게 되세요? is how desks and forms ask. You answer with your humble 이름; theirs stays a 성함.
題目 topic-eye: a title. 노래 제목이 뭐예요? — the K-pop survival question. This 목 is Sino 目 (eye/item), NOT your native neck (M14) — it's the same one aiming inside 목표 (M26): a goal is where the eye points.

Interview through the converter: V→ㅂ gives 뷰 (the F/V rule from the Konglish reading). This is the press kind — what M16's 기자 does after the 뉴스. Job interviews took a different word (면접), because Korean never borrows just one.

付託 entrust: a favor-ask. 부탁이 있어요 opens it; 부탁해요 seals it (M16 shipped the verb). And the untranslatable formula: 잘 부탁드립니다 (M9's humble 드리다) — 'I entrust myself to you well', said at every first meeting. See the gap deck for why nothing in English covers it.

表現 surface-appear: an expression — meaning surfacing into words. 한국어 표현 = a Korean expression, the exact species this app's gap deck collects. 이 표현을 자주 써요 = this one gets used a lot (M21's 쓰다, still on its fifth job).

文章 writing-piece: a sentence — the thing the anatomy drill has been dissecting since Module 1. This 문 is writing 文 (문법's, M10), NOT the door 문 (M6) or 신문's hearing-聞 — three 문s, exactly the collision S3 warned you about.

會話 meet-talk: 사회/회사's gather-회 + 전화's talk-화 — conversation, the classroom subject. 한국어 회화가 어려워요 is why the class exists. Awkwardly, a second 회화 (繪畫) means painting — talking class and art class collide in one sound; context referees.

稱讚 praise: the compliment, received like a gift — 칭찬을 받았어요 (M9's 받다). Korea's compliment economy runs hot (M26's 한국어를 잘하시네요 is guaranteed), and the gap deck long ago issued you the official deflection: 잘 못 해요.

情報 feeling-report: information. Yes — that 정 is 情, M19's warm affection-정, moonlighting in intelligence work (there the hanja reads 'situation'). 정보를 찾아요 (M6's 찾다); 개인 정보 = personal data, the checkbox you keep agreeing to.

俗談 folk-talk: a proverb — the 담 is 농담's talk-담 (談, M19). The gap deck has been feeding you 속담 since 금강산도 식후경 (M23); now the category has a name. Koreans deploy them mid-argument like trump cards, and this module's gap deck adds the best one about speech itself.

相對方 mutual-facing-direction: whoever's on the other end — of a conversation, a deal, a match. M32's facing-대 (對하다) sits in the middle; the 방 is direction 方, not room. 상대방 마음을 생각하세요 = consider the other side's heart — Korea's first rule of talk.

安否 peace-or-not: asking after someone is literally checking whether they're at peace. The 안 is 안녕's 安 — M1's hello was asking this question all along; thirty-three modules later the circle closes. 부모님께 안부 전해 주세요 = give your parents my regards.

萬若 ten-thousand-if: M9's 만 (10,000) counting hypotheticals. It's an adverb that ANNOUNCES a -(으)면 clause (M20): 만약 비가 오면… — the 면 still does the grammar; 만약 just clears its throat first. Speech says 만약에, and yes, there's a famous ballad by that name.

經驗 pass-through-test: experience is what passing through things leaves on you. The 경 is 경제's 經 (M32). 경험이 있어요/없어요 runs every job interview; 좋은 경험이었어요 is how Korean redeems every disaster after the fact.

機會 machine-meeting: opportunity is the moment the machinery lines up. The 기 is 비행기's machine-기 (M12); the 회 is 사회/회사/회의's gather-회. 기회를 주세요 = give me a chance; 다음 기회에 = 'next time' — how Korea declines you gently.
目的 eye-target: purpose is where the eye aims — same Sino eye-목 as 제목 and 목표 (M26), no relation to your neck (M14). 여행 목적이 뭐예요? is what immigration asks; answer 관광 (M23) and keep walking.

決定 decide-fix: 결정했어요! = I've decided (the drama line, hand slamming table optional). The noun rides free: 좋은 결정이에요 = good decision. That 정 is 定 (fix) — a THIRD 정 after affection 情 and politics 政 — and it works alone two entries down.
選擇 select-pick: to choose. The noun 선택 comes free — 좋은 선택이에요 (good choice). Every quiz this app has given you was a 선택; now the word for what you've been doing 3,000 times joins the deck.
定하다: lighter than 결정하다 — you 정하다 a time, a place, a rule: 약속 시간을 정해요 (M5's 약속). A bare Sino root moonlighting as a verb, exactly like 통하다 (M32) — the smallest decision machine Korean sells.

알다 + 듣다 welded: to hear-and-understand. 못 알아들었어요 = I didn't catch that — the honest learner's most-used sentence, and nothing to be ashamed of. Stays ㄷ-irregular like its parent (M2): 알아들어요. Its eye-side twin 알아보다 = to recognize/look into — the verb-welds of M28 keep paying.

물어보다's bow: you 여쭤봐요 UP the ladder — teachers, elders, bosses — the way 드리다 gives upward (M9) and 말씀 speaks upward (M27). The humble set grows to three. 선생님께 여쭤보세요 = ask the teacher (properly); the 께 (M27) travels with it.

謝過 apologize — and yes, 사과 is also the apple (M3). Different hanja (the fruit is 沙果), same sound, and the pun is national: Korean apology memes are just pictures of apples. 먼저 사과하세요 = apologize first; M19's 미안해요 ladder supplies the actual words.

拒絶 refuse: 부탁을 거절했어요 = turned down the favor — this module's noun and verb in one uncomfortable sentence. Korean softens refusals hard (다음 기회에…, 글쎄요…, a long breath) — a bare 거절 is rare and loud when it lands.

en: to excuse oneself, commit a discourtesy
notes: 失禮 lose-courtesy: the polite trespass. 실례합니다 = excuse me — the licensed way to approach a stranger; 실례지만… = pardon me, but… (M7's -지만 doing diplomacy). The 예 is 예의's courtesy-예 (M26): you announce you're spending some, and the announcement itself pays it back.

傳하다 transmit: 말을 전해요 (pass the word along), 안부를 전해 주세요 (send my regards — this module's 안부 in its natural frame). The radar sighs and files a FIFTH 전: electric 電, before 前, all 全, war 戰, now transmit 傳.

조용하다 (M13) + -히: the adverb factory from M32's 특히, now clearly a factory. 조용히 하세요! is what librarians say; 조용히 지내요 = keeping a low profile (M23's 지내다). The adjective keeps its badge jobs; -히 handles the manner.

솔직하다 (M24) + -히 — and as a sentence-opener, a license: 솔직히 말하면… (honestly speaking…) permits whatever follows. Korea's favorite preamble to mild treason. Said 솔찌키 — the ㅎ merges, per the sound reading.

That-much-and-no-more: 그만하세요 = stop it; 이제 그만! (M26's 이제) = enough! And the decode lands two rings late: M16's 그만두다 (to quit) was this word + 두다 (put/leave — a verb Ring 2 still owes you) all along. Quitting is putting down the that-much.

The conversation's gear-shift: 어쨌든, 밥 먹으러 가요 — ANYWAY, food. Built from 어찌+했+든 ('however it went'), which is why it shrugs; the -든 piece is a Ring 2 pattern still in the mail, so for now memorize the shrug and deploy it to escape any topic.
웃다 (M19) + -ㅁ: the nominalizer M32 previewed in 느낌, now unmistakably a machine — verbs freeze into nouns: 자다→잠 (M28), 꾸다→꿈 (M8), 웃다→웃음, 걷다→걸음. 웃음이 나요 = laughter erupts (M28's 나다, still erupting).

微笑 tiny-laugh: the quiet Sino smile (웃음 is the audible native one — a register ladder for your face). Radar: this 미 is 微 (tiny), NOT 미국's 美 (beautiful, M27). 미소를 지어요 = wear a smile — 짓다 is another verb Ring 2 owes you; the smile works on credit.

紹介: the noun of M16's 소개하다, promoted for one compound: 자기소개 (M32's 자기 + this) — the self-introduction that opens every Korean class, job, and blind date. Speaking of which: 소개팅 = a date-by-introduction — the -팅 clipped from 미팅 (Konglish reading, still paying).

順序 order-sequence: 순서를 지키세요 (M26's 지키다) = keep the order — wait your turn; 제 순서예요 = my turn. Korea queues hard, and this word is the reason it works. Also every recipe's skeleton: 순서대로 — in order (대로 arrives later in Ring 2).
狀況 state-of-things: 상황이 어때요? = how's it looking? 상황에 따라서 (M32's 따르다) = depends on the situation — Korean's official way of not answering. The news says it hourly; so does everyone dodging a decision.
態度 posture-degree: attitude — the 도 is 정도's degree-도 (度, M32), so attitude is literally your posture's setting. 태도가 좋아요/나빠요 — how teachers grade what isn't on the test.

Dialect — what 팔도 (M31's gap deck) actually sounds like. 경상도 사투리 stars in gangster movies (M31 said so), 전라도 사투리 in food shows, and 제주 사투리 barely counts as the same language. What this app teaches is 표준어 — standard Seoul speech, which no grandmother anywhere speaks.

記憶: a memory, and the frame it lives in — 기억이 나요 (M28's 나다: memories ERUPT, they aren't retrieved). M19 shipped the verb 기억하다; the noun runs the idiom. 기억이 안 나요 = it's not coming to me — the exam sentence.

理解: the noun of M10's 이해하다 — and M24's 오해 (오+해) decoded it in advance. The frame that matters: 이해가 안 돼요 = understanding doesn't happen = I don't get it (M10's 되다, negative). Softer and more common than any 몰라요.

苦悶 bitter-agonize: the decision-agony noun. 고민이 있어요 = something's on my mind (how Koreans open serious talks); 고민 중이에요 = still deciding (S2's ○○ 중 machine). Menu deliberation counts: 메뉴 고민 is real and daily.

精神 essence-spirit: the mind. A FOURTH 정 (affection 情, politics 政, fixing 定, now essence 精) — the radar wheezes but files it. The frame everyone actually uses is in the gap deck: 정신이 없어요 — no mind left.
느끼다 (M32) + -ㅁ: the feeling — promised in that module's note, official now. 느낌이 와요 = the feeling arrives (Korean intuition travels, M1's 오다); 좋은 느낌 = a good vibe. The -ㅁ factory's most-used product.
믿다 (M19) + -ㅁ: trust, frozen into a noun — the factory from 웃음 (M33) ships again. 믿음이 가요 = trust flows toward it (I find it credible). Also church Korean for faith — Sunday usage guaranteed.

希望 rare-gaze: hope — looking toward what's scarce. 희망이 있어요/없어요, and on every fan sign: 포기하지 마세요, 희망이 있어요 (M14's -지 마세요 doing encouragement). The 망 (望, gaze) returns in 실망 — disappointment, hope's fallen cousin, a note for later.

期待 appointed-time-await: looking forward. The frame is the word: 기대돼요! = I can't wait! (M10's 되다 — anticipation HAPPENS to you); 기대하세요 = look forward to it, says every trailer. Set 기대 too high and the review says 실망 — see 희망's note.

豫想 beforehand-think: the prediction. 예상보다 어려워요 = harder than expected — M22's 보다-particle measuring reality against the forecast. 예상 문제 = the questions you bet will be on the test (M15 culture, still running).
判斷 judge-cut: the call you make. 판단하기 어려워요 = hard to judge (M13's -기 nominalizer); 제 판단이에요 = my call. News panels demand 신중한 판단 — careful judgment — nightly.
疑心 doubt-heart: suspicion — the heart-심 of 관심/진심 (M24) gone skeptical. 의심하지 마세요 = don't doubt me; 의심이 가요 = suspicion flows toward it (믿음이 가요's evil twin, two entries up).

Idea through the converter, all vowels cushioned: 아-이-디-어, four syllables. 좋은 아이디어예요! is meeting-room applause. Korean also owns 생각 for the same job (M10's 생각하다) — the borrowed one sounds brainstormier, which is very Konglish of it.

The shape someone cuts — how they appear. 웃는 모습이 예뻐요 = the laughing-figure is lovely (M24's badge working on M19's 웃다). News-speak loves it: 새로운 모습 = a new look. Rank 164 on the B-list — this word was overdue.
表情 surface-feeling: M33's surface-표 + M19's affection-정 (情) — feeling, surfacing on a face. 표정이 왜 그래요? = what's with the face? The evidence-word for this module's glue: read the 표정, then say -나 봐요.

模樣 pattern-form: shape. 별 모양 = star-shaped, 하트 모양 = heart-shaped (bakery Korean). Radar: this 양 (樣) is NOT 동양/서양's ocean-양 (洋, M32) — same syllable, drier hanja. Bonus: ~모양이에요 can also mean 'seems' — this module's theme, moonlighting in a noun.
狀態 form-posture: the condition something's in. 배터리 상태 (M20's phone), 건강 상태 (M14's health), 지금 상태로는… = as things stand. The 태 is 태도's (M33) — attitude and condition share their posture.

想像: to imagine. 상상해 보세요 = picture it (M16's try-machine). The noun rides free — 상상이 안 돼요 = I can't picture it (the 이해가 안 돼요 chassis, one entry over). Fun fact: 상상 doubles the think-상 of 예상 — imagination is prediction unchained.

en: to resolve, make up one's mind
notes: 決心 decide-heart: 결혼 ties the knot (M25), 결심 ties the HEART — same 결, aimed inward, with 관심/진심's 심 (M24). 담배를 끊기로 결심했어요-style New Year vows are its natural habitat; noun form 새해 결심 = the resolution itself.

後悔 after-ache: M13's after-후 (後) + a heart that hurts late. 후회했어요 = I regretted it; 후회하지 마세요 = no regrets (M14's -지 마세요, life-coach setting). The proverb version sits in every drama: 나중에 후회해도 소용없어요 — regret later, and it's no use.

To hope for: 행복하기를 바라요 = wishing you happiness (M13's -기 turning the wish into a noun). Spelling scandal: standard is 바라요, but the whole country writes 바래(요) anyway — a live orthography fight your textbook loses to the group chat daily.

願하다: to want — but only NOUNS: 커피를 원해요. For verb-wanting, Korean already gave you -고 싶어요 (M3): 마시고 싶어요. The split is strict, and 원하다 runs formal — ads and ballads (원해요~) more than café counters. Bare Sino root + 하다, the 정하다 pattern (M33).
The native pick to M33's Sino 선택하다 — the register pair in action: shops say 골라 보세요 (pick one!), forms say 선택하세요. 르-family (M7's table): 골라요, 골랐어요. Three for a thousand won: 골라 골라! — the market cry.

緊張 tight-stretched: nerves as a drawn bowstring. 긴장하지 마세요 = relax (said right before things get worse); 긴장돼요 = I'm getting nervous (M10's 되다 — the tension happens TO you, same chassis as 기대돼요). Interviews, stages, and 시험 season run on this word.

確實 firm-real: certain. 확실해요? = are you sure?; 확실하지 않아요 = not sure (M28's long negation earning its keep). The 확 is 확인하다's (M20) — checking is how things get certain. Said 확씰- with the tense ㅆ the spelling hides.

當然 fitting-so: how it should be. 당연해요! = of course! — agreement with its feet up. As a comeback it out-warms 네: someone thanks you too hard, wave it off with 당연한 거예요 (that's just what one does). The full casual form 당연하지! arrives with Ring 2's -지 ending.

分明 divided-bright: clear as day. 분명해요 = it's obvious; and as an adverb, 분명히 봤어요 = I DEFINITELY saw it (M33's -히 factory, still open). 확실하다 checks the facts; 분명하다 trusts its own eyes — courtroom vs. eyewitness.

The missing basic, thirty-four modules late: glad. ㅡ-drop family (M7's table): 기뻐요. The joy ladder, assembled: 기쁘다 = the moment's spike (합격해서 기뻐요), 즐겁다 = fun-in-progress (M29), 행복하다 = the standing state (M7). Three altitudes of happy.

외 + ㅂ-family: the OUTSIDE-외 of 외국/해외 (M23/M31) turned inward — lonely is being outside, feelings edition. 외로워요. 혼자 있지만 안 외로워요 = alone but not lonely (M10's 혼자 knows the difference; 혼밥 culture, M18, agrees).

ㅂ-family: 부끄러워요 — shy or ashamed, the blush covers both. The stronger street word is 창피하다 (mortified, C-list); the K-drama collocation is 부끄러워하지 마 — don't be shy. Cheeks-red is the diagnostic 표정, two shelves up.

The untranslatable chest-tightness: slow wifi, dense friends, gridlock (M12's 길이 막혀요 causes it), buttoned collars, unspoken feelings — all 답답해요. Doubled syllable like 빨리빨리 (M8): the language squeezing the word the way the word squeezes you. No English gloss survives contact; you now own a feeling English can't say.
憂鬱 worry-dense: blue. 비 오는 날에는 좀 우울해요 — rain-day gloom (M11 weather, M9's 좀 softening the confession). The calendar version sits in the gap deck: 월요병, Monday as a diagnosis.

ㅂ-family: 아쉬워요 — the feeling when something ends too soon or falls just short: the trip's last day, a 99-point exam, leftover 치킨 someone else ate. Not regret (that's 후회 — your fault) and not sadness; English needs a sentence, Korean needs three syllables.

Irritation — and it ERUPTS: 짜증(이) 나다, the crankiest member of M28's 나다 family (화가 나다, 기억이 나다, now this). 짜증 나! is the national teenage anthem; 짜증 내지 마세요 = don't take it out on me (내다, the eruption's transitive twin, M28).
어찌 + -(으)면 fossilized: 'if things go however' = maybe. M24's 아마 guesses the likely; 어쩌면 wonders wilder — 어쩌면 우리가 이길 수도 있어요 (we might just win). Also a standalone gasp: 어쩌면! = how could that be!

왜 + -인지 (M33's indirect question, fossilized): 'why-it-is' compressed into 'somehow'. 오늘은 왠지 기분이 좋아요 = feeling good today, can't say why. Spelling trap even Koreans fail: 왠지 (this word) vs 웬 (what kind of) — the group chat gets it wrong daily.

The as-if announcer: 마치 꿈 같아요 = like a dream. Like 만약 (M33) announcing -(으)면, 마치 announces a 같다 (M24) — Korean posts the adverb up front so you hear the simile coming. Formal partner 처럼 arrives later in Ring 2.

For-no-reason: 괜히 걱정했어요 = worried over nothing (M29's 걱정); 괜히 왔어요 = shouldn't have come. Cousin of 괜찮다 (M7) — both from 관계하지 아니하다, 'not related': no-reason and no-problem share a bloodline. The -히 factory stamps it (M33).
Deliberately: 일부러 그랬어요? = did you do that on purpose? — the accusation; 일부러 와 줬어요 = you came just for this — the gratitude. One adverb, both readings; 괜히 (one entry up) is its no-reason opposite.

The bitter-choice adverb: when both options are bad, 차라리 picks the lesser — 차라리 걸어갈게요… better to just walk (than wait for this bus). Pairs naturally with M22's comparison kit: 차라리 A가 B보다 나아요 — A beats B, for what it's worth (M14's 낫다).

en: to be confusing, get mixed up
notes: The learner's verb, off the official list but non-negotiable here: ㅐ랑 ㅔ가 헷갈려요 = I mix up ㅐ and ㅔ — this app's confusables drill, described from the inside. Things 헷갈리다 TO you (it-confuses framing): 길이 헷갈려요, 이름이 헷갈려요. Welcome to the club; the drill is the cure.

어리다 (M21) + -ㄴ이: the-young-one. Coined in the 1920s by 방정환 to give children a dignified word — and it worked: 어린이날 (Children's Day, May 5 — M25's -날 shelf) is a national holiday. 아이 (M4) is everyday; 어린이 is the word on museums, menus, and crosswalk signs.

靑少年 green-few-years: the green years. The 청 is 청바지's blue-green-청 (M21 — Korean files young and blue under one color). 청소년 관람 불가 = the no-teens-allowed rating on movie posters; the word between 어린이 and 어른 (M24).

Children 자라요; so do plants, cities, and rumors. 서울에서 자랐어요 = I grew up in Seoul — the biography verb (vs 태어나다, M25: born there, raised here). Kids also just 커요 (M1's 크다 moonlighting as 'grow big') — but 자라다 is the proper verb for the whole process.

A VERB, not an adjective — Korean treats aging as something you do: 늙었어요 = has aged. Said 늑따 (the batchim cluster simplifies, sound-reading rules). Politer company prefers the frame 나이가 들다 (age comes in — M28's 들다, entering you). 젊다 (M24) is what it undoes.

살이 찌다 — the FLESH gains, not you: Korean grammar politely blames the 살 (M5's age-살's homograph — flesh). 살쪘어요? is unfortunately a normal greeting. Homograph bonus: 찌다 also steams food — 만두를 찌다 — so the diet and the dumpling share a verb.

en: to fall out/into; to come off
notes: The universal falling-verb: 살이 빠지다 (weight falls off), 물에 빠지다 (fall into water), 이가 빠지다 (a tooth falls out), 사랑에 빠지다 (the gap deck's entry — same metaphor as English). One verb for everything that drops out of place or sinks into something — including you, into K-dramas: 드라마에 빠졌어요.

Diet through the converter, vowels cushioned: 다-이-어-트. Konglish narrowing: only the weight-loss campaign, never 'what you eat'. 다이어트 중이에요 (S2's ○○ 중 machine) is the standard confession — usually delivered while ordering 치킨.
몸 (M14) + 무게 (weight — 무겁다's (M21) noun form): body-heaviness, fully decodable. 몸무게를 재요 = weigh yourself; the number 찌다 and 빠지다 argue over. Scales in Korea speak kilograms; the anxiety is universal.

習慣 practice-accustomed: the Sino habit. 좋은 습관을 만들어요 = build good habits — this app is one, hopefully. Radar: the 관 (慣) is neither 관심/관계's gate-關 nor 관광's see-觀 — a third 관, filed without ceremony. Its native register twin is next door.

The native habit, and it leans negative: 나쁜 버릇 (bad habit), 말버릇 (the way one talks), 손버릇 (sticky fingers). Kids get scolded about 버릇 (버릇없다 = no manners — the 있다-factory's disciplinary wing). The proverb built on it sits in the gap deck: three-year-old habits go to eighty.

成功 achieve-merit: to succeed. 성공했어요! covers everything from exams to fried chicken franchises. The noun rides free: 성공이에요 = it's a success. Korea's favorite drama arc: 성공한 사람이 고향에 돌아와요 (M23's return-verbs carrying the plot).

失敗 lose-the-attempt — and the 실 (失, lose) reveals a family: 실수 (M16, lose-your-hands = mistake), 실례 (M33, lose-courtesy = discourtesy), 실패 (lose-the-attempt = failure). Three losses, one hanja. 실패해도 괜찮아요 — M7's 괜찮다 doing its best work.

發展 unfold-expand: the 발 is 출발's (M8, 發 launch) — development is a launch that keeps going. 한국이 빨리 발전했어요 = Korea developed fast — the sentence behind every skyline photo. Noun 발전 rides free: 경제 발전 (M32's economy, growing).

抛棄 throw-away: to give up. M34's 희망 note promised this word; here it is, usually negated: 포기하지 마세요! (don't give up — M14's -지 마세요 in cheerleader mode). Korean study-culture's most-shouted verb, right after 화이팅 (M15's gap deck).
계속 (M28) + 하다: to keep at it. 계속하세요 = go on / carry on; 계속할까요? = shall we keep going? (M9's offer machine). The anti-포기하다 — this module seats them side by side on purpose.

To make real: 꿈을 이루다 = achieve a dream (M8's 꿈, M34's whole inner life, delivered). The do-form of a famous pair — its happen-twin is the next entry, and together they demonstrate this module's glue inside the dictionary itself.

이루다 + -아/어지다: the glue as a vocabulary word. YOU 이루다 a dream; the dream 이루어지다 on its own — do-form vs happen-form, the split M36 will industrialize. 꿈은 이루어진다 = dreams come true — the 2002 World Cup's national slogan, now parseable.

Skills, weight, worries — they all 늘어요. The learner's favorite frame: 한국어 실력이 늘었어요 (M26's 실력) = my Korean has improved — objectively true of you by module 35. ㄹ-drop conjugation like 살다/알다: 늘어요, 늘었어요.
늘다's opposite: 몸무게가 줄었어요 (weight went down), 시간이 줄었어요 (less time now). Sweaters also 줄다 in hot water — shrinkage is shrinkage. Same ㄹ-drop family as its twin.

To come by something: 정보를 얻다 (M33's 정보, acquired), 기회를 얻다 (M33's chance, seized), 힘을 얻다 (M14's strength, drawn from someone's kindness). Where 받다 (M9) is handed things, 얻다 works for them — or lucks into them.

시간이 남아요 (time to spare), 음식이 남았어요 (leftovers — the container culture's favorite verb). And the 남-radar files its promised third card (M32's 남성 note called it): man 男, south 南, remain 남다 — native, no hanja, just left over.

To stick — and Korea's exam verb: 시험에 붙었어요 = I PASSED (you stuck to the list; the fallen didn't). Its doom-twin 떨어지다 (to fall = to fail) is still in the pool — the pair arrives fully in M36's party. Said 붇따; stickers, tape, and destinies all 붙어요.

바꾸다's (M9) happen-twin: YOU 바꾸다 the plan; the plan 바뀌다 on you. 계획이 바뀌었어요 = plans changed (nobody's fault, says the grammar). 계절이 바뀌어요 = seasons turn. This do/happen split is M36's entire thesis — consider this the trailer.
To vanish: 돈이 사라졌어요 (the money's GONE), 스트레스가 사라졌어요 (the good kind of gone). Another -지다 native: things 사라지다 by themselves, no culprit named — the grammar of mysteries and magic tricks alike.

다르다 (M24) + -아/어지다, lexicalized: 서울이 많이 달라졌어요 = Seoul's changed a lot (returnees' first sentence). The 르-conjugation survives inside (달라-), so this one word rehearses two machines at once. 뭔가 달라졌네요 — noticing it takes M26's -네요.

Water, time, tears, music — Korean lets them all 흐르다: 시간이 흘러요 (time flows), 눈물이 흘러요 (M14's 눈물, flowing on schedule in every drama). 르-family (M7's table): 흘러요, 흘렀어요. The gentlest verb this module owns.

The make-grow verb: kids, dogs (강아지를 키워요 — M22), plants, dreams, even 실력. It's 크다 (M1) with a causative engine bolted on — the machinery M37 will formalize; for now it's just the word every pet owner conjugates daily.

키우다's 르-family twin (길러요, 길렀어요): a bit more formal, and the only one that grows HAIR — 머리를 기르다 (M8's 머리, lengthening). Also 습관을 기르다 = cultivate a habit — this module's nouns and verbs keep marrying each other.

過去 passed-gone: the past as a noun. With 현재 (next entry) and 미래 (M25), the tense trio is complete — 과거, 현재, 미래: what every grammar table in this app has been silently assuming. 과거는 과거예요 = the past is the past (copula therapy).

現在 appear-exist: now, officially. M32's 위치 note glossed 현재 위치 (current location) — decoded at last. Doubles as an adverb in news Korean: 현재 조사 중입니다 = currently under investigation (S2's ○○ 중, in its natural broadcast habitat).

歲月 years-and-months: time as the thing that passes, heavier than 시간. 세월이 빠르다 = the years fly; 세월이 약이다 = time is medicine (M10's 약!) — the consolation proverb. A word that gets more use the older its speaker.

Back-when: 예전에 = in the old days; 예전보다 좋아졌어요 = better than before (M22's 보다-particle measuring against memory). The time-ladder rounds out: 옛날 (M24, storybook-old), 예전 (within living memory), 최근 (M32), 요즘 (M26).

새 (M13) + -로: the adverb of fresh starts — 새로 생긴 카페 (the newly-opened café, M28's 생기다 + M24's badge), 새로 시작해요 (start over). Attach it to any verb and the thing just happened for the first time, again.

새 grown into a full adjective (ㅂ-family: 새로워요): not factory-new but new-to-the-heart — 기분이 새로워요 = feels like a fresh start; 모든 게 새로워요 = everything's new (first week abroad, in one sentence). The 새-family completes: 새 / 새로 / 새롭다.

成績 achieve-weave: your grades — the number Korean school life orbits (M15's 수능 culture, quantified). 성적이 올랐어요 (M22's 오르다 — grades CLIMB) / 떨어졌어요 (they fall — M36 delivers that verb properly). The fridge door's most feared document.

植物 planted-thing. Radar, and a good one: this 식 (植 plant) is NOT 음식/식당's eat-식 (食) — 식물 grows, 음식 gets eaten, and the syllable doesn't care. 식물을 키워요 = plant parenting (this module's 키우다, employed). Said 싱물 (ㄱ before ㅁ nasalizes).

오래 (M10, a long while) + 되다 (become): became-long-ago = old, for THINGS — 오래된 건물 (an old building, M24's badge), 오래된 노래 (an oldie). People 늙다; things 오래되다 — Korean keeps the verbs apart, and this one is this module's thesis wearing a dictionary entry.

The creep adverb: 점점 추워져요 = it's getting colder and colder — glued to -아/어지다 so often they're practically sold together. Sounds like M32's 점 (dot) doubled — dot, dot, further — though the hanja is 漸 (gradual); the mnemonic works, the etymology just won't sign it.
The formal finally — headlines and novel endings: 마침내 전쟁이 끝났어요 (M32's war, M16's 끝나다). Its spoken sibling is next door; keep 마침내 for prose and gravity.
The lived finally — relief you can hear: 드디어 금요일이에요! (Friday at last), 드디어 왔구나 (you're HERE). Where 마침내 narrates history, 드디어 exhales. Both stack onto this module's machines: 드디어 따뜻해졌어요.

보다 + 이: to be seen — things show THEMSELVES: 남산이 보여요 = Namsan is visible (from here). And the six-career verb confesses a seventh: M21's -아/어 보이다 (멋있어 보여요) was this word all along — 'is SEEN as cool'. The highest-frequency word left on the entire B-list, and now it's yours.

듣다 + 리: to be heard — 소리가 들려요 = there's a sound (reaching me). 보이다's ear-side twin: Korean perception runs passive — the world shows and sounds, you just receive. 잘 안 들려요 = I can't hear you (phone Korean, said daily).

en: to open (by itself); to be held
notes: 열다 (M13) + 리: the door opens — nobody opens it. 문이 안 열려요 = it won't open (the locked-out panic sentence). Second job straight from the news: events 열리다 — 콘서트가 열려요 = a concert is held. Doors and festivals, one passive.

닫다 (M13) + 히 — and say it carefully: 닫히다 is pronounced 다치다 (ㄷ+히 fuses to 치, the 같이=가치 rule from the sound reading) — a perfect homophone of M14's 다치다, to get hurt. 문이 닫혔어요 = the door closed; whether someone got hurt in it is context's problem. The sound-reading's finest exhibit.

잡다 (M28) + 히: to get caught — 도둑이 잡혔어요 (the thief got caught). Also the schedule sense: 약속이 잡혔어요 = a meeting got set (it caught YOU). The agent wears 한테: 경찰한테 잡혔어요 — M27's person-particle picks up the 'by' job, and the passive party has its grammar.
팔다 (M28) + 리: 잘 팔려요 = it sells well (the thing does the selling, says the grammar). 다 팔렸어요 = sold out — the sign on everything you wanted. Merchants conjugate 팔다; merchandise conjugates 팔리다.

en: to be placed; to be set at ease
notes: 놓다 (M28) + 이: to be set down — 책상 위에 놓여 있어요 = it's sitting on the desk. And the idiom that earns its gap-deck seat: 마음이 놓여요 — the HEART gets set down = relief. Korean worry is something you carry; relief is putting it down.

쓰다 + 이: to get used — 이 표현은 자주 쓰여요 = this expression gets used a lot (M33's 표현, in the passive it deserves). 쓰다's five jobs (write/use/wear/bitter/badge) mean 쓰이다 inherits the estate: things get written AND get used, context referees as usual.
끊다 (M20) + 기: to get cut — 전화가 끊겼어요 = the call dropped (nobody hung up; it HAPPENED, says 기). Also 인터넷이 끊겼어요, 전기가 끊겼어요 — modern life is a list of things that 끊기다 at the worst moment.

To bite: dogs, mosquitoes, and — gently — 물고 다니다 toddlers. ㄹ-drop family: 물어요. Radar: sounds exactly like water-물 (M1) with a verb ending — 물이 물어요 (the water bites) is nonsense Korean children find delightful. Its passive is next door, scratching.
물다 + 리: to get bitten — off the official list, but July doesn't care: 모기한테 물렸어요 (bitten by a mosquito — 한테 marking the tiny perpetrator) is the national summer sentence. Scratch, apply 물파스, repeat.

en: to fall, drop; to fail; to run out
notes: The great faller, three jobs deep: things fall (폰이 떨어졌어요), exam-takers fail (시험에 떨어졌어요 — 붙다's (M35) doom-twin, as promised), and supplies run out (커피가 다 떨어졌어요). 값이 떨어지다 = prices drop — M22's comparison shopping, now with physics.

넘다 + 지다: to topple — people, bikes, and 김치 towers all 넘어져요. The proverb pre-installed: 일곱 번 넘어져도 여덟 번 일어난다 — fall seven, rise eight (M8's 일어나다 doing resilience). Winter sidewalks teach this verb for free.

깨다 + 지다: glass's destiny — 컵이 깨졌어요 (the cup broke; no suspect named — the grammar of roommates everywhere). Screens, promises, and records also 깨지다: 약속이 깨졌어요 = the plan fell through. M35's machine on a verb, exactly as flagged.
켜다 (M13) + 지다: the screen lights up on its own — 불이 켜져 있어요 = the light is on (someone left it; the light isn't telling). With 갑자기 it's a horror-movie stage direction: 티비가 갑자기 켜졌어요.

끄다 (M13) + 지다: 핸드폰이 꺼졌어요 = the phone died (배터리's last words). Register landmine, clearly marked: 꺼져! alone means GET LOST — the power-off verb aimed at a person. Read it in webtoons; do not deploy at work.

en: to come untied; unwind, be relieved
notes: 풀다 + 리: knots loosen, and so does everything Korean ties: 스트레스가 풀려요 (stress unwinds — 노래방's official function), 화가 풀렸어요 (the anger let go), 날씨가 풀렸어요 (the cold snapped — weather unties too), 문제가 풀렸어요 (the problem cracked). One passive, half of self-care.

Two jobs in one verb: break it (컵을 깨다, 기록을 깨다 — records too) and wake from it (잠에서 깨다 — sleep is a thing you break OUT of; M28's 잠). 깨우다, waking someone ELSE, is M37's machine — one module of patience.

en: to untie; to solve; to relieve
notes: The untying verb, and Korean ties everything: 문제를 풀다 = solve problems (M15 school-life — exams are knots), 스트레스를 풀다 = de-stress, 화를 풀다 = let the anger go, 짐을 풀다 = unpack. ㄹ-drop: 풀어요. Its passive next door is where the relief actually happens.

To block — and the M12 mystery closes: 길이 막혀요 (traffic!) was 막다 + 히 all along; you've been speaking the passive party's dialect since Band 2. 귀를 막다 = cover your ears; 골을 막다 = keeper's job. Parent found, decode complete.

To go over: 산을 넘다 (over the mountain), 선을 넘다 (over the LINE — the boundary idiom Korea loves: 선 넘었어 = you went too far), numbers too — 백 명이 넘어요 = over a hundred (M9's 백). Its stumble-child 넘어지다 is above; the parent crosses, the child trips.

事故: the accident — and it ERUPTS: 사고가 났어요 (M28's 나다, in its grimmest job). 교통사고 = traffic accident (M12's 교통 doing the compounding). Radar: not the think-사고 (思考) of philosophy books — same sound, opposite amount of planning.

事件: the incident — what detectives and headlines call their work: 사건이 일어났어요 (M8's 일어나다 moonlighting as 'happen'). 사고 is bad luck; 사건 has a suspect. Every crime drama's episode title ends in this word.

The thief — who ENTERS: 도둑이 들었어요 (M28's 들다: a break-in is an entering). Caught, they wear this module's grammar: 도둑이 경찰한테 잡혔어요. The proverb bonus: 바늘 도둑이 소 도둑 된다 — the needle-thief becomes the cow-thief (M35's 되다, sliding downhill).

琉璃: glass — 깨지다's favorite customer: 유리가 깨졌어요. 유리창 = glass window (M6's 창문's fancier cousin), 유리컵 = the one you shouldn't have handed the toddler. Also a beloved K-drama heroine name, because fragile-and-clear is a whole aesthetic.

電氣 electric-energy: the FIRST 전 finally alone — 전화 (electric-talk) and 전기 share it, and now you hold the root itself. 전기가 나갔어요 = the power went OUT (M28's 나가다 — electricity leaves the building); 전기가 끊겼어요 = got cut (bills exist). 전기차 = the electric car.

Summer's tiny 한테-agent: 모기한테 물렸어요 is this module's most seasonal sentence. The 앵~ whine at 3 a.m. has its own national choreography: lights on, magazine rolled, family mobilized. 모기향 = the coil; 모기장 = the net; the war is eternal.

傷處 wound-place: the mark left — on knees (상처가 났어요, M28's 나다 again) and on hearts: 상처를 받았어요 = I got hurt (emotionally; M9's 받다 — wounds are received like unwanted gifts). 상처를 주다 = to hurt someone — give-and-receive (M9), in its saddest market.

多幸 much-fortune: the word for 'thank goodness' — 다행이에요 = what a relief (said after every near-miss this module describes). 다행히 = fortunately (M33's -히 factory). The gap deck holds its best compound: 불행 중 다행.

運: luck — 운이 좋아요/나빠요 = lucky/unlucky, the accident shelf's coin-flip. 운이 없었어요 = just wasn't my day. Buy 로또, blame 운; the 있다-factory's least reliable product. 행운 (good luck, below) is 운 with a blessing stapled on.

幸運 fortunate-luck: 행복's happy-행 (M7) + 운 = luck, blessed. 행운을 빌어요 = wishing you luck (the send-off before exams and interviews); 행운의 숫자 = lucky number. Where 운 is the weather, 행운 is the forecast you wanted.

돕다 (M28) + -ㅁ: help, frozen solid — the nominalizer factory (잠, 꿈, 웃음, 느낌, 믿음…) ships its most practical unit. 도움이 됐어요 = it helped (BECAME help — M35's 되다); 도움이 필요해요 = I need help. ㅂ-family fingerprint preserved in the 우.

安全 peace-entire: safe. Two owned roots collide beautifully — 안녕/안부's peace-安 (M33 closed that circle) + 전국's all-全 (M31): safety is peace, all the way through. 안전 운전 = drive safe; 안전벨트 = the belt; 안전하지 않아요 = the review that kills a product.
비에 젖었어요 = soaked by the rain (에 marks the weather-agent — rain outranks 한테). Clothes, shoes, moods: 젖은 머리 = wet hair (M24's badge). What 장마 (M11) does to everyone who trusted the forecast.

en: to dry; to be thin; be thirsty
notes: 르-family (말라요): laundry dries, people are skinny (말랐어요 = so thin! — a compliment in Korea, mind the culture gap), and throats go dry: 목이 말라요 (M14's 목) = thirsty — thirst is a drying, says Korean. Three jobs, one 르-verb.

en: to spoil, go bad; be hurt
notes: 傷하다 — 상처's wound-상 as a verb: food spoils (우유가 상했어요 — smell first, always) and feelings do too: 기분이 상했어요 = my feelings soured (M7's 기분, past its date). The fridge and the heart share a verb; check both regularly.

To burst: 타이어가 터졌어요 (the tire blew), 울음이 터졌어요 (tears burst out — M33's -ㅁ factory in the wreckage), and the slang everyone actually uses: 빵 터졌어요 = burst out laughing (빵! is the pop). Also phones: 데이터가 터지다 = signal actually works. Chaos, in one verb.

避하다: to dodge — 비를 피하다 (duck out of the rain; every convenience-store awning's purpose), 러시아워를 피하세요 (M12 would approve), and people too: 저를 피하는 것 같아요 = I think they're avoiding me (M34's hedge, aimed sadly). The accident shelf's only PREVENTIVE verb.

밀다 (S2's push-door) + 리: to get pushed — and the modern job: backlogs. 일이 밀렸어요 = work piled up (it pushed itself, honest); 차가 밀려요 = traffic's backed up (막히다's twin — blocked vs pushed, pick your metaphor); 월세가 밀렸어요 = rent's overdue. Adulthood, passivized.
먹다 + 이: make-eat — 아기한테 밥을 먹여요 (feeding the baby; 한테 marks the mouth). Pets, kids, and houseguests all get 먹이다; the noun 먹이 = animal feed/prey. The causative party's gentlest member, and its busiest.

죽다 (M14) + 이: make-die. Dramas need it nightly — but so does slang, inverted: 죽인다! = KILLER (amazing), 시간을 죽이다 = kill time (same idiom, both languages). Handle the register; Korean compliments have a body count.

붙다 (M36) + 이: make-stick — 스티커를 붙여요, 반창고를 붙여요 (the band-aid verb). Said 부치다 — a perfect homophone of the mail-verb 부치다 (편지를 부치다), so attaching a stamp and mailing the letter sound identical. Korean shrugs; context delivers.
높다 (M7) + 이: adjectives get causatives too — make-high: 소리를 높여요 (turn it up), 실력을 높여요 (level up — M26's 실력). With 낮추다 below, you hold both ends of every volume knob in Korea.
살다 + 리: make-live — the opposite number of 죽이다, filed two entries up. 의사가 환자를 살렸어요 (M14's cast, best outcome). The emergency shout lives in the gap deck: 사람 살려!

알다 + 리: make-know — M33 deliberately left this seat empty; the causative party fills it. 도착하면 알려 주세요 = let me know when you arrive (M20's -면 + M9's favor machine — the most-texted request in Korean). News 알리다s the nation; you 알리다 your 엄마.

울다 (M19) + 리: make-cry — 동생을 울리지 마! (don't make your sibling cry — every Korean household's first law). Second job, all sound: phones and bells 울리다 — 전화가 울려요 = it's ringing. Tears and ringtones, one causative.

돌다 + 리: make-turn — and the modern job is appliances: 세탁기를 돌려요 (run the washer — M13's machine, finally switched on), 청소기를 돌려요. Also heads (고개를 돌리다 = look away) and — idiomatically — 말을 돌리다: to change the subject. Spin, in every sense.

The parent: things 돌다 by themselves — 지구가 돌아요 (the Earth turns), 머리가 돌 것 같아요 (head's spinning — M34's hedge on the edge). ㄹ-drop: 돌아요. M23's 돌아오다/돌아가다 were this verb wearing travel shoes; the root finally stands alone.
M35's 늘다 + 리: make-grow — 단어를 늘려요 (grow your vocabulary — this app's whole business plan), 시간을 늘려요. The pattern clicks: 늘다 happens, 늘리다 is done — the M35/M36/M37 triangle in one pair of verbs.
M35's 줄다 + 이: make-shrink — 소리를 줄여 주세요 (turn it down — the neighbor's knock), 커피를 줄여야 돼요 (the annual resolution). With 늘리다 above: the do-side of every graph that goes up or down.

맡다 + 기: make-take-charge — hand it over and walk away: 세탁소에 옷을 맡겨요 (the dry cleaner), 짐을 맡기다 (luggage storage), 아이를 부모님께 맡겼어요 (the grandparent economy). 저한테 맡기세요! = leave it to me — confidence, conjugated.

en: to take on, be in charge of; to smell
notes: The parent, moonlighting: 맡다 = take a role (제가 맡을게요 territory — you'll hear it) AND to smell (냄새를 맡다 — the nose takes things on too, says Korean). A homograph of M15's 맞다 (correct) in sound alone — duties, odors, and right answers all land on one syllable.

M35's 남다 + 기: make-remain — 메시지를 남겨 주세요 (leave a message — voicemail's whole script), 음식을 남기지 마세요 (clean your plate — cafeteria law), 댓글을 남기다 (leave a comment). What remains, someone left: the pair tells you who.
To hide: 고양이가 침대 밑에 숨었어요 (M22's cat, M13's bed, M6's under — the usual suspects). The kids' game is pre-installed: 숨바꼭질 = hide-and-seek. You 숨다 yourself; hiding THINGS takes the causative next door.
숨다 + 기: make-hidden — 선물을 숨겼어요 (the birthday logistics verb), 감정을 숨기다 (hiding feelings — every drama's episodes 1 through 14). What you 숨기다 eventually 보이다s; the party suffixes narrate the whole arc.

M36's 깨다 + 우: make-wake — 일곱 시에 깨워 주세요 (the wake-up-call sentence; hotels and mothers both take the request). The 우-crew's flagship — and proof you met 키우다 (M35) early: 크다 + 이우, make-grow. The suffixes were always here.
자다 + 이우 fused: make-sleep — 아기를 재워요 (the 9 p.m. project). With 깨우다 above, the caretaking day has both ends: you 재우다 them at night and 깨우다 them for school, forever. Parenting, in two causatives.

en: to give a ride; to burn
notes: 타다 (M6) + 이우: make-ride — 공항까지 태워 주세요 (the airport favor; M23 route knowledge assumed). Second job from 타다's other life: to burn — 밥을 태웠어요 (dinner's obituary). Give a lift, scorch the rice: one causative, both kitchens and carpools.

비다 + 우: make-empty — 방을 비워 주세요 (checkout notice), 잔을 비우다 (the 건배 aftermath, M18). The philosophical setting is in the gap deck: 마음을 비우다 — emptying the mind, Korea's favorite prescription for wanting too much.

차다 (to be full) + 이우: make-full. 잔을 채워요 (the 건배 before-photo — 비우다's mirror), 빈칸을 채우세요 (fill in the blank — every worksheet you'll ever meet), 배를 채우다 = fill the belly. Empty it, fill it: the 우-crew runs the bar.
낮다 (M7) + 추: make-low — 소리를 낮춰 주세요 (the library whisper), 온도를 낮추다 (the A/C fight), 몸을 낮추다 (duck!). Also register: 말을 낮추다 = drop to 반말 (M19's 말 놓으세요, formal edition). The volume knob's other half.

맞다 + 추: make-fit — the tuning verb: 알람을 맞춰요 (set the alarm — M20's 알람 meets its verb), 답을 맞추다 (check answers against the key — M15's school), 눈을 맞추다 (make eye contact), 비위를 맞추다 (humor someone). Korea runs on things precisely 맞춘: schedules, outfits, couples' rings.

The parent M18 skipped: 물이 끓어요 = the water's boiling (it does it alone; you just watch). 끓이다 (M18's 라면 verb) was this + 이 all along — another mask off, one module late. Blood too: 피가 끓다 = blood boils, youth edition.

The state 비우다 manufactures: 방이 비어 있어요 (the room stands empty — M8's progressive holding the door), 자리가 비었어요 = the seat's free. 빈- in front of nouns is its badge form: 빈말 (M33's gap deck — empty words), 빈손 = empty-handed. Emptiness, fully productive.

앉다 (M9) + 히: make-sit — 아이를 의자에 앉혀요 (the booster-seat verb). Said 안치다. Low frequency, high ceremony: hosts 앉히다 guests at the best spot, and refusing the seat is its own etiquette event (예절, this module's shelf).

입다 (M21) + 히: make-wear — 아기한테 옷을 입혀요 (the morning wrestling match). M21's wear-verb taxonomy gains its caretaking wing: you 입다 your own coat, 입히다 the child's, and the child undoes both (벗다, uncredited).

人形 person-shape: the doll — 외국인's person-人 (M23) + a shape. 인형 뽑기 = the claw machine (a national money-drain), and couples give giant 인형 the way other countries give flowers. The 곰 인형 (teddy) is Korea's default comfort object.

幼稚園 young-tender-garden: kindergarten (a German idea, hanja-ified). The -원 (園/院, walled place) also stamps 병원 (M14) and 학원 (M15) — the institutions that bracket a Korean childhood. 유치원에 보내다 = send the kid off; the causative worldview, scheduled.

Rice porridge — Korea's official sick-day food: 아플 때 죽을 먹여요 (this module's 먹이다, at the bedside). 전복죽 (abalone) for recovery, 호박죽 for comfort; whole franchises sell nothing else. Homograph mercy: unrelated to 죽다 — the porridge is innocent.

The errand — what kids get sent on: 심부름을 시키다 (this module's 시키다 frame, in its natural home) and 심부름을 가다 (going on one). The corner-store 심부름 with permission to keep the change is a core Korean childhood memory; the word carries the warmth.

沐浴 wash-bathe: the bath — 목욕하다 to bathe, 목욕시키다 to bathe someone (the baby, the dog — 시키다's make-do career, below). The 목욕탕 is the public bathhouse: scalding pools, 때밀이 scrub-downs, and banana milk after — a whole culture in one noun.

洗手 wash-HANDS — that says hands, but 세수 means washing your FACE: the hanja drifted and Korean shrugged. 세수하다 = the morning face-wash; the 세 (洗, wash) also runs 세탁기 (M13) and 세탁소 (below). Morning routine, etymologically confused, universally practiced.

세탁 (washing — M13's 세탁기 minus the machine) + -소 (place): the dry cleaner's — 맡기다's natural habitat: 세탁소에 맡겼어요. The -소 place-suffix files alongside 주유소 (gas station) and 파출소 (police box); small shops, essential errands.

駐車場 park-car-place: where 차를 세워요 (M12's 세우다 — its park-the-car job, finally explained: making the car STAND). The -장 (場, grounds) also paves 정류장 (M12) and 운동장. 주차 금지 = no parking — S2's sign kit gains its most-ignored member.

用돈 use-money: the allowance — 용돈을 주다/받다 (M9's axis, family edition). Kids earn it via 심부름, spend it at the 편의점, and — the culture's full circle — grown children give PARENTS 용돈 at 설날 and 추석 (M25's holidays, with envelopes).

장난 (mischief, next door) + -감 (material): mischief-material — a toy, decoded. 장난감을 정리하세요 = the eternal parental sentence. The -감 suffix measures potential: 신랑감 (husband-material) awaits you in Band 5; Korean rates everything as material for something.

Mischief: 장난치다 = to mess around, 장난 전화 = prank call, and the essential 장난이야! = just kidding! Slang inverts it: 장난 아니야 = NOT a joke = seriously intense (이 매운맛 장난 아니야 — M3's tastes, weaponized). Play, and the denial of play, one noun.

花盆 flower-basin: the pot — where M35's 식물 lives and 키우다 happens indoors: 화분에 물을 주세요 (M9's give-machine watering — Korean waters plants by GIVING). Radar: this 화 is 花 (flower), a FOURTH 화 — speech 話, fire 火, harmony 和, now flowers. The syllable is a garden.

禮節 courtesy-section: manners as a teachable subject — 식사 예절 (table manners: the M18 chopstick laws, codified), 예절 교육 (M32's education, aimed at elbows). 예의 (M26) is the principle; 예절 is the curriculum — what 어른들 say kids these days lack, since forever.

同時 same-hour: 동시에 = at the same time, simultaneously — this module's thesis as a noun. 동시에 말했어요 = we said it at the same time (the jinx moment). The 동 is same-同, not east-東 (M27's compass) — a fourth 동 for the radar.

瞬間 blink-between: the instant — 시간's 간 (between) again, sliced thinner. 그 순간 = at that moment (every drama's freeze-frame); 순간의 선택 = a split-second choice. Its dramatic cousin 순식간 waits at the end of this shelf.

Dawn — but in Korea it starts at midnight: 새벽 두 시 = 2 a.m. (not 'two at dawn' — the word owns the whole 12-to-6 shift). 새벽까지 공부했어요, 새벽 배송 (dawn delivery — groceries at your door by 새벽). The hours this country famously refuses to sleep through.
終日 end-of-day: the whole day through — usually as 하루 종일 (M8's 하루 + this): 하루 종일 비가 왔어요 = it rained all day. The 종 is end-終 (not 종로's bell-鐘, M31) — the day, run to its end.

平素 flat-ordinary: the baseline — 평소에 = usually, on a normal day: 평소에 일찍 자요. The 평 is 평화's flat-平 (M32): peace and ordinary share a hanja, which is its own small philosophy. What 평소 is, this module's adverbs disturb.
日常 day-constant: the everyday — 일상생활 = daily life (M29's 생활 welded on), 일상으로 돌아가요 = back to the routine (M23's return verbs). Vlogs sell 일상 by the million: other people's ordinary, beautifully lit.

한 (one, big) + 참: a LONG moment — 한참 기다렸어요 = I waited forever (measured in sighs, not minutes); 한참 후에 = a good while later. M29's 참 (truly) is a different word wearing the same syllable; this 참 is a stretch of time.

요즘's (M26) street twin — same meaning, more slippers: 요새 어떻게 지내요? The time-ladder completes: 요새/요즘 (casual→neutral), 최근 (M32, tie required). Radar: the 새 here is a worn-down 사이 (gap, M6) — 'this gap of days' — not bird, not new.

當時 that-very-hour: 'at the time' — news and history's word: 당시에는 몰랐어요 = at the time, we didn't know (every documentary's saddest sentence). 당연하다's fitting-當 (M34) + M5's 시: the hour that fit. 그때 for talk; 당시 for print.

늦다 (M8) + 잠 (M28): the late-sleep — off the official list, but Monday knows better. 늦잠(을) 자다 = to oversleep: 늦잠 자서 지각했어요 is the excuse this compound was built to deliver. The -ㅁ factory's laziest product, and its most relatable.
期間 term-between: a bounded stretch — 시험 기간 (exam period: the library fills, M15 nods), 세일 기간 (sale window), 공사 기간 (S2's 공사, scheduled). The bureaucratic cousin of 동안: 동안 feels time; 기간 files it.

世紀 generation-record: the century — 21세기 = the 21st century (Sino numbers, M2's 이십일 on duty). 세상's world-세 (M22) zoomed all the way out. 세기의 대결 = the match of the century — sports pages love this word more than historians do.

걷다 (M6) + -ㅁ: the step — M33's 웃음-note promised it, here it lands. 첫걸음 = the first step (every textbook title), 걸음이 빨라요 = fast walker (Seoul's default setting). The ㄷ-irregular's ㄹ survives in the noun — the factory keeps fingerprints.

German 'Arbeit' (work), via Japan, into Korean — the long-haul immigrant path the Konglish reading mapped (빵's route, retraced). Five syllables, so the 준말 law strikes: everyone says 알바 — 알바 자리 (an opening), 알바생 (the part-timer). Convenience stores run on this word.

信號 trust-mark: the signal — 신호를 기다려요 (waiting at the light; M12's 신호등 was this + M11's lamp all along — decode complete). Also phones (신호가 약해요 = weak signal) and hearts: 그린라이트 is the borrowed version; 신호 is what you're squinting at either way.

道路 way-road: the official road — M31's province-道 doing street work, welded to 종로's road-路. 도로가 막혀요 (M36's passive, rush-hour edition), 고속도로 = the highway (high-speed-road, fully decodable). 길 (M12) is any path; 도로 has asphalt and a budget.
瞬息間 blink-breath-between: faster than 순간 — 순식간에 끝났어요 = over in a flash (concerts, vacations, 치킨). Always wears -에. When Korean wants you to know you missed it, this is the word.
方今 just-now: seconds ago — 방금 왔어요 = literally just walked in; 방금 뭐라고 했어요? = what did you JUST say (M32's machine, instant replay). Points backward only; its forward twin is next door.

今方 — 방금 flipped, and looser: points both ways. 금방 갈게요 = be right there (the text that buys ten minutes); 금방 끝나요 = almost done (universally optimistic). Korean's favorite unit of vague immediacy — the 사회/회사 flip pattern (M32), timekeeping edition.

Earlier today, and ONLY today: 아까 말했잖아요-flavored earlier — 아까 봤어요 = I saw it earlier. The recent-past ladder: 방금 (seconds), 아까 (hours, same day), 어제 (M2). Beyond today it stops working — 아까 has a curfew.

아까's mirror: later, and ONLY today — 이따가 봐요! = see you in a bit (clips to 이따 봐 in texts, 준말 law). Not 나중에 (M8 — someday, unscheduled); 이따가 is a promise with today's date on it. The pair bookends your day: 아까 behind you, 이따가 ahead.

Ahead of time: 미리 준비하세요 = prepare in advance (M9's 준비, scheduled early), 미리 말해 줬잖아요-energy: 미리 알려 주세요 (M37's 알리다 — tell me BEFOREHAND). The anti-미루다: one vowel apart, opposite life outcomes — see three entries down.

항상's (M10) native twin — one syllable, softer wool: 늘 고마워요 = thank you, always (the yearbook register). 항상 states a rule; 늘 strokes it. Ballads and handwritten cards run on 늘; procedure manuals on 항상.

The can't-stop adverb: 자꾸 생각나요 = you keep coming to mind (M34's 기억이 나다 machinery, on loop), 자꾸 웃음이 나요 = can't stop laughing. Carries a shrug of helplessness — 왜 자꾸 그래요? = why do you KEEP doing that? Repetition, minus the control.

어느 (M27, which) + 새 (the worn-down 사이 again): 'in which gap?' — time slipped through one: 어느새 겨울이 됐어요 = suddenly it's winter (M35's 되다, ambushed). The adverb of montages and parents looking at grown children.

主로 main-ly: 주말에는 주로 집에 있어요 = weekends, mostly home (the honest calendar). The 주 is owner/main-主 — 주인's (M27), promoted to adverb duty via M6's (으)로. What you 주로 do is what you actually do; the rest is 가끔 (M8).

The comparison amplifier: M22's kit gains a turbo — 훨씬 커요 = WAY bigger, 이게 훨씬 나아요 = this is much better (M14's 낫다 doing its comparative job). Where 더 nudges, 훨씬 shoves. Attach before any comparative and mean it.

每年: the 매-family assembles — 매일 (M5), 매주 (M17), 매년, with 매달/매번 riding the same rail (every month/time). 매 (每, every) is the Sino counterpart of M31's native 마다 — 매년 = 해마다, same promise, different register. 매년 여름에 = every summer, reliably.

Hold-still: 가만히 있어요 = stay put / don't move (said to kids, patients, and wobbly ladders); 가만히 들어 보세요 = just listen (M16's try-machine, hushed). The -히 factory (M33) stamps it. In dramas, 가만히 안 있어! is a declaration of war.

如前히 like-before-ly: unchanged — 여전히 아름다워요 = still beautiful (reunions, old cities, exes). The 전 is before-前 (전에's, M13). 아직 (M14) waits for change; 여전히 has stopped waiting — the difference between 'not yet' and 'same as ever'.

The hustle adverb, warm register: 얼른 와! = hurry over! 얼른 먹어 = eat up (grandmother's imperative — affection at speed). Cousin of M9's 어서 (service register) and 빨리 (M8, neutral). Three hurries; 얼른 is the one with food attached.

Three lift-offs in one verb: 눈을 뜨다 (open your eyes — waking's first act), 해가 뜨다 (the sun rises — 해 = sun; its setting is 지다, M17's lose-verb moonlighting), 물에 뜨다 (float). Slang inherited the rising: 요즘 뜨는 가수 = the singer blowing up right now. ㅡ-drop: 떠요.
The hurry verb: 서두르세요! = please hurry / 서두르지 마세요 = take your time (M14's -지 마세요, mercifully). 르-family (M7's table): 서둘러요, 서둘렀어요. The verb 빨리빨리 culture (M8's gap deck) conjugates all day.

The procrastination verb — S2's 밀다 note promised its 'procrastinating cousin'; here it is: 숙제를 미뤘어요 (M15's homework, deferred), 내일로 미루지 마세요 = don't put off until tomorrow (the proverb, pre-conjugated). 미리's evil twin, one vowel and one life philosophy apart.

밤 (M2's night) + 새다 (to dawn): the night... dawns on you — Korean for pulling an all-nighter: 밤새서 공부했어요 (시험 기간's official verb), 밤새 게임했어요. The adverb form 밤새 = all night long. A word this country's students wear like a badge.

지나다 (M25's 지난주 root) + 가다: to pass on through — 시간이 지나가요 (time walks past), 태풍이 지나갔어요 (the storm moved on — M11 weather, exiting), 잠깐 지나갈게요 = coming through! (the subway squeeze, M28's compound-motion table gaining a polite member). This too shall 지나가다.

急하다: urgent — 급한 일이 생겼어요 = something urgent came up (M28's 생기다 delivering the all-purpose excuse). People too: 성격이 급해요 = impatient by design — the 빨리빨리 temperament, diagnosed. 급하게 먹으면 체해요: eat in a rush and it backs up on you — grandma's slowest wisdom.
