때 (M25's when-noun) doubled + (으)로: time-time-ly — the written register of 가끔 (M8): essays and lyrics say 때때로; texts say 가끔. The doubling trick from 빨리빨리 and 점점, now telling time. Collect the ladder: 자주 > 가끔/때때로 > 거의 안 (M23).

Early — 아직 이르다 = it's still too early (said about marriage, dessert, and giving up). 르-family: 일러요. The 일찍 (M8) connection shows in the first syllable: 이르다 is the adjective 일찍 adverbs for. Second job in formal prose: to reach (결론에 이르다 = arrive at a conclusion) — recognize, don't chase.

그렇다 + -아/어도: M29's machine meets this module's glue — 'even it being so'. The comeback word: 어려워요. 그래도 재미있어요 (hard — even so, fun). Sentence-initial, load-bearing, and the exact spirit Band 4 closes on. The 그렇다 factory's last big shipment.

M29's 아무 (any) stretched into an adverb — the -아/어도 amplifier: 아무리 바빠도 (no matter HOW busy), 아무리 생각해도 모르겠어요 (however long I think…). It announces an -아/어도 the way 만약 (M33) announces a -면: adverb first, grammar second, drama guaranteed.

The clench verb: 웃음을 참다 (choke back laughter — M33's -ㅁ noun in a headlock), 눈물을 참다, 화를 참다. 못 참아! = I can't TAKE it anymore. Endurance as national virtue: 참는 자에게 복이 와요 — blessings come to those who hold it in (M25's 복, patiently).
참다's structural cousin: 참다 clenches a moment; 견디다 outlasts a season — 겨울을 견디다, 힘든 시간을 견뎠어요 (I got through it). Buildings 견디다 earthquakes; hearts 견디다 breakups; the drama OST 견디다s both at once.

The scrappy survivor of the endurance trio: 버티다 is white-knuckled — 조금만 더 버텨요! (hang on just a bit longer — 미리 warned you Korean loves this sentence). 참다 suppresses, 견디다 withstands, 버티다 refuses to fall over. Monday-morning conjugation: 버티는 중.

最善 most-good: your utmost — locked into one frame: 최선을 다하다 = give it everything (다 + 하다: to do-it-all, M9's 다 finally verbing). 최선을 다했어요 = I did my best — the sentence that closes exams, interviews, and this band. 최고's (M19) inward-facing sibling.

最惡 most-bad: 최고's evil twin — 최악의 하루 = worst day ever; 최악이에요 = it's the WORST (register: dramatic, daily). The 최-ladder completes: 최고 (M19), 최근 (M32), 최선, 최악 — Korean superlatives are a prefix, not a suffix.

條件 clause-item: the strings attached — 조건이 있어요 = there's a catch; 조건 없이 = no strings (M32's 없이, at its most romantic). Job postings, contracts, and blind dates all run on 조건 — the only-if noun for an only-if module.

無 (no) + 조건: zero-conditions — 무조건 갈 거예요 = I'm going, period. The 무- prefix is the 불-'s (M36) quieter sibling: it doesn't negate, it EMPTIES. Also the title of a trot anthem the whole country can sing; loyalty, with a beat.

規則 rule-standard: the rules — 규칙을 지키세요 (M26's 지키다: rules are KEPT, like promises and orders). 게임 규칙 = how to play; 규칙적인 생활 = a regular routine (the -적 suffix Ring 2 owes you, previewing itself). What 예외, below, exists to escape.

法: the law — and the root inside 방법 (M32) and 문법 (M10), finally alone: 법을 지키다 (keep the law), 법대로 하세요 (by the book). Second job as 'the way': 김치 만드는 법 = how to make kimchi — every recipe title ends in this syllable. Law and lore, one hanja.

例外 example-outside: the case standing OUTSIDE the examples — 예 (M33's example-예) + 외 (외국's outside-외): fully decodable. 예외 없이 = without exception; 저는 예외예요 = I'm the exception (everyone's favorite sentence). Grammar has 예외; this module's glue mercifully has few.

基準 base-level: the measuring stick — 기준이 뭐예요? = what's the criterion? (ask it about grades, prices, and 'spicy'). 내 기준으로는 = by my standards, the disclaimer Korean reviews run on. Where 규칙 binds, 기준 merely measures.

限界 limit-boundary: the wall — 한계가 있어요 = there's only so much; 한계를 넘다 = push past the limit (M36's 넘다, at the gym and in the anthem-lyrics sense). 인간의 한계 = the limits of the possible; sports commentary owns this word.

以下 from-here-down: M32's 이상 finds its floor — 스무 살 이하 = twenty and under; 만 원 이하 = under 10,000 won. The pair runs every sign, form, and dosage label in the country: 이상/이하, ceiling and floor, now both yours.

責任 duty-charge: what lands on you — 제 책임이에요 = it's on me (the grown-up sentence); 책임을 지다 = to bear responsibility (지다's third job: lose, set, and now carry — M17's verb keeps volunteering). 무책임하다 = irresponsible: the 무-prefix, already working.

代身 substitute-body: instead — 커피 대신 차를 마셔요 (tea instead of coffee); 대신에 제가 할게요-flavored offers: 제가 대신 할 수 있어요. Also the trade-off marker: 싸요. 대신 좀 멀어요 = cheap — in exchange, far. Korean bargains out loud with this word.

可能 can-able: possible — 가능해요? = can it be done? (the contractor's question); 배달 가능 = delivery available (the sticker on every door). Officialese prefers it to 할 수 있어요; your landlord will text it without the 하다.

불- (M36's gap deck, delivering) + 가능하다: not-possible — 불가능해요 = can't be done. The motivational-poster inversion arrives pre-quoted: 불가능은 없다 — impossible is nothing. Korean pessimism and optimism, one prefix apart.

充分 filled-portion: sufficient — 충분해요 = that's plenty (say it before the 이모 refills the 반찬 again, M18); 시간이 충분하지 않아요 = not enough time (M28's negation measuring the shortage). The word 밖에 spends this module lamenting the absence of.

不足 not-enough-foot: falling short — 잠이 부족해요 (sleep-deprived: the national condition, M28's 잠), 실력이 아직 부족해요 (the modest self-review — pair it with M26's deflections). 충분하다's shadow; between them they audit everything.

完璧 complete-jade: flawless as an unchipped jade disc (the hanja is a whole ancient story — a treasure returned intact). 완벽해요! = perfect!; 완벽한 계획 (M8's badge-ready 계획). S1's 완전 was the slang intensifier; 완벽 is the standard the intensifier aspires to.

甚하다: over the line — 너무 심해요 = that's too harsh (the friendship foul-call), 감기가 심해요 (M14's cold, upgraded), 장난이 심하다 (M37's mischief, past its limit). The adverb 심하게 bruises; the drama line 너무하네, 정말 is its cousin in spirit.

滿足 full-foot: satisfied — the foot is FULL, says the hanja, and no one knows why but everyone is happy. 결과에 만족해요 = satisfied with the result (M32's 결과, accepted). 만족스러워요 previews the -스럽다 machine Band 5 will formalize.

相關 mutual-connection + 없다: no-relation — 상관없어요 = doesn't matter / I don't mind, the concession module's soul: 비가 와도 상관없어요 (even if it rains — so what). Aggressive register available: 상관없잖아 = none of your business. The 있다-factory's most liberating product.

絶對 absolute: 절대(로) + a negative = never ever — 절대 안 돼요 (M10's veto, notarized), 절대 잊지 않을 거예요 (M15's 잊다, defied). It demands its negative partner the way 밖에 does — this module's grammar even shapes its adverbs. Promise-register: heavy.

全혀: M31's all-全 gone negative — 전혀 몰랐어요 = I had NO idea; 전혀 안 매워요 = not spicy at all (a lie, at any 매운탕 house). Another negative-polarity item: 전혀 without its 안/못/없다 sounds like a sentence missing its floor.

꼭's (M29) formal twin: 반드시 오세요 = you MUST come (wedding invitations, court summons — same adverb, different envelopes). Speeches and rulebooks say 반드시; texts say 꼭. Radar: no relation to 반 (half, M5) — the syllable just moonlights.

The desperate please — NOT 주세요's polite request but a hands-clasped plea: 제발 조용히 해 주세요 (M33's 조용히, begged for), 제발… (alone, eyes closed — before lottery numbers and exam results). English 'please' covers both; Korean splits courtesy from desperation.

The tables-turned adverb: 오히려 제가 고맙죠 = if anything, I should thank YOU (the gratitude reversal — memorize it whole); 오히려 더 좋아요 = actually better this way. When reality lands opposite to expectation, 오히려 files the report. Top-400 frequency wearing a C-grade disguise.

努力 exert-strength: effort, the noun (M26 shipped 노력하다; here's the substance) — 노력이 필요해요 (it takes work), 노력의 결과 (M32's 결과, earned). Study-culture's scripture sits in the gap deck: 노력은 배신하지 않는다. Said 노력 [노력]; spent daily.

苦生 bitter-living: the hard road — M26's gap deck taught you 고생했어요 (you've struggled well); now own the noun: 고생 끝에 낙이 온다 = joy comes at hardship's end (M28's 끝 keeping the promise), 헛고생 = wasted effort. Korea praises the struggle itself; this word is how.

勇氣 brave-energy: the 기 is 인기/기회's energy-氣 (M32/M33) — courage as a substance you summon: 용기를 내세요 = take courage (M28's 내다: you PAY it out from within), 용기가 필요해요. What every confession scene in every drama is short on until minute 58.

M26's 자신 (self-belief — 자신 있어요) + -감 (the feeling-stuff suffix from M37's 장난감 note): self-trust-material, bottled — 자신감을 가지세요 = have confidence; 자신감이 떨어졌어요 (M36's faller, at its saddest). The -감 factory also ships 책임감 (sense of duty) — file the pattern.

意志 intent-aim: the will — 의지가 강해요 = strong-willed (M14's 힘-adjacent virtue); 의지의 한국인 = 'Korean of pure willpower', the affectionate meme for anyone who refuses to quit absurdly. This module's endurance trio (참다/견디다/버티다), distilled to a noun.

The excuse — 핑계 대지 마세요 = don't make excuses (대다, to put forth — recognize it in this frame). 늦잠 (M38) is the excuse; 핑계 is the genre. The proverb goes 핑계 없는 무덤이 없다 — no grave lacks an excuse: everyone has reasons; the graveyard is full of them.

長點 long-point: where you run long — M32's 점 (point) measured in 長 (long — 사장님/부장님's chief-장, stretched literal). 장점이 뭐예요? = what are your strengths? — the interview question 최선을 다하다 answers. Its short twin is next door.

短點 short-point: where you run short. 장점과 단점 = pros and cons — the pair every review, resume, and relationship talk runs on. The honest interview answer: 단점은 완벽주의예요 (my weakness is perfectionism) — a 핑계 wearing a suit.

The face tour starts at the top: the forehead — where fevers get checked (a mother's palm, the original thermometer) and where 땀 (three shelves down) reports first. 이마가 넓어요 (M13's 넓다) = a wide forehead; fortune-tellers read generosity into it.

눈 (M14) + 썹 — a bound syllable with exactly one job. The 눈-compound family keeps compounding interest: 눈물 (M14, eye-water), and 속눈썹 — DEEP-set 눈썹, M28's 속 doing the placing — is the eyelash. Half of Korean beauty content is 눈썹 maintenance.

The cheek — specifically the one K-dramas slap and winter wind bites first. Everyday Korean keeps a softer word too: 볼 (rounder, cuter — babies get their 볼 pinched); 뺨 is the dramatic one. And the idiom: 프로 뺨치는 실력 (M26's 실력) — skill that slaps a pro's cheek — amateur work good enough to embarrass professionals.
Chin and jaw, one syllable — and where the next entry grows: 턱수염 = the chin-beard. Propping it on your palm is 턱을 괴다, the international bored-student pose (recognize it; deploy it in lectures).

鬚髥 — two hanja that BOTH mean facial hair: a beard written twice. Humans split it into 턱수염 (chin-beard) and 콧수염 (nose-beard — M14's 코 wearing a linking ㅅ = mustache); M22's 고양이 wears plain 수염, the whiskers. 할아버지 (M4) owns the archetype.
입 (M14) + 술 — and radar up: NOT M9's drink-술. This -술 is an ancient word for rim, worn smooth: the mouth's rim. 겨울엔 입술이 말라요 (M36's 마르다 — lips chap), hence 립밤, Konglish's smallest product.

The tongue — where taste lives and where every ㄹ you've ever fought was fought. 혀 짧은 소리 (M7's 짧다 + M19's 소리) = 'short-tongued talk' — baby-talk or a lisp. Korea reads sticking it out as pure cheek; doctors are the one exception.
To chew: 잘 씹어 드세요 — chew well, every grandmother's table law. The modern job is colder: 문자를 씹다 (M20's 문자) = to CHEW a text — read it, never reply. Being left on read, as digestion.

皮膚 hide-skin — radar first: this 피 is hide-皮, not M14's blood-피; the syllable just runs both ways. 피부가 좋아요 is the K-beauty compliment economy's base unit, and 아기 피부 (M25) is the gold standard — the one this module's 처럼 will be comparing things to.

Hair everywhere M8's 머리 isn't: arms, legs, sweaters, dogs. 머리 (with its full form 머리카락 for the strands) covers the head; 털 covers the rest of the mammal — 강아지 털 (M22) is what black clothes exist to collect.

The bone — what M35's flesh (살이 찌다's 살) hangs on. You've been eating them since M30: 갈비 is rib-뼈, grilled. And the idiom worth filing: 뼈 있는 말 — 'a word with bone in it' — the soft-sounding remark with structure inside.

Sweat — M28's 나다-note listed 땀이 나다 among the things that erupt; here's the noun, paid in full. It also flows: 땀이 흘러요 (M35's 흐르다 — water, time, tears, and now this). 식은땀 = the cold sweat, exam variety; the gap deck grips a fistful.

Breath — taken with 쉬다: 숨을 쉬다 = to breathe. Radar, and it's a good one: spelled exactly like M8's rest-쉬다 — Korean files resting and breathing under one sound, which is either a homograph or a philosophy. 숨을 크게 쉬어 보세요 (M16's try-machine, at the doctor's) = take a deep breath.

한 (the big-one prefix from M38's 한참) + 숨: one great breath = the sigh — 한숨을 쉬다, breathed with the same 쉬다 as its parent. Second job in the negative: 한숨도 못 잤어요 = I didn't sleep even one breath's worth (M3's 못, counting in breaths). The sound Monday makes.

The yawn — it comes out uninvited: 하품이 나와요 (M28's 나오다: you don't do the yawn, it exits). Famously contagious; reading this entry may already have triggered one. In class, reach for M39's 참다: 하품을 참았어요.
The sneeze — 재채기가 나와요; permission was never requested. Culture gap, and a real one: Korea has NO 'bless you' — a sneeze passes in polite silence, and nobody is being rude. 에취! is the Korean achoo.

To shake and shiver: 추워서 덜덜 떨었어요 (M11's cold, with 덜덜 — the shiver's own sound effect). And a retro-decode: M36's great faller 떨어지다 was this verb + M35's -아/어지다 all along — shake a thing until it lets go, and it falls.

떨다 + 리: M36's machine shipping its most emotional product — you don't tremble your hands; they tremble AT you: 손이 떨려요 (before the interview), 목소리가 떨렸어요 (during). The do/happen split (M35's 바꾸다/바뀌다 logic) aimed inward: Korean reports nerves as body weather.

The fist — made with the next entry: 주먹을 쥐다. 주먹밥 (M1's 밥) = fist-rice, the hand-pressed ball. And the classic restraint line, an old movie title the language kept: 주먹이 운다 (M7's 울다) — my fist is crying.

손 (M8) + 바닥 (M13's floor): the hand's floor = the palm — fully self-assembled from taught parts, and 발바닥 (the sole) rides the same logic free. The proverb: 손바닥으로 하늘 가리기 — covering the sky with one palm — denial that fools nobody.
손 + 톱: the fingernail — and the -톱 half ships 발톱 free: toenails on you, CLAWS on M22's 고양이 (same word; the cat means it differently). 손톱을 깎다 (M21's 깎다 — it peels prices AND nails) = clipping them.

M28's 손가락-note promised toes, and here they land: 발 + 가락 = foot-strands. The holey sock reports: 발가락이 나왔어요 (M28's 나오다 — a toe has exited). Stub one on a table leg and you'll learn every Korean pain sound in one lesson.

발 + 등: the foot's BACK — 등 is the body's back, a root landing here first (radar: S2's list-등, the etc.-등, is a different word entirely). 손등 = the back of the hand, same logic, free. The idiom every deadline lives by waits in the gap deck: fire, meet instep.

배 (M3) + 꼽: the navel — anchor of the 배꼽 인사 (M19's 인사): hands folded over it, the formal bow every Korean kid and department-store greeter has down cold. Hunger runs on it too: 배꼽시계 (M5's 시계) = the belly-button clock, the stomach that announces noon. Its laughing idiom sits in the gap deck.

To close the hand — what 주먹 exists for: 주먹을 쥐다. Radar against M28's 잡다: 잡다 CATCHES (taxis, fish, chances — motion toward); 쥐다 CLENCHES what's already in hand. Homograph bonus: 쥐 = mouse, and 다리에 쥐가 났어요 (M28's 나다) = a cramp — a 'mouse' erupts in your leg, and nobody apologizes for the metaphor.

To touch — fingertips, surfaces, curiosity: 만지지 마세요 (M14's -지 마세요) is every museum's favorite sentence. The grip ladder completes: 만지다 touches, M28's 잡다 catches, 쥐다 clenches — choose by how much hand commits.

To shake and to wave: 손을 흔들다 (hello, goodbye, taxi), 고개를 흔들다 = shake the head no (고개 — the head-as-it-turns — rides along free). ㄹ-stem like M36's 물다: 흔들어요, 흔드세요. Feed it to M36's machine and the bus does it to you: 버스가 흔들려요 — shaken, not shaking.

To tip forward — 고개를 숙이다: the head drops, the courtesy rises. It wears M37's causative -이- (you MAKE the head go down), and it completes the bow economy: 인사하다 (M19) is the greeting, 절 (M26) is the floor version, 숙이다 is the hinge inside both. Low doorways collect the involuntary ones.

Officially three verbs wearing one spelling; practically one syllable that closes, washes, and winds. 눈을 감다 — M38's 뜨다 finally meets its opposite; the eye pair completes. 머리를 감다 — hair demands its own private wash verb (M8's 씻다 handles hands and faces). 실을 감다 — wind the thread. Say 감아요 [가마요].

Soft — ㅂ-family (M21's 무겁다 rules): 부드러워요. Skin (아기 피부, the standard), voices (부드러운 목소리 — M19), and M18's 두부, the food this adjective was born to describe. The particle waiting two shelves down exists to compare things to all three.

Strong — 힘이 세요 (M14's 힘), 바람이 세게 불어요 (M11's wind, with muscle). Radar, twice: count-세다 (돈을 세다 — counting money) is a separate verb in the same clothes, and M5's 세 (three, before counters) is a third tenant. One syllable, three leases.

The outer surface — and the topology completes: 안 (M6) is inside-the-boundary, 속 (M28) is inside-the-substance, 밖 (M6) is beyond the thing, 겉 is the FACE of the thing itself. 겉과 속이 달라요 (M24's 다르다) = two-faced. 수박 겉 핥기 (M30's 수박) — licking the watermelon's rind — is studying the surface and calling it studying.

Smell — neutral on paper, suspicious in practice: bare 냄새 나요 usually means something's off. It erupts (냄새가 나다 — M28's door for happenings) and gets taken: 냄새를 맡다, the exact frame M37's 맡다-note promised. 빵 냄새, 커피 냄새 — attach any noun and inhale.

香氣 fragrance-energy: the GOOD smell — 냄새 with a five-star review. The 기 is the energy-氣 inside 전기 (M36) and 용기 (M39); the 향 is incense-香 — the root that was burning inside M36's 모기향 coil all along. Flowers and perfume (향수) carry 향기; garbage only ever manages 냄새.

The simile in one syllable, stuck straight onto the noun: 아기 피부처럼 부드러워요 — soft LIKE baby skin. It does mid-sentence what M24's 같다 does at the end (피부 같아요 files a verdict; 피부처럼 lets the real adjective finish). Like 마다 (M31): no conjugation, no ceremony.

To resemble — transitive, and frozen in the past: 아빠를 닮았어요 (the resembling already happened, at birth, says the tense). The ㄻ batchim reruns M24's 젊다 exhibit: 닮다 [담따], 닮았어요 [달마써요]. The slang certificate is 붕어빵 — the fish-shaped bread: one mold, two pastries.

M28's 생기다-note promised this one: 잘 (M10) + 생기다 = came-out-well = handsome — and like 닮다 it lives in the past: 잘생겼어요. The mirror is free: 못생기다 (M3's 못) = came out… otherwise. Korean grades faces as production runs; the grammar itself is the compliment.

美人: 미국's beautiful-미 (M27 — the hanja that flattered America by accident) + 외국인's person-人 (M23): a beautiful person, formal register. The useful spin-off is 팔방미인 (M2's 팔) — an eight-directions-beauty: someone good at everything.

눈 (M14) + 빛 (light — a root worth banking; 햇빛, sunlight, carries it too): the eye-light — not what eyes look like but what they're SAYING. 눈빛만 봐도 알아요 (M39's -아/어도) = I know just from the look. K-drama's entire acting curriculum is 눈빛 연기.

印象 stamp-image: what a face presses into memory — 첫인상 = the first impression (interviews give you seconds). 인상을 쓰다 = to WEAR a scowl: 쓰다's estate (M36's 쓰이다-note counted five jobs) gains a sixth. Radar: the news-인상 of 가격 인상 (price hike) is a different hanja — same sound, emptier wallet.

體重 body-heavy: M35's 몸무게 in a lab coat — same number, clinical register: doctors chart 체중, and the bathroom scale is sold as a 체중계. The 중 is heavy-重, the same weight sitting inside 중요하다 (M16) — important things are heavy things, says the hanja.

The mimetic 뚱, doubled like 빨리빨리 and M35's 점점 — sound as shape. Calibration, not endorsement: Korean discusses weight with a directness that startles English speakers — M35's 찌다-note warned that 살쪘어요? passes as a greeting, and M36's 말랐어요 lands as a compliment. Hear 뚱뚱하다 as blunt description; feel free never to deploy it.

感情 feel-affection: emotion as a category — feelings when you're managing them, not just having them. 감정을 숨기다 (M37's 숨기다 note hid this word in plain sight — the IOU pays today), 감정 표현 = emotional expression. The 정 is 情 — M26's untranslatable 정 in a clinical coat, the radar's FIRST 정 back on duty (affection 情, politics 政 M32, essence 精 M34); and the 감 is the 感 that bottled feelings in M39's 자신감/책임감, now leading words instead of trailing them.

마음 (M19) + 속 (M28): the heart's interior — M28's 속 note already filed 마음속 as 'where 마음 keeps its secrets'; now it's officially on the shelf. 마음속으로 = inwardly: 마음속으로 생각했어요 — thought it, never said it. Where everything this module names actually lives.

기쁘다 (M34) + -ㅁ: the noun factory, DECLARED open — M32 previewed it in 느낌, M33 named it in 웃음, and the back-catalog lines up on cue: 잠 (M28), 꿈 (M8), 믿음 (M34), 걸음 (M38). Joy as a holdable thing: 기쁨을 나누다 = to share joy — the arithmetic is in the gap deck.

슬프다 (M7) + -ㅁ: sorrow, nouned. Note the factory's fine print: -ㅁ attaches to the dictionary stem, so the ㅡ that drops in 슬퍼요 survives in 슬픔. 기쁨과 슬픔 = joys and sorrows — life's standard invoice, and every ballad's table of contents.

울다 (M7) + -음: batchim stems take the full -음, and the ㄹ survives — 걸음's rule (M38), holding. 울음이 나요 = crying erupts (M28's 나다, the door feelings always use); 울음을 참다 = hold back tears (M39's clench verb, at graduations and funerals both).

즐겁다 (M29) + -ㅁ: ㅂ-family roots wear their costume change into the factory — 즐겁- → 즐거우- + -ㅁ, the same ㅂ→우 as 즐거워요. 여행의 즐거움 = the joy of travel. Four factory products in one module: the -ㅁ machine is now load-bearing infrastructure.

幸福 fortune-blessing — and BOTH halves are already yours: the 행 is 다행's (M36) fortune-幸, the 복 is M25's luck-福. M7 handed you the adjective 행복하다 thirty-five modules ago; here's the Sino noun it stood on. 행복하세요! = be happy — the send-off at weddings and retirements, a wish conjugated straight out of this noun.

怯: fear as a substance — it erupts (겁이 나요, M28's 나다 again) and it's a possession: 겁이 많아요 = scaredy-cat, literally 'owns much fear' (said of dogs, kids, and everyone honest about horror movies). Radar: 무섭다 (M24) rates the scary thing or the scared state; 겁 is the stuff itself.

緊張 tight-stretched: M34 gave you 긴장하다 and decoded the drawn bowstring; here's the noun alone, because Korean handles it as a substance — 긴장을 풀다 = release the tension (M36's 풀다, at its most therapeutic), 긴장돼요 (M36's 되다-verb roster listed 긴장되다 — this noun was inside it all along).

衝擊 collide-strike: the shock — physical or emotional, Korean doesn't split them. 충격을 받았어요 = I was shocked: in Korean you RECEIVE shocks (M9's 받다 running an emotional inbox — 스트레스 받다 works the same shift). Headline vocabulary: big news arrives pre-labeled 충격.

感動 feel-move: emotion set in motion — the word for being moved, touched, gotten-to. 감동받았어요 = it moved me (받다's inbox again: shocks and 감동 arrive by the same courier); 영화가 감동적이었어요-style -적 forms exist — recognize the suffix, a later module owns the factory. The compliment every performance is fishing for.

便安: M12's 편하다 grows an 안 — and that 안 is 安, the peace inside 안녕하세요 (M1's first word, finally X-rayed). 편하다 says the sofa is comfortable; 편안하다 says YOU are at peace: 마음이 편안해요. Hotels wish you 편안한 밤 되세요 — M29's 되세요 send-off, in slippers.

不安: the same peace-安, revoked by the 불- machine (M36's gap deck named it; M39's 불가능하다 ran it). 편안/불안 sit one prefix apart — Korean's entire nervous system in two words. 불안해서 잠이 안 와요 = too anxious for sleep to come (M28's 잠이 오다, declined).

不滿 not-full — and the 만 is 만족하다's (M39) full-滿: satisfaction is fullness, complaint is the unfilled remainder. 불만이 있어요 = I have a complaint; 불만이 많아요 = chronically unsatisfied. The 불- ledger grows: 불가능, 불편, 불안, 불만 — file the prefix, it keeps paying.

Familiar — the 익 is ripeness: the same root Korean uses for fruit that's ready and rice that's cooked through; what you're used to has cooked all the way. 한국 생활에 익숙해요 = used to Korean life — note the 에: you're used TO a thing. The workhorse form is 익숙해지다 = to GET used to (M35's -아/어지다, doing exactly its job).

낯 (the old native word for face — 얼굴's (M8) ancestor, surviving only in compounds) + 설다 (unripe, strange): a face you can't place. 낯선 사람 = a stranger (badge form 낯선 — the ㄹ steps aside, as ㄹs do); 낯선 도시 = an unfamiliar city. 익숙하다's exact opposite: one ripens, one stays raw.

語塞 words-blocked: awkwardness as the moment speech jams — the 어 is the language-語 of 한국어 (M1), 단어 (M10), 언어 (M26). 분위기가 어색해요 = the vibe is awkward (M26's 분위기, suffering); 아직 어색한 사이예요 = still in the awkward stage. The foreigner's daily weather — and exactly what a misfired -잖아요 produces.

놀라다 (M26) grown into an adjective: the verb startles YOU, the adjective rates the THING — 놀라운 소식 = surprising news (ㅂ-family badge 놀라운, like M24's 무서운). 놀랍게도 = surprisingly enough. Korean keeps feeling-states and feeling-acts in separate words — this module's 밉다/미워하다 runs the same split the other direction.

en: to be flustered, caught off guard
notes: Flustered — caught without a script: 갑자기 질문을 받으면 당황해요 (M28's 갑자기 + M10's 질문: the ambush, diagrammed). Radar vs 창피하다 next door: 당황 is the system error IN the moment; 창피 is the shame replay afterward. 당황하지 마세요 = don't panic.

Everyday embarrassment: 아, 창피해! = so embarrassing! (said from behind your hands). Tripping in public, waving back at someone who wasn't waving at you — daily-life shame, minor but vivid. Off the A-list on paper, on the A-list in life; the gap deck files the official escape plan (a mouse hole is involved).

Unskilled, still-rough — 르-family (M7's table): 서툴러요, 서툴렀어요. 한국어가 아직 서툴러요 = my Korean's still clumsy — the most useful humble sentence this app will ever hand you; deploy it and watch patience appear. Radar: 서두르다 (M38, to hurry) sits one vowel away — and the logic connects them: rush and you fumble.

Pitiful — the ache at someone (or some street cat) worse off: 고양이가 불쌍해서 밥을 줬어요-grade mercy; 불쌍해 보여요 = looks pitiful (M36's 보이다). Radar catches its own false positive: despite the costume, this 불 is NOT the un-prefix — the word is a single native piece.

The near-miss ache: so close, and no — 정말 안타까워요 (ㅂ-family: 안타까워요), said at missed goals, missed trains, missed confessions. Sports commentary's favorite sigh. Division of labor: 불쌍하다 pities the person; 안타깝다 pities the situation.

Suffering with duration: 마음이 괴로워요 = it's eating at me (ㅂ-family: 괴로워요). Its causative is the dark one: 괴롭히다 — M37's party suffix -히- turning a private ache into something done TO someone: 동생을 괴롭히지 마! = stop tormenting your sibling. The adjective suffers; the causative bullies — M37's triangle at its bleakest.

Hateful-to-see — dislike with a face attached: 미워요 (ㅂ-family). Softer than English 'hate': kids say it to parents mid-tantrum, couples mid-quarrel — dislike INSIDE a relationship that isn't going anywhere. The gap deck files the proof: 미운 정, the jeong (M26) that grows even through this.

밉다 + -아/어하다 — and there's the machine: Korean turns feeling-adjectives into acting-verbs with -아/어하다, and you've owned its products since Band 1: 좋아하다 (M1) is 좋다 acted out, 싫어하다 (M3) is 싫다 with intent. 밉다 is how they seem to you; 미워하다 is what you DO about it. 미워하지 마세요 — the sermon, pre-conjugated.

Longing — for times, places, tastes: 고향이 그리워요, 그때가 그리워요 (ㅂ-family: 그리워요). For PEOPLE, M3 already gave you the idiom: 보고 싶다 doubles as 'I miss you' — Korean splits longing by its object. Folk-reading worth keeping: the root echoes 그리다 (M15, to draw) — to miss something is to keep drawing it in your mind.

사랑 (the noun inside M7's 사랑하다) + -스럽다: love-ish — lovable: 강아지가 너무 사랑스러워요 (M22's puppy, correctly assessed). You glimpsed -스럽다 once in M39's 만족스러워요: a suffix that paints a quality ONTO things. The Character module formalizes the whole family later; for now, own this one whole.

en: to be hurt, let down (by someone close)
notes: The let-down-by-someone-you're-close-to feeling — disappointment with the affection still attached: 친구가 약속을 잊어서 서운했어요 (M5's 약속, M15's 잊다 — the small bruise). Not anger (M19's 화나다), not 밉다 — the ache only 정 (M26) makes possible. English never named it; Korean relationships run on naming it early.

Heart-flutter — the GOOD nervous: before first dates, trips, new semesters: 내일 여행 가서 설레요 (M11's 여행, working its magic in advance). 마음이 설레요 = my heart's aflutter. Radar: 긴장돼요 is the exam's flutter, 설레요 is the vacation's — same heartbeat, opposite dread.

눈 (M14's eye) + 치: eye-measure — the gap deck's TWICE-filed untranslatable (and M19's group-chat warning), now officially on your checklist, in its rightful module: this chapter's endings manage what the listener knows, and 눈치 is the organ that senses it. 눈치가 빠르다/없다 = quick radar / none at all; 눈치를 보다 = anxiously reading the room.

M33's 표현 (surface-appear — meaning surfacing into words) gets its verb: 감정을 표현하다 = to put feelings into words, this module's entire assignment in one phrase. 잘 표현 못 하겠어요 = I can't quite express it — the intermediate learner's exact coordinates, now at least sayable.

M34's 기대 verbs up: 너무 기대하지 마세요 = don't get your hopes up — the review-culture disclaimer. Family radar: 기대돼요 = it excites me (the feeling happens TO you — M36's 되다-verbs); 기대하다 = you actively hold the expectation. One noun, two stances; the 하다/되다 split does the aiming.

M34's 고민 (bitter-agonize) + 하다: to turn something over and over — 아직 고민하고 있어요 = still deciding (menus, majors, confessions: all 고민 of equal rank). 고민 끝에 = after much agonizing (M28's 끝) — how Korean announces a hard-won decision.

아무리 + -아/어도 (both M39), fused and worn smooth: 'no matter how (I turn it over)' — the reluctant-conclusion adverb. 아무래도 안 되겠어요 = I'm afraid it won't work; 아무래도 감기에 걸린 것 같아요 = I think I'm coming down with something (M34's hedge riding along, as usual). Opens sentences the way bad news clears its throat.

어찌 (how — the stem of M33's 어쨌든 and M39's gap-deck 어쩔 수 없어요) + -ㄴ지 (M33's indirect question, fossilized exactly like 왠지): 'how-it-is'. Two jobs: the CLICK — 어쩐지! = no wonder!, the sound of a -거든요 landing on old confusion — and 왠지's (M34) near-twin: 어쩐지 이상했어요 = something felt off somehow. Radar: 왠지 wonders BEFORE the answer; 어쩐지 celebrates receiving it.

당연하다 (M34) through the -히 factory (M32's 특히 started it; M33 made it official): of course — 당연히 갈 거예요 = obviously I'm going. This module's -잖아요 is 당연히 as grammar: 'this is obvious to us both.' Agreement with its feet up, now in adverb form.

확실하다 (M34) + -히: definitely — 확실히 좋아졌어요 = it's definitely gotten better (M35's machine, measured and signed off). The hedge-killer: M34 taught you to soften claims; 확실히 stakes them. Say it 확씰히 — the tense ㅆ the spelling hides, as that module warned.

다행 (M36) + -히: fortunately — the adverb M36's own note pre-announced; the factory delivers on schedule. 다행히 비가 안 왔어요 = luckily, no rain. Sits at the front of the sentence like a sigh of relief taking its seat first.

그 + 만큼 (as much as) — you met 만큼 once, in S3's proverb 아는 만큼 보인다, where it was flagged as Ring 2 glue still to come. The full particle keeps its appointment later; until then, own the frozen adverb: 그만큼 중요해요 = it's THAT important. Radar: 그렇게 (M33) points at manner; 그만큼 points at amount.

材料 timber-stuff: the first word of every recipe video — 재료부터 준비하세요 (M8's 준비하다, apron on). The 료 is 음료수's stuff-料 (M18); the 재 is raw material. Cooking, crafts, and essays all start by listing their 재료.

The cutting-board verb: repeated knife strokes — 파를 썰다, 무를 썰다, the rhythm section of every Korean kitchen. ㄹ-verb like 만들다 (M3): 썰어요. Its neighbor 자르다 is one decisive cut; 썰다 is many small ones aimed at dinner.

One clean cut through: 머리를 잘랐어요 = I got a haircut (M8's 머리 — Korean cuts hair, not 'gets' it cut), 케이크를 자르다 (M19's cake). 르-irregular (M7's family): 잘라요. Also conversations (말을 자르다 = cut someone off) and — via M36's passive 리 — jobs: 잘리다 = get cut = get fired.

Combine things into one: 재료를 잘 섞으세요 — the recipe's assembly step. M18's 비비다 is the personal version (rubbing rice and sauce in your own bowl); 섞다 is the general one: colors, cards, playlists, and languages all get 섞다-ed. Says 석따.

Stir — and M14's ㅅ-irregular family (낫다: 나아요) finally gains its second member: the ㅅ vanishes before vowels, 저어요, 저은. Coffee, soup, and heads: 고개를 젓다 = shake your head no. Radar: sounds exactly like M36's 젖다 (get wet) — stir the soup, don't soak in it.

Sprinkle and scatter: 소금을 뿌리다 (M3's salt, airborne), 물을 뿌리다 (spray), and money — 돈을 뿌리다 = throw cash around, said of election seasons and regrettable Fridays. Farmers 뿌리다 seeds, which is where every harvest proverb begins.

en: to put in (a dish), to contain
notes: Put into a container, with intention: 그릇에 담다 (M18's bowl, receiving) — plating, where M28's 넣다 just inserts. Second job, sincerity: 마음을 담다 = put your heart into it (M19's 마음) — letters, gifts, and songs all claim to be 마음을 담아서 made. Says 담따.

담다's deep-end sibling: fully submerge — 발을 물에 담그다 (feet in a cold stream, summer's cheapest luxury) — and THE kimchi verb: 김치를 담그다. You don't 'make' kimchi; you immerse it into being. ㅡ-drop: 담가요. M26's 김장 finally gets its verb: what November does to a thousand cabbages.

The jeon verb: 전을 부치다 — shallow-fry in oil, the official sound of rain (Koreans swear rain on the roof sounds like frying, hence 비 오는 날엔 파전). Same spelling mails things: 편지를 부치다 — the exact homophone M37's 붙이다 note flagged. Now you hold all three: stick, mail, fry.

Boil the THING: 달걀을 삶다, 감자를 삶다, 국수를 삶다 (M18's noodles) — the food goes into the water. M18's 끓이다 boils the liquid itself (라면, soup); 삶다 cooks solids IN it. Says 삼따. Bonus register: Korea also 삶다-s laundry — 수건을 삶다 (M30's towel), hygiene at a rolling boil.

Done-ness as a verb: 고기가 다 익었어요 = the meat's ready (the BBQ referee's call), fruit ripens (감이 익다), and kimchi 익다-s too — ferments into its real self. A does-it-alone verb like M37's 끓다; bolt on the causative 이 (M37's party) and 익히다 cooks it through on purpose. Radar: no relation to 읽다 (read) — only the spelling rhymes.

Heat leaving: 국이 식었어요, 커피가 식기 전에 (M13's -기 전에, on a timer). Hearts too: 사랑이 식다 = love cools — dramas measure whole relationships in soup temperature. 식기 전에 드세요 (M4's 드시다) = eat before it gets cold: the Korean parent's I-love-you. Radar: NOT 식사's food-食 — this 식 is native cooling.

Water that stopped: 물이 얼었어요, and most winters 한강이 얼어요 (M22's river — the news photographs it annually). People freeze too: 겨울에 손이 얼어요 (M8's 손), and stage fright 얼다-s whole humans. Add M37's causative 리 and you get 얼리다 — freeze it yourself, the freezer's own verb: 얼려 두세요.

얼다 + -음: frozen-stuff = ice — the -ㅁ factory (웃음 M33, 걸음 M38) ships its coldest product. 얼음물 arrives free at every 식당. And the playground: Korean tag pauses when a kid shouts 얼음! (freeze!) and resumes at 땡 — the noun factory, running a national game.

간 (saltiness — the native seasoning word: 간을 보다 = to taste-check, 간이 맞다 = seasoned just right) + 장 (paste/sauce). M18's 된장 note promised this family's third jar — 된장, 고추장, and now 간장: the paste shelf, complete. The brown base note under half of Korean cooking.

The all-purpose flavor squad — the mixed sauce that makes 양념치킨 red and glorious (its menu rival: plain fried). One folk etymology reads it as 藥念, 'medicine-mindset' — seasoning as something you administer. When a recipe lists 양념 재료 separately, the real cooking has begun.

참- (true, real — M29's 참, working as a prefix) + 기름: the TRUE oil = sesame oil, the smell of a Korean kitchen winning. One spoon finishes 비빔밥 (M18's 비비다 insists), 나물, everything. Its country cousin 들기름 (perilla oil) waits at the market.
All oil, one word: the pan's (기름에 볶다 — M18's 볶다 demands a slick surface), the fried food's, and the car's — 기름값 = fuel prices, a national mood indicator. 참기름 above is this word wearing its medal.

고추 (chili — the fruit inside M18's 고추장) + 가루 (powder; 밀가루 is flour): the red in every red dish. Note the ㅅ wedged in the middle — the linking-ㅅ Korean compounds sometimes take (젓가락 wears one too, M18). Kimjang math: kilos per household.

食醋 food-vinegar: 식사's food-食 + 초 (vinegar). The sour corner of the shelf — cold noodles and 무침 dishes run on a splash of it. Dumped where it isn't wanted, it ruins everything — which is exactly the idiom the gap deck pours.
Sauce, the loanword — and the shelf's passport control: Korean-born sauces keep their 장 names; imports get 소스 (파스타 소스, 돈까스 소스). Two languages on one shelf, split by port of entry.
Butter — the traditional Korean kitchen had no slot for it, so the word arrived with the bread: M2's 빵 and 버터, same boat, same bakery. 버터 향 is that bakery smell; home fridges keep one modest block.

Cheese — the loanword Korea fell hard for: cheese on 떡볶이, corn-cheese at every 술집, cheese pulled over ribs for the camera. Speaking of cameras: Korean says 치즈~ for photos too — though 김치 also works, and this module stocks both.

Honey — and slang's sweetest prefix: 꿀팁 (golden tip), 꿀잼 (pure fun — 재미있다's 재미, sweetened), 꿀맛 (divine). Real honey goes into 유자차 and onto 호떡; metaphorical 꿀 goes onto anything effortless and great. 꿀 같은 주말 = a honey-like weekend.

달다 (M3) wearing M24's -ㄴ badge, frozen onto 맛 (M18): sweet-taste, the flavor as a NOUN. The whole rack builds this way — 짠맛 (짜다), 매운맛 (맵다, ㅂ softening first), plus sour 신맛 and bitter 쓴맛. Balancing 단맛 and 짠맛 is the entire science of 양념.

The national aromatic — Korean per-capita garlic consumption runs among the world's highest, and it goes founding-myth deep: in the 단군 story, a bear ate garlic and mugwort in a dark cave to become human. The first Korean was made BY garlic; the kitchen just keeps the tradition.

양 (Western — 서양's ocean-洋, M31, the same 양- that starts 양말, M21) + 파 (green onion, next door): the 'Western scallion' = onion. The 양- prefix stamps whatever arrived by ship; the kitchen kept the receipts.

The aromatic Korea buys by the armful — 파를 썰다 is knife skill number one, and 파전 (scallion pancake) is what 부치다 exists for on rainy days. Radar: no relation to 파란색 (M7) — though one folk story does claim the blue-green color was named after the onion's stalk. Believe responsibly.

The white giant of winter — 깍두기 is 무 cubed, 무국 is comfort in a bowl. Radar: NOT M39's 무- (無), the prefix that empties 무조건 and 무책임 — that 무 deletes things; this one weighs a kilo and sweetens after frost.

THE kimchi cabbage — 배추김치 is the default that M3's word 김치 quietly assumes. Every fall the news reports 배추 prices like a stock index, because M26's 김장 depends on them. A hundred heads per extended family is considered normal math.

Potato — 삶은 감자 is the humble snack; 감자튀김 the fries. Owner of Korean food's best naming dispute: 감자탕 (pork-bone stew) contains potatoes AND a bone by a similar name, and the country genuinely argues about which named the dish. The only vegetable with a controversy.

군고구마 (roasted) is the smell of a Korean winter street. Modern slang made it a feeling: a frustrating, stuck drama plot is 고구마 (dense, dry, lodged in your chest), and its cure is 사이다 — the fizzy relief of things FINALLY happening. Say it about episodes, meetings, group chats.
Into every 찌개 (M18) and onto every grill: 팽이버섯 (enoki, the hotpot crowd-pleaser), 표고 (shiitake), and 송이 — the pine mushroom priced like jewelry and gifted like it too.

The protein backbone: 콩나물 (bean sprouts), 콩국수 (cold soybean-broth noodles, summer's other answer), and M18's 두부 is this, pressed. The proverb keeps it honest: 콩 심은 데 콩 난다 — where you plant beans, beans come up. You reap what you sow, legume edition.

M3's 계란 note promised 'the native-Korean word 달걀' — here it lands: 닭 (M30's chicken) + 알 (egg), worn smooth by centuries. Same carton, two registers: markets lean 계란, textbooks lean 달걀. 삶은 달걀 plus 사이다 is the classic train-trip set.

What comes off first: 사과 껍질 (M3's apple, ribboned), 감자 껍질, and 양파, which is 껍질 all the way down — the crying joke writes itself. At the BBQ restaurant, 껍질 on the menu means pork skin, chewy and beloved.

The battered yellow pot 라면 (M3) demands — it heats faster, tastes right, and dents proudly. Borrowed long ago from Japanese nabe and fully naturalized, like 빵's route (M2) but from the other neighbor. The lid doubles as a plate; everyone knows this.

Lid — literal and figurative: 뚜껑을 열어 봐야 알아요 = you won't know until it opens (elections, exams, ovens). Slang runs hotter: 뚜껑(이) 열리다 — M36's 열리다 doing anger work — your lid flips open = you're furious. Bonus: Korea grills pork belly on an upturned 솥뚜껑, the old cauldron lid.

밥 (M1) + 솥 (the old iron cauldron): the rice cooker — modern Korea's talking appliance, announcing in complete sentences that your rice is ready. The venerable 솥 survives mostly in this compound and in that grill-lid 뚜껑 note above. 전기밥솥, 압력밥솥: job-description naming, M13's 냉장고 school.

가스 불 (M13's 불 — the burner flame: 불을 줄이세요 = lower the heat, M37's 줄이다 in every recipe), 가스레인지 (Konglish 'gas range' = the stovetop), and the national leaving-home litany: 가스 잠갔어? — did you turn off the gas? Half of Korean anxiety fits in four syllables.

국 (M3) + 물 (M1): soup-water = broth — said 궁물, and in Korea it's the POINT of the dish: 국물까지 다 드세요. M7's gap deck already taught you the paradox of calling it 시원해요 while it scalds. When 국물 is denied, all mercy is — the gap deck files the threat.

間食 between-food: 시간's between-間 (the one M38's 순간 sliced thin) + 식사's food-食 — the snack, structurally defined as what happens between meals. School 간식, office 간식, 새벽 간식 (M38 taught you the hour). Radar: NOT 간장's salt-간 — that one seasons, this one schedules.

床: the low table a meal arrives on — 밥상, 술상, 생일상 — folded away when the eating ends. Radar, four ways: 상처's wound-傷 (M36), 상황's state-狀 (M33), the prize-상 (賞) that award shows hand out — 상을 받았어요 = I won a prize, M9's 받다 receiving glory this time — and this one, which holds dinner. Its verb is next door.

To set out properly: 상을 차리다 = lay the table, feast-grade — the collocation this verb lives in. Then the mind: 정신을 차리다 (M34's 정신) = pull yourself together — 정신 차려! is every drama's slap line. Also 가게를 차리다 = open up shop. To 차리다 is to assemble something into readiness.

en: to pack, take along; to look after
notes: The caretaking verb M37's party was missing: 우산 챙겼어요? (M9's umbrella, remembered), 동생을 챙기다 (look after), and the love language itself — 밥 챙겨 먹어요 = make sure you actually eat, texted daily by every Korean parent. To 챙기다 is to keep someone provisioned, including yourself.

Put — and LEAVE in your keeping: 가방을 집에 두고 왔어요 = left my bag at home; 마음에 두다 = keep in mind (or on your mind). M28's 놓다 sets a thing down and lets go; 두다 keeps custody. Board games are 'placed' too: 바둑을 두다. Its biggest job here is as glue — -아/어 두다, the do-and-store ending.

en: going to work; the morning commute
notes: 出勤 out-to-duty — M16's 출근하다 was 출근 + 하다 all along; the noun steps out and stands alone: 출근 시간 = the morning crush, 출근길 = the road in. The 출 is the out-door of 출구 (M12) and 출발 (M8); the 근 is the duty that runs M16's whole workday family. Fused with its opposite it names rush hour itself: 출퇴근 시간.

退勤 retreat-from-duty: M16 called 퇴근하다 'the day's sweetest verb' — here's the noun it was carrying. 퇴근 후 = after work, where the evening actually lives; 퇴근길에 = on the way home, the drama's favorite scene marker. The office dream is 칼퇴 — knife-sharp, on-the-dot departure; say it wistfully, achieve it rarely.

勤務 duty-task — and both halves clock in from M16: the 근 of 출근/퇴근/야근 plus the 무 of 사무실 (the 사무 was office-TASKS all along). 근무 시간 = working hours, 야간 근무 = the night shift. The formal register: job postings and HR write 근무 where speech just says 일 (M2's 일하다). Radar: not M40's kilo of radish, not the nothing-無 of 무조건 (M39).

職場 duty-place: M16's 직 (직업, 직원) lands on the place-場 that paves 시장 (M3) and 주차장 (M37). The three-way radar: 회사 (M2) is the company that pays you, 직업 (M16) is what you are, 직장 is where you show up — you can change 직장 without changing 직업. 직장 동료 = coworker (M16's 동료, given its address); 직장 생활 = work life, M29's 생활 in a lanyard.

社員 company-member: 회사's 사 (社) + the member-員 already staffing 회사원 (M4) and 직원 (M16). 신입사원 = the new hire — Korea's spring cohort, suits still creased. Radar: this 원 is 員 the member, not the ₩ it gets paid in (M9), and not 병원's institution (M14).

報告書 report-document: 보고 (reporting upward) + the document-書 filed in 서류 (M16), shelved in 도서관 (M2), and sold in 서점 (M27). 보고서를 쓰다 = the office's homework, due before every 회의 (M10). Radar: this 보고 is 報告, not 보다 + M10's -고 — though your 사장님 does expect to 보고서를 보고 sign off.

就職 take-up-the-duty: the 직-family completes — 직업 the occupation (M16), 직원 the person (M16), 직장 the place (above), and 취직, the getting-in. 취직 준비 = job hunting (M8's 준비하다, in its grimmest deployment); 취직했어요! = I'm hired. No relation to 취미 (M17) — one 취 you chase for money, the other for love.

面接 face-contact: the face/surface-면 you've met in 화면 (M20's picture-surface) + 接, to touch — an interview is faces making contact. Korean sees interviews the way it sees exams: 면접을 보다. M33's 경험 note promised that 경험이 있어요/없어요 runs every job interview — this is that room. Radar: not the noodle-면 of 라면/냉면 (M3/M30), though you may deserve some after.

en: to seek and land (a job, a home); to rescue
notes: The verb of every listing site: 일자리를 구하다, 집을 구하다 — seeking with intent to LAND it (M6's 찾다 searches; 구하다 closes the deal). Shop windows post 사람 구합니다 = help wanted. The same spelling's second job is rescue (a different root, same sound — NIKL files both): 사람을 구하다 is what the hero does — M37's gap-deck scream 사람 살려! is answered by someone who 구하다-s. Hire me or save me; context decides which emergency.

契約 bind-promise: the promise-約 family files its paperwork — 약속 (M5) promises a person, 예약 (M18) promises a table, 계약 promises in ink. 계약서 = the contract itself (보고서's 書 again); 계약을 깨다 = break it (M36's 깨다, at its most expensive). Jobs, apartments, and phone plans all begin — and end — here.

賃金 hire-gold: the news-and-law register of pay — headlines argue 최저임금 (the minimum wage) while the break room says 월급 (M16's month-pay). Homograph alert, crown edition: 임금 is ALSO the old word for king — 임금님, in every folktale; NIKL lists both, context wears the crown. 임금이 올랐어요 means a raise (M22's 오르다, doing prices), unless a palace is involved.

封套 seal-sheath: what 편지 (M27) travels in — and at every counter, the bag question: 봉투 필요하세요? (M16's 필요하다, asked a thousand times a day). The cultural heavyweight is 월급봉투: the literal cash pay-envelope once carried home to the family — direct deposit killed the object, but the word still means the pay itself. M25's 세뱃돈 arrives in one too; some envelopes give instead of take.

월급 (M16) + 날 (M11): the day the month works toward — M16's note called it a small national holiday, and here's the word itself, said 월금날 (the ㅂ softens before ㄴ). On 월급날 evening everyone is briefly a 부자 (two shelves down); the gap deck files exactly how briefly.

通帳 through-ledger: the through-通 of 교통/보통 that M32's 통하다 finally conjugated, plus 帳 the account-book — a NEW 장 for the radar (M40's paste-醬, the place-場 of 시장/직장, and now the ledger-帳). Korea still prints 통장s — the little booklet the ATM fills line by line, a national comfort object. 통장을 만들다 = open an account (M3's 만들다, doing banking); where 월급 lands and, per the gap deck, barely pauses.

貯蓄 store-and-stockpile: saving as a discipline, not an accident — 저축하다 is the verb your 통장 wishes you conjugated more often. The formal partner of everyday 돈을 모으다 (M17's collector's verb, pointed at won instead of photocards). This module's own financial advice lives in the glue: 조금씩 저축하세요.

積金 piled-gold: the savings plan Korea actually runs on — a fixed sum marches from 통장 to 적금 every month, on schedule, no excuses. Touching it early is a minor moral event: 적금을 깨다 = to BREAK it (M36's 깨다 again), said in the tone of breaking a promise. Finishing one is adulthood's report card.

銅錢 copper-money: a new 동 (copper — not 동생's, not 동네's) on a new 전 (money-metal — not 전화's electric-電, not 전에's before-前; the radar logs both and moves on). The 500원 coin is the vending machine's favorite; a jar of 동전 is every household's accidental 저축. Korea went nearly cashless and kept the word — nostalgia is also a currency.

計算器 count-machine: M9's 계산하다 (where paying IS calculating) + the machine-기 of 세탁기 (M13) and 비행기 (M12). The market's diplomacy tool: a price typed and turned to face you beats a price spoken — 할인 negotiations run through it. Phone apps killed the object; the market grandmothers never noticed.

稅金 tax-gold: the 금 you've held since metal-day 금요일 (M5) and counted as 현금 (M9), now owed to the state. 세금을 내다 — M28's 내다, whose pay-job was built for exactly this. Every Korean receipt quietly includes it; every 월급 quietly excludes it. Radar: this 세 is 稅, not the native 세 that counts 세 시간 — one taxes your money, the other your time.

保險 guard-the-cliff-edge: 險 is the steep danger inside M12's 위험하다; 保 is keeping-safe — insurance, decoded, is protection purchased against the drop. 건강보험 (M14's 건강) covers the nation; 보험에 들다 = to take out a policy — M28's 들다, entering you into the rolls. The phone calls selling it are their own national weather.

費用 spend-use: the use-用 you've owned since 사용하다 (M10) and pocketed in M37's 용돈 (use-money), attached to 費, the spend-away root. 비용이 많이 들어요 = it costs a lot — M28's 들다 on its cost shift: expenses ENTER. What the 소비자 (same 費, further down) generates just by existing.

事業 affairs-work: the 사 of 사무실 (M16's office was an 事務-room) + the work-業 running through 수업 (M10) and 직업 (M16). 사업을 하다 = to run a business — plans, capital, and a 사업가's business card implied. For commerce at street level, see 장사 next door; the two words size each other up constantly.

The native word for selling-for-a-living — no hanja armor, older than the paperwork: 장사가 잘돼요 = business is good, said over market stalls and chicken shops. 사업 is the boardroom; 장사 is the counter. M35's 남다 runs its best idiom here: 남는 장사 = a deal that leaves something over — worth doing. 장사꾼 = the wheeler-dealer; affectionate or suspicious, entirely by tone.

貿易 exchange-trade: the business of borders — 무역 회사 hires half the business majors; 무역 전쟁 (M32's 전쟁) makes the evening news. Radar, twice: this 무 is 貿 — not the nothing-無 of 무료 (M20) and M39's prefix, not M40's kilo of radish — and this 역 is 易, not the subway's 역 (M6). Resource-poor Korea's whole modern story fits in this word.

輸出 ship-out: 輸 transports, and 出 is the out-door of 출구 (M12), 출발 (M8), and this module's own 출근. 수출하다 sends the semiconductors, cars, and dramas abroad; the news tracks 수출 the way it tracks weather, because for Korea it is the weather. The importing mirror is one entry down.

TWO words in one spelling, and both are money — the module's homograph exhibit. 輸入 ship-IN (入, the in-door of 입구 M12): 무역's other half — 수입 맥주 (M3's beer, well-traveled), 수입차. And 收入 gather-in: income, what your work collects — 수입이 늘었어요 (M35's 늘다, the happiest verb in finance). NIKL lists both; Korean lets the sentence sort it out, and this module owns both readings.

經營 manage-and-run: the 經 of 경제 (M32) and 경험 (M33), now steering a company — 회사를 경영하다. 경영학 = business administration, Korea's most crowded major. No relation to M17's 경기 (the match) — though shareholders treat quarterly results like one.

工場 work-grounds: 工 is the craft-work hiding inside 공부 (M1 — studying was workmanship all along), and 場 paves 시장 (M3), 주차장 (M37), and this module's 직장. 공장에서 만들어요 — where the next shelf's 제품 is born. The 공-syllable stays crowded (공항 flies on sky-空 M12, 공원 rests on public-公 M6); the hanja never collide.

製品 made-goods: 品 stacks three boxes into 'goods'; 製 is the making. What the 공장 outputs: 신제품 = the new product every launch event exists for, 한국 제품 = made in Korea, said with feeling. Its shelf-twin 상품 is the same object one register later — priced and shelved.

商品 commerce-goods: the same 品 as 제품, now wearing a price tag — 제품 leaves the factory; 상품 meets the customer. 인기 상품 = the bestseller (M17's 인기, doing retail). And the 상-radar seats a FIFTH member: M40 filed the meal-table 床, the wound 傷 (M36), the state 狀 (M33), and the prize 賞 — commerce-商 completes the shelf it's sold on.

販賣 sell-sell — two selling roots, doubled for business. 판매 중 = now on sale; 판매 가격 = the selling price (M21's 가격). The Sino register of what M28's 팔다 does barehanded — the verb form waits next door. Radar: this 매 is 賣, not the every-每 of 매일/매주 (M5/M17) — one sells daily, the other just means daily.

판매 + 하다: M28's 팔다 in a suit. Register twins, one counter apart: the shop window shouts 팝니다 (팔다's ㄹ bowing out, as M28 showed); the website and the receipt say 판매하다. 온라인 판매, 판매 직원 — when selling becomes a job title instead of an act, Korean switches to Sino.

割引 cut-and-pull: slice the price, drag it down — the word doing the math behind M9's Konglish 세일. 학생 할인 = the student discount your ID exists for; 할인 중 = discounts running now. 세일 shouts from the window; 할인 itemizes on the receipt — same event, two registers, and now you read both.

消費者 spend-away-person: 消 makes things vanish, 費 is 비용's spend, and 者 is the person-suffix M27's 환자 note introduced (기자 M16 records, 환자 suffers, 소비자 spends). The news says 소비자 where the ad says 손님 (M9) — same human, opposite camera angle. 소비자 가격 = the retail price. This module's whole economy aims at exactly this word: you.

利益 edge-plus-increase: 利 is profit as the blade's cutting margin, 益 adds the growth. 이익이 남다 = profit remains — M35's 남다 counting what the 장사 kept after costs. 이익을 보다 = to come out ahead. Its shadow, 손해 (the loss), waits on a later shelf; may your ledgers never need it early.

不動産 not-moving-property: wealth that can't run away — land, buildings, and the national obsession. The 불- machine (M42's 불안/불만 ledger) shows its dress code: 不 reads 불 except before ㄷ and ㅈ, where it slims to 부 — M39's 부족하다 obeyed the same rule, and now you know why. The 동 is 운동's move-動 (M8), denied; the 産 is property, banked next door in 재산. Street meaning too: the corner realty office itself is 'a 부동산'.

財産 wealth-holdings: 財 is money-wealth — radar it against M40's 재료, whose 材 is timber: one 재 builds dinner, the other builds portfolios. 전 재산 = everything one owns, the phrase dramas bet whole plots on; 문화재 (M26's 문화 + this 財) = a cultural treasure. And no mountain here: M11's 산 (山) only sounds like the property-産 closing 재산 and 부동산.

富者 wealth-person: the person-者 payroll (기자 M16, 환자 M27, 소비자 above) admits its most envied member. 부자가 되고 싶어요 powers half the self-help aisle; the proverbial route there is in the gap deck — dust, patiently, into mountains. Radar: a different 부자 (father-and-son) shares the spelling; the inheritance plots usually connect them anyway.

The blunt opposite of 부자 — native Korean, no hanja armor, no euphemism: 가난한 학생 (badge -(으)ㄴ, M24, on the classic broke student), 가난한 동네. Nouned as 가난. 돈이 없어요 reports today's problem; 가난하다 names the condition — dramas build first episodes on it, grandparents build entire lectures.

en: particle — or; a whole; or something (after a vowel)
notes: One tiny particle, three attitudes. Job 1, the flat or: 커피나 차 — coffee or tea. Job 2, the whopping reading: 세 시간이나 걸렸어요 = it took three WHOLE hours (the speaker's eyebrows are in the particle). Job 3, the settling shrug: 커피나 마셔요 — coffee, I guess; nothing better going. After vowels; batchim words take 이나. Swallows 이/가 and 을/를 whole, like 마다 (M31) and 만 (M30).

en: particle — or; a whole; or something (after a consonant)
notes: 나's after-batchim form, same three jobs: 빵이나 우유 (bread or milk — the flat or), 두 시간이나 (two WHOLE hours — the amount, editorialized), 라면이나 먹어요 (ramen, I guess — the shrug). And a receipt from Band 1: 얼마나 (M11) has been wearing this 나 all along — 'how much', with the amount-attitude built in.

en: particle — apiece, each at a time
notes: The distributor: 하나씩 = one apiece, 조금씩 = little by little, 한 달에 한 번씩 = once a month, every month. It rations an amount across people or across time — where (이)나 editorializes an amount, 씩 schedules it. Sticks straight onto the number or amount word, no ceremony — 마다's (M31) school of manners. The module's financial plan in one syllable: 조금씩.

入學 enter-study: the 입 is 입구's enter-入 (M12) — NOT M14's mouth — walking through the school gate for the first time. 입학식 is the March ceremony M25's 결혼식 note promised the -식 suffix would build; 대학 입학 is what the whole 수능 machine (M15's gap deck) aims at. Its bookend is the next entry.

卒業 finish-the-work: the 업 is 수업 (M10) and 직업's (M16) work-業 — schooling filed as labor, which no Korean student disputes. M15's 졸업하다 handed you the verb; here the noun stands alone: 졸업 후에 = after graduation, 졸업식 = the February ceremony (flowers everywhere, per that same note). With 입학 above you hold both bookends: enter-study, finish-work.

學期 study-period: the 기 is 기간's term-期 (M38), cut to academic size. 이번 학기 (M16's 이번), 한 학기 = one semester — and 새 학기 starts in MARCH, not September: the whole ladder M15 built (초등 → 중 → 고등 → 대) resets in spring, with M11's 방학 between the halves.

대학교 (M15 — 'casually just 대학') + 원 (the institute-院 M15's 학원 note filed, from 병원): the school after the big school. 대학원생 = grad student, a person defined by coffee and the 논문 owed below. 대학원에 다니다 — M16's attend-verb — is the standard phrasing for this standard grind.

博士 broad-scholar: the doctorate and its holder — addressed as 박사님, because M16's 님-ladder takes no days off. The rungs above 대학: 학사 (bachelor's) → 석사 (master's) → 박사; file the ladder, aim for the top. Also honorary slang: any impressive know-it-all is a 박사 — 컴퓨터 박사, your uncle.

專攻 sole-attack: pick one field and lay siege to it. 전공이 뭐예요? = what's your major — the university icebreaker, campus Korea's version of weather talk; 전공하다 = to major in. Radar: your FOURTH 전 — M31's 전국 note counted three (electric 電, before 前, all 全); this sole-專 completes the set.

留學 stay-study: staying somewhere ELSE to study — 유학을 가다 = go study abroad, and 유학생 (M4's 학생, with a visa) may be your own job title if you're reading this in Korea. Radar: a rarer homograph 유학 (儒學) means Confucian studies — the OLD national curriculum; same syllables, five centuries apart.

奬學金 encourage-study-money: the 금 is money-金 — 현금 (M9) and 요금's (M12) gold, aimed at tuition. 장학금을 받다 is M9's 받다 at its most welcome; a 장학생 is the student it funds. The dream exit from the 학원-fee economy M15 toured.

科目 branch-item: the 과 is 과학 and 교과서's branch-科 (M15) — knowledge sorted into labeled drawers. 제일 좋아하는 과목이 뭐예요? = favorite subject — and the shelf that follows is the answer key. Radar filed in advance: 과제, later this module, wears a DIFFERENT 과.

en: Korean (as a school subject); national language
notes: 國語 nation-speech: the country-國 family on parade — 한국 (M1), 외국 (M23), 전국 (M31) — meets 언어's speech-語 (M26). The inside name for Korean: foreigners study 한국어; Korean kids sit through 국어 시간 — same language, different door. Every country's schools run this trick: at home, the national language is just 'Language'.

體育 body-raise: the 육 is 교육's raise-育 (M32 decoded teach-raise) — education, but for the 몸 (M14). 체육 시간 = PE, the hour the 교실 empties gladly; 체육관 = the gym it empties into. The subject shelf's only entry conducted in shorts.

美術 beauty-skill: the 미 is 미국's beauty-美 (M27 — accidental flattery there, load-bearing here). And meet the OTHER 술: not M9's drinkable one — this 術 is skill, and it runs a trio through this shelf: 미술, 예술, 기술. 미술관 = art museum; 미술 시간 is where M15's 그리다 earned its keep.

藝術 craft-skill: art itself, the whole category — 미술 hangs in it, 음악 (M2) plays in it; 예술가 = artist. Rank 205 on the frequency list, startlingly high, because Koreans deploy it as a compliment: 예술이에요! = it's a masterpiece — said of paintings occasionally and of food constantly.

文學 writing-study: 문화 (M26) and 문장's (M33) writing-文, promoted to a discipline — and the -학 suffix M15's 수학 note told you to watch for ('names every field') collects another member: 수학, 과학, 문학. 한국 문학 = Korean literature; a 문학 소년/소녀 is a bookish kid. The three-문 radar (writing, door, hearing-聞) holds steady.

技術 craft-skill: the 術-trio completes — 미술 makes beauty, 예술 makes meaning, 기술 makes things WORK. One word spans a welder's hands and a chip fab: skill and technology, undivided. 기술자 = technician — the person-者 that 기자's note (M16) filed. Korea's proudest self-description is built from this word.

講義 explain-the-meaning: the university word for class — 교수님 (M15) gives 강의 in a 강의실 (the room-실 of 교실, M15). Students attend it, or watch it later at double speed: 인터넷 (M20) + 강의 = 인강, the recorded lecture that runs Korea's entire exam-prep economy.

硏究 grind-probe: to research — grinding at a question until it opens. 연구실 = the lab (room-실 again), 연구원 = researcher. It's what 박사s do for a living, and what you are doing to Korean right now, minus the funding.

論文 argument-writing: a 문장 (M33) army with a thesis — the paper every 대학원생 owes. 논문을 쓰다 (M10's 쓰다, at its most caffeinated); 박사 논문 is the final boss. The 논 is argument-論 — hold that hanja: it returns two entries down wearing a different sound.

討論 strike-argue: structured disagreement — 토론 수업, the class Korean students famously dread, since raising a hand to argue runs against every instinct M42's 눈치 named. And there's 논문's 論 again, now sounding 론: word-initial ㄹ softens to ㄴ (論文 → 논문) but keeps its ㄹ mid-word (討論 → 토론). One hanja, two spellings, zero mystery.

資料 asset-stuff: the 료 is the stuff-料 running through 음료수 (M18), 무료 (M20), and M40's 재료 — here it's research-stuff: 자료를 찾다 (M6's 찾다, in the library), 발표 자료 = presentation materials. Radar: this 자 is asset-資, not the self-自 of 자신/자연/자유.

調査 tune-examine: finding out, systematically — 조사하다 = to investigate, 자료 조사 = background research, 시장 조사 = market research (M3's 시장, studied instead of shopped). A wink for grammar people: Korean calls its particles 조사 too (助詞, 'helper words') — different hanja, same sound; you have been failing 조사 quizzes about 조사 since M1.

檢査 check-examine: the look-it-over — 숙제 검사 = homework check (M10's 숙제, under the teacher's eye), 눈 검사 = an eye exam, 검사하다 = to inspect. The 査 is 조사's examine-査, one entry up. Radar, and every legal drama depends on it: the homograph 검사 (檢事) is the PROSECUTOR — 검사님 in a suit, zero interest in your homework.

發表 launch-surface: M16's 발표하다 note already told you '발표 = the presentation' — today the noun reports for duty. The 발 is launch-發 (출발 M8 launches trips, 발음 M26 launches sound); the 표 is 표현's surface-表 (M33): send it out, let it surface. 합격 발표 = results announcement — the refresh-the-page day this module's exam shelf orbits.

記錄 record-engrave: the 기 is 기자's record-記 (M16 — the person whose entire job is this verb). Write it down so it keeps: 꼭 기록해 두세요 — M40's -아/어 두다, because recording IS do-and-store. The noun 기록 rides free and moonlights in sports: 세계 기록 = world record (M23's 세계) — same word whether you're keeping minutes or breaking them.

課題 task-topic: the 제 is 문제 (M7) and 숙제's (M10) topic-題 — the family's formal member. 숙제 is what school assigns; 과제 is what universities and offices assign — the same suffering on better stationery. And the promised radar: THIS 과 is task-課, not 과목's branch-科. Two 과s, one module, no refunds.

學習 study-practice: the 습 is 연습하다's practice-習 (M10) — learning defined as study PLUS reps, the most honest definition on record. The formal word on textbook spines and app-store listings: 언어 학습 = language learning (M26's 언어 — hello). 학습지 = the worksheet subscriptions Korean childhoods run on.

復習 again-practice: going back over it — what this app's review queue does to you daily, now named: 복습하세요 is every teacher's closing line. Its mirror is 예습 (豫習, previewing tomorrow's lesson); Korean pedagogy names both directions. Radar: this 복 is again-復, not M25's luck-福 (복 많이 받으세요) — though reviewed flashcards do bring luck.

集中 gather-middle: the 중 is 중학교 and 중국's middle-中 (M15/M27); the 集 is 'gather' — M17's 모으다 in a suit. Pull everything to one point: 집중하다 = to focus, and 집중이 안 돼요 = I can't focus — the library's truest sentence, usually typed into a phone. 수업 시간에 집중하세요 — every 선생님's refrain.

能力 able-strength: the 력 is 힘 (M14) in a suit — the 力-family M39's 노력 note decoded (努力, exert-strength) and M26's 실력 embodies. Sort them: 실력 is skill you've built, 노력 is strength you spend, 능력 is what you CAN do. 능력이 있다/없다 quietly sorts the workplace; slang crowns anyone impressive a 능력자.

正答 correct-answer: M15's 답 note planted this exact word ('정답 — the quiz-show word'); the debt clears today, checked by M15's 맞다/틀리다 pair. The 정 radar now reads four hanja — affection 情 (M26/M42), politics 政 (M32), essence 精 (M34), and correctness 正, which was hiding inside 정말 (M11, 'true-speech') all along. Life advice arrives as 정답은 없어요 = there's no right answer.

合格 fit-the-frame: the 격 is 성격 (M19) and 가격's (M21) frame-格 — you match the standard, you're in. The Sino noun for what M35's 붙다 does natively (시험에 붙다 = stick to the list): 합격했어요! is the phone call home. The opposite, 불합격, runs the 불- machine (M36's gap deck named it; 불가능하다 M39, 불안하다/불만 M42) — the prefix keeps its promise to keep paying.

成功 achieve-merit: M35's 성공하다 note said 'the noun rides free' — today it lands properly, with 성적's (M35, 成績) achieve-成 up front. 성공을 위해서 = for the sake of success — this module's glue aimed at the national target. Korea's favorite drama arc in one noun; its partner-in-failure is next.

失敗 lose-the-attempt: M35's 실패하다 note filed the 失-family — 실수 (M16, lose-your-hands), 실례 (M33, lose-courtesy), 실패 (lose-the-attempt) — and here stands the noun itself. 실패는 성공의 어머니 = failure is the mother of success: the proverb on every classroom wall, and this module's sentence deck co-signs it.

知識 know-recognize: knowledge as inventory — 지식이 많다 = knows a lot; 지식인 = an intellectual (외국인's person-인, M23, on suffix duty). Meet 식 number three: 음식's food-食 (M1), 결혼식's ceremony-式 (M25), now knowing-識 — and M40's 식다 already warned you its cooling-식 was native. Four 식s, four jobs.

The one native word on this imported shelf — and Korean's most affectionate insult: 바보야! lands nearer 'you dope' than cruelty; dramas use it as a love confession's rough draft. Also the standard self-diagnosis right after seeing the 정답. M15's 똑똑하다 is its official antonym; the distance between them is usually one 복습.

筆筒 brush-tube: the 필 is 연필's writing-tool-筆 (M15 filed it); the 통 is the all-purpose container syllable (물통, 쓰레기통) — NOT 교통's through-通 (M12). At rank 19,748 this is the deepest word in the course's pool, included because every desk owns one: the humble case the whole module fits in.

特徵 special-mark: the trait that picks a thing out of a lineup — M24's 특별하다 supplied the special-特, and 徵 stamps it visible. 특징이 있어요 = it's distinctive; 얼굴의 특징 = the features on a face. Sibling worth filing: 특성 (special-NATURE) — science says 특성 about materials where people-watching says 특징.

性質 nature-substance: 성격's (M19) nature-性 + the substance-質 hiding inside 질문 (M10 — a question asks after the substance). Of people AND things: 소금의 성질 = the properties of salt; 성질이 나요 = losing your temper (M28's 나다, the eruption door); 성질이 급해요 (M38's 급하다) = short-fused. Radar: 성격 is the personality profile; 성질 is the raw material — and the fuse.

魅力 charm-force — the 력 is 力, the strength family in its best suit: 실력 (M26) is built, 노력 (M39) is spent, 능력 (M44) is raw, and 매력 pulls. The 魅 is a bewitching spirit — charm as literal magic. 매력이 있어요 = attractive; and once Part 3's machine runs, 매력적이에요 says it with the suffix stamped onto its own shelf-mate.

The loanword *image*, doing Korea-specific work: not the picture (that's 사진, M17) but the personal brand — 이미지가 좋아요 = has a clean image; 이미지 관리 (image management — 관리 waits on a later shelf) is a national sport for celebrities, politicians, and anyone with in-laws. What 겉 (M41) is to a thing, 이미지 is to a career.

欲心 desire-heart: the heart-心 already beating in 조심하다 (M12, guarded heart), 관심 (M24, hooked heart), 열심히 (M10, hot heart). 욕심이 많아요 cuts both ways — grabby, or hungry to achieve; Korean lets the context deliver the verdict. 욕심쟁이 = greedy-guts, the affectionate register, said to kids reaching for a third cookie.

固執 firm-grip: holding position past all incoming evidence. The frame is M41's 세다: 고집이 세요 = strong-willed, stubborn — said of grandfathers, toddlers, and anyone who won't update. Whether it counts as a flaw or a spine depends, as with 욕심, on whether it worked.

The loanword *humor* — on Korea's ideal-partner checklist since checklists began: 유머가 있는 사람 (M24's badge) = someone genuinely funny. The full set phrase is 유머 감각 = sense of humor (감각, the sense itself, waits on a later shelf). Being funny in a second language is the final boss; this word at least lets you nominate candidates.

餘裕 surplus-slack: room to spare — in the schedule (시간 여유), in the wallet, and in the temperament that having either one buys. 여유가 없어요 = stretched thin, the national self-diagnosis; 여유가 있는 사람 = someone with enough margin to be gracious. Part 3's footnote factory makes it an adjective: 여유롭다 = unhurried.

理性 principle-nature: the reason-理 of 이유 (M24) and 이해하다 (M10) + the nature-性 of 성격 (M19) and 여성 (M32). M42 stocked the 감정 shelf; 이성 is its counterweight — 이성과 감정 = head and heart. Radar, mandatory: a second 이성 (異性, different-nature) means the opposite sex — 이성 친구 = a friend of the opposite sex, standard 소개팅 (blind-date) vocabulary — and only context chaperones the two apart.

純粹 — both hanja mean 'unmixed'; the word says pure twice and means it. Of hearts: 순수한 마음 (M19's 마음), 순수한 사람 = guileless — a compliment, usually. Of substances: 순수 한국어 = pure native Korean, no hanja and no loanwords — this module's exact opposite.

平凡 flat-common: the 평 that flattens 평일 (M16 — the ordinary weekday). 평범한 사람, 평범한 하루 (M8's 하루) — the anti-특별하다 (M24). Every K-drama lead claims to be a 평범한 회사원 (M4); the premise never survives episode two.

活潑 alive-splashing: the life-活 inside 생활 (M29), plus water hitting rocks. 활발한 성격 — the kindergarten report card's highest honor, and the self-description shy people rehearse before interviews. Also said of markets and discussions when they've got proper churn.

的 — the '-ish/-al' stamp: a dependent noun that bolts onto a Sino noun and turns it into a quality-word; fifteen of this module's words come off this one machine, and Part 3 runs it. M42's 감동 note promised 'a later module owns the factory' — this one does, paid in full. Radar, mandatory: a freestanding 적 (敵) is the ENEMY — 적이 많아요 = has many enemies. The suffix always hangs off a noun; the enemy stands alone.

個人 individual (unit-個 + the person-人 of 외국인, M23) + 적. 개인적인 질문 (M10's 질문) = a personal question — the fence Korean politely names before hopping over it; 개인적으로 = personally, in my own view. First off the assembly line because it's the product you'll deploy in week one — and proof the machine reads roots you've never formally met.

一般 one-kind: the general run of things. 일반적으로 = generally, as a rule — the essayist's opening move; 일반적인 생각 = the conventional view. On signage, bare 일반 marks the regular tier — the unmarked door, the standard lane — which is exactly what the word means everywhere else too.

具體 equipped-with-a-body: an idea you can poke. 구체적으로 말해 주세요 = give me specifics — the meeting room's favorite demand, and the tutor's favorite reply to 'I'll study harder.' The essay kit's workhorse; everything vague is its enemy.

全體 whole-body: the whole-全 that stretched across 전국 (M31 — the whole country), now measuring any whole at all. 전체적으로 = overall, on the whole — the reviewer's first word, spoken while inhaling before the 'but.' With 구체적 it brackets the essay kit: zoom out, then zoom in.

代表 stand-in-and-show: 대신's (M39) substitute-代 + 표현's (M33) show-表 — the one that steps forward and shows the group's face. 한국의 대표적인 음식 (M1's 음식) = Korea's signature dish; every guidebook's load-bearing adjective. Bare 대표 is also the boss — the representative on the business card.

積極 piled-to-the-pole: effort stacked as high as it goes — proactive, all-in. 적극적인 사람 is the answer every Korean job interview is fishing for. Its mirror 소극적 (pulled-back, passive — not yet taught) flips the polarity with one syllable. And enjoy the stutter: root 적극 + suffix 적 — the machine stamps without listening.

肯定 consent-settle: inclined to say yes to what is — positive. 긍정적으로 생각하세요 = think positive, the national coping strategy; mirror 부정적 (negative — recognize it now, a later shelf owns it). With 적극적 it forms interview Korean's power pair: proactive AND positive, hire me.

사회 (M32) + 적: social — 사회적 문제 (M7's 문제) = a social problem, the phrase M32's news register was waiting for. The suffix's core competence on display: it turns the nouns of the news into the adjectives of the op-ed.

세계 (M23) + 적: world-class — 세계적인 가수 (M4's 가수) = a world-famous singer, the headline K-pop taught the planet to read; 세계적으로 유명해요 (M17's 유명하다) = famous worldwide. M23's atlas-world, upgraded into a superlative.

경제 (M32) + 적, wearing two English hats at once: economic (경제적 문제 = economic trouble) and economical (경제적인 방법, M32's 방법 — the cheap way). English splits them into two words; Korean lets the context pay the difference.
정치 (M32) + 적: political — 정치적인 질문 = the question best dodged at the 명절 (M25) dinner table. The 정 here is the politics-政 your 정-radar filed back in M32; the suffix just gives it an opinion.

역사 (M15) + 적: 역사적인 날 = a historic day — the adjective anchors drop half an octave to deliver. One Korean word covers both English ones: momentous (historic) and merely about-history (historical); the speaker's gravity tells you which shipment arrived.
과학 (M15) + 적: scientific — 과학적인 방법 = the scientific method; 과학적으로 = scientifically(-proven, as every cosmetics ad insists). The factory at its most institutional: attach 적, gain authority.

전통 (M26) + 적: traditional — 전통적인 결혼식 (M25's 결혼식) = a traditional wedding, 한복 (M21) and all; 전통적으로 = traditionally. M26 taught the noun as a living inheritance; the suffix lets it modify everything the inheritance touches.

정신 (M34) + 적: mental, psychological — 정신적으로 힘들어요 (M15's 힘들다) = mentally drained, the honest answer that 괜찮아요 usually covers for. Korean splits exhaustion in two — 정신적 vs 육체적 (bodily; a later shelf) — and this module hands you the half people actually admit to.

자연 (M22) + -스럽다, the factory's flagship: nature-quality — unforced, no seams showing. 자연스러운 발음 (M26's 발음) is the compliment this app is aiming you at; ㅂ-family: 자연스러워요. Its negative image is M42's 어색하다 — awkward is exactly what natural isn't.

조심 — the guarded heart inside M12's 조심하다 — + -스럽다: cautious in MANNER, gingerly. Radar: 조심하다 is what you do (조심하세요!); 조심스럽다 is how you come across — 조심스럽게 물어봤어요 (M15's 물어보다, M33's -게) = I asked, carefully, the way you bring up salary or hair loss.

걱정 (M29) + -스럽다: the factory demonstrating on stock you've owned since Ring 1. 걱정스러운 얼굴 (M8's 얼굴) = a worried face — the quality painted on the surface, where M29's 걱정돼요 reports the feeling from inside. One noun, three angles on worry: have it, feel it, wear it.

자유 (M23) + -롭다: -스럽다's vowel-stem sibling — same job, older license, and M35's 새롭다 was its product all along (새 + 롭다, retro-decoded at last). 자유로운 분위기 (M26's 분위기) = a free-and-easy atmosphere; ㅂ-family: 자유로워요. Slice-mate 여유 runs the same machine: 여유롭다 = unhurried.

作家 make-house: the 家 is 가족's (M4) house-家 — in the maker-suffix reading, a skill so practiced it's the house you live in. Today's shelf runs five careers off this one machine (M45 taught suffix-thinking; here is the media wing's own factory). The job is broad — novels, dramas, webtoons: if it gets written, a 작가 signed it. Radar: 가수 (M4) wears a different 가 — song-歌, plus a hand to hold the mic.

小說 small-talk, literally — the old catalogues filed fiction under 'minor discourse,' and the name stuck. The 설 is 설명하다's (M24) explain-說. 추리 소설 (mystery), 연애 소설 (romance), 웹소설 (the phone-first kind) — and the accusation the gap deck files: told 소설 쓰지 마, you are being charged with fiction, not praised for it.

소설 + 家: the factory's first product, stamped while you watch. The register sort matters: 작가 is the working title (any writer), 소설가 declares the genre, and 저자 — two shelves down — is for paperwork. Introduce one as 소설가님 and watch the bookstore line form.

詩人 poem-person: poem-詩 + the person-人 of 외국인 (M23). The 시-radar M31's 시청 note opened (city-市, o'clock-時, test-試) seats a fourth tenant — and Korea gives this one public housing: subway platform doors print poems, so the nation's 시인들 publish at rush hour. 시를 쓰다 = to write poetry; 윤동주 and 김소월 are the names every Korean carries.

著者 write-person: authorship-著 + the person-者 suffix M27's 환자 note introduced and M43's 소비자 formalized. The colophon word — copyright pages, citations, invoices: 저자: 김OO. The split from its shelf-mates: 작가 is a person; 저자 is a field on a form.

畵家 picture-house: the professional of 그림 (M15) — 그림을 그리는 사람, promoted by the suffix. The collision is the module's best joke: M19's 화나다 puts anger next door, so 화가가 화가 나면 — when the painter gets angry — is fully grammatical and fully cursed. Painter and temper share no hanja, just a stage.

音樂家: 음악 (M2) + 家 — the musician, classical register first: composers, pianists, the conservatory crowd. The idol on stage is a 가수 (M4); the person who wrote the string arrangement is the 음악가. Same industry, different floors of the house.

藝術家: M44's 예술 note promised '예술가 = artist' — paid, with the house-家 attached. The whole-category maker: painters, dancers, installation people, and anyone difficult enough to earn 예술가 기질 (an artistic temperament) as a family diagnosis.

俳優 — both characters mean performer, so the word is doubly an actor. Radar the obvious: NOT 배우다 (M2), though the syllables match perfectly and actors do spend their lives learning lines — 대사를 배우는 배우, if you want the tongue-twister. 영화배우, 뮤지컬 배우; the credits print their names, the fans say 배우님.

演技 perform-skill: perform-演 + the craft-技 inside M44's 기술. 연기를 잘하다 is the actor's whole report card. RADAR, and the frequency list insists: 연기 is also smoke (煙氣) — 연기가 나다 (M28's 나다) is fire-drill vocabulary, smoke coming OUT — and a third 연기 (延期) postpones things: 공연이 연기됐어요 = the show got pushed back. Acting, smoke, delay: a theater can suffer all three in one evening.

Konglish 'announcer' (M20's corner taught the port of entry), but the Korean job is specific and prestigious: the broadcast professional — news desks, live events, flawless 발음 (M26). The big 방송국s hire a handful a year from thousands of applicants; it's an exam-culture career like any other. The stadium loudspeaker is not an 아나운서; the nine-o'clock news is.

作品 make-goods: 작가's make-作 + the goods-品 of M43's 제품/상품 — the 품-shelf gains its art wing. A made thing signed with pride: paintings, novels, and films are 작품; the factory's output stays 제품. Koreans also hand it out as a compliment — a plated dinner or a perfectly parked car earns 작품이네요 from the right audience.

主題 master-topic: 주인's (M27) master-主 + the topic-題 of 문제 (M7) and 숙제 (M10) — the topic that RULES the piece. 소설의 주제, 오늘의 대화 주제, and whatever your essay grader says you wandered from: 주제를 벗어나다 = to drift off-topic, the seminar's gentlest scolding.

人物 person-thing: the person-人 of 외국인 (M23) + 물건's (M9) thing-物 — a person weighed as a piece on the board. Three jobs: a story's cast (등장인물 = the characters), history's roster (역사 인물 — M15's 역사), and looks — 인물이 좋다 = fine-featured, the grandmother's appraisal.

主人公: 주인 (M27) + 公, an old lord-suffix — the story's owner, ennobled: the protagonist. 드라마의 주인공, 소설 속 주인공. And the word leaves the page on your birthday: 오늘의 주인공 = the person the day belongs to — sung to, photographed, handed the first slice.

場面 place-face: 장소's (M27) place-場 + the face/surface-面 of 화면 (M20) and 면접 (M43) — the face a place turns to the camera. Films are cut from 장면s; 명장면 = the legendary scene every retrospective replays. Off-screen it's any vivid tableau: 그 장면을 잊을 수 없어요 — some scenes need no director.

日記 day-record: day-日 + the record-記 M16's 기자 note filed — a note that name-checked 일기 itself; the IOU clears thirty-two modules later. 일기를 쓰다 = to keep a diary — today's glue turns it into a resolution. RADAR, per the frequency list: a second 일기 (日氣) is the day's WEATHER — 일기 예보 = the weather forecast. One 일기 records the day that happened; the other predicts the one coming.
