童話 child-tale: child-童 + the speech-話 of 전화 (M20) and 대화 (M24), sized for bedtime. 전래 동화 is the traditional canon — tigers, magpies, filial daughters; 동화책 is the shelf it lives on; 동화 같다 = like a fairy tale, said of weddings and first snows. The one audience that never reviews harshly.

옛날 + 이야기 — both M24, and both notes pointed here: 옛날's note said every 옛날이야기 opens with 옛날 옛날에, and 이야기's filed the word as Korean for fairy tale. A compound that self-assembled two bands ago and waited. The register split: 동화 is what the bookstore sells; 옛날이야기 is what 할머니 tells — no ISBN, better sound effects.

雜誌 assorted-record: 雜 is the everything-drawer hanja — mixed, sundry — and 誌 is a record-character, bookish cousin to 일기's 記. A magazine is literally a miscellany on a schedule: 패션 잡지, 시사 잡지, and the entire library of every waiting room. One of the course's few grade-A debts, settled here.

웹 (web) + 툰 (cartoon): Konglish that ran the trade route in reverse — Korea coined the word and the format (M20's 셀카 precedent: named before English had it), and the world now says 'webtoon' back. M17's 만화 gone vertical, free-to-start, and thumb-scrolled; half of today's 드라마 (M17) list one in the credits.

방송 (M32) + 局: the office-국 of 약국 (M6) and 우체국 (M27) — the bureau where broadcasts live. Today's suffix pair in one line: -가 houses a skill, -국 houses an institution. KBS, MBC, SBS are the big three 방송국; a field trip there — with luck, an 아나운서 sighting — is a Korean childhood staple.

Konglish 'channel' — one word, two careers. Career one: 채널을 돌리다 = turn the channel (M9's 바꾸다 also serves; the 돌리다 version still remembers the dial). Career two: the 유튜브 채널, which turned everyone with a phone into a small 방송국. 채널 고정! = don't touch that dial — now said by streamers who never owned one.

撮影 snatch-shadow: filming is catching shadows before they move on. 촬영 중 — mid-shoot — is the sign on every studio door (the busy-sign 중 the written-register interlude systematized), and 사진 촬영 금지 is the museum's favorite sentence. Radar: 영화 (M2) hides a different 영 (映, projecting onto screens) — same light business, different hanja.

錄音 engrave-sound: the engrave-錄 of M44's 기록하다 + the sound-음 running through 음악 (M2) and 발음 (M26). M44's 토론 note taught the spelling law that governs it: the ㄹ softens word-initially (錄音 → 녹음) but survives mid-word (기록). 녹음하다 = to record; 목소리를 녹음해 봤어요? — nobody survives hearing their own.

公演 public-perform: 공원's (M6) public-公 + the perform-演 inside 연기 — a performance is acting done where the public sits. 공연을 보다, 공연장 (the venue), 길거리 공연 (busking). When the poster says 공연 연기, read carefully: the show is postponed, not acting.

記事 record-affair: what 기자 (M16) writes — reporter (記者) and article (記事) share the record-記; one records, the other IS the record. RADAR, and M12 saw it coming: 기사님 the driver is a different word (技士, a licensed-skill title) — the taxi 기사님 has never read your 기사. 인터넷 기사 come with comment sections; brave 기자들 still read them.

言論 speech-discourse: 언어's (M26) speech-言 + the argument-論 of M44's 논문. The press as an institution — not one 기사 but the whole apparatus that produces them. 언론의 자유 = freedom of the press (M23's 자유, on constitutional duty); 언론사 = a news organization. When Koreans criticize the media, this is the word that takes the hit.

通信 through-trust: 통하다's (M32) through-通 — the message getting through — plus trust-信, the belief inside 자신 (M26: self-trust, worn as confidence). 통신사 = your phone carrier, collector of the monthly bill; 통신이 안 돼요 = no signal, the mountain hiker's report. Old word, new pipes: it covered letters long before it covered LTE.

大衆 great-crowd: 대학교's (M15) big-大 + crowd-衆. The crowd as an institution, with services named after it: 대중교통 = public transit (M12's 교통), 대중문화 = pop culture (M26's 문화), 대중 앞에서 말하기 = public speaking — which polls scarier than the dentist in every language.

觀客 view-guest: subtract the 광 from 관광객 (M23 — 'guests of the view') and the tourist takes a theater seat. The audience with tickets: cinemas, 공연장, stadiums. Korea's box office counts in 관객 수, and 천만 관객 — ten million admissions, a fifth of the country — is the club every director dreams of.

視聽者 watch-listen-person: watch-視 + listen-聽 + the person-者 of M43's 소비자 — the audience measured in living rooms. M31's 시청 note promised '시청자 = viewers'; paid, and the homograph holds: 市廳 is city hall, 視聽 is what you do to a screen. 시청자 여러분 — 'dear viewers' — is how the news addresses the nation.

讀者 read-person: 독서's (M17) read-讀 + person-者. The audience trio completes by medium: 관객 fills seats, 시청자 fills living rooms, 독자 turns pages. 독자 여러분 opens every author's letter; 애독자 = a devoted reader. The quietest audience — and the only one a 작가 never gets to watch.

아버지 (M4) climbing M16's 님-ladder: the honored father — someone else's father always, your own in formal settings, and, the big job, your spouse's. Married Koreans call their in-laws 아버님/어머님; the moment a boyfriend says 아버님 to a girlfriend's father, the subtitles know it's serious.

어머니 (M4) + 님: the honored mother — the address for a mother-in-law, a friend's mom, and (in shops working a certain charm) any customer who might be one. The proverb keeps 어머니 (실패는 성공의 어머니, M44's deck); the moment she is in the room and outranks you, she's 어머님.

年歲 year-years: M4's 나이 note promised 'for elders, the word itself upgrades: 연세' — paid in full, 43 modules later. 연세가 어떻게 되세요? is the polite age question, asked early because Korean grammar needs the answer to pick its endings. The 연 is 작년's (M25) year-年, dressed for company.

生辰: M5's 생일 note filed the upgrade order ('an elder's birthday upgrades to 생신') — delivery day. 생신 축하드려요, with M9's 드리다 doing the humble giving, because congratulations travel upward too. Same cake, better paper: the 생 is 생일's life-生; 辰 is a stately old 'day'.

The third row of M4's swap table (자다 → 주무시다) finally conjugates: 할머니께서 주무세요. And the national goodnight: 안녕히 주무세요 — sleep peacefully — what you say up the ladder, while 잘 자요 travels down it. 자다 (M1) never takes plain -시-; it gets replaced entirely.

드시다 (M4) with more ceremony — the eat-verb aimed at the grandparents' generation: 할머니, 많이 잡수세요. The full ladder now reads 먹다 → 드시다 → 잡수시다, three rungs on one appetite. The old-school greeting 진지 잡수셨어요? ('have you eaten?') runs it over 진지 — 밥's own honorific upgrade, the swap system reaching even the rice.

The humble see-meet: YOU 뵙다 an elder; the elder 보다-s (M1) you — the mirror half of the honor system, lowering yourself the way M9's 드리다 does for giving. M15's 처음 note filed the formula 처음 뵙겠습니다; here is the verb inside it. Before vowels it writes 뵈-: 내일 봬요 (see you tomorrow, upward), 뵈러 가요 (going to see an elder).

en: to attend to, serve, escort (an elder)
notes: Serve, escort, keep provisioned — upward: 부모님을 모시고 살아요 = we live with (and care for) our parents, the load-bearing sentence of Korean family life; 할머니를 모시고 병원에 가요 escorts her there. 챙기다 (M40) provisions anyone; 모시다 aims the care specifically up the ladder.

돌아가다 (M23, go back) + -(으)시-: the honored RETURN — Korean's gentle verb for an elder's death: 할아버지께서 돌아가셨어요. Never M14's 죽다 for someone you respect: they aren't gone, they've gone back. You will meet it almost only in the past tense, which is where it lives.

親戚 close-kin: 친하다's (M19) close-親 + kin-戚 — the whole extended web, the people 명절 (M25) assembles under one roof: 명절에 친척들이 다 모여요. Also the people culturally licensed to ask about your grades, job, and marriage plans, in that order.

三寸 three-degrees: M2's 삼 + 촌 (寸), the kinship-distance unit — Korea MEASURES family: parent-child is 1촌, siblings 2촌, so dad's brother sits three steps out and is literally named his distance. Kids also deploy it warmly on any uncle-aged man. Your cousin lives one step further: 사촌, the four-degree relative — same arithmetic.

외 (outside-外 — the 외 of 외국, M23) + 삼촌: mom's brother. Traditional kinship files your mother's entire family under OUTSIDE — the 외가, the outside house — a patriarchy fossil the language never buried. The warmth survived the filing: the 외삼촌 is the classic fun uncle.

姑母 father's sister — the 모 is mother-母, 부모님's (M4) second syllable. Her mirror is 이모, mom's sister: the word you've been shouting at restaurant servers since M18's gap deck taught the summons — the actual aunt outranks the 반찬 refills. Korean has no plain word for 'aunt'; every aunt is filed by side.

외 + 할머니 (M4): mom's mom. In a country where grandmothers run the childcare economy, the 외할머니 is statistically the one doing school pickup — the 'outside' grandmother, managing the inside of everything. The prefix maps her whole household: 외할아버지, 외삼촌, 외가.

孫子 grandchild — and 손 number three: M8's hand-손, 손님's (M9) guest-손, now grandchild-孫. The 자 is child-子, hiding in plain sight inside 남자 and 여자 (M4) — man-child, woman-child. 손자 바보, a grandparent gone foolish over the boy, is the gap deck's 딸 바보 pattern run one generation up.

孫女: grandchild-孫 + woman-女 — the same 女 that runs 여자 (M4), spelled 녀 here by the initial-sound law M44's 토론 note documented for 論: soft at the front of a word, full strength inside one. 손자, 손녀, and the gender-neutral 손주 (the one grandparents actually count in) — the grandchild shelf, complete.

Nephew AND niece in one native word — where the aunt shelf splits by side (고모/이모), the sibling's-kid shelf doesn't even split by gender; add M4's 딸 for precision (조카딸). 조카 바보 is a certified personality type: the aunt or uncle whose camera roll is 90% somebody else's child.

兄弟 older-brother-younger-brother: 형 (M4) finally shows its hanja 兄, paired with younger-弟. Brothers strictly, siblings loosely — 형제가 어떻게 되세요? is standard small talk about your sibling lineup. Church Korean calls fellow members 형제님: the family metaphor, institutionalized.

男妹 man-and-younger-sister: 남자's (M4) man-男 + sister-妹. The mixed set: 삼 남매 = three kids counting both kinds (M2's 삼 doing the counting) — the word for somebody's brood, family portraits, and every drama's scheming siblings. 형제 is the brothers' word; 남매 is the ensemble's.

新郎 new-young-man: 신문's (M8) new-新 — the same 신 신혼여행 (M25) unpacked — + 郎, the classical young gentleman. The groom, and then some: in married-couple talk, a wife's 우리 신랑 keeps him 'my groom' decades past the wedding hall.

新婦 new-bride — 신랑 신부 입장! is the ceremony's opening call, the pair walking in together. Radar, courtesy of Korean Catholicism: a priest is ALSO 신부 (神父, god-father) — 신부님, in a collar. One spelling, two vocations, and only one of them is getting married today.

en: one's husband's family, the in-laws' house
notes: The husband's household — the house a bride traditionally married INTO, which is why 시집가다 = (a woman) marries: she literally goes to the in-laws'. The 시- prefix (媤, husband's side) stamps his whole family: 시어머니, 시아버지, and the polite form 시댁 (there's M27's 댁 upgrade, working). Radar: a same-spelled 시집 (詩集, poem-collection — 집중's (M44) gather-集 applied to verse) sits on bookstore shelves; context never confuses the in-laws with the anthology.

시집's groom-side counterpart: 장가가다 = (a man) marries — historically 'moves to the wife's family's house,' from the era when grooms did exactly that. The asymmetric pair is the culture lesson: women 시집가다, men 장가가다, and modern Korean increasingly says 결혼하다 (M25) for both. 장가 survives mostly inside its verb and in relatives' teasing: 언제 장가가?

시- + 어머니: the husband's mother — K-drama's most reliably employed antagonist and the axis the gap deck's 시집살이 turns on. To her face she is 어머님; the prefix does the sociology — hers is the household the bride traditionally entered. Modern in-law relations renegotiate all of it, loudly.

시- + 아버지: the husband's father — at rank 27,910 the deepest word in this module's pool, because Korea discusses the 시어머니 relationship an order of magnitude more. The quieter in-law: addressed 아버님, analyzed rarely.

The daughter-in-law — historically a ROLE more than a person: in the traditional 시집 she joined the labor force. The 며느리/사위 asymmetry is proverbial (her chore list, his chicken), and the whole folk genre of 시집살이 songs is sung in her voice. Address from the in-laws runs affectionate; the word itself stays third-person.

The son-in-law — the honored guest: 사위는 백년손님, 'a son-in-law is a hundred-year guest' (M9's 백, M25's 년, M9's 손님 — assembled entirely from your own shelf): treat him formally forever, feed him the good chicken. The proverb's unspoken other half is the 며느리's workload; the asymmetry runs exactly one direction.

離婚 part-marriage: 결혼's (M25) marriage-婚 with leave-離 prefixed. 이혼하다 = to divorce; 이혼율 is the rate demographers track. Korean handles the word exactly this plainly — a legal noun, not a melodrama — though the dramas respectfully disagree.

妊娠 pregnancy: 임신했어요 = we're expecting — the announcement sentence, usually followed by every 친척 in the phone tree knowing within the hour. 임신부 is the expectant mother the subway seats are marked for; the 아기 (M25) arrives one entry down the shelf.

Give birth: 아기를 낳다, 딸을 낳았어요. Pronunciation radar, the course's best homophone exhibit since the 젓다/젖다 collision M40 staged: the ㅎ falls silent, so 낳아요 sounds exactly like 나아요 — which is ALSO what M14's 낫다 (recover) conjugates to. Korean spellers crash here daily: 병이 빨리 낳았으면 is the internet's favorite typo, wishing an illness a safe delivery.

쌍 (雙, a pair) + -둥이, the affectionate kid-suffix Korean pins on types: 막둥이 (the baby of the family), 귀염둥이 (the cutie), 바람둥이 (the flirt). The pair-kid: a twin, or the twins collectively. 쌍둥이를 낳았어요 doubles everything upstream of it — names, strollers, grandparents' joy.

아이 (M4) worn smooth by speech — that note promised 'often shortened to 애 in speech,' and the 준말 interlude's shrinking law delivers it, the same clip that made M27's 아줌마 from 아주머니. 애가 둘이에요 = we have two kids; 애들 = the kids; 우리 애 = our kid. 아이 is for writing and pediatricians; 애 is for living rooms.

子息 offspring: child-子 (the 자 inside 남자/여자, M4, and 손자 above) + breath-息 — your children at any age: 자식이 둘이에요; 부모와 자식 = parent and child, the relationship's formal name. Register double-agent: aimed at a non-relative — 이 자식! — it flips into a scolding word, roughly 'you punk.' Context and volume tell you which one arrived.

The youngest — the maknae, exported globally by K-pop, where every group has one by law of nature. M30's 첫째/둘째 ladder finally gets its bottom rung: 첫째, 둘째, … 막내 — birth order as a lifelong job title, exactly as 첫째's note warned. Offices run it too: the team 막내 does the coffee run regardless of age.

Look after: 아이를 돌보다, 부모님을 돌보다 — sustained, eyes-on tending; the 보다 inside is M1's see-verb, caring as watching. Sort the caretaking shelf: 챙기다 (M40) provisions in bursts (pack the umbrella, confirm they ate); 돌보다 tends continuously; 모시다 does it upward with the honorifics on.

家庭 house-courtyard: the home as INSTITUTION, completing a three-way radar — 집 (M1) is the building, 가족 (M4) is the people, 가정 is the unit civics discusses: 가정을 이루다 (start a family), 가정 교육 (upbringing — M32's 교육, administered at home). May is 가정의 달, Family Month, with Parents' Day and Children's Day back to back.

老人 old-person: old-老 + the person-人 of 외국인 (M23). The demographic word — news Korean for the world's fastest-aging society; polite speech softens it to 노인분들 or reaches for 어르신, the warmer street honorific (an address word — recognize it, this list doesn't drill it). Radar: this 노 (老) is not 노력's (M39) exert-努 — one is old, the other is trying.

世代 world-age: 세계's (M23) world-世 + 시대's (M26) age-代 — a generation, and the gaps between them: 세대 차이 = the generation gap, the phrase Korean families reach for mid-argument. MZ세대 is marketing Korean for everyone under 45; every generation gets a label and objects to it.

The honorific SUBJECT particle: when the doer outranks you, 이/가 (M1) steps aside — 할아버지께서 오세요 — and the verb agrees with -(으)시-, M4's marker finally meeting its particle. It stacks like its plain twins: 께서는, 께서도. M27's 께 sends things TO an elder; 께서 marks the elder DOING — the set 께's note said 'moves as a set,' now complete.

en: particle — as much as, to the extent of
notes: The equative: 아버지만큼 커요 = as tall as father — not more, not less, THAT much. Three IOUs clear at once: S3's proverb (아는 만큼 보인다), M41's 처럼 lesson ('the measuring cousin waits for a later module'), and M42's 그만큼 ('keeps its appointment'). Calibrate the trio: 보다 (M22) ranks, 처럼 (M41) paints a likeness, 만큼 declares the amounts equal.

現代 now-era: 현재's appear-現 (M35) + 시대's era-代 (M26) — the era that includes today. 현대 미술 (M44's 미술), 현대 사회: the word history books use for 'modern.' And yes, the carmaker — the chaebols shop this shelf for names, and calling your company The Modern Era is ambition with a hanja budget. Same syllables, different parking lot.

年代: M25's 년 + 시대's 代 (M26) = the decade machine — 90년대, read 구십 년대, is the nineties. Korea narrates itself in decades: 70년대 growth, 90년대 pop, and the 응답하라 dramas answering to three of them by name. The same 代 counts age brackets too — 20대, one's twenties — a few shelves down from here.

오늘 (M2) + 날 (M11): today's-day — 'nowadays,' the essay-and-broadcast register. Spoken Korean says 요즘 (M26); written Korean opens paragraphs with 오늘날의 한국은. A register pair, exactly like the pay words M43 sorted — one meaning, two dress codes.

以前 from-before: the 전 of M5's 오전 and M13's -기 전에, finally standing alone — 그 이전에 = before that, 조선 시대 이전 = before the Joseon era. The 이 is 以, 'taking as the line': set a boundary, point backward. Radar: neither M29's this-이 nor the number two — a new job for Korean's busiest syllable.

以後: 이전's mirror — M5's 오후 and M13's -(으)ㄴ 후에 carried the 後 for you; now it takes any noun straight: 졸업 이후 (M44's 졸업), 수업 이후. Where -(으)ㄴ 후에 needs a verb, 이후 rides nouns and dates — the officialese of timelines. 그 이후로 = ever since.

지나다 (M12) wearing M24's badge + 해 — M11's sun moonlighting as 'year,' the job its note filed under 새해. The NEWS word for last year: anchors say 지난해, the break room says 작년 (M25) — the same register split M43 filed for the pay words. One passed year, two dress codes.

The 지난- prefix M25's 지난주 note promised would work the whole calendar (지난달, 지난번) — paid in full: 지나다 + badge + M12's counter-번 = the time before this one. 지난번에 말한 카페 = the cafe I mentioned last time. Vague on purpose: whenever it was, you both know which time.

이 (M29) + 날 (M11): THIS day — but almost never yours. It's newspaper anaphora: name a date, then write 이날 오후 = 'that afternoon.' M29's 그날 points from memory; 이날 points from the page. You now read datelines like a subscriber.

年末 year-end: M25's 년 in word-initial dress — the initial-sound law M44's 토론 note decoded (論 → 논/론) also bends 년 → 연 up front — plus end-末, a new hanja with no relation to M4's speech-말. 연말 is party season, deadline season, and 연말정산, the year-end tax reckoning every office worker suffers in January.

en: one's days, a time of life
notes: 時節 time-season: 시간's 時 (M1) + the season-節 inside M11's 계절 — the seasons of a life. 학생 시절 = one's student days; 어린 시절 = childhood, M21's 어리다 wearing M24's badge. Nostalgia's favorite noun: 그 시절 means 'those days' and arrives pre-sighed.

平生 flat-life: the ordinary-平 of 평일 (M16) and 평소 (M38) + the life-生 of 학생 (M4) and 생활 (M29) — the whole level stretch of a life. 평생 친구 = a lifelong friend; 평생 공부 = the studying that never ends, this course's honest job description. K-dramas sell 평생 사랑; teachers sell the other one.

將來 about-to-come: the come-來 inside M25's 미래 with 將 (about-to) in front — the future, but specifically YOURS. Said [장내], the ㄹ ducking to ㄴ after ㅇ. 장래 희망 (M34's 희망) is the school-form blank for 'future dream' — every Korean adult once wrote 과학자 or 가수 in it. 미래 belongs to cities and robots; 장래 is the one your parents worry about.

언제 (M10) + -ㄴ가, the wondering syllable (the same one that hedges guesses in -(으)ㄴ가 보다, from M34's seeming machinery): some-when. It points both ways — 언젠가 한국에서 살 거예요 = someday I'll live in Korea; 언젠가 봤어요 = I saw it sometime. The dream-tense adverb; half of K-pop runs on it.

한 (M5's 하나 in combining form) + M25's 때: one-time — a chapter that closed. 한때는 가수였어요 = I was a singer, once; the topic-는 does the distancing. Everyone owns a 한때; slang imported a deluxe version, 리즈 시절 — 'Leeds days,' from a footballer's best years — for when the 한때 was glorious.

The determiner M24's 옛날 note pre-decoded (옛 + 날): old, worn only in front of a noun, exactly like M13's 새 — the shelf's matched bookends. 옛 친구 = an old friend, 옛 모습 (M34's 모습) = how it used to look, 옛 노래 = the oldies. 새 breaks things in; 옛 breaks your heart.

永遠 long-far: a NEW 영 — eternal-永, no relation to 영화 (M2) or 영어 (M10) — welded to far-遠, your fourth 원 after M6's hospital-院 and park-園 and M9's ₩. 사랑은 영원해요 is K-drama's thesis statement; 아무것도 영원하지 않아요 — M28's long negation doing philosophy — is its series finale.

영원하다 through M42's -히 factory — 당연히, 확실히, 다행히, and now forever: the rack keeps stamping. K-pop's favorite adverb: 영원히 함께 (M29's 함께) is carved into fan signs, rings, and at least one bridge padlock per couple. Say it sparingly; mean it once.

The prefix M26's 첫눈 note pre-decoded ('처음's prefix form') goes free-standing: first, worn before a noun like 새 and 옛 — the determiner shelf seats three now. 첫 만남, 첫 월급 (M16's 월급), 첫사랑: Korean firsts get their own words because firsts are a genre here. Radar: M15's 처음 stands alone ('for the first time'); 첫 must hold something.

M12's counter-번 + -째: the ordinal machine. Native numbers drive it in combining form (M5's 하나/둘/셋 → 한/두/세): 두 번째, 세 번째 — but first place belongs to 첫: 첫 번째. 몇 번째예요? (M5's 몇) = which one in line — the question the 차례 shelf below runs on.

첫 + M11's 날, said [천날] — the same nasal slide 첫눈 taught. 입학 첫날 (M44's 입학), 새해 첫날, 출근 첫날: the day everything is hardest and most photographed. Its opposite number uses M15's 마지막 — 마지막 날 — so you now hold both ends of anything.

最初 most-first: the most-最 of 최고 (M19) and 최근 (M32) + beginning-初 — the third 초, exactly the one M25's candle note radar'd (candle, the clock's second, and 초등학교's start-syllable: this is that one). 세계 최초 (M23's 세계) = world's first, news-Korean's favorite boast. Radar: 처음 is YOUR first time; 최초 is history's.

次例 next-in-line: order and turns — 제 차례예요 = it's my turn; the 례 is M33's example-예 in mid-word dress, the initial-sound law again. And the homograph that owns the holidays: 차례 (茶禮), tea-차 (M2) + the courtesy-예 of 예의 (M26) — the ancestral table set on 명절 mornings, the ceremony M25's 추석 note fed. 차례를 지내다 — M23's 지내다, on ritual duty. One spelling: your turn at the counter, and the rite at dawn.

初盤 opening-board: 최초's beginning-初 + a board-盤 — the Go board, where games phase 초반/중반/후반 as the stones fill. Now it phases everything: 20대 초반 = early twenties (시대's 代 counting age brackets), 영화 초반 = the film's first act. English says 'early on'; Korean sees a board position.

後半 after-half: M5's 오후-後 + — surprise — M5's actual half-반, where 초반's 반 was the board-盤. Different hanja, same shelf: your third 반 overall, counting M15's classroom one. 후반전 = the second half of a match; 인생 후반 (M25's 인생) = life's second half. Same whistle, longer game.

當場 the-very-spot: the fitting-當 inside 당연하다 (M34) + the place-場 of 장소 (M27) — on this spot, this instant. 지금 당장! = RIGHT now, the parent's ultimatum register, zero installments accepted. It has a softer job too: 당장은 괜찮아요 = for the moment, it's fine.

當分間 this-portion-interval: 당장's 當 + M5's minute-分 (the portion that cuts hours) + the between-間 of 시간 (M1). For now, until things settle: 당분간 쉬세요 = rest for the time being — the doctor's word, the coach's word, and the sign taped to every temporarily closed shop door (당분간 휴업).

en: for a while, for some time
notes: 한 (one) + M28's 동안: one-stretch — a while long enough that you noticed it. 한동안 못 만났어요 = we didn't see each other for a while. It joins 그동안, which M28's 동안 note already runs, on the rack — and the next entry stretches the same rack further.

M10's 오래 + M28's 동안 with the linking-ㅅ wedged in — the same wedge M40's 고춧가루 note filed: a LONG stretch. 오랫동안 기다렸어요 = I waited a long time. Its cousin 오랜만 (M19) measures the gap between two meetings; 오랫동안 measures the stretch itself. Gap or stretch, Korean clocks both.

M27's 어느 (which) + 덧, an old sliver of time: at-some-unnoticed-point. The sigh adverb: 어느덧 연말이에요 = somehow it's already year-end; 어느덧 십 년 = ten years, gone. Its sibling 어느새 says the same thing slightly faster. The gap deck files what this word feels like from the inside.

The fuzzy 때: around-when. It takes a noun straight — 저녁 무렵 (M2's 저녁, going amber) — or rides M25's third badge exactly like 때 does: 해가 질 무렵 = around sunset, M17's 지다 working the sunset job its note promised. 때 pins a moment; 무렵 admits that dusk has no timestamp.

M6's 앞 + M40's 두다: to have a thing PLACED in front of you — 시험을 앞두고 있어요 = the exam sits ahead, parked there by the calendar. News-Korean's setup verb: 선거를 앞두고 = with the election ahead. The grammar of looming, built from M40's calm put-and-keep verb.

M28's 계속 grew 하다 in M35 (계속하다); swap in 되다 — the move M36 formalized for the whole 하다-family (시작하다 → 시작되다) — and things continue BY THEMSELVES: 회의가 계속되고 있어요 (M10's 회의, refusing to end), 전쟁이 계속되면 (M32's 전쟁). You 계속하다 your studies; the rain just 계속되다-s. The news verb for whatever won't stop.

The stopwatch noun: [verb + M24's past badge] + 지 + duration + 됐어요/지났어요/넘었어요 — how long it's been SINCE. Always spaced, always after -(으)ㄴ: 배운 지, 만난 지, 산 지. RADAR, three 지-jobs in one syllable: this counting-지, a noun that wears a space · the glued -지 of -지 않다 (M28) and -지 마세요 (M14) · the question-folder -는지 (M33). The space is the tell — if 지 stands apart, someone's counting.

소리 (M19) + 치다 (M17): STRIKE a sound into the air — the hit-play verb's loudest career yet, after pianos and rackets. 크게 소리쳤어요 = shouted out loud; fans do it at concerts, parents do it at 씨름 broadcasts, and drowning dialogue does it in every drama. 부르다 (M19) calls a person; 소리치다 just launches the voice.

크다 (M1) wearing M24's badge + 소리 (M19): the big sound — 큰소리로 읽으세요 = read it out loud. Radar for the second job: 큰소리치다 (치다 again) = to talk big, bluster, promise what you can't deliver — 큰소리만 치고 아무것도 안 해요. A loud voice and an empty boast share one word; Korean noticed the overlap first.

en: to make a racket, chatter loudly
notes: The teacher's verb: 떠들지 마세요! — M14's don't-machine, aimed at the back row. ㄹ-verb like 만들다 (M3): 떠들어요. M13's 시끄럽다 is the STATE of noise; 떠들다 is the activity producing it — one describes the room, the other convicts the people in it.

노래 (M7) + 소리 (M19), welded with the linking-ㅅ that M40's 고춧가루 flagged (젓가락 wears one too, M18): song-sound — singing heard from somewhere, as a sound in the air. Joins M19's 목소리 on the -소리 shelf: 목소리 is a voice; 노랫소리 is a voice at work on a melody, usually drifting through a wall.

들리다 (M36) + 오다 (M1): heard-and-arriving — sound that travels TO you. 옆집에서 노랫소리가 들려와요 = singing drifts in from next door. M36's passive party taught that Korean perception receives; this verb adds the journey: the world's sounds commute to your ear.

흐르다 (M35 — whose note already let music 흐르다) + 나오다 (M28): flow-and-emerge. What cafes, radios, and open doors do to songs: 문 밖으로 음악이 흘러나와요. The 르-family conjugation comes pre-applied — the 흘러 is frozen mid-flow. Light and secrets 흘러나오다 too; anything that escapes a container in a stream.

Radar before the reflex: this 들리- is NOT M36's be-heard — it's M37's causative party, MAKE-heard — plus M9's -아/어 주다 do-it-for-me frame: make it heard, as a favor. 노래 들려주세요 = play me a song; grandmothers 들려주다 old stories, playlists 들려주다 moods. Same surface as the passive, opposite direction of travel.

en: to turn on, put on (music, TV, fan)
notes: The play button. Radar vs M13's 켜다: 켜다 lights it up (lamps, screens, engines); 틀다 sets it FLOWING — 음악을 틀다, 에어컨을 틀다, the tap, the fan. Anything with a stream inside gets 틀다-ed. ㄹ-verb: 틀어요 — 노래 좀 틀어 주세요 is how every road trip starts.

M48's 녹음 decoded 錄音 (engrave-sound) and promised this verb in the same breath — paid: 노래를 녹음하다, 수업을 녹음하다, and the app-era default 통화 녹음 (Korea records its phone calls; ask before you're surprised). Video gets its own sibling, 녹화 — engrave-picture — waiting on a later shelf.

樂器 music-tool: the 악 has been hiding at the end of 음악 (M2) since Module 2 — music-樂, finally alone in the light. The 기 is tool-器 — a different hanja from 비행기's machine-機 (M12), same career. 악기를 다루다 is the formal phrase, but each instrument brings its own verb, and the next two entries prove it.

The barrel drum — 북을 치다 (M17's 치다, in its original percussion job), heartbeat of 사물놀이, the farmers' four-instrument ensemble, and of every stadium cheering section. RADAR, and it's a big one: the 북 of 북쪽 (M27) and 북한 (M31) is north-北, a Sino syllable; this 북 is native and hollow. The compass and the drum share a spelling and nothing else.

Rhythm through the Konglish converter: the r survives as ㄹ (the interlude's one-liquid-fits-all rule) and the impossible -thm tail gets an ㅡ cushion — 리듬, two syllables where English mumbles one and a half. 리듬을 타다 = ride the rhythm — Korean surfs its beats. Also 생활 리듬 = the rhythm of daily life, what jet lag breaks.

Violin, converter-standard: v → ㅂ (the 비디오/서비스 rule). The verb is the surprise — 바이올린을 켜다, M13's turn-on verb, whose older native job was sawing friction (you 켜다 a saw, and once upon a time, fire). Bowed strings saw; keys and drums 치다 (M17). Korean sorts its orchestra by hand motion.

拍手 strike-hands: the 수 is 세수's hand-手 (M37), and the verb is — inevitably — 박수를 치다: M17's 치다 collects applause too. Korean audiences clap ALONG, on the beat, unprompted — 박수 문화 turns every concert into a rhythm section. 박수를 받다 (M9's 받다) = to be applauded; the gap deck files the proverb about when to stop.

en: Korean pop song, K-pop (as a genre)
notes: 歌謠 song-ballad — the song-歌 that M48's 작가 note filed for 가수 (M4), plus ballad-謠. Radar vs 노래 (M7): 노래 is A song, any song; 가요 is the GENRE — Korean popular music as a category, the word radio charts used before 'K-pop' went abroad. Grandma's lane of it is 트로트; all of it is 가요.

歌詞 song-words: what you're reading on the 노래방 screen. 가사를 외우다 (M15's 외우다 — this app's business model, applied to choruses); 가사가 좋아요 is the compliment for songs that mean something. Radar: a homograph 가사 (家事) means housework — 노래 가사 you memorize, 집안 가사 you postpone. Context sorts the chores from the chorus.

舞踊 — both hanja mean dance; the word is doubly dancing, the way M48's 배우 was doubly an actor. Radar vs M17's 춤: 춤을 추다 at the club and the 노래방; 무용 at the theater — 한국 무용, 현대 무용, a 무용가 on a poster. Same body, different ticket price. The dance-舞 returns two entries down, holding up a stage.

舞臺 dance-platform: 무용's dance-舞 + platform-臺 — the raised floor performance happens on. 무대에 오르다 (M22's 오르다: mountains, stairs, prices, and now performers) = to take the stage; 첫 무대 = a debut stage, K-pop's sacrament. Figurative too: 세계 무대 = the world stage, where the news likes to put Korea.

Concert, with the converter's ㅡ-cushions installed (the 테스트 rule: crowded consonants get vowels). Register: M48's 공연 is the umbrella — any live show, plays included; 콘서트 is the music one. 콘서트장 = the venue (the place-場 economy, still hiring); when the act is big enough, the venue is the next entry but one.

en: to be in fashion, be trending
notes: M21's 유행 finally conjugates — and decodes: 流行 flow-go. Trends FLOW; the hanja agrees with M35's 흐르다 about how fashion moves. 요즘 유행하는 노래 = the song going around; 유행가 = a hit song, 유행어 = a catchphrase — the flow-family stamps whatever the whole country is suddenly doing. M21 warned that last season is archaeology; now you can say why.

Konglish, with a clean division of labor: M22's 별 keeps the sky, 스타 takes the famous — 톱스타, 스타가 되다 (to become a star). English made the metaphor; Korean imported only the showbiz half and left the astronomy at customs — the false-friend pattern's gentler cousin: specialization.

The converter's f → ㅍ rule runs twice and lands both English words on one syllable: FAN — 팬클럽, 팬미팅 (a real meet-your-fans event, no relation to the interlude's blind-date 미팅), 저 그 가수 팬이에요 — and PAN, the kitchen kind, usually 프라이팬. Fandom is the sense Korea runs on; the skillet just shares the spelling.

Show — 토크쇼, 쇼 프로그램 (M32). But the word's best work is sarcastic: 쇼를 하다 = to put on an act, and 쇼하지 마 (M14's don't-machine, dropped to 반말 like M48's 소설 쓰지 마) = quit the theatrics. Deny a drama queen the -를 and you've diagnosed one: 쇼하네.

One clip, two careers. M32's 프로그램 note promised that a TV show is often just 프로 — paid: 무슨 프로 봐요? = what shows do you watch? Job two is professional: 프로 선수 (M17's 선수 gone salaried), and the register wink 프로의 세계 — 'the world of the pros,' said gravely about any craft done seriously, including yours.

Series through the converter: both s-sounds survive, the z lands on ㅈ (the 피자/사이즈 rule). 드라마 시리즈 (M17's 드라마, now with seasons), book 시리즈 — and baseball's 한국시리즈, the championship round where M17's 야구 crowns its year. English plural, Korean singular: one 시리즈, many episodes.

The false-friend file (미팅, 컨닝 — the Konglish reading's table) gains its TV wing: NOT talent, but a television drama actor — a title from the era when broadcasters trained their casts in-house. Radar vs M48's 배우: 배우 acts anywhere (film, stage); 탤런트 is specifically the drama-screen kind, and the word itself now reads a little retro — like the shows it starred in.

en: to appear (on a show, in a film)
notes: 出演 out-perform: the out-出 whose whole family M43's 수출 note counted (출구, 출발, 출근), plus the perform-演 that M48 decoded inside 공연 and 연기 — to step OUT and perform, i.e., to appear on. 방송에 출연하다 (M32's 방송), 드라마에 출연하다; the credits call the cast 출연진. The particle is 에: you appear ONTO the program.

大會 great-gathering: the great-大 of 대학교 (M15) + the gather-會 running through 회사 (M2), 회의 (M10), and 사회 (M32) — a gathering big enough to crown somebody. 노래 대회, 요리 대회, and the one with your name on it: 한국어 말하기 대회 — speaking contests for learners are a real circuit, and M13's -기 builds their names.

參加 join-add: add yourself to the roster. The particle is 에 — 대회에 참가하다, 올림픽에 참가하다: you participate INTO the event. 참가자 = participant (the person-者 M43's 소비자 filed), 참가비 = the entry fee that finds you at every marathon and 축제 (M25).

M17's 경기 + the place-場 that paves 시장 (M3), 주차장 (M37), and 공장 (M43): the grounds where matches happen. 축구 경기장, 야구 경기장 — and on off-days the biggest 콘서트s move in, because only a stadium holds that many 팬. When an act 'books the 경기장,' they've made it.

The Olympics — and in Korea the word means a year before it means a sport: 1988. The 서울 올림픽 was the country's coming-out party, the moment postwar Korea stood up on the world 무대 — and the city still navigates by it: 올림픽공원, 올림픽대로. 올림픽에 참가하다, 겨울 올림픽 (평창, 2018) — the word stays warm.

World + M18's 컵 — the trophy is right there in the name. In Korea the word means June 2002: the home-soil semifinal run, entire cities in red shirts, M23's 광장 doing exactly what its note said Seoul gathers there to do. The sound of that summer — 대~한민국, five claps — waits in the gap deck, because M31's 대한민국 note promised you a stadium chant.

優勝 excel-win — the excel-優 also fronts M48's 배우 (俳優). Radar vs M17's 이기다: 이기다 wins a MATCH; 우승 wins the whole thing — you 이기다 six times and 우승 once. 우승하다 = to take the title; 우승컵 = the trophy (M18's 컵, again, engraved this time). What every 대회 exists to award.

The sand-ring folk sport: two wrestlers grip each other's belt, and the first to touch ground loses. 추석 (M25) afternoons traditionally run 씨름 대회 on TV, and the champion earns the title 천하장사 — 'strongest under heaven' — plus, classically, an ox. Bonus career: 씨름하다 = to wrestle WITH anything — 시험 문제하고 씨름해요 (M7's 문제): studying, as full-contact sport.

Throw: 공을 던지다 (M17's ball — the ceremonial first pitch is a national honor roll), but Korean also throws intangibles — 질문을 던지다 (M10's 질문): to POSE a question, lobbed into the room; 몸을 던지다 = throw yourself into something, bodily commitment. If it leaves your hand or your comfort zone, 던지다.

Pull and drag — 의자를 끌다, a suitcase, a reluctant 동생 — but its star job is magnetism: 인기를 끌다 = to draw popularity (M17's 인기, upgraded from having to ATTRACTING), 관심을 끌다 = pull attention, 시간을 끌다 = drag time out, stalling. ㄹ-verb: 끌어요. Feed it to M36's machine and the pull reverses: 마음이 끌려요 — I'm drawn to it.

大都市: the big-大 fronting 대학교 (M15) and 대중 (M48), stamped onto 도시 (M22). Korea is a nation of them — roughly nine in ten Koreans live urban, and the 대도시 roll call (서울, 부산, 인천…) doubles as the KTX timetable. The 대- prefix sizes up whatever it touches; it is not done working.

en: center, heart (of a place or matter)
notes: 中心 middle-heart: the middle-中 of 중학교 (M15) and S2's busy-sign 중, plus the heart-心 beating in 관심 and 진심 (both M24) — the center, located exactly where anatomy would put it. 시내 중심 = the heart of downtown; 관심의 중심 = the center of attention. Korea measures everything by distance from one 중심 — the next word is what lies beyond it.

地方 land-direction: 지역's land-地 (M31) + 방향's direction-方 (M31) — the regions, which in practice means everywhere that isn't 서울 and its orbit. The 중심-vs-지방 pull is Korea's oldest tension: jobs, universities, and drama plots all migrate capital-ward. Radar, mandatory: a second 지방 (脂肪) is body fat — 트랜스 지방 glares from every snack label. Same spelling; one is on the map, the other on the nutrition panel.

市民 city-people: the city-市 that M31's 시청 note filed + 국민's people-民 (M32). 서울 시민 = a Seoulite — but the word also does civic duty: the news praises 시민 who return lost wallets and line up in disasters. 국민 answers to the country; 시민 answers to the town.

Konglish 'building' — but narrower than its English parent: a 빌딩 is the tall, glassy, elevator-ed kind. M22's 건물 is ANY building, down to the two-story 치킨집; when a 건물 grows into the skyline, Korean switches languages — the same passport rule M40's 소스 note found on the sauce shelf. 63빌딩, Seoul's gold tower, wears the loanword officially.

建築 build-erect: building as a discipline. The 건 retro-decodes 건물 (M22) — build-建 + thing-物 — and springs a radar: 물건 (M9) is 物件, thing-item. 건물/물건 look like mirror twins, but only the 물 (物) is shared; one 건 builds, the other itemizes. A 건축가 designs the 빌딩 above — the person-suffix parade continues below.

施設 lay-out-and-set-up: anything installed for people to use. The realtor's favorite line is 편의 시설 — convenience facilities, the same 편의 that names the 편의점 (M6): gym, parking, the works. 시설이 좋아요 is the entire text of most hotel and gym reviews.

空間 empty-between: 공항's sky-空 (M12 — the hanja M43's 공장 note filed) + the between-間 of 시간 (M1), the one M32's 인간 does philosophy with. Emptiness between things = space itself: 주차 공간 (a parking spot), 공간이 없어요 (no room). 자리 (M12) is a spot with your name on it; 공간 is the volume around it.

M31's 위치 (place-put) + 하다: to sit somewhere, in writing — 시청은 시내 중심에 위치해 있어요 is how a guidebook says it; a mouth just says 있어요. The written city's verb shelf opens here and continues at 향하다 below: Korean keeps a spoken city and a printed one, and this module stocks both.

길 (M12) + 거리 (M27), welded: the street as the place you're standing in. M27 split the pair — 길 the way you take, 거리 the street-scene; 길거리 is the pavement itself, which is why it fronts Korea's finest institution: 길거리 음식, street food. 길거리에서 = out on the street.

골목 (M22) + 길 (M12): the alley-road — technically redundant, emotionally precise. 골목길 is the nostalgia register: childhood games, corner shops, dramas shot in warm light before the 재개발 (redevelopment) crews arrive. M22 measured Korean urban charm in 골목s per block; 골목길 is that charm, paved.

高速道路 high-speed-way-road: 최고's high-高 (M19) + speed-速 (new — the 속 inside everything fast Korea builds) + 도로 (M38), whose note promised this word was 'fully decodable.' Debt paid, at 100 km/h. Every 명절 (M25) turns it into a parking lot, relieved only by the 휴게소 — the rest stop, a food court with a highway attached.

Konglish 'tunnel,' and geography's favorite loanword here: Korea is two-thirds mountains, so every intercity drive alternates 터널 and bridge, and 남산 (M31) alone keeps three numbered ones. Warning shot for the next entry: 터널 and 터미널 sit one syllable and a world apart.

Konglish 'terminal': where the intercity buses live — 고속버스 터미널, the set piece of every hometown visit and army send-off. The promised radar: add 미 and the mountain hole becomes a building full of buses. Seoul's 고속터미널 names a subway stop, a mall, and a flower market that never sleeps.

맞다 (M15) wearing M24's badge + the side-편 of 건너편 (M23) — the same 便 that relaxes in 편하다 (M12): the side that faces you. 은행 맞은편에 있어요 = it's across from the bank (M6's 은행). Kin sorted: 건너편 is the side you cross TO, 맞은편 the side squared up opposite you — across one street, the same asphalt.

곳 (M12) doubled: place-place = all over — the WRITTEN everywhere: headlines say 전국 곳곳 (M31's 전국, rained on in parts). Doubling is a Korean production line — 빨리빨리 set the tempo from M8's gap deck; 곳곳 does the geography.

여기 + 저기 (both M6), welded: the SPOKEN all-over, 곳곳's register twin. 여기저기 다녔어요 = I went all around (M16's 다니다); 여기저기 아파요 = I hurt everywhere — the clinic's most-heard opener. Print writes 곳곳; mouths say 여기저기 — file the pair beside M16's 월급 and M43's 임금.

大衆交通: the compound M48's 대중 note pre-assembled — the great-crowd, now with a fleet. The 교통 is M12's, its through-通 the one M32's 통하다 finally conjugated: traffic that moves the masses THROUGH. Korea's is genuinely world-class — clean, cheap, tapped into with the 교통카드 — which is why a carless 서울 시민 is a lifestyle, not a hardship.

電鐵 electric-rail: 전기's electric-電 (M36) + the rail-철 of 지하철 (M6). The radar: 지하철 says underground, but much of the metropolitan network runs in daylight — 전철 is the technically-correct, wider word (수도권 전철, the capital-region network; 수도 M31). Mouths still say 지하철; route maps and announcements reach for 전철.

列車 row-of-carts: cars in a row = a train, in its announcement register — 이번 열차 is the phrase every platform speaks. 기차 (M12) is what mouths say; 열차 is what the PA system says, and what the KTX officially is: 고속열차, the high-speed one. The register ledger gains another row.

自動車 self-moving-cart — a three-character poem for the horseless carriage, and a grade-A debt paid: the self-自 of 자유 (M23) and 자신 (M26), the move-動 inside 운동하다 (M8), and M2's 차, whose tea-note flagged the car meaning on day two. Register: 차 is what you SAY; 자동차 is what forms and news say. Its pedal cousin confesses too — 자전거 (M10) is 自轉車, the self-TURNING cart: you are the motor.

乘用車 riding-use-car: the passenger car in its census register. The 용 is the use-用 of 사용하다 (M10); the 승 is boarding-乘, the one that also lifts 승객 (passengers) and elevators — winks only. The trio completes: 차 in the mouth, 자동차 on the form, 승용차 in the statistics. If you ever say 승용차 aloud, you are probably reading a police report.

運轉者: 운전하다 (M10) finally shows its parts — carry-運, turn-轉 — plus the person-者 from 기자's note (M16): the one turning the wheel. This is the law's word; the news counts 운전자s. Face to face you say 기사님 — the different word (技士) that M48's 기사 note radar-flagged. On paper a 운전자, in the mirror a 기사님.

교통 (M12) + 사고 (M36): the compound M36's own note pre-built, now official. It happens with M28's 나다 — 교통사고가 났어요 is the sentence every insurance call opens with — and it is why every Korean windshield carries a 블랙박스 (Konglish: dashcam) that saw the whole thing.

駐車 stationed-car: parking itself — the 주차 that 주차장 (M37) has carried since Band 4, finally standing alone. You have held the parking LOT for two bands; today you receive the parking. 주차 금지 = no parking (S2's sign kit), 주차 공간 = a spot, scarcer in Seoul than forgiveness; 주차하다 parks the verb.

The everything-mover, rank 491 because everything does it: bodies (움직이지 마세요! — M14's don't-machine, doctor's edition), vehicles (차가 안 움직여요, rush hour's verdict), hearts and plans (마음이 움직였어요 = I was moved, M19's 마음). Runs both ways: things 움직이다 on their own, and you 움직이다 them.

방향's facing-向 (M31) + 하다: to head toward — the written register of 가다. 기차는 서울로 향했다 is a novel's sentence; a mouth says 서울로 가요. Faces and hearts aim with it too: 문을 향해 (facing the door, M6's 문). Shelved beside 위치하다 above, in the printed city.

en: to step out; to step forward, meddle
notes: 나 (the out- of 나가다, M8) + 서다 (M14): step out — 길을 나서다 = set out from the door, every journey's first verb. Second job, the radar: stepping FORWARD where you weren't invited — 나서지 마세요 (M14's don't-machine) is what Korean tells the meddler and the over-volunteer. Out of the house: good. Into other people's business: 나서다, frowned upon.

en: to step into; to go up (be built)
notes: 들어 (the entering of 들어가다, M28) + 서다 (M14): step into — 골목길에 들어서면 (M20's -(으)면) the traffic noise drops away. Second job: buildings step into streets — 새 빌딩이 들어서다 = a new tower goes up (M13's 새). A city where things constantly 들어서다 is exactly the city this module lives in.

오다 + 가다 (both M1), welded nose-to-tail — the tightest compound in the course. 사람들이 오가는 거리 (M24's badge on M27's 거리) is the establishing shot of every city scene; messages, seasons, and glances also 오가다. M28 built [action]+가다; this one welds the compass to itself.

건너다 (M12) + 가다: M28's compound-motion machine admits its crossing member — go across, away from the speaker: 길을 건너가다. Its mirror 건너오다 comes across toward you, per the M6 compass that governs the whole family. M23's 건너편 named the destination; here is the verb that reaches it.

Move a THING from here to there: 짐을 옮기다 (M13's 짐), 자리를 옮기다 (change seats — M12's 자리 — or jobs). 이사하다 (M13) is this verb at whole-house scale. Radar: 말을 옮기다 = carrying words from room to room — gossip's official verb. Some cargo shouldn't ship.

Sweep a place with your eyes: 시장을 둘러보다 (M3's 시장), 동네를 둘러보다 (M22's 동네). M16 gave 보다 its compound careers; this one browses. Radar vs 구경하다 (M22): 구경 enjoys the sights, 둘러보다 surveys the perimeter — festival stroll vs realtor's walkthrough. 그냥 둘러보고 있어요 = just looking (M24's 그냥, repelling shopkeepers nationwide).

다가 (up close) + 오다 (M1): to approach — footsteps, buses, strangers, and everything on the calendar: 시험이 다가와요 (M10's 시험, gaining on you), 겨울이 다가와요 (M11's 겨울, likewise). Mirror 다가가다 approaches AWAY from you, M6-compass as always. When a drama wants dread or romance, something 다가오다-s in slow motion.

The general-purpose stop: feet, machines, music, hearts — 버스가 갑자기 멈췄어요 (M28's 갑자기), 시간이 멈춘 것 같아요 (M34's hedge, tourist's review of a 골목길). The stop-shelf sorts itself: 그치다 (M11) is weather-only, 세우다 (M12) makes a VEHICLE stand from the driver's seat, 멈추다 stops anything — including itself: 멈춰요 it stops, 멈추세요 stop it.

지나다 (M12) pushed past its target: to pass by WITHOUT stopping — 정류장을 지나쳤어요 = I missed my stop (M12's 정류장), this module's most useful confession. Mandatory second sense, and NIKL grades it higher: as an adjective, excessive — 지나친 농담 (M19's 농담, gone too far), 지나치게 비싸요 (M33's -게). One word walks past and overdoes; both senses are 'too far' — one on foot, one in judgment.

To bump, collide: 어깨를 부딪치다 (M14's 어깨) — the involuntary greeting of any crowded street, 명동 on a Saturday being the national championship. Cars do it too, which is where 교통사고 above begins. Says 부딛치다. Its done-to sibling 부딪히다 files with M36's passive party: 치다 collides, 히다 got collided with.

Light itself — and the shelf's root: 햇빛 (sun's), 달빛 (달 M16), 별빛 (별 M22); tacked after a color it names the glow (금빛 = gold-hued). Feed it to M28's 나다 machine and it shines: 빛나다 = light emerges = to shine, the verb inside half of K-pop's choruses. Says 빋; the ㅊ resurfaces before a vowel — 빛이 = 비치.

太陽 great-sun: the sun as astronomy and anthems say it — 태양계 = the solar system, and the drama title 태양의 후예 ('Descendants of the Sun') runs on its blaze. Everyday Korean keeps M11's 해 for the same star. Radar: this 양 is sun-陽, NOT the ocean-洋 stamped on 서양 (M31) and M40's 양파 — same syllable, opposite elements.

地球 land-ball: the 지 is 지역's land-地 (M31), the 구 is 야구/축구's ball-球 (M17) — Earth is literally 'the land ball', which is exactly what it is. 지구 온난화 = global warming, the word's busiest beat. NIKL radar: a homograph 지구 (地區) is a zoned DISTRICT — 재개발 지구, 아파트 지구 — city-hall Korean, same sound, much smaller planet.

해 (M11) + linking-ㅅ (the wedge from M40's 고춧가루 note) + 빛: sun-light, the one you SEE — 햇빛이 밝아요 (밝다 M13), sunglasses weather. The 해-triple starts here and sharpens as it goes: 햇빛 you see, 햇살 slants, 햇볕 warms. Says 핻삗.

The sun rendered as THREADS: 아침 햇살 — morning light slanting through a window, the word ballads and apartment ads reach for. The 살 is the rib-and-spoke word (an umbrella's frame is 우산살 — M9's 우산 has 살 too). 햇빛 is plain light; 햇살 is light with texture.

The sun you FEEL on your skin: 햇볕이 뜨거워요 (뜨겁다 M18 — hot to the touch, because 볕 is heat, not glare). Laundry, grandmothers, and cats all seek it, and the 1998 햇볕 정책 — the Sunshine Policy — was named for the fable where warmth, not wind, gets the coat off. The triple completes: see 햇빛, admire 햇살, sit in 햇볕.

The cast shadow — it carries 그림 (M15) inside, and earns it: the picture your body draws on the pavement. M41's 처럼 makes it the stock simile — 그림자처럼, like a shadow: anyone who never leaves your side. Radar: the next entry is NOT its synonym — Korean splits what English blurs.

Where the light isn't: the cool patch under the tree — 나무 그늘에서 쉬어요. 그림자 is the shape a thing CASTS; 그늘 is the shelter you STAND in. The metaphor runs deep both ways: 부모님 그늘 = the shelter of your parents' care, and a worried face 그늘이 지다 — wears a shadow.

氣溫 air-warmth: the 기 is 공기's air-氣 (M22 — the same energy-氣 inside 전기 M36 and 용기 M39) + 온천's warm-溫 (M23). The forecast's own word: 아침 기온, 최고 기온 — when the TV reads out numbers, it says 기온. Every other temperature lives next door.

溫度 warm-degree: 온천's 溫 again + 정도's degree-度 (M32) — temperature of ANYTHING: 물 온도, 방 온도, the aircon's setting. 기온 is the sky's temperature; 온도 is everything's. The counter it reads out is that same 도: 이십 도 = twenty degrees.

덥다 (M11) pressed into a noun: the ㅂ softens to 우 (the same softening that makes 더워요) and -이 rides in — 더위, THE heat, the season-long thing you survive rather than describe. What the heat does to you personally is 더위를 타다 — the gap deck files 타다's strangest ride.

춥다 (M11) through the same press: 추워요 → 추위. Korea's cold keeps a schedule with names — 꽃샘추위 is the spiteful late-March snap that returns 'jealous of the flowers' (꽃 M7). File the pair 더위/추위 together: weather as something you ENDURE, nouned.

The native season-word — 계절 (M11) is the calendar's term; 철 is the market's: 딸기 철 (딸기 M30) = strawberry season, 제철 과일 = fruit in ITS season. One syllable, three careers, all on the NIKL ledger: 철이 들다 = your seasons come in = to grow up (a kid still green is 철없다); and iron-鐵 — the rail inside M6's 지하철 and all of 철도. Season, sense, steel.

The summer downpour that arrives loud and leaves in twenty minutes — you don't fight a 소나기, you wait under an awning. If M11's 비 is rain the weather, 소나기 is rain the EVENT. Hwang Sun-won's 1950s novella 소나기 — the first-love story every Korean reads in middle school — made the word permanently bittersweet.

Fog — and its verb is M21's 끼다: 안개가 꼈어요 = fog has settled in. The snug-fit verb for rings and gloves is also what mist does to a valley: it slots itself in (clouds and smoke 끼다 too). 안개등 = fog lights, driving-school Korean.

Lightning — the flash, and everything fast: M41's 처럼 gives you 번개처럼, quick as lightning. Slang made it social: a 번개 is a spur-of-the-moment meetup, announced an hour ahead in the group chat — 오늘 저녁에 번개 어때요? The rumble that answers it is next door.

Thunder — nearly always in the fixed pair 천둥 번개, and its verb is M17's 치다: 천둥이 쳐요 = thunder strikes, the racket-and-piano hit-verb moonlighting as weather. The word descends from 天動 — 'heaven moves' — which is exactly what it sounds like.

The ground itself — soil, dirt, what seeds want. Says 흑; the ㄺ batchim plays by 맑다's rule (M11): ㄱ alone at the end, both letters alive before a vowel — 흙이 = 흘기. Modern Korea sorted itself by spoons, and this word holds the bottom rung: 금수저 born golden, 흙수저 born to dirt — M18's 수저, graded by birth.

Sand — what 바닷가 (M23) is made of, poured through hourglasses and children's fists. 모래성 (+ 성 M23) = the sand castle, the tide's favorite demolition project; 모래사장 = the proper sand-beach. Anything built on it is proverbially doomed — Korean and English agree on that one.

Rock at boulder scale: 돌 (M22) you can throw; 바위 you climb on. You've chanted it since someone first taught you 가위바위보 — scissors-ROCK-paper, Korea's universal tiebreaker. Proverbs lean on its stubbornness: 계란으로 바위 치기 (계란 M3, 치다 M17) = hitting a boulder with an egg — a hopeless fight, fought anyway.

波濤 wave-billow, both hanja pure water. What the sea says out loud: 파도 소리 (소리 M19). You ride it — 파도를 타다 (M6's 타다): surfing, and the stadium crowd-wave both. Radar: this 파 has nothing to do with M40's 파 — one crashes, one garnishes.

風景 wind-scene: 태풍's wind-風 (M11) + 경치's view-景 (M22) — the landscape as a composition. Register pair: 경치 is what you EXCLAIM (경치가 좋아요!); 풍경 is what you describe, photograph, paint. Bonus tenant: the little bell under a temple eave is also 풍경 (風磬, wind-chime) — different second hanja, same wind.

en: to gaze at, look out at
notes: The scenery verb: not just see (M1's 보다) but face something and take it in — 바다를 바라보다, gazing where 보다 merely registers. Radar the stem: this is NOT M34's 바라다 (to hope), though Koreans feel the pun — gaze at something long enough and you're halfway to wishing. Works on people too: 눈을 바라보세요 = look into the eyes (눈 M14).

The root — literal (나무 뿌리) and every metaphor you'd hope for: 한글의 뿌리, one's 뿌리 = heritage. 뿌리 깊은 나무 — 'Deep-Rooted Tree', 깊다 (M22) wearing M24's badge — titles both a Sejong drama and the 1447 poem it honors: the deep-rooted tree fears no wind. Radar: no kinship with M40's 뿌리다 — seeds get sprinkled, roots grow.

솔 (the old pine word) + 나무 (M22), the ㄹ stepping out at the weld: Korea's national tree, green through every winter and therefore the emblem of constancy. The anthem sings a line you can now fully decode: 남산 (M31) 위 (M6)에 저 (M29) 소나무. The 송 in 송편 (M25) is this tree in hanja — the 추석 cakes steam on its needles.

나무 + linking-ㅅ + 잎 (leaf — the bare word waits its own turn; today it rides the compound). The same mortar-ㅅ as M40's 고춧가루, with a pronunciation party on top: an ㄴ sneaks into 잎 and the ㅅ matches it — 나뭇잎 says 나문닙. Autumn's whole plot happens to this word.

落葉 fall-leaf: autumn's second act. 단풍 (M11) is the color show ON the tree; 낙엽 is the show on the ground — 낙엽이 떨어져요 (떨어지다 M36, doing what the hanja promises). Kicking through them is a national October pastime; quoting poetry about them, another. Says 나겹.

虎狼 tiger-wolf, two beasts fused into Korea's apex icon: the mountain spirit's sidekick in temple paintings, both Olympic mascots' species, the shape patriots see in the peninsula itself. Folktales open on it (the gap deck lights its pipe) — and in the most famous one, the tiger flees a 곶감 (dried persimmon), having judged it scarier than himself (무섭다 M24). Even predators fear the unknown.

The bear — and Korea's first mother: in the 단군 myth (M40's 마늘 note told it), the bear who endured the cave on garlic and mugwort became human and bore the founding king. Daily sightings: 곰 인형 (인형 M37) = the teddy bear. And relax about 곰탕 — that 곰 is from an old simmer-verb, not the animal; the soup contains no bears.

The rabbit — and on clear nights, the one IN the moon: Koreans see a 토끼 up in 달 (M16), pounding 떡 (M18) with a mallet. Fourth animal of the zodiac, the folktale trickster who talks his way out of the Dragon King's palace — and modern slang for bolting: 토끼다 = to rabbit = to run for it.

날다 (M28) + the tool-suffix -개 (the one inside 지우개, M15): the flying-tool = wing. An IOU finally paying out: M21's gap deck ruled 옷이 날개다 — clothes are wings — and M28's 날다 note pointed straight back at them; the noun lands here. Birds, airplanes (비행기 M12), angels, and the fried-chicken menu all file under it.

M28's assembly line ([action]+가다), airborne: 날다 + 가다 = fly AWAY (날아오다 flies toward you). Birds do it, hats do it in wind — and so does anything lost at a stroke: 돈이 날아갔어요 = the money's gone; 파일이 날아갔어요 = the unsaved file, mourned in every office. When Koreans lose something suddenly, it flew.

en: to rise up; to come to mind
notes: 뜨다 (M38's float-rise) + 오르다 (M22's climb): float-up — the sun over the horizon (해가 떠올라요) and the thought into your head: 좋은 아이디어가 떠올랐어요 (아이디어 M34) = it surfaced. One verb for dawns and ideas — Korean files inspiration as a sunrise. 르-family (M7): 떠올라요.

The adjective that was hiding inside M7's 파란색 all along — split it: 파란 (badge form) + 색. ㅎ-family: the ㅎ walks out before a vowel and the vowels fuse — 파래요, 파랬어요 — the exact trick M24's 어떻다 taught you with 어때요. 하늘이 파래요 = the sky is blue; for forests and green lights, see the family outlier at the end of the shelf.

하얀색's engine (M7): 하얘요, 하얬어요 — the fusion keeps its ㅑ. Snow-white, paper-white, and going-pale white: 얼굴이 하얘졌어요 (얼굴 M8, through M35's -아/어지다) = the color drained from their face. Its starched sibling 흰색 (M30) dressed the 백의민족; 하얗다 is the softer, spoken white.

M7's 검은색 note tipped you off — '까만색 is the everyday synonym' — and here is the adjective under it: 까매요, 까만. Storm skies, midnight hair, and total amnesia: 까맣게 잊었어요 (잊다 M15, M33's -게) = forgot it to blackness, clean forgot. Korean forgets in color.

노란색's engine (M7): 노래요, 노란 — and yes, 노래요 collides head-on with 노래 (M7's song) plus 요; context referees. The color of 개나리 (the forsythia that yellows every Korean spring), school buses, and autumn ginkgo streets. Its intense sibling 누렇다 waits in the pool — Korean shades its colors by vowel.

빨간색's engine (M7): 빨개요, 빨간. The color of 고추장 (M18) heat and of embarrassment: 얼굴이 빨개졌어요 = I went red — M35's -아/어지다 welded straight onto the ㅎ-drop. The whole shelf conjugates like M29's 그렇다, because it IS that family: the ㅎ-machine, now in five colors.

The old, wide blue M7's gap deck promised you: sky, sea, AND forest — 푸른 하늘, 푸른 바다, 푸른 산 — which is why the go-light is 파란불: 푸르다 owned green first. Grammar rebel twice over: not ㅎ-family, and not even M7's 르-rule — 푸르다 adds 러 instead (푸르러요), the textbook's one famous 러-irregular. Its hanja twin is 청: 청바지 (M21), 청소년 (M35), and 청춘 — 'blue spring', youth itself.

旅行社: M11's 여행 + company-社 — the 사 that M32's 사회 note flipped (社會/會社) and M43's 사원 staffed. The storefront where trips are sold by the package: flights, 숙소, and a 가이드, stapled into one price. Its posters are where the next word lives.

M31's 해외 note promised 'the compound on every travel-agency poster' — filed. 해외 (beyond-the-sea) + 여행: with the land border sealed, leaving South Korea means crossing water, so every trip abroad IS overseas. 첫 해외여행 — the first-passport trip — is a stock life milestone, photographed at the gate.

M18's 예약하다 note glossed '예약 = reservation' — today the noun stands alone and shows its hanja: 豫約 ahead-promise, 예상's beforehand-豫 (M34) + 약속's promise-約 (M5 — M43's 계약 note filed the family: promise a person, a table, in ink). 예약을 하다, 예약을 확인하다 (M20), and — next entry's business — 예약을 취소하다.

豫買 ahead-BUY: the same beforehand-豫, but money moves now — KTX seats, concerts, movies: 기차표를 예매하다. Radar on the 매-file: 판매's sell-賣 (M43), 매일's every-每 (M5), now buy-買 — selling and buying are near-twins in hanja as in life. 예약 holds a promise; 예매 already owns the seat.

取消 take-and-erase: the booking economy's undo button — 예약을 취소하다, 약속을 취소하다. Every Korean screen runs on the button pair 확인/취소 (M20's 확인하다, nouned, vs cancel) — OK or walk away. 취소됐어요 = it got cancelled, said of flights and, in a heavier register, concerts.

The noun under M8's 출발하다 finally checks in — M16's 출장 note already pointed at its 출 ('the one in 출구 and 출발': out-出). 출발 시간 on every board, 도착하다 (M8) at the other end, and 출발! shouted alone is the starting gun of every race and road trip.

途中 road-middle — the 중 is the ongoing-中 of S2's ○○ 중. Two jobs, both listed: ON THE WAY (여행 도중에 = mid-journey, somewhere between 출발 and 도착) and MIDWAY THROUGH anything scheduled (회의 도중에 나갔어요 = left mid-meeting). Every process is a road; 도중 is the part with no exits.

宿所 stay-place: 숙제's 宿 (M10 — 宿題 is literally the 'lodges-overnight problem'; homework was a sleepover guest all along) + 장소's place-所 (M27). The neutral word every booking app sorts by — 호텔 (M23), 여관, 민박, 펜션 all shelve under it. 숙소를 예약하다 is step one of any trip.

旅館 travel-hall: 여권's travel-旅 (M23) + the hall-館 that M23's 박물관 note said 'builds public buildings' — the suffix's oldest client. The old-style inn: thin walls, floor bedding, a fading register — dramas check in when the past calls. Booking apps mostly say 모텔 or 숙소 now; 여관 is the word your grandfather's trips used.

Stay a while: 호텔에 머무르다. 르-family (M7's table): 머물러요 — and it even clips to 머물다. Radar vs M23's 묵다, whose note ruled '묵다 spends nights': 묵다 counts the nights, 머무르다 spans the whole stay — and needs no bed at all: 시선이 머무르다 (a gaze lingers), 마음이 머무르다.

M8's 하루 was never alone — it heads the native 흘-family: 하루, 이틀, 사흘… native spans for native trips. 이틀 동안 (M28's 동안) books the weekend; 하루 이틀 = 'a day or two,' said precisely of problems that won't be fixed in one. The famous TV itinerary 1박 2일 (one night, two days) is 이틀 with a bed in the middle.

THREE days — despite the 사 sound, and Korea itself trips on it: when a holiday notice once said 사흘, half the internet read M2's Sino 사 (four) and the word trended nationally for a day. The native family doesn't count in hanja; four days is 나흘, five 닷새 — the shelf's untaught tail. File 사흘 = 3 and you know more than the trending tab did.

M5's native 열 in the 흘-family uniform: ten days, the shelf's roundest span — 열흘 동안 여행했어요. The classics keep it humble: 열흘 붉은 꽃이 없다 — no flower (M7's 꽃) stays red ten days; no glory lasts. Trips, holidays, and hype cycles all get measured in 열흘.

M2's 어제/오늘/내일 finally get their fourth panel: the day-line runs 그저께·어제·오늘·내일·모레, one word per stop, no 'the day after' assembly required. 내일모레 = 'any day now' — and aimed at an age it winces: 내일모레 서른 (M30's 서른) = thirty is at the door.

A fossil weld: 어제 (M2) + 그저께 (the day before yesterday — untaught, carried inside the compound) = 'just a day or two ago.' Its real career is figurative: 엊그제 같아요 = it feels like yesterday — snap it onto M46's -(으)ㄴ 지 stopwatch and you can sigh like a native: 졸업한 지 십 년인데, 엊그제 같아요.

案內 plan-inside: a guiding paper (案) + 국내's inside-內 (M31) — to walk someone through the inside of a place or a procedure. 길을 안내하다 (M12's 길), and 안내 방송 (M32's 방송) narrates every platform and cabin. M27's 장소 note glossed its 소 with 안내소 — the information booth this verb staffs, decoded at last.

Konglish guide — the human form of 안내하다: 여행 가이드, 관광 가이드 (M23's 관광), flag up, umbrella raised, headcount running. 가이드북 rides in the backpack, and 가이드라인 runs the office — the loanword got a desk job too.

The people-porter, and the grid rule of the module: THINGS ride 가지다 (M28); PEOPLE and pets ride 데리다. It almost never stands alone — it works as 데리고 + a travel verb: 아이를 데리고 왔어요 = I brought the kid. Aim the same escort UP the ladder and it becomes M47's 모시다 — grandmother never gets 데리다.
데려 + 가다: take someone along, away from here — the M6 compass geometry still governing. 아이를 학교에 데려가요; and the tagalong's eternal cry: 저도 데려가요! = take me too! Its 오다-mirror is next in line.

The homeward mirror: bring someone HERE. 친구를 집에 데려왔어요 — every parent's doorbell surprise — and the adoption verb: 강아지를 데려왔어요 (M22's 강아지, now family). Person comes toward you: 데려오다; away from you: 데려가다.

M28's 가져오다 note promised 'its mirror 가져가다 takes things away' — paid. 가지다 (M28) + 가다: have-and-go. 우산을 가져가세요, 여권을 꼭 가져가세요. Grid check: take a PERSON and the verb must switch to 데려가다 — things are carried, people are accompanied.

가져다 + M9's -아/어 주다 welded in: carry it TO someone as a favor — the delivery verb. 물 좀 가져다주세요 (restaurant Korean at its politest), 서류를 가져다줬어요. Spoken Korean clips it to 갖다주다 — the same squeeze M28's 가지다 note filed under 갖다.

Going out to RECEIVE someone: 공항에 마중(을) 나가요 — M8's 나가다 does the going. In Korea you don't wait for arriving guests; you intercept them at the gate, the platform, the bus stop. A native word, no hanja to split — just the warmth. Its send-off twin is next.

마중's mirror: the send-off. 역까지 배웅했어요 — you walk them to the gate or the security line and wave until they're out of sight; leaving early is bad form. 마중 receives, 배웅 releases: arrivals and departures, staffed by family. 배웅하다 to verb it.

M28's 다녀오다 ran the round trip from the traveler's seat; 다녀가다 reports it from the HOST's: someone came, stayed a while, and left. 손님이 다녀갔어요 (M9's 손님); 어머니가 다녀가셨어요 — and now the fridge is inexplicably full.

外出 outside-go: 외국's outside-外 (M23) + the out-出 of 출구 and 출발. Stepping out — from home, the office, or a hospital ward: 외출 준비 = getting ready to go out, and 외출 중 (S2's ○○ 중) is the sign on a thousand doors: out at the moment. 외출하다 to verb it.

出入 out-in: M12's 출구 and 입구 compressed into one word for the traffic through a door. 출입문 = the boarding door (M6's 문) announced on every bus and train; 출입국 = entering-and-leaving countries — the immigration desk where every 해외여행 shows its 여권 (M23). Signage register: where 출입 appears, rules follow.

小包 small-wrap: 소설's small-小 (M48) + a wrap-包. M27's 우체국 note ended 'where 편지 and 소포 begin their journeys' — the parcel finally checks in. Its verb came in M40: 부치다 mails as well as pan-fries — 소포를 부치다. 기념품 (M23) travels home in one.

葉書 leaf-writing: 낙엽's leaf-葉 (M49) + the document-書 filed in 서류 (M16) — a letter the size of a leaf. 그림엽서 is the picture postcard, and the travel ritual is eternal: write it 여행 도중에, mail it 현지에서, land home before it does.

郵票 mail-ticket: 우체국's mail-郵 (M27) + M12's 표 — whose note glued vehicles on the front (기차표, 비행기표); here the ticket rides the envelope instead. 우표를 붙이다 (M37's 붙이다, doing its sticker job). 우표 수집 — stamp collecting — is where the hobby shelf keeps its quietest members.

現地 the actual-place: 현재's appear-現 (M35) + 지역's earth-地 (M31) — the place ITSELF, as opposed to the brochure. 현지 음식 = local food, the traveler's grail; 현지인 = a local; 현지 시간 = local time, which your body refuses to accept for three days.

僑胞 sojourner-sibling: 僑 (living abroad) + 胞 (from the same womb) — Koreans overseas, named as family who happen to live elsewhere. 재미교포 (in America), 재일교포 (in Japan). The word does emotional work no passport can: wherever born, still 胞.

M44's 유학 note called it early — '유학생 (M4's 학생, with a visa) may be your own job title' — and M44's scholarship sentence already spelled it: 유학생을 위한 장학금. Today it gets its own card: 留學生 stay-study-student. The 교포 was born abroad; the 유학생 commutes there.

歸國 return-country: homing-歸 + the country-國 of 국민 (M32) — the 국 that M27's 우체국 note triaged (country, soup, office). The 유학생's and 교포's homecoming verb: 십 년 만에 귀국했어요. The 귀-family runs on the same instinct — 귀가 (return home) and the holiday exodus 귀성, both untaught, both pointing the same direction: back.

M37's 돌다 (turn) + 보다: turn and look at what's BEHIND you — 뒤를 돌아보다 (M6's 뒤) when someone calls your name — then in time: 지난 여행을 돌아보다 = look back on the trip. Radar vs M50's 둘러보다 ('sweep a place with your eyes'): 둘러보다 sweeps the space around you — the market; 돌아보다 turns toward what's behind you — the memory.

The maker-verb, and this module's heavyweight: Korean BUILDS more than houses — 집을 짓다, 밥을 짓다 (rice is built, not just cooked — the rice cooker below agrees), 이름을 짓다 (names are built), 표정을 짓다 (M34's 표정 — faces assemble their expressions), even 약을 짓다 (M10's 약 — the pharmacist builds your prescription). To 짓다 is to compose something whole out of parts. ㅅ-irregular: M14's 낫다 and M40's 젓다 finally seat their third member — the ㅅ melts before vowels (지어요, 지은 집) and holds before consonants (짓고, 짓기로).

移徙 move-migrate: M13's 이사하다 note said it verbatim — '이사 is the move itself' — and today the noun unpacks. Direction rides Ring 1 verbs: 이사(를) 가다 = move out, 이사(를) 오다 = move in. 이삿짐 — the moving load M13's 짐 note pre-taught — wears the linking-ㅅ (M40's 고춧가루 wedge), and M50's 옮기다 note already called 이사하다 'this verb at whole-house scale.' Korea moves often; the boxes have their own industry.

下宿 down-lodge (the 하 is 지하's down-下, M12) + 집: a room in someone's home, meals included — the setting of every campus drama worth its ramen, complete with the 하숙 아주머니 who cooks and worries. Its modern heirs charge more and feed you less: the 고시원 (exam-cram cubicle) and the 원룸 (one-room studio).

Office + hotel, welded in Korea — the made-in-Korea shelf the Konglish interlude built (핸드폰, 원피스) gains a building: a tower of small units zoned for working AND living, urban Korea's one-room compromise. 호텔 (M23) lent the second half; no English speaker would recognize the whole. Real-estate listings measure your twenties in 오피스텔 floor plans.

The roof — grown out of 집 itself, worn smooth by centuries. The curved tile roof on the 한옥 postcard is 기와 지붕; 한 지붕 아래 = under one roof, the phrase families and sitcoms both live by. Modern Korea mostly builds flat tops instead — which is why 옥상, below, has a whole culture.

大門 great-gate: big-大 + M6's 문 — and M31's 동대문 note already split the syllables (동 + 대 + 문): the Great East Gate was a 대문 wearing a compass, and 남대문 its southern twin. Every walled house had one; apartment Korea keeps the word for the building's front door and its keypad. 대문 앞에 두세요 = leave it at the gate, the delivery-app default.

The yard — the packed-earth stage of the traditional house, where kimjang, weddings, and laundry all happened. NIKL lists a second sense Korean still uses: 마당 as a SCENE or round of something — 노래 한 마당, and 마당놀이 is the courtyard theater named for it. The yard was never just ground; it was the venue. 정원, next door, is the garden you look at instead.

庭園 courtyard-garden: the 원 is the garden-園 inside M6's 공원 — a DESIGNED green space, planted and admired. Register split with 마당: the 마당 is lived ON (dirt, work, play); the 정원 is looked AT (flowers, 나무 — M22 — arranged just so). Apartment Korea mostly rents its 정원 back as the 공원.

屋上 house-top: the flat rooftop — laundry lines, pepper-drying, and every drama's confession scene (the 옥상 is where Korean television goes to feel things). The 상 is top-上, hiding inside M22's 세상 (世上, the world) all along — a FIFTH 상 for the file M40's 상 note opened (wound-傷, state-狀, prize-賞, table-床). Its famous tenant: the 옥탑방, the rooftop shack above the top floor — cheap, freezing, cinematic.

M6's 위 + M13's 층 counter, fused into a noun: the floor above — and in apartment Korea, the people on it. 위층 사람 = the upstairs neighbor, a relationship conducted mostly through the ceiling. The gap deck names the war: 층간 소음.

M6's 아래 + 층: the floor below — the direction apologies travel in an apartment block. When the 아래층 rings your doorbell at 10 p.m., everyone already knows why. With 위층 above, the vertical neighborhood is complete.

en: the house next door, neighbor's home
notes: M13's 이웃 + M1's 집: the house next door and the people in it — 이웃집 강아지 (M22), 이웃집 아저씨 (M27): Korean narrates its neighbors by address. M13's 이웃 note already whispered 이웃사촌 — neighbors as cousins; the gap deck pays that debt today.

The wooden floor — historically the raised, breezy platform at the heart of the house (the grand version: 대청마루), summer's answer to the 온돌 winter M13's gap deck filed. Radar vs M13's 바닥: 바닥 is any floor or bottom; 마루 is the wooden one — and older Koreans still say 마루 where M13's 거실 now stands. Floors have registers too.

浴室 bathe-room: M37's 목욕 supplies the bathe-浴, and the room-실 family — 화장실 (M6), 침실/거실 (M13), 교실 (M15) — finally gets its bath. In Korean homes it's usually one wet room: drain in the floor, everything splashable. 화장실 is what you politely SAY; 욕실 is what the floor plan writes.

沐浴湯: M37's 목욕 note already toured the bathhouse — scalding pools, 때밀이 scrub-downs, banana milk after — so today just add the 탕: hot-water-湯, the same syllable that ends soup names (M40's 감자 note litigated 감자탕). The neighborhood 목욕탕 is fading; its heir, the 찜질방 M17's gap deck filed, took the towels and kept the ritual.

水道 water-channel (the waterworks) + linking-ㅅ + M1's 물: tap water — said 수돈물, the ㅅ turning nasal. M31's 수도 note promised exactly this: '수도 is also the water supply (수돗물 = tap water)' — the capital and the plumbing share syllables, and context sorts the head from the pipes. Seoul's tap water is certified drinkable and even branded (아리수); Koreans mostly boil it into 보리차 (barley tea) or filter it anyway. Trust, but simmer.

家具 house-gear: furniture — the 가 is house-家, the same one that makes 가족 (M4) the house-people. 가구를 놓다 (M28), 가구를 옮기다 (M50). And a second 가구 shares the spelling: 家口, house-mouths — the HOUSEHOLD, the census-taker's unit. 1인 가구 = the single-person household, statistically Korea's fastest-growing way to live; the news counts 가구, the store sells 가구.

The drawer — 책상 서랍 (M6's desk, opened for pencils and secrets). Every home maintains one 서랍 of cables, coins, and expired coupons; emptying it is the boss level of 정리, later this shelf. 서랍장 = a chest of drawers — furniture named by what it stacks.

Curtain, taken straight from English — the 창문 (M6) gets dressed in a loanword because the traditional house used paper doors and bamboo blinds instead. Modern Korea's favorite model is the 암막 커튼, the blackout curtain — the 해 (M11) rises early, and shift work runs late.

箱子 box-thing: the -자 is the noun-capping 子 that also ends 의자 (M6) and 모자 (M9) — Sino-Korean's little 'thing' suffix, finally pointed out. 택배 상자 — the parcel box (택배 = home delivery, riding frozen here) — towers by the elevator every recycling day, and 이사 turns a whole life into numbered ones.

M13's 쓰레기 + 통 (桶, the bucket): the trash can — M44's 필통 note called 통 'the all-purpose container syllable' and named this very word; 물통 and 휴지통 (wastebasket, and your computer's recycle bin) fill out the family. Korea's real civics exam is 분리수거 — separated recycling, frozen here as a concept: which 통 does this go in, and the neighbors are watching.

M36's 전기 + M40's 밥솥 — exactly the compound M40's note promised ('전기밥솥, 압력밥솥: job-description naming'). The talking appliance of every Korean kitchen: it announces, in complete polite sentences, that the rice is done. 밥을 짓다 is this machine's entire career — the maker-verb from the top of this shelf, automated.

扇風機 fan-wind-machine: the 풍 is wind-風 (태풍 M11, 풍경 M49), the 기 the machine-機 of 비행기 and M13's 세탁기. Home of Korea's most famous urban legend: fan death — the belief that a 선풍기 running overnight in a closed room can kill you. Generations of grandmothers enforced the timer dial; science shrugs; the dial remains. 선풍기를 틀다 — M51's flow-verb — starts the summer.

Scissors — M49's 바위 note has had you chanting 가위바위보; today the scissors third is officially yours. Korean kitchens keep 가위 beside the tongs: noodles, 삼겹살 (M18), and kimchi all get cut with scissors, and nobody apologizes. Radar: an unrelated 가위 names sleep paralysis — 가위에 눌리다, pressed by the night-hag; context holds the scissors.

The dishes, as a chore — a rare native noun on this shelf; 설거지하다 does the scrubbing. Grammar of the sink: 그릇 (M18) pile up, someone claims the glory of M3's 요리하다, and 설거지는 내가 할게 — I'll do the dishes — is Korean's most negotiable love language. Cooking has prestige; 설거지 has virtue.

The laundry — both the chore and the pile: 빨래(를) 하다, and frozen inside rides 빨다, the wash-clothes verb, untaught and waiting in the pool. 빨래를 널다 (= hanging it out) happens on the 옥상, the 베란다 (M13), or the drying rack that lives in every Korean living room — the dryer is a recent immigrant.

洗濯 wash-rinse: the Sino base FINALLY under its own machines — M13's 세탁기 (wash + machine) and M37's 세탁소 (wash + place) both ran on credit, and M37's 세수 filed the wash-洗 they draw on. 세탁하다 is the formal wash; 빨래 is the same job in house slippers. Register, as ever, is the real laundry.

Clear it away: 방을 치우다 (M8's 방), 상을 치우다 (M40's 상, after dinner). The parental register lives here — 방 좀 치워라! — and so does the server's 치워 드릴까요? (shall I clear this? — M9's 드리다, on duty). NIKL also lists an auxiliary sense: -아/어 치우다 = do it OFF completely — 먹어 치웠어요 = polished it off. To 치우다 is to make space, by force if necessary.

整理 order-arrange: M13's 정리하다 note already defined it — '정리 = order, arrangement' — and today the noun stands alone: 책상 정리, 서랍 정리, 짐 정리. Bigger things get tidied too: 마음을 정리하다 (M19's 마음) = to sort out your heart, the breakup's official verb phrase. Says 정니 — the ㄹ nasalizing, as its verb already showed you.

Decorate: 방을 꾸미다 — the move-in imperative (마음대로 꾸미세요, says the landlord, within reason of the deposit). Yourself, too: dressing up counts as 꾸미다. Radar: stories get 꾸미다-ed as well — 이야기를 꾸미다 = to MAKE UP a story, 꾸며 낸 말 = a fabrication. What decorating and lying share: arranging surfaces until they convince.

Cover: 이불을 덮다 (M13's 이불, the floor-sleeper's shield), 뚜껑을 덮다 (M40's lid, closing), 책을 덮다 = close the book — endings are covers too. The rice bowl wears it as a suffix: 덮밥 = 'covered rice', anything ladled over M1's 밥. Radar for the ear: says 덥따 — exactly like M11's 덥다 (hot). In summer you 덥다; under a blanket you 덮다.

Worn out — age you can SEE: 낡은 집, 낡은 가구, the elbow-shine of long use. Says 낙따 (the ㄺ cluster simplifies, like M35's 늙다 → 늑따) — and that's the radar: one vowel apart, 늙다 ages people, 낡다 wears out things, and M35's 오래되다 note already ruled that merely-old is neutral. 낡다 is 오래되다 plus scars.

The used-determiner: 헌 옷 (M7's 옷, donated), 헌책방 = the secondhand bookstore, smelling of every previous owner. It completes the shelf M46's 옛 note called 'matched bookends': 새 (M13) breaks in, 옛 looks back, 헌 is worn-by-hands. Every Korean child knows the sandpile chant: 두꺼비야, 헌 집 줄게 새 집 다오 — toad, take my old house, give me a new one. Real estate's first lesson.

Sturdy — built to last: 튼튼한 집, 튼튼한 가구, and the grandmother's highest compliment, 튼튼한 아이. The doubled 튼튼 is Korean's mimetic pattern for soundness — you can hear the knock on good wood. Bodies use it constantly: 이가 튼튼해요 = strong teeth (M8's 이), and the kindergarten anthem promises 몸도 튼튼, 마음도 튼튼.

M13's 넓다 through M37's causative machine (히): MAKE it wide — 길을 넓히다, 집을 넓히다. Says 널피다, the ㄼ and ㅎ merging. The move-up idiom: 집을 넓혀 가다 = to move somewhere bigger, Korean's standard life-progress phrase. Horizons take it too: 세상을 넓히다 (M22's 세상) — what this app is allegedly doing to yours.

그 + 대로: as-it-is — rank 340, the fossil trio's workhorse. 그대로 두세요 (M40's 두다) = leave it exactly as it stands; 지금 그대로 = just the way it is now, the compliment K-ballads run on. This is the glue, frozen solid: the 대로 that follows nouns took 그 and never let go.

M19's 마음 + 대로: as your heart points — 마음대로 하세요 is a blessing from a friend and a threat from a parent; tone is the entire dictionary here. The junmal interlude's 맘 clips it to 맘대로, home of the idiom 엿장수 맘대로 — 'as the taffy-seller pleases' (M44's gap deck sold you that 엿): arbitrary, whimsical, house rules.

제 + 대로: as-it-properly-should-go — rank 619, one of spoken Korean's busiest adverbs. 제대로 하세요 = do it RIGHT; 제대로 된 식사 = a real meal. Radar: this 제 is one's-proper-own, not M17's humble my — it's the reflexive 제 that M49's tiger proverb walked in on. When Korean wants to say something actually works, it says 제대로.

The conformity particle, three settings: noun + 대로 (약속대로 M5, 계획대로 M8, 순서대로 — paying M33's IOU by name); M24's badge + 대로 (도착하는 대로 = the moment you arrive, 들은 대로 = as heard); and the fossils above — 그대로, 마음대로, 제대로 — where it fused permanently. Radar: the -대로 ending 강남대로 is 大路, a boulevard — M31's 종로 note stamped street names with road-路; this 대로 takes orders, that one takes traffic.
