症狀 illness-shape: the 상 is the state-狀 of M33's 상황 — the shape your sickness takes, finally itemizable. 어떤 증상이 있으세요? is the consultation's opening move; M14 let you say 아파요, this word lets you answer like a chart.

症勢 illness-momentum: 증상's twin, with 勢 (force, tendency) in the back seat — how the sickness is TRENDING. Doctors' paperwork leans 증상; worried families say 감기 증세가 있어요. A register pair, not a synonym exam — use either, hear both.

頭痛 head-pain: M8's 머리 territory in hanja, and your first 痛. The mold is a vending machine — 복통 (stomach-ache), 치통 (toothache) — read the pattern, buy the one pill: 두통약, job-description naming from M13's 냉장고 school.

아프다 (M14) through the -ㅁ factory M33 named (웃음 — and M40's 얼음): hurting, nouned. In the wild it's mostly the heart's: 이별의 아픔 = the ache of parting — song-lyric and book-jacket register. A hurting knee still just says 아파요.
苦痛 bitter-pain: the bitter-苦 of M39's 고생 + the pain-痛 of 두통, at soul scale. The ladder now reads: 아픔 aches, 고통 crushes — news anchors and novels reach for this one. 고통을 받다: M9's 받다, at its heaviest.

The overwork illness English can't name: M14's 몸 calls a general strike — everything aches, chills, no single cause except too much of everything. It erupts (몸살이 나다 — M28's 나다) or catches you like M14's 감기 (몸살에 걸리다); either way, announce it and Korea nods. The legitimate excuse, because everyone knows how it was earned.

온 (whole — a little determiner the course hasn't taught; it rides in frozen) + M14's 몸: the whole body, reporting as a unit. 온몸이 아파요 is the 몸살 sentence; 온 세상 = the whole world, same prefix. When every part checks in at once, this is the word.

en: to be dizzy; to be messy
notes: Dizzy — the room spins: M11's ㅂ-family (ㅂ → 우 before vowels) gives 어지러워요. Second job, same physics: a desk, a room, an era can be 어지럽다 — cluttered, disordered. Vertigo and mess share one adjective; context holds the handrail.

en: to suffer from, be sick with
notes: To suffer THROUGH: 감기를 앓다 takes the cold as a siege, where M14's 아프다 only reports the state. Says 알타. Also inward: 속을 앓다 = to ache privately over something. And the national performance: 앓는 소리 — the audible groan produced so the household knows; complaint as broadcast.

M14's 병 + M28's 들다 on its enter-job (the 들 of 잠이 들다): illness moves IN — long-term, chronic, lived-with, where 병에 걸리다 merely catches. ㄹ-drop like its parent. Societies take it too: 병든 사회 is the editorial page's favorite patient.

身體 the body, formal register: forms, news Korean, and 신체검사 — the school physical every Korean kid lines up for. M14's 몸 in a suit; a register pair like M50's 가다/향하다. Your 몸 hurts; your 신체 gets measured.

The tooth ladder, rung by rung: M8's 이 is neutral, 이빨 is the casual-to-animal rung — tigers bare 이빨, toothpaste ads flash it, buddies say it about their own molars. Aim it at grandmother's dentures and you've filed her with the tigers. (The formal top rung, 치아, gleams from dentist brochures — one wink, no card.)

M8's 머리 note said head and the hair on it share one word — 머리카락 is the STRAND: what clogs the drain, lands on sweaters, and gets counted 하나까지 (down to the last one). 머리를 자르다 cuts the hairstyle; the single fallen hair is always 머리카락.

M8's 손 + M14's 목: hand-neck = wrist — Korean builds joints by finding the neck in them. 손목이 아파요 is the desk worker's diagnosis; 손목시계 = the watch named for its address. M21's 목걸이 already proved how much 목 loves compounds; 팔목 names this same joint from the arm side.

M14's 발 + 목: foot-neck = ankle, the joint machine's second shipment. 발목이 아파요 after the hike. The idiom earns its keep: 발목을 잡다 — to grab someone's ankle — is how old scandals, old contracts, and old habits hold you back.
治療 govern-heal: treatment — what the 병원 (M6) actually dispenses. 치료를 받다: M9's 받다 again, because treatment — like M36's 상처 — is received. The verb 치료하다 belongs to the one in the white coat.

齒科 tooth-branch: the 과 is the branch-科 of M15's 과학 that M44's 과목 filed — hospitals sort into -과 departments (내과 internal, 안과 eyes; read the pattern, learn this one). 치과 is where 이를 빼다 happens, which is why the whole country shares one 치과 공포. Radar: this formal tooth-齒 is the 치아 rung of 이빨's ladder.

手術 hand-art: the wash-hands 手 of M37's 세수 + the craft-術 of M44's 기술 trio — surgery is literally handiwork. 수술을 받다: operations, like M36's 상처 and 치료 above, are RECEIVED (M9's 받다, in scrubs). 큰 수술 = a major one; the drama cliché is the corridor outside it.

入院 enter-the-institution: the enter-入 of M12's 입구 + the walled -원 of 병원 (M6) that M37's 유치원 note mapped — the institutions with gates. 입원하다 = to be admitted, and Korea admits lightly: a bad 몸살 can earn you a night and an IV drip.

退院 retreat-from-the-institution: the 퇴 of M43's 퇴근 — the day's sweetest retreat — aimed at the hospital gate. 퇴원하다 = to be discharged; with 입원 above you hold the arc's bookends, exactly the way M44 held 입학/졸업. A C-grade word for an A-grade day.

回復 turn-back-restore: recovery as a round trip — what M23's 돌아오다 does natively, 回 does in ink. 건강을 회복하다; when it happens on its own, 회복되다 rides the 되다-machine from M36's passive party. And 피로 회복 — fatigue recovery — is the two-word promise printed on little brown bottles; next entry explains.

疲勞 worn-labor: fatigue as a noun — M7's 피곤하다, filed as a substance. 피로가 풀리다: M36's 풀리다, whose whole portfolio is untying exactly this. 피로 회복 is the slogan of 박카스, the pharmacy energy drink Korea has poured on tiredness since 1963 — fatigue so institutional it has a beverage.

Worn down — past tired, out of fuel: 일에 지치다 (worn out BY the work — the dictionary's own example), 더위에 지치다. M7's 피곤하다 is tonight; 지치다 is the accumulation — almost always past tense, 지쳤어요, because you only notice after it's done.

Massage through the converter (the Konglish reading's rules, vowels cushioned: 마-사-지). 마사지를 받다 — M9's 받다 yet again: like 치료 and 수술, relief arrives as something received. 발 마사지 is the trip-weary traveler's reward.

Vitamin, converter-standard: v → ㅂ, the 비디오/서비스 rule from the Konglish reading. 비타민 C (say 씨) is Korea's default gift of concern — visiting the sick, you bring fruit or these. 비타민을 챙겨 먹다: M40's 챙기다, provisioning yourself on purpose.

M1's 좋다 through M35's -아/어지다: to get better — the patient's chart, plotted upward, with M35's 점점 glued on as always: 점점 좋아지고 있어요. Hearts run the same machine: 그 사람이 좋아졌어요 = I've come to like them. Improvement and affection, one verb.
M29's 나쁘다 through the same machine, ㅡ-drop first (나쁘 → 나빠): to worsen. 눈이 나빠졌어요 — M14's 눈, dimmed by screens — is the national optometry confession. The chart's down-slope; 좋아지다's shadow.

M39's 심하다 (severe, over the line) + -아/어지다: worsening with momentum — 기침이 심해졌어요 is the sentence that upgrades you from the 약국 (M6) to the 병원. The trajectory trio closes: 좋아지다 up, 나빠지다 down, 심해지다 accelerating.

The removal verb, many exits: the dictionary's base sense pulls OUT (가시를 빼다 — a thorn), the 치과 pulls M8's 이 — 이를 빼다 — and the gym finally answers M35's 찌다: 살을 빼다 — the flesh that note said gains is what you subtract. Also tension: 힘을 빼다 = un-tense, the massage table's one instruction.

Not enough — the native half of a register pair with M39's 부족하다, which already diagnosed 잠이 부족해요 as the national condition; 잠이 모자라다 is the same diagnosis, groaned at home. Humble-mode too: 제가 많이 모자라요 = I fall short. Careful with the badge: 모자란 사람 shades into 'dim' — aim this verb at sleep and budgets, not people.

The IOU clears: M36's passive party listed this exact word among its 되다-verbs (시작되다, 준비되다, 걱정되다 — swap the 하다, get the happen-form), and M29's 걱정 note has said 걱정돼요 since Band 3. Worry that arrives on its own: 걱정하지 마세요 asks someone to stop DOING it; 걱정돼요 just reports the weather.

不安 peace-less: the peace-安 M33's 안부 decoded, revoked by the 不 of M39's 불가능하다. M42 taught the adjective 불안하다; here stands the bare noun, because Korean handles anxiety as a substance, like M42's 긴장: 불안이 크다, 시험 불안. Peace, subtracted — and measurable.

The honorific sick — M12's 편하다 negated into 편하지 않다, then squeezed by the 준말 law into one soft word: the honored elder is 'not at ease,' never bluntly ill. 어디가 편찮으세요? is how you ask UP the ladder M47 built; 할머니께서 편찮으셔서요 is how you explain the visit. Off the word list, but the second ladder doesn't work without it.

M14's 죽다 through M33's -ㅁ factory: death, the noun — plain, heavy, and needed, because life keeps filing it: 죽음 앞에서 = in the face of death. Korean keeps a gentler register beside it — M47's 돌아가시다: the honored haven't died, they've gone back. The factory's weightiest product; no jokes on this shelf.

癌 — cancer, and Korean says it exactly that plainly: 암에 걸리다, the same catch-frame as M14's 감기, for the diagnosis nearly every family has heard once. 암 검사 (M44's 검사) is the screening; catching it early is why the odds keep improving. A word taught because it is needed — factually, and without flinching.

禁煙 forbid-smoke: M14's no-smoking sentence told you to 'read it off every wall in Korea as 금연' — the wall's word is finally yours. As a verb, 금연하다 = to quit: what M20's 끊다 note already did to 담배, made official. Its licensed opposite, 흡연, hangs on the glass smoking booth — read it, don't enroll.

禁止 forbid-stop, verbed: S2's sign kit taught the noun (주차 금지, 사용 금지 — M50's 주차 note read the parking sign for you); this is the verb that issues them — M4's 의사 forbidding M9's 술: 의사가 술을 금지했어요, a hard week. Radar: forbid-禁 is NOT the gold-金 of 금요일 (M5), 현금 (M9), and 세금 (M43) — same syllable, opposite relationship to your wishes.

그런데 (M7), squeezed by the 준말 law — that note promised it 'shortens to 근데 in speech,' and at rank 563 the clip now outranks most of what it connects: spoken Korean and every group chat run on it. One more thing it's been carrying: the -ㄴ데 in its tail is this module's glue — see the glue Part, where the machinery finally comes out of hiding.

en: to reveal, make known; to light up
notes: M13's 밝다 through M37's causative party (the adjective wing that gave you 높이다/낮추다): make-bright. Lamps do it literally — 불을 밝히다 (M13's 불) — and the news does it daily: 사실을 밝히다 = bring the facts into the light. Every 'officials revealed…' headline is running this one bulb.

M8's 일어나다 filed three jobs — get up, stand up, happen — and M37's party makes all of them transitive: raise a fallen 아이 (M4), and raise events — 문제를 일으키다 = cause trouble, 사고를 일으키다 (M36). What 일어나다 does by itself, 일으키다 makes happen; the news mostly reports the second kind.

M32's 나타나다 (appear) welded to M28's 내다 (the put-it-out verb): put an appearance out = express, show — 뜻을 나타내다 (M10's 뜻), 기분을 나타내다 (M7). The pair mirrors: 결과가 나타나다 = the results show up; 결과를 나타내다 = the chart shows them. Radar: M42's 표현하다 puts it in WORDS; 나타내다 shows it in anything — graphs, colors, faces.

M37's 알리다 (make-known) through M35's -아/어지다: become-known — fame with no named publicist. 이름이 알려졌어요; wearing M24's badge it's the adjective every profile wants: 잘 알려진 가수 (M4's 가수). Print loves it precisely because nobody has to say who did the telling.

M35's 늘다 + M28's 나다: an increase erupting into view — stretched longer and more visible than plain 늘다. The triangle completes: 늘다 grows (M35), 늘리다 you grow it (M37's party), 늘어나다 grows where everyone can see — which is why statistics prefer it: 이용하는 사람들이 늘어나고 있다.

M28's 가지다 note filed the receipt — 'Spoken Korean squeezes it to 갖다' — and the squeeze turns out to be a NIKL headword of its own, ranked 190. Two mechanics: it only works before consonants (갖고, 갖게, 갖는 — before a vowel it reopens: 가져요), and the written register trusts it with abstractions: 관심을 갖다 (M24), 회의를 갖다 (M10 — meetings are HAD in print). Speech runs the auxiliary too: 사 갖고 왔어요 = bought-and-brought, the squeezed -아/어 가지고.

Finish, announced from a podium: 일을 마치다, 회의를 마치겠습니다 — the rung above M8's 끝나다 (it ends) and M16's 끝내다 (you end it): 끝나다 happens, 끝내다 you do, 마치다 you declare. Radar: M34's 마치 (as-if) is one syllable short and a total stranger — 마치 opens similes, 마치다 closes ceremonies. And M35's 마침내 (at last) was smuggling this stem all along: 마침 + 내, 'at the finishing.'

Divide AND share — Korean refuses to split the two. Math and cake: 반으로 나누다 (M5's 반); the table: 나눠 먹다, the default verb of Korean eating (one 찌개, several spoons); and talk: 이야기를 나누다 (M24) — conversations are shared, not held. Both spellings serve: 나누어 = 나눠.

Launch something that sprawls: 일을 벌이다 = start a whole THING (said fondly or wearily), 잔치를 벌이다 (M25's feast, spread wide) — and the news wages its campaigns and investigations with it. Radar, three ways: M16's 벌다 earns money, M13's 버리다 throws away — and 벌이다 is even pronounced 버리다, context standing guard — while untaught 벌리다 (spread open: 입을 벌리다) rides frozen here. 일을 벌이다 spends energy; 돈을 벌다 earns it back.

The 보다-compound shelf (M15's 물어보다, M49's 바라보다, M50's 둘러보다) hires its inspector: look with CARE, detail by detail — 자료를 살펴보다 (M44's 자료), 먼저 살펴보고 결정하세요 (M33). Radar vs M50's 둘러보다: 둘러보다 sweeps a place, 살펴보다 sweeps the details — realtor's walkthrough vs building inspector's clipboard.

M9's 받다 + 들이다 — 들다's enter-sense (M28: the 들 inside 들어가다) run through M37's party: let-IN. Receive at the door, then let into the house: 결과를 받아들이다 (M32), 다른 문화를 받아들이다 (M26) — verdicts, cultures, and bad news all get accepted this way. 받다 alone takes the package; 받아들이다 signs for what's inside.

Arrange into existence — the pure-Korean verb of providing: 자리를 마련하다 (M12's 자리 — set up the occasion), 돈을 마련하다 (scrape it together — 어렵게 마련한 돈 carries the sweat in M24's badge), and the government's beloved 대책을 마련하다 (대책, countermeasures — riding frozen) in every third headline. Where M8's 준비하다 gets ready FOR the thing, 마련하다 procures the thing itself.

發生 launch-into-life: the launch-發 M35's 발전하다 decoded from 출발 (M8) + the life-生 of 학생 (M4) and 생활 (M29). This is M36's 사고가 났어요 wearing a press badge — a true register pair: 나다 (M28) speaks, 발생하다 prints: 사고가 발생했습니다. What M28's 생기다 lets arise in conversation, this verb files as a report.

發見 shoot-forth-see: launch-發 again + the view-見 inside M24's 의견 — to discover is to fire your seeing at what was already there. 새로운 사실을 발견했어요 (M35's 새롭다, M24's 사실) for science and police work; 새로운 맛집을 발견했어요 (M18) for the rest of us. The passive rides free on the 되다-machine (M36): 발견되다.

發達 launch-arrive: 發 a third time + the arrive-達 that gets 배달 (M18) to your door. Radar vs M35's 발전하다, a pair the news never confuses: 발달 grows a CAPABILITY — 기술이 발달하다 (M44), muscles, even the storm clouds the forecast calls developed — while 발전 advances a STATE: 나라가 발전하다 (M23), 경제 (M32). Skills 발달; skylines 발전.

M44's 조사 (調査 tune-examine) finally conjugates: 경찰이 사고를 조사하고 있습니다 (M16, M36) — to look into something systematically. 설문 조사 (설문 — questionnaire, riding frozen) is the survey every app begs you to take. M44 warned you about failing 조사 quizzes about 조사; now you can run the investigation yourself.

利用 benefit-use: radar vs M10's 사용하다, and the line is sharp — 사용 uses a THING in your hand; 이용 uses a SERVICE or an opportunity: 지하철을 이용하다 (M6), the verb of every PA announcement ('이용해 주셔서 감사합니다'). The sharp edge: 사람을 이용하다 = to use a person like a service — exploit. Choose your object carefully.

比較 compare-compare — both characters mean it, so the word can't mean anything else. M22's 보다-particle finally gets its formal verb: B보다 A가 커요 becomes A와 B를 비교하다 (M30's 와/과 doing the pairing). 다른 사람과 비교하지 마세요 — the advice every 부모님 (M4) needs and no ranking culture takes. Wink: 비교적 = comparatively (riding frozen — M45's -적 factory, one badge early).

解決 untie-decide: untie-解 (frozen) + the decide-決 of M33's 결정하다 — NOT the tie-結 of M32's 결과, though solving does tie off results. M36 already told you Korean problems are knots — you 풀다 them, they 풀리다 loose on their own; 해결하다 is the formal completion: untie it AND rule on it. 문제를 해결했습니다 is what the press release says after somebody quietly 풀었어요.

包含 wrap-contain: the wrap-包 of M52's 소포 (the small-wrap parcel) + contain-含 (frozen) — to include is to wrap into the parcel. Usually met wrapped itself, in the 되다-machine (M36): 아침 식사가 가격에 포함되어 있어요 (M3's 식사, M21's 가격) = breakfast is included — the hotel sentence worth the whole rank.

主張 master-stretch: 주인's master-主 (M27) + stretch-張 (frozen) — to claim is to stretch your position out and stand on it as its owner. Content arrives by M32's quote machine: 사실이라고 주장해요 = insists it's a fact — the verb the news uses when it declines to agree. One rung above 말하다 (M4) in force, one below proof.

強調 strong-tune: strong-強 (frozen) + the tune-調 of M44's 조사 — to emphasize is to turn the tuning up LOUD. 중요하다고 강조했어요 (M16's 중요하다, through M32's quote machine) — teachers, editorials, and parents share this verb. Underlining, as speech.

要求 need-seek: the need-要 hiding inside M16's 필요하다 + seek-求 (frozen) — to demand is to point your need at someone. Top rung of the assertion ladder: 말하다 says, 주장하다 insists, 강조하다 underlines, 요구하다 sends the bill. Demands arrive by M33's favor-quote: 돈을 달라고 요구했어요 — give-me, quoted and invoiced.

en: to be according to; ~에 의하면 / ~에 의해
notes: 依 lean-on — and like M32's frame verbs (대하다/위하다/통하다/따르다: 'the dictionary forms are just their ID cards'), you'll never conjugate it raw. Frame one: [source]에 의하면 = according to — the 에 따르면 frame (M32) with the verb swapped for pure hanja stiffness. Frame two: [agent]에 의해(서) = by, the passive agent of print: M36 dressed the spoken agent in 한테 (경찰한테 잡혔어요); the written record promotes it — 경찰에 의해 발견되었다. Speech says 한테; documents say 에 의해.

關 the connecting gate — 관심's (M24) and 관계's (M32) 관, now conjugating, barely: it lives entirely in [topic]에 관해서 and 에 관한 + noun = concerning. The formal sibling of the 에 대해서 frame (M32)/에 대한: 대하다 faces a topic, 관하다 gates it — 이 문제에 관해서 (M7's 문제). Reports and 논문 (M44) reach for 관해서 where conversation says 대해서.

關聯 gate-link: 관하다's gate + link-聯 (frozen). 관계 (M32) ties PEOPLE; 관련 ties TOPICS: 관련(이) 있다/없다 = related or not, and stacked bare before a noun it's every news site's furniture — 관련 기사 (M48's 기사) = related articles, 관련 뉴스 (M24). The frame extends: [noun]와 관련해서 = in connection with.

M29's 또 (again/also) in a suit: moreover. Where speech stacks with 도 and 그리고, print pivots its paragraphs on 또한 — S2's stiff-connective shelf (및, 또는, 즉) gains its and-also officer. Reading word first; say it aloud only from a podium.

한 (one — M5's 하나, clipped before a noun) + 편 (side-便 — the 편 of M23's 건너편 and M27's 남편): one-side. As the news' pivot: 한편, … = meanwhile, over on the other side of the story — how broadcasts change scenes without changing breath. As a noun it seesaws arguments: 한편으로는 … = on the one hand.

或 perhaps: S2's 또는 note made a promise — 'its literary twin 혹은 haunts older books' — and the twin walks in, mostly through essays and exam questions: 커피 혹은 차. The or-ladder, register-complete: speech says (이)나 (M43), forms say 또는 (S2), older print says 혹은. Same fork; only the paper stock changes.

于先 at-the-front: first of all — M8's 먼저 with an agenda: 우선 이것부터 합시다 = first things first, the sentence that opens meetings. Radar: the 우선 of 우선순위 (priority ranking — riding frozen) is a DIFFERENT word, 優先 superior-first, wearing the same sound; this one just runs the agenda.

各各 each-each — the character doubled because the meaning is: each one, respectively. 의견이 각각 달라요 (M24) = everyone's opinion differs, each their own. It distributes one-to-one where M29's 모두 lumps: 모두 gathers the crowd, 각각 hands each person their portion.

直接 straight-touch: no middleman between you and the thing — in person, firsthand. 직접 만든 케이크 (M19) = made it MYSELF, the craft flex; 직접 가서 보세요 = go see with your own eyes. Its shadow twin 간접 (indirect — riding frozen: the between-間 of M40's 간식) touches through a layer; interviews prize 직접 들은 이야기, heard with no layer at all.

en: by oneself, of one's own accord
notes: By oneself — radar vs M10's 혼자, and the line matters: 혼자 is alone in SPACE (nobody around — 혼자 살아요), 스스로 is alone in AGENCY (nobody made you — 스스로 결정했어요, M33). A child eating 혼자 is unsupervised; a child eating 스스로 is growing up. It moonlights as a noun for the self: 스스로를 믿으세요 (M19's 믿다).

完全 complete-whole + -히 (천천히's adverb tail, M10): completely, in the licensed register. S1 taught 완전 as the slang intensifier, and M39's 완벽하다 note called 완벽 'the standard the intensifier aspires to' — 완전히 is the form that passes the editor: 완전히 달라졌어요 (M24's 다르다 through M35's -아/어지다). 완전 맛있어! texts; 완전히 바뀌었습니다 prints.

若干 some-amount: the measured 조금 (M9) — a-little, with instruments. 약간 달라요 = slightly different; 약간의 시간 = a bit of time, the 의-form print prefers. M9's 조금 shrinks to 좀 and softens requests; 약간 stays exact and never begs. Recipes, reviews, and weather reports all measure in 약간.

The know-how noun: -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다 = to know / not know HOW — the glue Part runs the machine, mistaken beliefs included. Radar vs Ring 1: M10's 수 asks whether a way exists (운전할 수 있어요?); 줄 asks whether your hands have learned it. Same syllable, physical job: a rope or a line — 줄을 서다 (M14's 서다) = stand in line, Korea's civic sport — and 한 줄 = one line of text. Rope, row, know-how: one syllable, three careers.

Rank 62 in the whole language, and you've been saying it since M7: M24's 그런 note confessed that 그런데 was 그런 + 데 all along, and M53's -는데 is this little noun fused into glue. Alone it's the spoken place, spot, or situation: 가까운 데 = somewhere near, 아픈 데 = the spot that hurts. M12's 곳 names places in print; 데 names them out loud — and only 데 also does situations.

The places-counter, riding M5's counting frame with 데 visibly aboard: 한 군데, 두 군데, 몇 군데 = how many spots (M5's 몇, still demanding its counter). When a Korean says they checked 여러 군데 (M29's 여러), the shopping around was thorough.

Only-ness as a noun. On nouns directly: 너뿐이야 = it's only you — M19's 너 plus M19's 반말 copula, the chorus of half of K-ballad history. On verbs through the prospective badge: 웃을 뿐이에요 (M7's 웃다) = I merely smile. Radar vs M30's 만-glue: 만 picks one item off the menu; 뿐 declares the menu has one line.

Ground, two ways. The literal sense is a site: 집터 is where a house stands, and M26's 놀이 note already shelved 놀이터 — the play-ground. The grammar sense is ground a plan or expectation stands on: -(으)ㄹ 터 squeezes to 테 and runs two frames you'll hear daily — 피곤할 텐데 (M53's -ㄴ데 riding inside) = you must be tired, given that; 금방 갈 테니까 (M10's -니까) = I'll be there soon, so. Expectation is intention with the ground shifted.

As-if for whole clauses: 다 아는 듯이 말해요 = talks as if he knows it all (M24's badge doing the knowing). Radar vs M41's 처럼: 처럼 rides a noun (피부처럼); 듯이 rides a claim. M34's 마치, the as-if announcer, escorts this one too: 마치 모르는 듯이 = as if they didn't know. Headlines clip it to bare 듯: 비 올 듯.

式 the way-hanja: 그런 식으로 말하지 마세요 (M24's 그런, the -지 마세요 don't-machine M14 built) = don't talk in that manner — the sentence 식 lives in. Style by nation: 한국식 (M1) = Korean-style. And the payoff M25 banked: 결혼식's note filed 식 as 'ceremony — the suffix behind 졸업식 and 입학식' — same 式, because a ceremony is a way of doing, formalized until it wears a hall.

外 the outside-root, finally solo: [noun] 외에 = besides, apart from — 그 외에 = besides that, 수업 외에도 (M10) = outside class, too. You've owned its compounds since 외국 (M23, outside-country) and 해외 (M31, beyond-the-sea). S2's register warning applies: 외 is sign-Korean — 관계자 외 출입 금지 (staff only; 관계자 = 'persons concerned', riding frozen) guards half the doors in Korea.

間 between, standing alone at last: 서울과 부산 간 (M30's 와/과) = between Seoul and Busan — the 間 you've carried inside 시간 (M1), M38's 순간, and M40's 간식, and the one M54's gap deck spelled into 층간 소음. Radar, three organs deep: seasoning-간 — M40's 간장 note taught 간을 보다 = taste-check — and liver-간: 간이 크다 (M1's 크다) = big-livered = fearless. Between, salt, and liver: mind the 간.

篇 the piece-counter for anything authored: 영화 한 편 (M2), 드라마 몇 편 (M17). Radar: the side-便 you've collected in 건너편 (M23), 맞은편 (M50), and the 편 that relaxes in 편하다 (M12) — 우리 편 = our side, our team, and -는 편이에요 = 'tends to be on that side': 일찍 자는 편이에요 (M8, M1) = I tend to sleep early. Third booking, transport: 기차 편으로 (M12) = by train. Pieces, sides, rides.

臺 the machine-and-vehicle counter M5's emergency 개 was covering for: 컴퓨터 두 대 (M10), 자동차 한 대 (M50). Second job, 對 versus — every scoreline: 2 대 1로 이겼어요 (M17's 이기다). And M46's 년대 note promised the age-bracket 代 was 'a few shelves down from here' — shelf reached: 20대 = one's twenties, 30대 = the thirties. Three hanja under one syllable; context referees.

Whole, stamped on the front of a noun: 온 세상 (M22) = the whole world, 온 가족 (M4), 온 동네 (M22). M53's 온몸 note filed it as 'a little determiner the course hasn't taught; it rides in frozen' — the ride ends here. Slots exactly like M13's 새: never alone, always in front.

Two 맨s. The edge-finder: 맨 위 (M6), 맨 앞 (M6), 맨 처음 (M15) = the VERY top / front / first — a superlative for positions. A different 맨 strips things bare: 맨발 (M14's 발) = bare feet, 맨손 (M8's 손) = bare hands — the empty-handed hero of every success story. Edge-맨 points; bare-맨 undresses.

M29's 다른 through the street press: 딴 생각 = thoughts that wandered off (M10's 생각하다, nouned) — the classroom's favorite crime; 딴 얘기 = a different story; 딴 사람 같아요 (M24's 같다) = like a different person. Print writes 다른; the street says 딴.

單 single, the drama determiner: 단 하나 (M5) = just ONE, 단 한 번 (M12) = one single time — smallness with a spotlight on it. It has hidden in this app's own name since M10: 단어 = 單語, the SINGLE word. Radar: M13's 계단 climbs a different 단 — step-段.

各 each: 각 나라 (M23) = each country, 각 반 (M15) = each class — the written-notice determiner. Speech mostly trails M31's 마다 after the noun (나라마다); documents stamp 각 in front. Same census, opposite ends of the noun.
M5's 몇 doubled and done asking: 몇몇 사람 = several people, 몇몇 군데 = a few spots. Single 몇 is a question that demands a counter; doubled, it's a quiet answer — some, a handful.

Korean estimates by welding neighbors — no word for 'about' needed; the weld IS the approximation. M5's counter-forms 한 + 두: 한두 번 (M12) = once or twice, 한두 명 = one or two people. First rung of the ladder.
Rung two: 두 + 세 — 두세 시간 = two or three hours, 두세 개 = a couple-three. The same M5 shapeshifters, still welded, still refusing to commit.

Rung three, with fossils inside: 서 and 너 are 셋 and 넷's elder counter-forms — older than the 세/네 counter-forms M5 ships, surviving in this weld and in market grandmothers' speech. 사과 서너 개 = three or four apples. Past this the ladder re-welds (네다섯) or shrugs.

이 아이 pressed flat — M47's 애 note showed the first squeeze (아이 → 애); the pointer fuses next: 이 애 → 얘, this kid. Doubles as an interjection: 얘! = hey, you! — for kids and close friends only. Radar: 얘기 is a DIFFERENT squeeze, M24's 이야기 at speed; no children involved.

그 애 → 걔: that kid — casual Korean's actual he/she, because a full 그 사람 sounds like a deposition between friends. M29's pointer + M47's 애, one syllable after the 준말 press. Strictly casual: fine about classmates, unthinkable about anyone M47's 께서 bows to.
저 애 → 쟤: that kid over THERE — the far pointer at kid-height, completing the trio: 얘/걔/쟤 = M29's 이/그/저 row, squeezed. 쟤는 누구야? (M10's 누구, M19's 반말) = who's that? Point with your chin, not your finger.
M19's 너, pluralized: 너희 집 = your (all's) place, 너희들 with M27's optional 들 for extra crowd. Same WHO rules as 너 — 반말 only, friends and juniors. A teacher's 너희 to a classroom is the canonical sighting.

M4's 우리 bowed low: humble WE, built on M1's humble 저 — 저희 회사 (M2), 저희 집, said upward to customers and strangers. One national exception, drilled into every announcer: never 저희 나라. You may humble yourself and your company before a listener, but not the country — 우리나라 stays 우리, always.

The middle of a squeeze the course taught backwards: M10 shipped the clip 뭐, M29 the full suit 무엇 — 무어 stands between them, alive in print, dialect, and grandmothers' 무어라고? Recognition vocabulary: read it anywhere, keep saying 뭐.

The formal parent of a family you know from its children: 이러하다 contracts to 이렇다, whose badge M24 sold you as 이런. Full-length, it lives in S2's written register — 이러한 문제 = 이런's Sunday suit, the form headlines, textbooks, and terms-of-service wear.

en: to be like that, be so (formal)
notes: M29's 그렇다 — 'the connective factory's engine' — turns out to be this word's 준말: a squeeze so old the short form got the factory job. Written Korean still files the long form: 그러한 이유로 = for such reasons. Recognize it; let 그렇다 keep doing the talking.

The spoken trio closes: 어떻다 (M24), 그렇다 (M29), and now 저렇다 — to be like THAT over there. Same ㅎ-family collapse (저래요, 저랬어요), and M24's 저런 — the national sympathy noise — was its badge all along. 왜 저렇게 말해요? = why does he talk like that?

Hither — direction, not location: M6's 여기 names the spot; 이리 names the drift toward it. 이리 오세요 = come this way; historical dramas bellow the archaic 이리 오너라! at every gate. Wink: 이리 is also the wolf — in a folk tale, 이리 와 may be a warning, not an invitation.
이리's far twin: 저리 가! = shoo, that way — deployable on pigeons and 동생s (M4). Welded double, 이리저리 = this way and that, the aimless wander. Mostly heard, occasionally barked; aim it with love.

이것 + 저것 welded, the same forge as M50's 여기저기 — that one wanders places, this one rummages THINGS: 이것저것 물어봤어요 (M15's 물어보다) = asked about this and that; 이것저것 샀어요 = bought odds and ends. Speech clips it to 이거저거 by M17's 것 → 거 law.

M29's 아무 + M17's 것. With the 도-negative frame, nothing at all: 아무것도 없어요, 아무것도 몰라요 (M4's 모르다) = I know NOTHING. M29's note emptied rooms with 아무도; this empties hands. Flip it open with M43's (이)나: 아무거나 괜찮아요 = anything's fine.

Likewise, verdict-grade: 저도 마찬가지예요 = same here; 월요일도 마찬가지예요 (M5) = Monday's no different. Radar vs M24's 같다: 같다 runs a comparison; 마찬가지 announces the comparison already settled. Underneath, a fossil sentence: 마치 한 가지 — 'as if one kind' (M34's 마치, M32's 가지) — worn smooth into one word.

크다 (M1) + M13's -기 nominalizer: big-ness = size, the measure factory's first product — 신발 크기 (M9), 화면 크기 (M20), 방 크기. Korean builds its rulers out of its adjectives; four more roll off the line below.

길다 (M7) + -이, the noun-maker that turned 놀다 into 놀이 (M26): long-ness = length — 머리 길이, 바지 길이 (M21), the tailor's first question. Radar: M12's 길 (road) wearing the subject particle spells 길이 too — 길이 막혀요 is traffic, not geometry; context holds the ruler.

높다 (M7) + the same -이: high-ness = height — 건물 높이 (M22), 파도 높이 (M49). The identical spelling also works as an adverb: 높이 날아요 = fly HIGH. Kin, not product: M37's 높이다 is the causative that CHANGES the number; 높이 is the number. For people, M27's 키 keeps the job.

The IOU M35's 몸무게 note wrote — it called this word 무겁다's (M21) noun form and the compound fully decodable — paid in full: 무게 stands alone. The factory's one irregular casting (the ㅂ melts, -에 caps it): 가방 무게, and 무게가 나가다 = to weigh — weight GOES OUT, says Korean. With 몸무게 (M35) and 체중 (M41) the whole scale shelf is now yours.

速度 — the factory's one Sino ruler: 고속도로's (M50) speed-速 + 정도's (M32) degree-度. 속도가 빠르다/느리다 (M12's pair), and 인터넷 속도 (M20) — a national pride statistic. Radar: this 속 is speed-速, not M28's inside-속 (물속, 마음속) — same syllable, different physics.

全體: 전국's (M31) all-全 + 신체's (M53) body-體 — the all-body = the whole thing: 나라 전체, 이야기 전체. M45's -적 lesson ran 전체적으로 (overall) off this root as a demo before you owned it; today the root lands and the adverb is officially yours. The fraction trio opens here: the whole, a part, the rest.

一部: M2's Sino 일 + 부분's (M32) section-部 — one-part, literally. 학생 일부 = some of the students; 일부만 = only a portion. The fraction trio's middle slice; news Korean leans on it hard (일부 지역 = some regions, every weather report).

Native in a shelf of suits: M35's 남다 (remain) nouned — what's left over. 나머지 시간 = the time that remains; math's remainder; and the group project's meaning of life: 나머지는 제가 할 수 있어요. The trio closes: 전체 − 일부 = 나머지.

差異 differ-differ — two hanja that both mean 'not the same', stapled for emphasis. 나이 차이 (M4), 성격 차이 (M19 — the official cause of every drama breakup). Differences ERUPT in Korean: 차이가 나다, through M28's 나다, the same door feelings and nosebleeds use.

效果: effect-效 + 결과's (M32) fruit-果 — the fruit your method bears. Runs on the 있다-chassis: 효과가 있어요/없어요 = it works / it doesn't — medicine, diets, and study plans all stand this trial. M45's stamp makes 효과적 = effective, 광고's (M32) favorite adjective.

가능하다 (M39) + -성 (性): possibility-nature. Name the factory: M39's 자신감 note filed the -감 suffix; -성 is its sibling — it bottles a thing's NATURE the way -감 bottles a feeling, and ships 중요성 and 필요성 off the same belt. The 性 has stood inside 여성/남성 (M32) and 이성 (M45) all along. 가능성이 높다/낮다 — Korean maybes are HIGH or LOW; today's 높이 measures even the odds.

決定: M33's 결정하다 said the noun rides free — today it dismounts and stands alone: 결정을 내리다 (M6's 내리다) = to hand a decision DOWN; 아직 결정 못 했어요, the restaurant-menu state of being. The 정 is fix-定, 정하다's (M33) — not affection-情, not politics-政. Radar: 결심 (M34's 결심하다) ties the heart, inward; 결정 fixes the matter, outward.

發展: M35's 발전하다 already decoded it — unfold-expand, with 출발's launch-發 (M8) — and pre-filed 경제 발전; today the noun reports alone: 기술 발전 (M44), 자기 발전 (M32's 자기) = self-improvement, the caption under every dawn gym photo. Radar, one line: a second 발전 (發電) generates — 발전소 = the power plant. Progress and electricity share a spelling; context flips the switch.

活動 live-move: 생활's (M29) activity-활 + the move-動 that 자동차 (M50) decoded out of 운동하다 (M8). What you DO, as a filed category: 취미 활동 (M17), 경제 활동 (M32). Add 하다 and it verbs — 활동하다 = to be active in a field, which is what idols do between albums.

豫定: 예약's (M52) ahead-豫 + 정하다's (M33) fix-定 — the decided-in-advance. The 豫-family now files three ways: 예상 (M34) THINKS ahead, 예약 (M52) PROMISES ahead, 예정 FIXES ahead. 예정보다 늦어요 = running behind schedule (M22's 보다-particle auditing the plan); its real job is the frame in Part 3 — ~(으)ㄹ 예정이다.

管理: pipe-管 (control, as plumbing) + the reason-理 of 이유 (M24) and 이해하다 (M10) that M45's 이성 filed — keeping a thing running on principle. 건강 관리, 시간 관리, 피부 관리 (M41) — self-management is a national hobby with an industry attached — and 관리비 is the maintenance fee on every 아파트 bill. Says 괄리. Radar, one line: a historical homograph 관리 (官吏) is the Joseon official — sageuk dramas only.

業務: the work-業 of 수업 (M10) and 직업 (M16) — the one 사업 (M43) and 졸업 (M44) already filed — + the duty-務 of 사무실 (M16, an 事務-room). M2's 일하다 gave you work as a thing you do; 업무 is work as FILED: 업무 시간, 업무 이메일 (M16), and the door sign 업무 중 — S2's busy-sign machine, on the clock.

役割 duty-portion: the part you play. 역할을 하다 = to do one's role — team members, vitamins, and 김치 in a stew all 역할을 해요; 중요한 역할 (M16's 중요하다, M24's badge) = a key role. In drama credits 역 stands alone: 왕 역 = the role of the king.

行動: the go-行 that flies in 비행기 (飛行 — M28's 날다 note glossed it) and flows in 유행 (流行 — M51's decode) + the same move-動 as 활동 above: going-and-moving = how you act. 말보다 행동 = actions over words (M22's 보다-particle keeping score); 행동으로 보여 주세요 = show it in actions — M36's 보이다 handing over the proof via M9's 주다.

代表: 대신's (M39) stand-in-代 + 발표's (M44) surface-表 — the one who SURFACES in everyone's place. 회사 대표 = the CEO, and 대표님 is how the whole office says boss; 국가 대표 (M31's 국가) = the national team, worn like armor every Olympics. M45's stamp mints 대표적인 = classic, most-representative: 한국의 대표적인 음식? 김치.

相對 mutual-facing: M33's 상대방 minus the 방 — the facing one, with 대하다's (M32) facing-對 exactly where that note filed it. 대화 상대 = someone to talk to; 경기 상대 (M17) = the opponent. The verdict form: 상대가 안 돼요 = no match for them — the facing-one doesn't even register.

個人: the counter 개 (M5) in its hanja suit — 個, one unit — + 외국인's person-人 (M23): one-unit-person = the individual. 개인 정보 (M33) = personal information; 개인 시간 = time to yourself; 개인적으로 (M45's -적으로) = personally, the throat-clear before every opinion. Where 사회 (M32) gathers, 개인 stands alone.

自體: the self-自 of 자동차 (M50) and 자유 (M23) + 신체's (M53) body-體 — the self-body: the thing ITSELF. 그 자체 = in itself: 예술 그 자체 (M44) = art itself, the compliment that needs no adjective. Also the in-house stamp: 자체 제작 = made in-house (제작 rides frozen: 製作, manufacture) — how streaming credits brag.

基本: base-基 + 일본's (M27) origin-本 — the base everything starts from: 기본 재료 (M40), 인사는 기본이에요 = greeting people is the bare minimum (M19's 인사하다 filed 인사 = the greeting itself). The damning verdict: 기본이 안 돼 있다 = the basics aren't even in place — filed against restaurants, rookies, and governments alike. Its precision twin is next.

基礎: the same base-基 + cornerstone-礎 — what you BUILD on: 기초부터 배우세요 = learn from the ground up; 기초 문법 is where this course began. Buildings agree: 기초 공사 is the foundation pour (S2's 공사, downward). The split: 기본 is the floor already expected of you; 기초 is the footing that carries what comes next.

一般: one-一 + sort-般 — 'of the common sort'. 일반인 = an ordinary person (외국인's person-인, M23) — the civilian in every celebrity story; M45's -적 demo ran 일반적으로 (generally) before you owned the root — paid today. Radar: M8's 보통 is usually, the felt average; 일반 is the-ordinary-as-CATEGORY — the checkbox on the form, not the shrug.

專門: sole-專 + the gate-門 that M54's 대문 decoded (M6's 문 was hanja all along) — ONE gate, entered deeply. 삼겹살 전문점 (M18's 삼겹살 + M27's shop-店): the signage promise that a restaurant does one thing perfectly. The person is 전문가 — the expert — a wink now, a word later.

特別: M24's 특별하다, rootward — M32's 특히 already split out the special-特; the 별 is separate-別: special = set apart. Bare, it prefixes: 특별 메뉴 (M3), 특별 방송. And the adverb comes free: 특별히 = especially, particularly — the -히 of 천천히/열심히 (M10) on 특별, the aimed version of M32's 특히.

主要: 주인's (M27) master-主 + essential-要 — the 요 that has been sitting inside 중요하다 (M16) and 필요하다 (M16) all along, finally named. Determiner-like, always parked before a noun: 주요 뉴스 (M24), 주요 도시 (M22). Radar: 중요 (重要 — M41's 체중 note weighed its heavy-重) says it MATTERS; 주요 says it LEADS the list.
種類 seed-sort: things filed by what they grew from. 무슨 종류예요? (M10's 무슨) = what kind is it?; 이런 종류의 영화 (M24's 이런) = this kind of movie; 여러 종류 (M29). Says 종뉴 — the ㄹ bows to the ㄴ.

綜合: gather-綜 + 합격's (M44) fit-合 — everything fitted together. 종합 병원 (M6's 병원) = the general hospital, every department under one roof; 종합 선물 세트 = the assorted gift box (M9's 선물; 세트 rides frozen — Konglish 'set') every Korean childhood remembers. M45's stamp: 종합적으로 = all things considered.

秩序: rank-秩 + 순서's (M33) sequence-序 — public order, the subway-platform virtue. 질서를 지키다 (M26's 지키다) = keep order: boarding arrows, queue lines, festival crowds that file out row by row. Radar: 순서 (M33) is whose TURN it is; 질서 is everyone agreeing the turns are real.

周圍: 주변's (M31) around-周 + enclose-圍 — the ring around. 주위를 보세요 = look around you; 주위 사람들 = the people around you — a job it shares with M31's 주변, and the two swap freely (주위 hugs a touch closer). Radar, one vowel over: S2's 주의 is caution — 주위 is where you stand; 주의 is what the yellow sign wants from you.

背景: back-背 (what's at your back) + the view-景 of 경치 (M22 — M31's 경-pileup sorted it): the scenery behind. 사진 배경 (M17), 배경 음악 (M2) = BGM. And the heavier ledger: a person's 배경 — family, money, connections — where 배경이 좋다 means well-connected, said with an eyebrow.

元來: origin-元 + 미래's (M25) coming-來 — what came from the origin. 원래 그래요 = that's just how it is: the national shrug, deployed daily against traffic, in-laws, and printers; 원래 계획 (M8) = the original plan, moment of silence. Spoken constantly despite the Sino suit; says 월래 — the ㄴ+ㄹ→ㄹㄹ merge that says 절라도 (M31's 전라도).

M1's 밥 먹었어? through the 경상도 press: 먹었나 → 뭇나 — the vowels shed weight and the question lands on -나, because in the southeast EVERY yes/no question does (the fork is Part 2's big rule). Same job as the standard greeting: it isn't about lunch, it's about you. Answer 응, 뭇다 and you've passed.

The other prong of the fork: questions with a question-WORD (M10's 뭐/어디/왜 kit) end in -노, never -나. 뭐 하노? = 뭐 해? So 밥 뭇나? asks yes-or-no, 뭐 하노? asks open-ended — a grammatical distinction 표준어 gave up centuries ago and 경상도 kept running. Hear the ending, know the question type.

뭐라고 하노 pressed flat: what-are-you-saying — bewilderment, pushback, or delight, by tone. The 준말 interlude's law (frequency is pressure) works overtime down south: 뭐라고 → 머라꼬, 하니 → 카노 (the ㅋ is 경상's signature — 하다 hardens to 카다 in speech). The whole family follows: 와 이라노 = 왜 이래?

경상도's -잖아: 맞다 아이가! = it's right, ISN'T IT — the shared-knowledge tag M42 taught you, in regional dress (아이가 = 아니야's local shape, flipped into a tag). Media exported this one nationwide; you'll hear it in Seoul from people who've never lived south of the 한강. Radar: not M4's 아이 (child) wearing a particle — context and the exclamation mark sort it.

One syllable of pure 부산: hey / oi / LOOK — thrown before a sentence to seize the room (마! 니 뭐 하노?), or alone at the stadium, where forty thousand people yell it at the umpire in unison (사직구장's second national anthem). Friendly between friends, fighting words between strangers. Recognition only — this word has a dress code.

M6's 어디 + the southern courtesy tail -예: literally 'where?', actually the humble wave-off — 잘하시네요! → 어데예 = oh no, hardly. The same deflection M10's 잘 못 해요 gap item taught, in regional uniform. 경상도 politeness runs -예/-교 where Seoul runs -요: 맞아예, 뭐라카는교.

단단히 (firmly — the standard adverb, riding frozen) pressed to two syllables: 단디 해라 = do it PROPERLY / take care — the send-off every southern parent issues at the door. So beloved it's now branding: Busan startups and city campaigns wear 단디 as a badge of local trust. The 준말 press, with a hometown.

경상's intensifier: 억수로 싸다 = crazy cheap, 억수로 좋다. 억수 is a downpour — rain by the bucket — so the region intensifies things by weather: good LIKE A FLOOD. Files next to M11's degree ladder (아주/너무/진짜) as the southern rung, and next to S1's 완전 as proof every register grows its own turbo.

M4's 할머니 through decades of southern mouths: 할매 — and 할아버지 wears down to 할배 the same way. Not rude, just worn smooth like a doorsill; 국밥집 signs say 할매 국밥 as a WARRANTY (grandma's hands made this). The pair anchors half of Korea's food-stall branding.

The southern shape of M27's 아줌마 (itself squeezed from 아주머니 — the press never stops): the market vendor, the restaurant owner, the neighborhood's operating system. 아지매! across a 시장 stall is how business opens in 부산 and 대구. Same respect economics as 아줌마: fine for the stall, risky for a stranger in heels.

전라도's universal placeholder — noun, verb, adjective, alibi: 거시기 좀 갖고 와 (bring the, y'know, the thing), 좀 거시기하네 (it's a bit... you know). Standard dictionaries actually list it, but the southwest runs on it: a whole conversation can be conducted in 거시기 if both sides share enough context — which, in 전라도, they do. The word is a trust exercise.

전라's turbo: 겁나 맛있다 = scary good — literally 'fear rises' (겁 = fright, the noun inside 겁이 나다) worn down into an intensifier. Variety shows and rappers carried it out of the southwest; it now lives in every group chat, regional passport expired. The nationalization pipeline in one word — S1's refresh loop should expect more like it.

The southwest's all-purpose exclamation — admiration, exasperation, warmth, all in the delivery: 아따, 겁나 좋네! Files beside M29's 아이고 as regional kin: 아이고 sighs nationwide; 아따 flavors it 전라. Dramas use a single 아따 as a whole costume — one syllable and you know where the character's grandmother lives.

M7's 괜찮아요 with the 충청도 tail: -요 relaxes into -유, and the sentence reclines with it. The stereotype says 충청도 speaks SLOWLY; the truth (Part 4) is it speaks INDIRECTLY — 괜찮아유 can mean yes, no, or 'ask me again tomorrow', and the region considers that a feature. The gentlest syllable in Korean dialectology.

충청's counterpart to 머라카노: 뭐라는 거야 → 뭐라는겨 — the -겨 ending (거야 pressed flat) is the region's other signature: 뭐 하는겨? 가는겨? Same 준말 physics as everywhere, different vowel. Deployed deadpan; 충청도 humor is dry enough to need a fire permit.

제주's 어서 오세요 — and the distance between those two sentences is why linguists file 제주어 as a separate LANGUAGE (UNESCO lists it as critically endangered, its fluent speakers mostly past seventy). 혼저 = quickly/please, 옵서예 = come-honored. It greets you at the airport, on tourist mugs, over every 흑돼지 restaurant door — the island's own hello, kept polished even as the language beneath it fades.

제주's 할아버지 — and the island's icon: 돌하르방, the stone grandfathers (M22's 돌!) standing guard at every gate, bulging eyes, mushroom cap, hands on belly. 할망 is the grandmother; 제주 myth runs on 설문대할망, the giantess who built the island. Half of Jeju's souvenirs are this word carved in basalt.

제주어 for 가십니까 — the -ㅂ니까 machinery replaced wholesale by -수광/-쑤과. A 1977 혜은이 ballad titled 감수광 carried the word to the mainland, chorus and all, and it never left the karaoke book. One word demonstrating the island's grammar runs on different rails, and one 십팔번 (M51's gap deck) ready-made for your 제주 trip.

강원도's calling card: the -드래요 ending — a folksy they-say/it-turns-out quotative (M32's -다고 해요 machinery in mountain dress): 결혼했드래요 = word is, they got married. Dramas hand it to any character from the east coast, one ending as a whole biography. 강원's other stereotype is M40's 감자 — the potato province owns it with pride.

The civilization staple, finally: Korean splits rice into three words where English has one — 벼 the plant in the paddy (riding frozen), 쌀 the raw grain in the sack, and M1's 밥, cooked and on the table. 쌀밥 = plain white rice, 쌀국수 = the rice noodles under M18's 국수 category. Pronunciation drill: tense the ㅆ or you're saying 살, the age counter (M5) — the shop will hear your years, not your grain.

農事 farm-affairs: the 사 is the affairs-事 running through 사고/사건 (M36) and 사업 (M43). Its verb completes M54's maker list: 짓다 built houses, rice, names, expressions, and prescriptions — now add the oldest job of all, 농사를 짓다 = to farm. Composing a year's living out of soil and weather is exactly what the maker-verb is for.

農業 farm-work: the work-業 of 수업 (M10), 직업 (M16), and M57's 업무 — farming filed as an industry. Calibrate against its sibling: 농사 is what a grandfather does; 농업 is what the ministry manages — 농업 기술, 농업 국가. Radar: the 농 is farm-農, not the basket-농 of M17's 농구.

農村 farm-village: 村 is the village — the same 촌 the -스럽다 factory (M45) uses to build 촌스럽다, 'so-countryside-it-hurts' = unfashionable. Radar vs M22's 시골: 시골 is the countryside you're FROM — grandmother, clean air, healing dramas; 농촌 is the agricultural sector the news worries about — 농촌 인구, 농촌 문제. One is a memory, the other a policy area.

The dry field: 고추밭, 감자밭 — M40 grew both crops' words. Its wet partner 논 (the rice paddy — riding frozen) completes the pair 논밭 = farmland, and the two split Korean agriculture between them: 논 grows the 쌀, 밭 grows everything else on this shelf. Final ㅌ softens on contact: 밭에 says 바테.

To plant: M22's 나무를 심다, M7's 꽃을 심다 — and every April Korea does it as a nation on 식목일 (Arbor Day — riding frozen). The planting chain closes: M40's 뿌리다 scatters the seed, 심다 sets it in the ground, M49's 뿌리 takes hold. Minds take plantings too: 마음에 심다 = plant an idea in someone.

To tend into shape — the gardener's verb: M54's 정원을 가꾸다, M3's 채소를 가꾸다. Where M35's 키우다 raises a thing BIGGER, 가꾸다 grooms it BETTER — which is why it moved indoors: M41's 피부를 가꾸다, 몸을 가꾸다. Fields and faces, one verb.

en: to pick, pluck; to earn (a license)
notes: To pick — detach what's attached: 사과를 따다 from the tree, 고추를 따다 from the row, and M40's 뚜껑을 따다 off a bottle, because caps count as fruit here. Korean also picks its achievements: 메달을 따다, 자격증을 따다 (자격증 = license/certificate, riding frozen) — you don't win credentials, you pluck them off the exam tree.

One spelling, a whole toolshed — and you get every sense. Grind: M1's 커피를 갈다, fresh each morning, and M8's 이를 갈다 — dentists mean it literally, dramas mean revenge. Plow: 밭을 갈다, the field turned over for spring. Replace: 물을 갈다 (change the fish's water), M6's 핸드폰을 갈다 (swapped out). ㄹ-verb like 만들다 (M3): 갈아요, 갈아서.

To rot: fruit forgotten in the drawer, M8's 이가 썩다 — the dentist's verdict — and everything metaphor can reach: 썩은 정치, M32's politics wearing the -(으)ㄴ badge (M24). Parents claim it happens internally: M28's 속이 썩다, rotted by worry, teenagers the usual cause. Wherever nothing circulates, Korean says 썩다.

新鮮 new-fresh: the new-新 fronting 신문 (M8) and 신랑/신부 (M47), plus 鮮, vivid — the produce-aisle adjective: 신선한 재료 (M40's ingredients at their best), 신선한 회 (M18's raw fish, where freshness is the whole dish). Ideas earn it too: 신선한 아이디어 (M34) is praise for the genuinely new.

The chili itself, finally on the vine: M18's 고추장 opened with '고추 (chili) + 장 (paste)' and M40's 고춧가루 named it again — today the fruit lands. It reddens whole rooftops every fall: the harvest dries in the sun before becoming that 가루. Mild versions exist, but 청양고추 (the hot one — riding frozen) is served as a dare.

The summer coolant: sliced into 김밥 (M3), floated in cold soups, laid on spa-day faces. Korea maintains a famous anti-cucumber minority — 오이를 못 먹는 사람 is a recognized identity with its own online club — so 오이 빼 주세요 is a well-rehearsed sentence. Radar: nothing to do with numbers, though yes, 오 and 이 (M2) technically spell five-two.

The carrot — and modern Korea's favorite pun: 당근이지! = 'obviously!' (당연하지 with a vegetable swapped in), which is how the used-goods app 당근마켓 got its name and its carrot logo. In the kitchen it's the orange dice in 김밥 (M3) and the sweetness hiding in curry.

The wrap leaf: at the 삼겹살 table (M18) you don't eat lettuce WITH the meat — you build with it: leaf in the palm, meat, sauce, one bite, no exceptions. The whole move is called 쌈 (a wrap — riding frozen), the greenest thing about Korean BBQ. 상추 wilts fast: buy small, eat tonight.

You own both halves: 양- (Western — the ocean-洋 prefix M40's 양파 decoded) + 배추 (M40's napa cabbage) = the round Western cabbage. Same naming logic, one shelf over: whatever arrived by ship got stamped 양-. It's the shredded crunch beside every 돈까스 and inside every street-toast.

The seasoned-greens CATEGORY — spinach, bracken, sprouts: blanched, squeezed, dressed with 참기름 (M40) and garlic. 비빔밥 (M3) is mostly 나물 by volume; the 명절 table (M25) sets out three kinds minimum on the 상 (M40); spring markets sell 봄나물 foraged off hillsides. Learn it as a system, not a single dish.

콩 (M40's soybean, whose note already listed this compound) + 나물: the bean, sprouted into Korea's cheapest vegetable. 콩나물국 is THE morning-after soup — the national hangover repair. And a packed subway car is a 콩나물시루 (the sprouting crock — riding frozen): commuters, growing shoulder to shoulder.

Corn — 강원도's crop (M31 mapped the province; the dialect appendix filed its potato reputation, and corn is the other half of that mountain pantry). Summer trucks sell it steamed; winter cafés pour corn tea. Its silk brews the triple-수 tongue-twister 옥수수수염차 — corn-beard-tea, a real product on real shelves.

땅 (M22's ground) + 콩 (M40's bean): the ground-bean = peanut — the compound is straight botany, since peanuts ripen underground. Sold roasted at every rest stop, and married to squid in 오징어땅콩, the snack-aisle couple two entries below. 맥주 안주 royalty.

The palindrome vegetable — 토마토 reads the same both directions, a fact every Korean kid discovers in hangul class. The older generation eats it SWEET: 토마토에 설탕 (M3's sugar, sprinkled on chilled slices) was a whole era's summer dessert. Korea never settled the fruit-or-vegetable debate — it's 채소 (M3) at the market and dessert at grandmother's.

Shrimp — the sea section opens: 새우튀김 on the noodles, 새우젓 (the fermented brine that seasons soups — riding frozen), and 새우깡, the 1971 shrimp cracker that is Korea's oldest snack brand (M9's 과자, industrialized). Sleeping curled on your side is 새우잠 — shrimp-sleep, the posture of cold rooms and short sofas.

Squid — dried and shredded, the national screen snack: baseball games, movie nights, and highway rest stops all smell of 오징어 구이. Yes, THAT 오징어: the 2021 series made it the one Korean word the whole planet learned (M8's 게임 completes the title). Slang runs cruel — stand next to someone too handsome and you become an 오징어.

人蔘 person-root: the person-人 of 인간 (M32), because the forked root looks like a little person — the hanja is a portrait. Korea's signature crop and oldest export brand, sold as 고려 인삼 since the dynasty of that name; steamed and aged it becomes 홍삼 (red ginseng — riding frozen), the default health gift. Radar: this 삼 is root-蔘, not three (M2) — though it IS the 삼 floating in 삼계탕 (ginseng-chicken soup — riding frozen).

The ox — the animal Korean agriculture ran on: patient, uncomplaining, worth more than its barn. M56's gap deck already fixed that barn — 소 잃고 외양간 고친다 shipped with 소 riding frozen; today it unfreezes and the proverb is fully yours. M18's 소고기 was always 소 + 고기, and the hanja cow hides in M2's 우유 (牛乳, cow-milk) — you've been drinking this animal's character since Module 2.

소 + -아지, the young-animal suffix: calf. The suffix now decodes backwards: M22's 강아지 was 개 (the dog — riding inside its own puppy) + 아지 all along, and 망아지 (foal — riding frozen) completes the barnyard set. Every Korean child sings 송아지 송아지 얼룩송아지 — the spotted-calf song — long before they can spell it.

The egg, the grain, the pellet — Korean's all-purpose small-round-thing. M40's 달걀 note already split it open (닭 + 알, the chicken's 알, worn smooth); fish 알 is roe; and pills go down by M5's native counting — 한 알, 두 알, one pellet at a time — which is why a pill is an 알약: M10's 약, in round form. Berries, bullets, and grapes all count in 알.

The fruit a plant BEARS — any plant, edible or not: 나무의 열매, the red 열매 on a winter branch. Radar vs M3's 과일: 과일 is the sweet kind you buy; 열매 is botany's word — which is why effort uses it: M39's 노력 finally bears fruit in 노력의 열매, the graduation-speech phrase. Its verb, 맺다 (to form/bear), rides frozen for now.

Powder — a paid IOU: M40's 고춧가루 note glossed itself '가루 (powder; 밀가루 is flour)', and today the base word lands. The whole powder shelf snaps into place: 고춧가루 behind you, 밀가루 and 후춧가루 next door, 가루약 (powdered medicine) at the pharmacy. What 갈다 does, 가루 is.

밀 (wheat — riding frozen) + 가루: wheat-powder = flour, the base of the other half of Korean carbs — 국수 (M18), 빵 (M2), 라면 (M3), and every 전 that M40's 부치다 fries. Rice was the civilization; 밀가루 was the postwar pivot — American wheat aid rewired the national menu in a single generation.

후추 (black pepper — riding frozen) + 가루, welded by the linking-ㅅ that M40's 고춧가루 note flagged (젓가락 wears one too): pepper-powder. The tabletop pair completes — 소금 (M3) and 후춧가루 — and every beef-broth soup arrives expecting you to add both. Same seam as the chili powder: you've now seen the ㅅ-weld twice on one spice rack.

食用油 eat-use-oil: 식사's food-食 (M3) + use-用 (the 용 inside M10's 사용하다) + oil-油 — cooking oil, named like a job description (the 냉장고 school of naming, M13). Says 시굥뉴. Radar: M40's 기름 is the native word for all oil everywhere; 식용유 is what the label on the bottle says. And this 유 is oil-油, not the milk-乳 of M2's 우유 — one syllable, two liquids.

食品 food-goods: food-食 again + the three-boxes-品 that M43's 제품 note stacked into 'goods'. The supermarket register: 식품 코너 = the food section, 건강식품 — M14's 건강 in capsule form — and 냉동식품, frozen food wearing the cold-냉 of M13's 냉장고. M1's 음식 is food you eat; 식품 is food that gets manufactured, shelved, and recalled.

飮料 drink-stuff: the stuff-料 running through 재료 (M40) and 자료 (M44), aimed at drinking — the beverage CATEGORY on menus, vending machines, and convenience-store fridges. M18's 음료수 was this word wearing 수 (water); bare 음료 is what the sign above the aisle says. 탄산음료 = carbonated drinks, the parental enemy.

Thick — but only for ROUND things: 굵은 팔 (M14 — the arm, whose note counted two, not eight), 굵은 손가락 (M28), a 굵은 목소리 (M19) rumbling from the chest, and rain once it means business. English hands out 'thick' to everything; Korean checks the geometry first. Says 국따, wakes fully as 굵어요 (굴거요).

The round-thin partner: 가는 국수 (M18), 가는 손가락, a 가는 목소리 that barely carries. ㄹ-drop badge: 가늘 + the badge = 가는 — which reads exactly like 가다 on its way somewhere; 가는 국수 is thin noodles, 가는 길 is the road you're on, and context referees.

Flat-geometry thick: 두꺼운 책 (M1), a 두꺼운 코트 (M21), river ice you may walk on (M40's 얼음). ㅂ-irregular, the 덥다/춥다/맵다 family: 두꺼워요. The idiom worth its rank: 얼굴이 두껍다 (M8) — a face too thick to blush through — is Korean for shameless.

두껍다's other end: 얇은 옷 (M7) is why you're cold, an 얇은 책 is why the exam went fine, and an 얇은 지갑 (M21) is the universal broke-joke. Says 얄따. Pair discipline: books, coats, and ice run 두껍다/얇다; arms and noodles run 굵다/가늘다 — swap them and every Korean ear catches it.

M22's 깊다 finally gets its floor: 얕은 물 (M1) is where the kids stay, 얕은 잠 (M28) is the sleep that doesn't stick. The metaphors mirror too — knowledge and thinking can be 얕다, judged exactly as 깊다 praises them. Says 얃따.

Round: 둥근 얼굴 (M8), the 둥근 달 (M16 — the orbiting half of that note's two jobs), and the schoolroom fact 지구는 둥글어요 (M49). ㄹ-drop family, like 살다/알다: badge 둥근, formal 둥급니다. Doubled, it rounds PEOPLE: 성격이 둥글둥글하다 = an easy, no-corners personality — high praise.

Hard-and-stiff, and nearly always a complaint: 딱딱한 빵 (M2) is yesterday's, a 딱딱한 의자 (M6) is why 허리가 아파요 (M14), a 딱딱한 분위기 (M26) is a meeting nobody exhales in — even textbook prose gets called 딱딱하다. Radar vs M54's 튼튼하다: sturdy is praise, stiff is the complaint. The doubled 딱딱 is the same mimetic mold 튼튼 came from — you can hear the knuckle-rap in it.

津 the strength dial, turned up: 진한 커피 (M1) keeps you up, 진한 색 saturates, 진한 화장 (makeup, riding frozen) took an hour, and a 진한 국물 (M40) took all day. Order 커피를 진하게 — the -게 adverbializer (M33) — and the barista nods once.

軟 soft — the dial's other end: 연한 색 = a pale wash of color, 연한 고기 (M3) = tender meat, 연한 커피 for the evening nerves. One dial, two knobs: 진하게 for strength, 연하게 for mercy — cafés and grill houses both take the setting.

Dense-dark: 짙은 안개 (M49 — the fog its module rolled in, adjective finally attached), 짙은 눈썹 (M41), 짙은 녹색 on the written page. Calibration: 진하다 measures STRENGTH (coffee, makeup), 짙다 measures DENSITY (fog, brows, prose colors). Homophone radar: says 짇따, exactly like M54's 짓다 — one builds, one darkens; the first vowel splits them (지어요/짙어요).

The formal white that was hiding inside M30's 흰색 all along — 흰 is this adjective wearing the badge, and that module dressed the 백의민족 in it. M49's 하얗다 note already called 흰색 'its starched sibling': 하얗다 chats, 희다 writes — 흰 눈 on year-end cards, 흰 머리 arriving with dignity. Says 히다: after a consonant, ㅢ relaxes to ㅣ — hold that rule; 무늬 below runs it too.

The formal black under M7's 검은색 — 검은 + 색, the badge in there all along, exactly as M49's color table showed for 빨간색. 검은 머리 is the poetic default hair; 검은 밤 broods through half of K-lyric history. Says 검따. With 희다 you hold the written pair; M49's ㅎ-family (하얗다/까맣다) keeps the spoken shift.

The literary red — prose, poetry, and one immortal proper noun: the 붉은 악마 (the Red Devils — 악마, devil, riding frozen), the national-team supporters whose shirts M51's 월드컵 note painted as 'entire cities in red.' A 붉은 해 (M11) rises on every novel's first page; M49's 빨갛다 stays the spoken red. Says 북따.

M49's ㅎ-family table did colors; the family does SIZE too: 크다 (M1) inflated through the degree-suffix -다랗다 into storybook bigness. Same machinery — 커다래요, badge 커다란: a 커다란 곰 (M49), a 커다란 구멍 (below). Not really bigger than 크다 — just drawn at picture-book scale.
The size wing's other end — tiny, and a little fond: a 조그만 가게 (M1), a 조그만 구멍. ㅎ-family conjugation: 조그매요, badge 조그만. M1's 작다 states the smallness; 조그맣다 smiles at it.

A payoff scheduled twice: M7's 검은색 note said '까만색 is the everyday synonym,' and M49's 까맣다 note pointed straight at it — today the noun itself lands. Spoken Korean's default black: 까만색 머리, a 까만색 티셔츠 (M21). M49 supplies the badge 까만; this entry is just that badge wearing 색 — M7's rule that every color is [something] + 색.

Black number three — the checkbox black of order forms, shoe boxes, and the color-option line in every catalog: 색상 (color, riding frozen): 검정 — bare 검정 works alone. The trio sorts by register, not shade: 검은색 written, 까만색 spoken, 검정색 the product listing. English owns one black; Korean asks where it will be printed.

褐色 coarse-cloth-color: 갈색 머리, 갈색 눈, 갈색 가죽 (below). Keep the hanja honest: this 갈 is NOT 갈비's (M30) — the ribs are native Korean; the brown is 褐, the color of undyed hemp cloth, which is what brown WAS for most of history.

灰色 ash-color: a 회색 하늘 (M11) before rain, 회색 건물 (M22) by the block — the concrete-and-overcast national palette. Radar: this 회 is ash-灰, not the meeting-會 you commute to in 회사 (M2) and sit through in 회의 (M10). The metaphor imported with the color: 회색 지대 (zone, riding frozen) = the gray zone, where the rules blur.

綠色 green-color, the formal green of maps, documents, and tea: 녹차 (green tea, riding frozen) is this 綠 poured over M2's 차. Calibration vs M7's 초록색: same stretch of spectrum — 초록색 holds the crayon box, 녹색 signs the paperwork. The 신호등 (M12) turns 녹색 in the traffic report and plain green at the crosswalk.

Pattern: 꽃무늬 (M7) florals on grandmother's everything, 호랑이 무늬 (M49) on every folk painting. Says 무니 — after a consonant, ㅢ relaxes to ㅣ, the rule 희다 filed above. The wink the gap deck expands: 무늬만 [X] = X in pattern only — all stripe, no tiger.
M55's 줄 — the rope-and-line syllable — stamped onto 무늬: line-pattern = stripes. A 줄무늬 셔츠 (M21) for the office, and the 호랑이's coat is the national 줄무늬. Says 줄무니.

幅 width — the dimension noun missing from M57's ruler shelf (크기, 길이, 높이): 길의 폭이 좁아요, measured with M13's 넓다/좁다 pair now doing ruler work. News Korean loves 대폭 (大幅, 'by a wide margin,' riding frozen) — prices, budgets, and policies all swing 대폭.

金 the metal itself, at last — the syllable you've paid as 현금 (M9) and 세금 (M43, whose note built the ledger: 'the 금 you've held since metal-day 금요일'), now standing alone: 금 가격 (M21), a 금메달 (gold medal — 메달 riding frozen), and the top spoon M49's 흙 note graded — 금수저 born golden, 흙수저 born to dirt. Second sense, all native: a 금 is a drawn line or a crack — 컵에 금이 갔어요 (M1's 가다) = the cup cracked, and friendships crack the same way. Radar: the 금 on walls forbidding things is 禁 — 금연 (M53), 금지 on the S2 signs — that one costs you; this one pays.

Skin that became material: a 가죽 가방 (M6), 가죽 구두 (M21), 가죽 장갑 (M21) — on the animal it's hide, off the animal it's the jacket's whole personality. The proverb every Korean knows runs on it: 호랑이는 죽어서 가죽을 남기고, 사람은 죽어서 이름을 남긴다 — the tiger dies and leaves its hide; a person dies and leaves a name (M49, M14, M37's 남기다 — every word yours).

A hole: 양말에 구멍이 났어요 (M21, M28) — holes ERUPT through 나다, the same door anger and memories use. A 구멍가게 (M1) is the hole-in-the-wall corner shop, named generations before convenience stores ate them. And the schedule metaphor: 숨 쉴 구멍 (M41's 숨) — a breathing hole — is what a packed week lacks.

Two careers, and NIKL lists both: the piece — 케이크 한 조각 (M19), 얼음 조각 (M40) — with counter duty included (한 조각만 주세요), and 彫刻 carve-carve: sculpture, the museum sense. A 조각가 makes the second kind — the maker suffix M48 stamped through 작가 and 화가, now stamping the sculptor. At a wedding buffet, 얼음 조각 could be either; the pedestal decides.

Unfold and spread: 책을 펴세요 (M1) opens every class in the country, 우산을 펴다 (M9) opens the sky-lid, 허리를 펴세요 (M14) is the physiotherapist's refrain. Radar vs M22's 피다: flowers bloom on their own (꽃이 피다); 펴다 needs your hands and an object — though half the country writes 담배를 피다 anyway, to the dictionary's despair (M14's 피우다 is the licensed form).

펴다's undo: 종이를 접다 folds paper — 종이접기 (M15's 종이 + the -기 nominalizer, M13) is origami, a kindergarten pillar — and 우산을 접다 (M9) closes the sky-lid. The slang every planner needs: 접었어요 = I folded it — the shop, the plan, the dream is OFF. Korean gives up in card-player's vocabulary.

Stretch out and extend: 다리를 쭉 뻗다 (M14, with M12's 쭉 measuring the relief), 손을 뻗다 (M8) reaches for the top shelf, and roads and branches 뻗다 across maps on their own. Slang bonus: 뻗었어요 = conked out flat — what the legs do after the marathon does the rest.

Open a gap: 입을 벌리세요 (M14) says the dentist, 팔을 벌리다 (M14) opens the hug. M56's 벌이다 note carried this word frozen — 'untaught 벌리다 (spread open: 입을 벌리다) rides frozen here' — and today it thaws. Keep the trio straight: 벌리다 opens a GAP, 벌이다 opens a PROJECT, and M16's 벌다 pays for both.

Tie and bundle: 머리를 묶다 (M8) makes the ponytail, 하나로 묶다 makes the package deal — telecoms 묶다 your phone and internet the way M55's 줄 ties anything else. Says 묵따, exactly like M23's 묵다: 호텔에서 묵다 spends the night, 머리를 묶다 spends a hair tie.

The knot-fastener: 넥타이를 매다 (M21 — that note dressed you with the all-purpose 넥타이를 해요; this is the tie's OWN verb), 목도리를 매다 (M21), and the sticker in every taxi: 안전벨트를 매세요 (seatbelt, riding frozen). One-line radar: the homophone 메다 SHOULDERS things — 가방을 메다 — a pool word for later. 매다 knots at the front; 메다 hangs from the shoulder.

會長 gather-chief: the gather-會 of 회사 (M2), 회의 (M10), and 대회 (M51) meets 長 — the chief-장 that M39's 장점 note named ('사장님/부장님's chief-장'). The top of the tower: a 사장님 (M9) runs a company; the 회장님 above runs the GROUP of them — chaebol org charts stop here. The title scales down as happily as up: every club, alumni group, and fan club elects a 회장 too.

總長 all-chief: 總 (gathers-everything — riding frozen) + 長. The head of a 대학교 (M15) — the campus's final boss: M15's 교수님 answers to the 총장님. The same all-chief logic runs upward off campus: the UN Secretary-General is a 사무총장 (frozen gloss — chief of all the affairs).

課長 task-chief: 과제's (M44) task-課 + 長 — head of a 과, the office section. The org chart's middle: the 과장님 approves what the 사원 (M43) drafts and answers to the 부장님 next door. Radar: a same-sounding 과장 (誇張) is exaggeration — 과장하지 마세요 = don't overdo it; the office and the context never confuse them.

部長 section-chief: 부분's (M32) section-部 + 長. M16's 부장님 note put him 'mid-floor' on the title ladder; today the bare title lands, and the ladder gets all its rungs: 사원 (M43) → 과장 → 부장 → 사장 (M9) → 회장. Bare 부장 is for org charts and gossip — to his face it is 부장님, always.

班長: M15's 반 (the 3학년 2반 classroom) + 長 — the class president, elected every semester and in charge of quiet and roll call. Grown-ups keep the word: work crews and cleaning teams have a 반장 too. The smallest chair in the 長-machine, and the first one most Koreans ever sit in.

責任者: 책임 (M39 — 제 책임이에요) + the person-者 of M27's 환자 note — the person the responsibility lands ON. 책임자가 누구예요? = who's in charge here? — the escalation sentence, politer than it feels. Where 사장님 is a title, 책임자 is an accusation waiting for a name.

秘書 secret-documents: 비밀's (M19) secret-秘 + the document-書 filed in 서류 (M16) and shelved in 도서관 (M2) — the keeper of the boss's calendar, calls, and confidences. 비서실 = the executive office; K-drama's 비서 is forever hyper-competent and semi-secretly in love. Addressed by surname plus title: 김 비서님.

師母 + 님: teacher-師 rides frozen; the 모 is mother-母, the 부모님 syllable M47's 고모 note decoded. Originally your teacher's wife, now the honorific for the wife of any titled man — the boss's, the professor's, the pastor's — and how upscale shops flatter married women of a certain wattage. No English seat: 'madam-wife-of-the-important-man.'

先輩 ahead-cohort: 先 is the syllable 선생님 (M4) has worn since Module 4 — 先生, born-ahead: your teacher simply got to the material first — and the at-the-front-先 of 우선 (M56); the cohort-輩 rides frozen. Anyone who entered your school, company, or field before you: age is irrelevant, ENTRY DATE is everything, so a 25-year-old gives 존댓말 (M19) to a 23-year-old 선배 without blinking — M47's honor-the-rank rule, sorted by admission year. Address: 선배님 at first, 선배 once you're close.

後輩 after-cohort: the after-後 that 오후 (M5) and -(으)ㄴ 후에 (M13) have carried all along, plus the same cohort-輩. Your junior — arrived after you, gives you the honorifics, inherits your class notes. The pair runs Korea's campuses, offices, fandoms, and crime films; the sentence deck stages its most important ritual: who pays.

新入生 new-enter-student: 신문's (M8) new-新 (the 신 that dressed 신랑/신부, M47) + 입학's (M44) enter-入 + student-生 (학생, M4). The March freshman, blinking in the fluorescent light. M43's 사원 note already filed the office twin — 신입사원, 'suits still creased' — same 신입, different building.

卒業生: 졸업 (M44) + student-生 — the graduate, February's flower-holder per the 졸업식 that M44's 졸업 note scheduled. Also the alumni register: 우리 학교 졸업생 = our school's graduates. With 신입생 above, the -생 economy gets its bookends: enter new, leave finished.

專門家: 전문 (M57) + the maker's house-家 of 작가/음악가/예술가 (M48). M57's 전문 note signed off: '전문가 — the expert — a wink now, a word later.' The word has arrived; the wink is paid. Korean TV mints one per topic — 부동산 전문가, 교육 전문가 — and the sentence deck tells you when to call one.

公務員 public-duty-member: 공원's (M6) public-公 (M43's 공장 note pinned it) + duty-務, the syllable sitting quietly inside 사무실 (M16, 事務 = affairs-and-duties) + the member-員 of 사원 (M43). The civil servant — and modern Korea's most-competed-for job title: the 공무원 시험 (M10's 시험) has entire prep neighborhoods, because the pension is forever.

國會議員, decoded end to end: 한국's country-國 (M1) + the gather-會 of 회사/회의 + discuss-議, the syllable that has sat silently inside 회의 (M10 — 會議, gather-and-discuss) all along + the member-員 of 사원 (M43). Country-gather-discuss-member: the assemblyman. 국회 is the assembly itself (the domed building in 여의도 — frozen landmark); 의원님 is the address; 300 of them hold the seats.

勞動者 labor-move-person: labor-勞 (riding frozen — NOT 노력's exert-努, which M39's 노력 note filed) + the move-動 that 자동차 (M50) decoded out of 운동하다 (M8) + the person-者 of M27's 환자 note: 기자 records, 환자 suffers, 소비자 spends — 노동자 labors. The news-register word for worker: May 1 is 노동절 (Labor Day — frozen), and the unions in every headline are 노동조합, clipped to 노조.

從業員 follow-work-member: follow-從 rides frozen; the 업 is the work-業 of 수업 (M10) and 직업 (M16); the 員 staffs 사원 (M43). The neutral, count-them-all word for staff — signs and statutes say 종업원, faces get warmer words: you summon a 직원 (M16) or flatter a 사장님 (M9). 종업원 몇 명? is how the tax office asks.

會員 gather-member: the gather-會 a third time + member-員 — a member of anything with a signup form: the gym, the app, the fan club (whose president is, of course, its 회장). 회원 가입 (joining — 가입 rides frozen) is the first button on every Korean website, and 회원님 is what the gym's front desk calls you: the 님-economy extends to anyone holding a membership card.

顧客 regard-guest: look-after-顧 (riding frozen — the merchant turning to attend you) + the guest-客 of 관광객 (M23) and 관객 (M48). The formal 손님 (M9): shops have 손님, corporations have 고객. M43's 소비자 note split the camera angles — news says 소비자, ads say 손님 — and 고객 completes the shot list: what the company calls you TO YOUR FACE, always as 고객님. The sentence deck picks up on the first ring.

人員 person-member: the person-人 of 인간 (M32) + the member-員 of 사원 (M43) — people as a NUMBER. The field-trip liturgy: 인원 확인 (M20's 확인하다) before the bus moves, 인원수 체크 (frozen gloss: headcount check) after every rest stop. 몇 명 (M5) counts the people; 인원 is what the clipboard calls the answer.

主婦: 주인's (M27) master-主 + the bride-婦 of 신부 (M47) — the master-of-the-house, official title. 전업주부 (frozen gloss: full-time homemaker — 전업, sole occupation) is the census box; daytime TV chases the 주부 audience by name. The 노동자 entry above should take notes: nobody who has run a household calls it not-work.

少年 few-years: the few-少 that 청소년 (M35) decoded — 'green-few-years' — + the year-年 of 내년 (M25). A boy, in the register of news and novels: M44's 문학 note already cast the bookish 문학 소년. Radar: NOT 소설's small-小 (M48) — 少 counts FEW, 小 measures SMALL; a boy is few-years, fiction is small-talk.

少女: few-少 + the female-女 inside 여자 (M4 — 女子). A girl — and since 소녀시대 ('Girls' Generation,' riding frozen) half a genre: girl-group members debut as 소녀들. M44's 문학 note filed the bookish 문학 소녀 beside her brother; the frequency list ranks her (960) above the 소년 (1078), which tells you who Korean pop culture writes about.

젊다 (M24) wearing the badge -(으)ㄴ (M24), welded to the person--이 that minted 어린이 (M35: '어리다 + -ㄴ이' — the-young-one): the-young-one, adult edition. Editorial register: 요즘 젊은이들은… has opened every generation complaint since newspapers were invented, and now you can read one. The mold's other casting, 늙은이 (old-one — frozen), exists and is rude: respect runs UP the age ladder, so the downward mold sours.

成人 achieved-person: the achieve-成 of 성공 and 성적 (M35) + the person-인 of 외국인 (M23) — the completed human: a legal adult. Sort the shelf: 어른 (M24) is 'the person 존댓말 was invented for,' a status you respect; 성인 is a category you age into (만 19세 — frozen gloss — is the line). 성인 영화 = adults-only cinema: the word on the rating sticker, never on the birthday card.

The young-lady address: 아기 (M25) fused centuries ago with the name-suffix 씨 (M4) into the noble house's unmarried daughter. REGISTER WARNING: from a market 아줌마 (M27) it's ordinary service-speech; from a man on the street it can land as a catcall; in nightlife contexts it's a job euphemism. Understand it everywhere, deploy it almost never — a 사장님 (M9) or 이모 (M18) lands better in any restaurant.

Licensed disrespect on a sliding scale: from a grandfather, 이 녀석! is pure affection with eyebrows; from a stranger it's an insult; between friends, 그 녀석 = that guy, 반말 (M19) seasoning. The rule is direction: never upward, never to strangers — the warmth lives entirely in who's allowed to say it. Drama grandpas conjugate whole relationships through this word.

형 (M4) + the 님-ladder (M16): the honored big brother — 형제's (M47) 兄, saluted. Three worlds run on it: respectful juniors to seniors in business and sport; the entire gangster-film genre, where 형님 is RANK (the Busan classic the dialect gap deck quoted runs on it); and — kinship outranking gender — a married woman calls her husband's older sister 형님 too. When a drama's 동생 switches from 형 to 형님, the temperature just changed.

The spouses' 'honey' — and you know its bones: 여보세요 (M20) was 'worn smooth' from 여기 보세요, per its own note, and 여보 is the same look-here, worn smoother still and aimed across the breakfast table. Couples graduate into it: dating pairs say 자기야 (M32's 자기 note filed the staple); rings on, the switch flips to 여보. One look-here dialed out and became the phone hello; the other stayed home and became a marriage.

軍 the military: 군인's (M27) army-군 standing alone — 우리 군 = our forces; 육군, 해군, 공군 (army, navy, air force — frozen glosses) file the branches. Sense collapse, mandatory: the dictionary's other 군 (君) is a Mr.-suffix for young men — 김 군, the name-suffix 씨 (M4) with a schoolmaster's accent: dated, formal, surviving in ceremonies and old novels. (A third, 郡, is the rural county on addresses.) One syllable, three government jobs.

軍隊 army-ranks: 軍 + unit-隊 (riding frozen — troops in a line). The army as institution and address: 군대에 가다 = to enlist. M27's 군인 note counted the ~18 months and warned that 군대 'is where friendships pause' — conscription is the bend in every Korean man's twenties: enroll, serve mid-degree, come back a 복학생 (frozen gloss: returning student). Korea handles the subject factually and constantly; the gap deck files its standard opening question.

將軍 commander-of-the-army: 將 — the same character 장래 (M46) read as 'about-to'; in uniform it means commander — + 軍. In Korea one name owns the word: 이순신 장군 (riding frozen — the 16th-century admiral who won with thirteen ships), on the 100원 coin and in giant bronze over 광화문 광장 (M23). Board-game bonus: 장군! is 'check!' in 장기, Korean chess — declare it like you mean it.

찾다 (M6) + the softening 보다 that M15's 물어보다 flagged and M16's try-machine formalized — seek-and-see. The roster completes: 물어보다 (M15), 바라보다 (M49), 둘러보다 (M50), 살펴보다 (M56), and now the one you'll use daily. 모르는 단어는 사전에서 찾아보세요 (M26's 사전) — though the dictionary is a phone now: 인터넷에서 찾아봤어요 is Korean for 'I googled it.'

찾다 pointed home by M6's come/go compass: seek your way TO the speaker — visit, come calling. 손님이 찾아왔어요 (M9's 손님) = a guest showed up at the door. Korean extends the courtesy to the calendar: 봄이 찾아오다 = spring comes calling — seasons, chances, and hard times all 찾아오다, uninvited but punctual.

en: to go visit, seek out (in person)
notes: The compass flipped: seek your way AWAY from here — go to someone, in person. 사무실로 직접 찾아갔어요 (M16's 사무실, M56's 직접) = I went to the office myself, the verb of complaints too urgent for the phone. Second job at the lost-and-found: 지갑은 여기서 찾아가세요 — find it AND carry it off.

en: to come up; to get posted (online)
notes: M28's compound table left this cell literally empty — 올라가다 climbed away with no partner to climb back. Filled: come up toward the speaker. 서울로 올라오다 = come up to Seoul (the capital is 'up' from everywhere, per the same M28 convention that sends you 내려가다 to the provinces). And the internet's favorite: 사진이 올라왔어요 = the photo's up — M20's 올리다 uploads it, 올라오다 is how the feed announces it.

en: to go over, move on; to let slide; to fall for
notes: M36's 넘다 (cross over) + the compass: go over and onward. Pages and agendas turn with it (다음으로 넘어가요 = let's move on), the sun 넘어가다-s the ridge at dusk, and — swallowed whole — 속아 넘어가다 = fall for it (속다 = to be fooled, frozen here). Best sense of all, mercy: 이번엔 넘어갈게요 = I'll let it slide this once.

어찌하다 (do-how) compressed into the how-did-this-happen verb — same family as M34's 어쩌면 (maybe). 어쩌다가 여기까지 왔어요? = how did it come to this — the drama sigh, delivered over a drink. 어쩌다 보니 = one thing led to another (gap deck), Korea's standard opener for unplanned lives. Radar: standing alone as an adverb it means once in a blue moon — 어쩌다 한 번.

en: to take out; to bring up (a topic)
notes: The out-verb: it ends in M28's 내다 (put forth), and it undoes M28's 넣다 — what 넣다 put in, 꺼내다 takes out. 지갑을 꺼내다 (M21) at the register, 냉장고에서 반찬을 꺼내다 (M13, M3) before dinner. Topics live in pockets too: 이야기를 꺼내다 (M24) = bring it up — the verb for finally saying the thing.

en: to put out, set out; to put up for sale
notes: M28 + M28: 내다 (put forth) + 놓다 (set down) — put it OUT and leave it standing, the same result-stays logic 놓다 brought to M40's glue. 쓰레기를 내놓다 (M13) = put the trash out; 집을 내놨어요 (M1) = the house is on the market; 의견을 내놓다 (M24) = lay an opinion on the table.

내다 (M28) + 밀다 (push — S2): push it forth, stick it out. The collocation to keep is 손을 내밀다 (M8) = extend a hand — literal at the handshake, figurative whenever help is offered or money is demanded; Korean does both with the same outstretched palm. ㄹ-verb like its parent: 내밀어요.

en: to detach, peel off; to take (first steps)
notes: Detach on purpose — the undo of M37's 붙이다: stickers, price tags, and posters all come down by 떼다. Gazes too: 눈을 뗄 수 없어요 (M14) = can't take my eyes off it. Babies 첫 발을 떼다 (M46's 첫, M14's 발) — lift the first foot — and so does every new project. M36's 떨어지다 falls off by itself; 떼다 is your hand doing it.

en: to pull out; to pick, elect
notes: Pull out what resists: 이를 뽑다 (M8's tooth, at M53's 치과), weeds from the garden, cash from the machine. The civic sense pulls PEOPLE out of the crowd: 대통령을 뽑다 (M32) = elect, 반에서 대표를 뽑다 (M57's 대표) picks the class rep. M13's -기 mints 뽑기 — the claw machines and capsule toys funding every arcade.
